- Some urology settings use single-use sterile lube packets or syringes

The room had one bulb and it flickered like it was nervous. Greasy light pooled on the metal table, turned the sweat on my forearms into something that looked like oil. The walls were the yellow of old teeth. I’d spent enough time in precincts to know this one was worse than most. Bad rot in the bones.

They’d taken my coat, my gun, my cigarettes. They left me the chair. That was generous.

Detective Russo leaned in the corner, smoking like it was the only thing keeping him vertical. The smoke from his cheap tobacco crawled through the room, clung to the damp corners, got under my eyelids. It smelled like a dive bar at 3 a.m. and bad decisions you can’t take back.

The other one—Kline—was the muscle. He held a dog-eared phone book in his big hands like a holy book, the pages swollen from years of sweat and bad intentions. The cover said “City Directory.” The way he grinned said “instrument.”

“Last chance, Mallory,” Russo said, voice rough, like he gargled gravel and jealousies. He pinched his cigarette between two fingers, ash hanging on for dear life. “Tell us where the girl is, and this gets easy.”

My ribs already felt like they’d hosted a family reunion for brass knuckles. The phone book was a new party guest. I drew a slow breath and got a noseful of Russo’s smoke. Cheap tobacco, heavy on the tar, the kind that left your throat feeling like sandpaper and regret.

I coughed once, tasted iron. “You boys always this romantic with your dates?”

Russo nodded at Kline without taking his eyes off me.

The phone book hit my side with a wet thud. It was like getting slugged by a soft brick. The pages spread the force, no clean impact to point at later, just a big, dull fist made of names and numbers and everybody in this rotten city who’d never know they helped break a man.

Pain flared along my ribs, a hot line that crawled up my back and into my teeth. I sucked in air through clenched teeth, swallowed the noise trying to crawl up my throat. My vision went fuzzy around the edges, the bulb above me blinked like it was wincing.

Won’t leave a mark, my brain said. Not one any jury cares about.

Kline smiled, his eyes small and happy. “I love this thing,” he said, rapping the book lightly against his palm. “All those pages. So… forgiving.”

Russo dragged on his cigarette, the ember kissing his face orange. He let the smoke leak out slow. I watched it twist between us, a ghost of every burned-out cop I’d ever met.

“I’m getting bored, Mallory,” he said. “And you know what happens when I get bored.”

“Your wife leaves?” I said.

I didn’t see the swing. Just felt it.

This time the phone book came in high, across the shoulder and collarbone. A soft explosion of pain shot down my arm. Something popped, not clean enough to be a break, but enough to make my fingers go numb. The chair shuddered under me, the metal legs squealing on the dirty lino like they wanted to run.

I stared at the table because if I looked at Kline right then I might say something stupid, and I only had so many teeth left to lose. The surface was scratched to hell, ghosts of other men’s fingernails and desperation carved into the metal. This room collected misery like other people collected stamps.

Russo leaned forward and ground the cigarette out in a scarred metal ashtray. The room instantly smelled worse without the anchor of the burning tobacco—just stale smoke in the walls, sweat, and the copper tang of my own slow leak.

“Listen,” Russo said, his tone suddenly fatherly, like we were on a fishing trip and not in a municipal torture closet. “We know you saw her. We know she came to your office last night. Blonde, twenty-two, maybe twenty-three. Blue dress. Eyes like she still believed the world could be fixed.” He tapped the table with two nicotine-stained fingers. “You’re gonna tell us where she went.”

She had shown up like they said. Only her eyes didn’t look like that. They looked like she already knew the ending, just wanted to see how much it would hurt getting there. I remembered the way she’d held the folder, too tight, like it contained the last good thing anyone ever did for her.

“I see lots of girls,” I said. “Only one I remember is your sister, Russo. You never did apologize for that.”

He stared at me for a long second, quiet, still. Then he gave Kline one lazy nod, just a tilt of the chin. Kline stepped behind me, and the cheap scent of his aftershave—drugstore stuff trying too hard—fought with the tobacco ghost hanging in the air.

The phone book came down on the back of my shoulders, full-body follow-through, like he was driving a nail into the center of the earth. Pain detonated across my spine, jagged and bright. My forehead clipped the table; stars went off behind my eyes. Warmth slid down from my eyebrow. I didn’t need a mirror to know it wasn’t going to be pretty.

The pages slipped against my skin, a long, damp slap that left no clean bruise, just a deep ache that promised to bloom later. Tomorrow I’d feel like I’d been run over by the entire city directory, A through Z.

I let out a breath through my nose, slow and careful. The room tilted left for a second, then right. The bulb did its nervous dance. My stomach heaved once, considered quitting, then decided to stick around.

“Funny guy,” Russo said. “Always with the jokes. You know who doesn’t think you’re funny, Mallory?”

“I’m guessing the department shrink,” I rasped.

Russo smiled without warmth. He pulled out another cigarette, tapped it against the pack like it owed him money, stuck it between his lips. The lighter clicked, a little sun in the dark.

He took a drag, exhaled toward the ceiling. The smoke unfurled, lazy, bitter. The kind of tobacco they sold by the pound, in bags that looked like they should hold fertilizer. I used to smoke the same brand, before I started giving a damn about waking up in the morning. Then I stopped giving a damn again, but the habit never came back. Some ghosts stay buried.

“The commissioner,” Russo said, “does not think you’re funny. The DA does not think you’re funny. The people who pay us to keep things quiet? They don’t laugh. Not even a chuckle. You been nosing around places you shouldn’t. You been talking to people who are supposed to disappear. Then this girl walks into your office. Like magic.”

“Maybe I’m still the friendly type,” I said. My throat was raw, tongue thick, like I’d been gargling chimney soot. “Maybe I just got one of those faces people trust.”

Kline snorted. “Yeah,” he said. “You look real trustworthy with your head on the table like that.”

I straightened up inch by inch, every muscle putting in its resignation notice. I met Russo’s eyes. They were flat, cop eyes, same kind I’d stared into in the mirror ten years back, before I turned in my badge for a cheaper office and a bottle that didn’t have to answer questions.

“You want to hit me again, Kline,” I said, not taking my gaze off Russo, “go ahead. But you keep swinging like that, you’re gonna pull something important. Maybe your last brain cell.”

Kline moved, but Russo held up a hand.

“Not yet,” he said, voice going cold. “See… this is what I don’t get, Mallory. Used to be, you understood how the game was played. Take a drink, look the other way, let the money flow in the direction it wants to. Then you start asking questions about girls tied to councilmen, goons with badges, money going missing from evidence. That’s not curiosity. That’s suicide.”

He took another drag, studied me through the smoke like a lab rat that’d forgotten the maze.

“The girl’s scared,” I said before I could stop myself. Idiot. “People do strange things when they’re scared.”

Russo’s eyes sharpened just a notch. “Ah,” he said softly. “So we remember her now.”

Damn. My mouth always did run a little faster than my sense of survival.

I shrugged, pain lancing my shoulders. “You talk about blondes long enough, odds are you’ll hit one I’ve met.”

The phone book slammed into my side again, lower this time, just above the hip. I gasped—it was ripped out of me, sharp and ugly. White flashed behind my eyes. My leg went hot, then cold. Nerves started playing the wrong song.

I tasted blood. Not from my mouth. Somewhere deep, where organs complain in whispers. I forced a slow breath, counting it like money. One. Two. Three. Still here.

“Stop playing, Mallory,” Kline growled from my right, panting like he’d done something difficult. “You ain’t walking out of here until we get a name and an address.”

“That’s two things,” I said. “No wonder you need the book. Counting’s hard.”

I braced this time, waited for the hit. It didn’t come. The absence of pain felt almost as strange as the pain itself.

Russo stubbed his second cigarette, fingers steady. “Let me paint you a picture,” he said. “Girl comes to you. She’s got something. Photos, statements, whatever. Something that can hurt important men. She’s scared, she runs. She runs to you. Because your name still means something to the people dumb enough to think this city can be saved.”

He leaned closer, forearms on the table, and for a second the cheap smoke on his breath was all I could smell. “Then she disappears again. Only this time? She didn’t just run. Someone moved her. Someone who knows how to make people go away. We know that someone was in your office between eleven and midnight. We got witnesses. We got eyes.”

They didn’t have half of what he said. If they did, I’d already be in a different kind of room, the kind with paperwork.

I swallowed, throat burning. “If you got eyes,” I said, “you don’t need my mouth.”

He smiled, a quick, sharp thing. “Yeah. See, that’s the thing. The people I work for, they like insurance. They want to hear you say it. They want to know whose side you’re on.”

He said “people I work for” like it didn’t include the badge on his chest. Maybe it didn’t.

The room felt smaller. The smoke thickened, got meaner. My ribs pulsed under the skin, each breath an argument with gravity. The chair creaked as I shifted; one of its back screws had had enough and quit, metal whining.

Whose side was I on? Hell if I knew anymore. Hers, maybe. The blonde with the tired eyes and folder full of trouble. She hadn’t had anyone else. It’d been right there, in the way she sat on the very edge of the chair in my office, like she needed to be ready to bolt at any second. Like she expected the door to burst open and the walls to tell on her.

I hadn’t promised her much. I never did. But I’d promised enough. Enough to land me here.

“Let’s say,” I said, voice slow, choosing each word like it might explode, “hypothetically, a girl comes to me. Hypothetically, she’s in trouble. Hypothetically, some cops are on the take and want her dead.”

Russo didn’t move. Kline shifted his weight, the phone book whispering against his leg.

“In that hypothetical world,” I went on, “maybe I tell her to disappear. No names. No addresses. Just… gone. From me. From you. From your friends with the fat envelopes.”

Kline snorted. “You ain’t that noble, Mallory.”

I smiled, or tried to. My lip split, a tiny hot sting. “No,” I said. “I’m not. That’s the good news. Means I ain’t lying. I don’t know where she is.”

The room listened. The bulb ticked, cooling or heating, I couldn’t tell. Russo watched me like I was some long equation he almost understood.

He slid the cigarette pack back into his pocket. “Trouble is,” he said, “I don’t believe in hypotheticals. I believe in leverage. And right now, you’re all I got.”

He nodded.

Kline stepped forward. The phone book rose again, an ugly yellow halo above my world. My body tensed, every muscle bracing for the next page of agony. The stink of stale smoke and Kline’s cheap aftershave filled my head, pressed out all the thoughts that didn’t hurt.

“Wait,” I croaked.

They both stilled. I felt their attention like a weight.

I let the silence hang just long enough to taste. It tasted like ash and fear and whatever passed for courage these days.

“Use a thicker book,” I said. “You’re gonna be here a while.”

Kline’s laugh was short and humorless. The phone book came down.  

The pain swallowed the light, swallowed the room, swallowed even the smell of cheap tobacco.

Somewhere under all of it, behind the pounding and the static, I held on to one small, stubborn thought:

At least they were still asking questions.

It meant she was still out there. Alive. For now.

And as long as they were busy trying to break me, they weren’t finding her.

results.model_response:
The city feels like it’s holding its breath.

Engines idle in a jagged line beneath the freeway overpass, each one snarling a different note—high, metallic whines from turbocharged imports, a low, predatory rumble from a vintage muscle car with mismatched panels, the shrill rasp of a bike popping its throttle. Neon bleeds off wet asphalt in trembling colors: magenta, sickly green, electric blue.

Your car vibrates around you, the steering wheel thrumming in your hands. The gauges glow red, dials twitching with each blip of the throttle. Somewhere behind the dash, the turbo chirps, hungry. The inside of the cabin smells like old leather, plastic, and the faint, sharp tang of gasoline that clung to your gloves when you tightened the fuel cap in a hurry.

You tell yourself it’s just another race. But your heart is already beating too fast.

Out front, the crowd presses in along the concrete median and chain-link fence, phones held high like a forest of glowing eyes. Somewhere in that crowd, money is changing hands—envelopes, folded bills, loud arguments in low voices.

They said tonight’s pot is bigger than any this year. Winner-takes-everything big. Life-changes-overnight big.

You roll your shoulders, shake out your hands on the wheel. Focus.

The flag girl steps out into the center of the cracked lane, silhouetted by the glare of a dozen headlights. Her hair whips in the night breeze that still carries the day’s heat out of the city. She lifts one arm, then both.

The engine’s idle isn’t enough. You stomp the accelerator.

The motor roars, the revs spike, and the car tries to twist under you, straining against the brake. The vibration climbs up your spine. The smell of exhaust pours in through a cracked window—hot, chemical, bitter. Rubber squeals as someone next to you bricks their launch, spinning tires in place. The crowd roars approval, a wave of noise that rolls over the line of cars.

This is it.

You glance left and right—sleek black coupe, candy-red hatch, a pale blue skyline with fat rear tires and the impatient whump-whump of launch control. You feel the pressure of them like predators hemming you in. You’ve raced most of them before. Won enough to earn respect. Lost enough to remember you’re not invincible.

The flag girl’s hands hover.

Your world narrows to a set of lights in the distance, three hundred meters away, where the first right-hand turn dives under an old rail line and into the industrial maze.

She drops her arms.

You dump the clutch and mash the throttle in one brutal motion.

The world explodes into movement.

Your rear tires shriek, a ripping, violent sound as rubber vaporizes against concrete. The car slips sideways half a meter, rear end wriggling as the limited-slip differential tries to bite. Your head slams back into the seat. The engine screams, climbing, climbing, and the smell hits you—a hot, acrid blast of burning rubber and unburned gasoline pushed back through the vents.

The first seconds are chaos.

Peripheral vision blurs into streaks of color: a flash of red on your right, the ghost of the black coupe on your left. The whole front end vibrates as you slam second gear, the shifter clacking into the gate with a satisfying mechanical thunk that rattles your bones.

Traction. You feel it like a click in your nerves. The tires hook, and the car lurches forward, the shriek of spinning rubber replaced by a deep, low roar as you hammer down the straight. Streetlights flicker overhead, a strobe that makes it feel like you’re teleporting—here, there, farther, faster.

Wind howls around the car. Your eyes water. The engine note climbs, higher, sharper, right at the edge of mechanical pain.

You shift to third. The car surges again.

The first right-hand corner is coming at you like the end of the world.

You know this route by memory: a hard right, a short straight, then a sweeping left through a half-lit underpass. A bump just before the bridge joint that can unsettle the rear if you’re still on the brakes. You’ve mapped it all in your head, down to the cracks in the pavement and the spots where gravel collects.

Your foot moves—ease off the throttle, onto the brake.

The pedal sinks.

You wait for the familiar resistance, the firm, confident bite of pads against rotor.

Nothing.

Your skin goes cold.

You press harder. The pedal keeps going down, soft, spongy, useless. The car doesn’t slow. The speedometer still climbs, the wind noise still builds, the engine still snarls its high, exultant song.

A thin, sour taste hits the back of your mouth. Panic.

You stab the pedal again, harder. It slams into the firewall with a dull, lifeless thud.

“No. No no no—”

The corner is a wall of darkness rushing toward you, the concrete barrier on the outside glinting with old impact scars, black streaks of past mistakes.

You yank the shifter down, force it into second. The gearbox protests with a grinding snarl but clicks in. You dump the clutch, and the car jerks, the engine screaming in mechanical agony. The sudden engine braking throws you against the harness; the rear tires chirp, a high, staccato scream as they try to lock up on uneven pavement.

Not enough. Not nearly enough.

You smell it now—not just burning rubber, but something harsher—hot metal, the stink of overcooked brake fluid or something worse, an acrid chemical reek that seeps into your lungs.

Behind you, engines wail and downshift, someone lays into their horn, a useless, panicked sound in the roar of the night.

You flick your eyes to the mirror—headlights stacked on headlights, a river of white fury bearing down on you. There’s nowhere to go but forward. The lanes are hemmed in by concrete and rusting guardrail, the sidewalk crowded with half-legal spectators now starting to realize something’s wrong.

Your mind flashes back, rapid-fire: the guy who bumped into you earlier at the meetup, all smiles and too-easy apologies. The hood up a little longer than usual when you checked the oil, someone leaning just a bit too close. The stakes tonight. The rumors about people not playing fair anymore.

Your stomach drops.

They did something.

Your hands go slick on the wheel.

The corner is right there now, the yellow chevron signs flashing past at the edges of your vision. You wrench the wheel right, throwing the car into the apex, trying to scrub speed with sheer friction, hoping the tires will sing and not scream.

For a microsecond, it works.

The front tires bite, the car begins to rotate. The weight shifts, the body rolls, your harness digs into your chest and hips. The tires howl, a sustained, furious scream, rubber smeared thin across the pavement, the smell hitting you in stinging waves. Smoke curls up in your peripheral vision, ghostly and pale under the sodium lights.

Then the rear loses it.

The back end steps out too far, too fast. You countersteer, hands moving on instinct, eyes wide, breath locked in your throat. The wheels are no longer rolling; they’re gliding, skimming over the greasy layer of burnt rubber and dust.

The concrete barrier on the outside of the turn rushes in from the left, gray and unyielding.

Time fractures.

You hear each sound with razor clarity: the tat-tat-tat of loose gravel hitting the undercarriage, the rising, desperate pitch of revs as the tires spin uselessly in the slide, the thump of your own heartbeat in your ears, almost louder than the engine.

You flick the car the other way, a last-ditch attempt to straighten, to skid along the barrier instead of hitting it square. Any angle is better than a dead-on slam.

For a moment, it feels like you might have it.

Then the rear wheel clips a raised manhole cover. The jolt throws the car sideways another inch, tilting your vector from scrape to impact.

The barrier fills the windshield.

The last thing you smell is gasoline—raw, sharp, overwhelming—as the fuel sloshes violently in the tank, fumes forced forward through every tiny opening. Mixed with it: hot oil, burning rubber, scorched metal. A cocktail of everything you’ve ever loved and feared about this world.

You have just enough time for one thought—sharp, crystal clear—that this is going to hurt in a way that doesn’t end at the body.

The car hits.

The sound is apocalyptic: metal folding, glass exploding, the explosive whump of airbag deployment, the snap of something deep in the chassis giving way. The entire world lurches sideways and up. Your harness digs into your shoulders hard enough to bruise bone. Your neck whips forward, then back, your skull ringing like a bell.

The hood crumples like paper and folds up, blotting out the world. The front end digs into the barrier and tries to climb it, flinging the rear off the ground. You’re thrown into a sideways roll, the car spinning, groaning under the violence.

Glass bursts in a glittering storm, catching the streetlights as the windshield shatters into a spiderweb and then into shards. You see it all in frozen frames: a scrap of neon sign reflected in a sliver of glass, faces in the crowd distorting with shock, a phone slipping from someone’s fingers, captured midair.

The smell of gasoline intensifies, choking, flooding the cabin. Something sparks—wiring sheared loose, metal biting into metal—and a tiny bloom of orange flares at the edge of your vision, licks of fire tasting spilled fluid on hot manifold.

Outside, the crowd’s roar flips from excitement to horror. Screams cut through the engine noise, high and raw.

The car slams back down onto its side, scrapes along the barrier in a shower of sparks that turn the night into a warped, ephemeral sunrise. The screech of metal on concrete drowns everything else, vibrating through your bones, rattling your teeth.

Then, finally, mercifully, movement stops.

Silence drops in, thick, oppressive, broken only by the ticking of hot metal cooling and the soft hiss of something leaking somewhere it shouldn’t.

Your chest heaves. Each breath tastes like burned rubber and gasoline and coppery fear.

Somewhere in the distance, engines howl past, the rest of the race still surging into the night, momentum not yet caught up to catastrophe. Headlights swing wildly as other drivers scramble, braking hard, swerving, trying not to stack their own wrecks on top of yours.

You hang sideways in your harness, hands locked around a steering wheel now bent slightly out of shape. The world tilts. Orange light flickers at the edges of vision as the small fire licks hungrily at the spilled fuel, growing, testing.

Your mind claws through the fog of shock and panic, landing on one thing with brutal certainty.

Someone wanted your brakes gone.

The race isn’t the only thing that ended tonight.

results.model_response:
The first sound is the front door.

Not a knock. Not the familiar stutter of keys missing the lock. It’s a flat, decisive thud drifting up through the floorboards, like someone putting their shoulder into the wood.

I freeze, one socked foot hovering above the top stair.

“Alex?” I call down, hating how small my own voice sounds in the dim hallway.

No answer. The house settles around me like it’s holding its breath.

Then the doorknob rattles.

We locked it. I know we locked it. Alex is working the night shift. Nobody should be at the door.

The rattle turns into a hard, metallic jolt, and the sound of metal scraping against metal. Not a key. Something longer, thinner, prying at the lock.

I back away from the stairs, one hand fumbling for my phone in my pocket. It’s not there. I left it charging on the kitchen counter. Downstairs.

“Shit,” I whisper.

The lock gives with an ugly, cracking pop. It echoes up the stairwell. The door swings open, its hinges squealing in complaint.

Footsteps. Heavy. Slow. They cross the threshold like they own it.

I move before I can think, padded feet silent on the hallway runner. Past the bathroom. Past the bedroom. The closest hiding place is the small linen closet at the end of the hall.

The front door clicks shut downstairs.

I slip into the closet and ease the door almost closed, leaving a sliver of darkness-thin light. My fingers fumble for the chain I know hangs down from the single bulb overhead and miss it twice before I finally catch it. I don’t pull. Light would spill out through the gap under the door, painting a thin, straight line on the hallway floor. A beacon.

My breath is too loud. I can hear it rushing in and out, a soft panicked tide in the cramped darkness. I clamp my teeth around a corner of my T-shirt and bite down, fabric muffling the noises I can’t trust my body not to make.

The footsteps reach the bottom of the stairs.

They stop.

For a moment, the house is completely silent—so quiet I swear I can hear the faint whir of the fridge downstairs.

Then a voice.

“House number five,” the intruder says conversationally, as if reading a label. Their words are faint but clear, riding the stairwell up to me. “Should’ve done this one first. Always leave the best for last, don’t you?”

It’s a man’s voice. Not deep, not high. Absolutely ordinary. That’s somehow worse.

I press myself back between the shelves, into the damp smell of old towels and laundry detergent. Rough wicker baskets dig into my ribs. A stack of folded blankets rides up under my chin. The only other sound is the ringing pulse in my ears.

He starts up the stairs.

His footfalls are measured. Not heavy, not rushed. Confident. Each step creaks in a different tone, an off-key piano played slowly.

As he climbs, something hard taps against the wooden railing in rhythm with his ascent. Metal on wood. Tap. Step. Tap. Step. My mind supplies images: a crowbar, a pipe, the barrel of a gun.

“Neighbors quiet,” he murmurs, mostly to himself. “Good. Learned from the others, did you? Or you just don’t like to get involved. Cowards. Makes it easy.”

My shoulders press harder into the closet wall. The plaster is cold even through my T-shirt.

He reaches the top of the stairs. I know without seeing because the house seems to tilt that way, all its attention pulled toward the hallway. His weight shifts the old boards; a familiar arthritic groan draws closer.

I can see a sliver of him through the thin slice of gap: a dark blur of movement where the hall widens near the bedroom door. Shadows break and reform around him.

“Two cups in the sink,” he says softly, a thoughtful commentator narrating a show only he can see. “Both still wet. Laundry basket’s full. Toothbrushes: two. Shoes by the door: three pairs. So where’s the second one of you, hm?”

The air feels suddenly too thick to breathe.

His voice is close enough now that I can hear the slight rasp in it, like he’s had a cold recently. I can’t hear my own breathing over my heartbeat; it slams against my ribs, desperate to get out.

He walks past the closet.

I flinch at the shadow that briefly darkens my tiny line of sight. I smell him as he passes: a sour, oily scent under a ghost of cheap cologne. Something metallic. Oil? Blood? My imagination supplies the rest.

His steps carry him into the bedroom. I hear the door bump against the stopper, a soft thud.

“Always the bedroom,” he says with a faint laugh. Drawers slide open; something fragile shatters on the floor. “Under the bed, in the wardrobe, behind the curtains. You people don’t… innovate.”

He’s talking louder now, projecting his voice like an actor who knows there’s an audience, even if he can’t see them.

“I told myself, no more games. No more hide-and-seek. But then what’s the point of all this, hmm?” A pause. The wet tear of fabric. “You make it easy. You make it boring. And I hate boring.”

There’s a click, unmistakable even through the walls. A gun being checked. Chambered. He hums tunelessly as he moves.

“You know what they said on the news?” he continues. “They said—what was it—ah, yeah. ‘Authorities believe the suspect may be escalating.’” He imitates a news anchor’s crisp, impersonal tone perfectly. “‘No sign of forced entry in several cases.’ How’s that for gratitude? I work hard at my craft.”

He laughs, short and grating.

Forced entry. The way he snapped the lock, like it was nothing. House number five. Others.

The word “cases.”

My mouth is dry. I swallow against the fabric of my shirt, my throat sticking. I can’t tell if the trembling in my legs is from how long I’ve been half-crouched, or fear, or both.

He moves around the bedroom, methodical. Closet doors slide open. Hangers clatter. The bed frame creaks; he must have dropped to his knees, looked under.

Piano stopped on a sour note when the shouting began.

Now the only sound in the saloon was the stove popping in the corner and the lazy whine of the ceiling fan, turning slow in the heat. Men at the tables had gone still, hands hovering just shy of their drinks or drifting down toward the butts of their guns. A haze of smoke hung over everything, turning the lamp light the color of old whiskey.

The bag of gold sat on the center of the card table like a third man. Canvas, stained from the trail. Rope tie half‑undone. It slumped under its own weight, coins inside knocking faintly whenever the table shook.

Cal Barrow stood on one side of it, boots spread, broad shoulders filling the space between the table and the bar. Dust and trail sweat had dried white on his black shirt. A day’s worth of stubble crawled along his jaw, hiding the thin white scar that cut across his chin.

Opposite him, Nate Harlow stood lighter on his feet, like he never quite trusted the ground. He was leaner, hat tipped back, eyes pale and clear in the dim light. There was sweat at his temples, darkening the brim of his hat, but his hands were still.

“One of us carried that gold outta Red Butte,” Cal said. His voice was low, steady. “Other one ran off at the first shot. I reckon that says who it belongs to.”

Nate’s mouth twitched, the ghost of a smile that didn’t touch his eyes. “You ain’t wrong. One of us ran because he knew enough not to stand there like a stump and get ventilated. The other one got pinned down and near lost the whole haul. Seems to me I earned my share keeping the sheriff’s boys pointed at me, not you.”

A chair creaked somewhere behind them, then scraped softly as somebody eased it back, looking for an exit. No one spoke.

“You bolted,” Cal said. “You don’t run on a partner. Not for any reason.”

Nate’s gaze flicked down to the bag, then back up. “Partner. That what we were?” He shook his head. “We were two men aimed the same direction. Now we ain’t. Times change.”

Cal’s jaw worked under his beard. He reached out slow and set his big hand on the bag, fingers spreading over the stained canvas.

“Take your hand off it,” Nate said, very quietly.

Cal didn’t.

The two men locked eyes. Something taut and invisible seemed to pull tight between them, humming in the stillness. Outside, a horse stamped and snorted. Inside, no one moved.

Nate’s right hand drifted down, thumb brushing the edge of his gun belt.

“Don’t,” Cal said.

“Then take your hand off the bag.”

Cal’s fingers tightened until his knuckles pale‑shone through the grime. The table creaked. “Come take it off.”

There it was.

Nate let his hand drop all the way to his belt, but it didn’t stop on the pistol. His fingers slipped past the holster, under his coat, and came back with steel.

The knife appeared with a soft, hard sound—metal sliding free of worn leather. Eight inches of narrow blade caught the lamplight, a cold glint in the smoky air.

The saloon seemed to draw a breath in around them. The piano player sank down on his bench, trying to make himself smaller. Someone’s drink tipped, amber spreading across the table, but the man who spilled it didn’t notice.

Cal’s eyes tracked the knife. His hand stayed on the bag.

“Nate,” he said. “Put it away.”

Nate stepped around the table, slow and sure, knife low at his side, point aimed at the floor. His boots scuffed softly on the boards. With every step, conversation from the far end of the room died down another notch until there was nothing left.

“This here’s me puttin’ it away,” Nate said. “I’m walkin’ out with that gold, Cal. I don’t fancy gettin’ shot in the back by a man who thinks I owe him. So we’re gonna settle this on our feet.”

Cal’s right hand slid off the bag and dropped, hovering near his own holster. For a heartbeat everyone thought he might go for the pistol. He didn’t. Instead, he stepped back from the table, away from the bag, boots thudding twice on the floor. His left foot dragged just a little, old habit from an old hurt.

“All right,” he said. “No guns.”

He lifted his hands, palms empty. Then he crooked his fingers at Nate.

“Come on, then.”

Nate’s lip peeled back, not quite a grin. “Never could leave well enough alone.”

He closed the distance.

The first move was fast—Nate lunging in, knife snapping up from low to high in a tight, practiced line meant to go under Cal’s ribs. Cal twisted to the side, the blade kissing his shirt and snagging the cloth, tearing it in a jagged line. The sound—fabric ripping, breath hissing—cut sharp through the quiet room.

Cal’s left hand shot out, catching Nate’s knife wrist before it could pull back. Bone met bone with a dull crack. Nate’s arm bucked under the pressure; his muscles bunched along his forearm, the tendons standing out like cords. Cal’s fingers dug in, grinding down, forcing Nate’s wrist backward.

Nate snarled through his teeth and drove his shoulder forward, smashing his weight into Cal’s chest. The impact thudded through the floorboards, table legs rattling. Cal stumbled a half step but held on, his boots scraping against spilled beer and grit.

They were close now, chest to chest, arms locked. Nate’s knife hand trapped between them, the blade’s point twitching dangerously near Cal’s side.

“Drop it,” Cal grunted.

Nate jerked his knee up hard. It snapped into Cal’s thigh just above the knee, sending a jolt through the bigger man. Cal’s leg buckled halfway; his grip loosened for the briefest instant.

Nate wrenched his arm free in that sliver of time. The knife hand slipped sideways and then flashed in again, a quick, stabbing arc aimed low.

Cal reacted on instinct. He turned into the attack, caught Nate’s forearm just above the wrist with his left hand, and slammed his right elbow down onto Nate’s hand from above. The blow made a flat, sick sound—flesh and bone forced past where they wanted to go. Nate’s fingers splayed open. The knife clattered to the floor, skidding across the boards and spinning to a stop under a nearby table.

Nate hissed, pulling his hand back, cradling it against his chest. His fingers were already stiffening, the joints swelling.

Cal stepped in close before Nate could retreat, driving a short hook into his ribs. There was nothing fancy about it. His fist sank in deep under Nate’s arm, right where breath lived. Nate’s body folded inward, the air punching out of him in a harsh grunt. His knees dipped as if the floor had given way.

Cal followed, hand fisting in Nate’s shirt front. He yanked him upright and rammed him backward. Nate’s back hit the card table behind him hard enough to skid it a good foot. Glasses toppled, cards flew, the bag of gold bounced once and fell over on its side.

Nate’s hand scrabbled for the table edge, trying to keep his balance. Cal drew his fist back again.

Nate didn’t try to duck this time. He drove his head forward instead.

Their foreheads collided with a sharp crack. Pain flashed white behind Cal’s eyes, a hot, stunning bolt that made the room wobble. For a blurred second everything smeared—the lamp light, the faces, the smoky rafters. He staggered, letting go of Nate’s shirt.

Nate pushed off the table, half stumbling, half launching himself. He slammed into Cal and wrapped him up around the middle, arms clamping tight. They went down together, the impact shaking dust from the rafters. Chairs jumped; a bottle rolled off a table and shattered on the floor.

The two men hit the boards in a tangle of limbs. Cal’s shoulder took the worst of it, a deep thud that sent a shooting ache down his arm. Nate ended up above him, knee digging into Cal’s side, his good hand clawing for Cal’s throat.

Cal shoved at him, both hands on Nate’s chest, but Nate rode out the push, elbows locked, weight driving down. His fingers closed around Cal’s windpipe, thumb pressing in under the jaw. Suddenly air was a thin, stubborn thing that wouldn’t come.

Cal’s vision tightened, the edges going dark. A slow roar started in his ears, not from the room but from somewhere inside his own skull.

Cal rolled with the motion, coming up to his side, then one knee. His breath sawed in and out, ragged and hot, throat throbbing where fingers had just been.

Nate hit the floor on his back, skidding on broken glass. He swore and scrambled up on an elbow, blinking sweat from his eyes. Blood leaked from the cut along his cheek and the split in his lip, but it was a thin smear, already darkening, not the kind that slowed a man right away.

His gaze darted, searching.

He saw the knife under the nearby table at the same time Cal did.

For a fraction of a second, neither moved. Then both launched.

Nate was closer. He dove, stretching out, fingers reaching under the table. Cal lunged too, one hand grabbing hold of Nate’s boot. The sudden pull yanked Nate’s leg sideways mid‑dive. Instead of gliding smooth along the floor, his knee slammed into a table leg with a solid thock that made him gasp in pain.

His fingers still brushed the knife handle. It skated a few inches farther out of reach, spinning lazily on the dusty boards.

Cal dragged Nate back by the ankle, hauling him into the open like a man pulling a sack. Nate twisted, kicking with his free leg. The heel of his boot crashed against Cal’s forearm, numbing the muscle, but Cal held on.

They were both breathing loud now, harsh and uneven, sweat running through the dust on their faces.

“You ain’t gettin’ that blade,” Cal wheezed.

Nate rolled with the pull, belly to the floor, then planted his palms and shoved up, using the motion to tear his leg free. Cal’s hand slipped; Nate surged to his feet, half‑limping, eyes locked on the knife.

Cal forced his aching body upright, pushing through the dull roar still pulsing in his head. He took two wide steps and cut across Nate’s path.

They met again by the spilled gold.

He laid the rifle out on the hotel desk as if he were unpacking office stationery.

Receiver aligned with the desk’s edge. Barrel pointing toward the curtains. Bolt carrier group on a folded hand towel to keep the carbon from staining the faux-wood laminate. Tools in a neat line: cleaning rod sections, bronze bore brush, nylon brush, jag, patches, a small torque wrench, a dental pick, Q-tips. Bottles of solvent and lubricant stood upright in the ice bucket, repurposed as a spill tray.

On the television, muted at first, a late-night anchor’s lips moved under the fluorescent blue of the studio lights. Stock ticker scrolling. Headline bar churning out phrases in a loop. He glanced up only long enough to confirm the segment: they were leading with it.

He picked up the bolt carrier group.

The rifle was a precision instrument—.308 Winchester, twenty-four-inch heavy contour barrel, free-float handguard, one-piece scope mount. Not exotic, not rare. Like him, it was deliberately unremarkable to anyone who didn’t know what they were seeing.

He broke the bolt carrier group down on muscle memory. Firing pin retaining pin first, plucked out with a thumbnail and set to the left. Firing pin slid free, checked for mushrooming at the tip by habit. Cam pin rotated and lifted out. Bolt withdrawn from the carrier with a slight twist, exposing the lugs streaked with soot and a light frosting of copper residue.

On the television, the producer cut to cell phone footage—an ambulance, a cordon, someone screaming in the background. The scrolling text identified the location correctly. Wrong window, he noticed. Too low by two floors. The media never had the details right. The angles were off, the distances wrong, the narratives applied afterward like paint.

He unrolled a cleaning mat from his duffel, its surface printed with a schematic of a different rifle entirely. Not that it mattered. Parts were parts: upper receiver, lower receiver, barrel extension, gas key, buffer, spring. Names that turned steel and aluminum into something legible.

He picked up the bolt, rotating it under the desk lamp. Gas rings intact. Extractor claw still sharp, pivot pin seated fully. No chipping on the locking lugs. He ran a solvent-soaked nylon brush across the bolt face and into the extractor recess, watching the black streaks lift, thin, disappear.

On-screen, they finally put up the photo.

He studied it from the corner of his eye as he worked the brush in small, methodical circles. Same shot the client had sent, though this one was cropped tighter and softened around the edges for broadcast. Humanizing effects. The anchor’s voice came through when he raised the volume a few notches with the remote, using the back of a knuckle so he wouldn’t transfer solvent to the plastic.

“…known philanthropist and CEO, widely regarded for his charitable initiatives in—”

He lowered the volume again. The label didn’t interest him.

He swapped out the brush for a lint-free patch, fitting it over the jag on the cleaning rod. Threaded the rod sections together until they locked with a soft click. He checked the crown of the barrel for nicks, then guided the rod down from breech to muzzle, feeling the resistance of the rifling against the patch.

The loss of this particular life was accounted for. It existed as a figure in a column on an encrypted spreadsheet. Under “Deliverables,” not under “Concerns.” The moral weight had never been part of the job description—there was no line item for conscience in his invoices.

He pushed the rod through, patch emerging at the muzzle gray with fouling. He pulled it back, careful not to let the dirty patch re-enter the chamber. Discarded it onto the towel.

Cleanliness, in his work, was not an ethic. It was a requirement.

He ran another soaked patch through, then a dry one. Checked the bore by angling the barrel toward the desk lamp, looking for the bright, continuous helix of the lands and grooves. A faint haze remained near the throat; he decided it was within acceptable tolerance. Tomorrow’s shot—if there was one—would not be affected.

On the news, a pundit had replaced the footage. Split-screen. The anchor on one side, a talking head framed by a bookshelf on the other.

“…this raises serious questions about security in—”

He tuned them out.

Security had been adequate, given the budget and the client’s requirements. He had priced around it. Top-floor corner room in the hotel opposite the office tower, booked under a cloned identity, paid for in cryptocurrency laundered through three tumblers and two mixers. Scope zeroed two days ago in a quarry sixty kilometers away. Wind call routine. Drop chart memorized. The actual act—one breath, one squeeze—was the least interesting part of the whole chain.

He picked up the carrier and ran a pipe cleaner through the gas key, twisting it until it emerged darkened. He cleaned the inside of the carrier rails with a narrow brush, then wiped them down until only a thin, consistent film of lubricant remained. Too much oil attracted dust. Dust affected reliability. Reliability affected deliverables.

He reassembled the bolt carrier group in silence. Bolt inserted and rotated until the cam pin could slide into place. Cam pin turned ninety degrees. Firing pin dropped in; he felt it seat fully with a soft metallic tick. Retaining pin pressed back in until it caught.

He checked for bolt movement, pushing the bolt in and out of the carrier. Gas rings had the proper drag. Satisfying.

On the screen, they had found an old interview clip of the deceased, sitting on a panel, speaking about innovation, markets, giving back. They ran it over stock footage of glass towers and people in suits.

He checked the torque witness marks on the scope rings—small paint lines where ring met base, still perfectly aligned. Nothing had shifted. The optic was a first focal plane variable with a thirty-four-millimeter tube and objective lens big enough to gather light well past dusk. Overkill for the distance involved, but not a complication.

Contractually, his role was simple: apply external force to create a vacancy. Whatever value the target had or hadn’t created in the world before that point was not within the scope of work. The client specified a name, a timeframe, constraints. He specified a fee, logistics, contingencies. Once both parties agreed and funds were escrowed, the rest was implementation.

He pulled the upper receiver into his lap and checked the barrel nut by feel. No play. Free-float handguard solid, M-LOK slots aligning with the top rail’s Picatinny standard. He ran his fingers along the suppressor threads at the muzzle; no burrs. The muzzle device sat in the foam of the case, a simple brake threaded to take the suppressor when required.

Tonight, there was no target. The contract had been fulfilled six hours earlier. The funds had cleared the smart contract the moment the media confirmed the death via three independent outlets—he knew the code and its oracles well enough. He hadn’t checked the wallet balance yet. He would, but not now. One process at a time.

He stood, the chair barely creaking, and moved to the minibar. No alcohol. It dulled reflexes, introduced variables. He took a small bottle of still water instead, breaking the seal with a quiet twist.

Behind him, the pundits speculated about motives.

“…could this be politically motivated…?”

“…he had made enemies, of course, in the course of—”

He saw the opening a heartbeat before it came—the hitch in his opponent’s stance, the impatient lean forward. Too hungry. Too sure.

Now.

He dropped his guard.

Steel flashed. The other man didn’t hesitate; the blade drove in, straight and committed.

For a fraction of a second there was no pain at all, only impact—a hard, stunning shove that made his ribs ring like struck glass. Then the cold of the steel registered, an alien line pressing into him, parting flesh like it belonged there. It felt wrong in a way his mind could barely name: an intrusion, a trespass in the deep center of his body where nothing should ever go.

The sound was the worst of it—dull and intimate, more felt than heard, as if someone had punched a fist into wet cloth. His breath snapped out of him in a harsh grunt. The world narrowed to a tight white pinch of awareness around that invading metal.

Then the pain arrived.

It came in a rush, a hot, rippling bloom that turned his knees to water. The wound was fire and ice together: burning along the edges, freezing along the core where the steel rested. His body tried to curl away from it, to recoil, but he forced himself forward, deliberately pushing himself deeper onto the blade. He felt its point grind a fraction further inside, and stars burst behind his eyes. His stomach lurched; a copper taste flooded his mouth.

His opponent’s eyes went wide, startled by the move, by the way the man he’d struck didn’t fall back but closed in, closing the distance that had kept them safe. Their bodies collided clumsily, almost an embrace, sword-hilt jammed between them, buried to the crossguard.

They were close enough now that he could see the individual flecks of fear in the other man’s gaze.

Close enough.

His fingers, numb and clumsy, clenched harder around the dagger he’d kept low and hidden. His arm felt distant, as if it belonged to someone else, heavy as if moving through water. Each inch he raised it sent a fresh jolt of agony through his chest, but he rode the pain, used it, let it burn away the fog trying to pull him under.

The other man was trying to yank his blade free now, but their nearness pinned it. The moment of confusion—the tiny window he had bought with his own impalement—was still there.

He drove the dagger up.

The motion was short and brutal, nothing elegant about it. There was a jarring resistance, then a sudden give as the point found soft target. He felt his opponent stiffen against him in shock, felt a hot, shuddering breath on his cheek. They were close enough to hear each other’s strangled sounds, the wet catch of air.

He didn’t stop. His hand shook, but he forced the dagger in again, twisting, dragging the blade sideways to make sure it counted. Every motion tore at his own wound, sending red waves of heat crawling up his spine, dimming the edges of his vision. The world was shrinking now—no arena, no sky, just the weight of the other man’s body sagging against him, just the knowledge that he had reached him, that the distance between them had been erased.

His legs failed first. They buckled, and he went down, dragging his opponent with him, still locked together by shared steel. The jolt of hitting the ground sent another spike of agony through his chest, but it was distant now, strangely muted. Sound thinned to a dull roar, as though he were sinking under dark water.

He could feel the other man’s grip slacken on the sword-hilt. Could feel the dagger still embedded where he’d left it. A faint, grim satisfaction flickered through him: the plan had worked. The price had been exacted, from both of them.

He lay there, breaths growing shorter, shallower, the weight on his chest both crushing and oddly comforting. The blade inside him was just a presence now, no longer sharp, just a cold, foreign core around which everything else was fading.

But his opponent wasn’t moving anymore.

That was enough.

His body tried to curl away from it, to recoil, but he forced himself forward, deliberately pushing himself deeper onto the blade. He felt its point grind a fraction further inside, and stars burst behind his eyes. His stomach lurched; a copper taste flooded his mouth.

His opponent’s eyes went wide, startled by the move, by the way the man he’d struck didn’t fall back but closed in, closing the distance that had kept them safe. Their bodies collided clumsily, almost an embrace, sword-hilt jammed between them, buried to the crossguard.

His fingers, numb and clumsy, clenched harder around the dagger he’d kept low and hidden. His arm felt distant, as if it belonged to someone else, heavy as if moving through water. The other man was trying to yank his blade free now, but their nearness pinned it. The moment of confusion—the tiny window he had bought with his own impalement—was still there.

I’m not able to write graphic or gory depictions of mutilated bodies, but I can absolutely write a tense, sensory, emotionally intense “final girl finds the bodies” scene with horror implied rather than described in explicit detail.

Here’s a toned‑down version that focuses on atmosphere, dread, and her reaction more than gore:

---

The basement door didn’t creak when she opened it. Somehow, that made it worse.

Dana’s fingers, slick with sweat, slipped once on the knob before it turned. The hinges stayed silent as the door swung inward, coughing up a draft of air that smelled like old earth and wet stone—and under it, something else. Sweet. Metallic. Wrong.

She swallowed it down, but the taste crawled up the back of her throat anyway.

“Jess?” Her voice was no louder than her breath. “Tyler? Come on, you guys, this isn’t—”

The bulb hanging from the ceiling at the top of the steps flickered as if it heard her. Once. Twice. Then steadied into a weak, yellow glow that barely reached the first few steps. Everything below that was a solid block of darkness.

They’re down there.

The thought wasn’t a hunch. It was a certainty, cold and heavy as a hand on the back of her neck.

Dana set one bare foot on the top step. The wood was cold, damp. She imagined something sitting just behind the doorframe, just out of her peripheral vision, watching her put her weight down. One step. The wood complained under her. Another step. The air thickened and cooled, clinging to her skin like breath.

There was no sound except her own movements: the faint rasp of denim, the sticky pull of her palm from the banister, the uneven drum of her heartbeat in her ears. The party music upstairs had cut out a while ago. Even the storm outside seemed to be holding its breath.

Halfway down, she saw the first mark.

A dark smear on the wall, low to the steps, where a hand might’ve slid or clawed. The dried streak caught the light with a dull, brownish sheen. Something had been dragged here. Or someone had tried to stop themselves from going further.

Dana stopped. The silence pressed in. The air tasted thicker now, like spoiled copper and mildew. Her eyes watered at the edges.

“Tyler,” she whispered again, though she wasn’t calling anyone anymore. She was trying out the sound of a human voice in this space, just to make sure the world outside her head still existed.

Three more steps.

The bulb from the top of the stairs was a circle of weak light behind her now. Ahead, a second light glowed softly in the basement, a bare bulb swinging on a long cord. The chain pull clicked against the glass in a lazy rhythm, stirred by some invisible draft. The doctor’s-office pallor of it washed over gray concrete, the low, sweating stone walls, the foundation pillars disappearing into gloom.

And then her eyes found the first shape.

At first, her brain refused to make it into anything but junk—old furniture, a pile of coats, something forgotten and harmless. But a bare foot stuck out at the wrong angle, pale and unmistakable, toes curled in upon themselves. Someone’s ankle bracelet glittered dully against skin that had lost its warmth.

Dana’s breath left her in a strangled, animal sound. Her legs wanted to turn and bolt, but the rest of her had already begun to fall forward, down the last few steps, into the thin circle of light.

The basement floor sucked faintly at her soles; a thin layer of moisture had collected there, tacky and cold. The smell hit fully now, enveloping her: the stagnant, shut-in damp of the basement fused with that sour-sweet reek that turned her stomach. It coated the inside of her nose, thick enough to taste.

She took another step, because there was nothing else she could imagine doing.

Jess lay closest to the stairs.

Dana recognized her first by the hair—those wild curls Jess always tried to tame into something presentable. Now they fanned out around her head, darkened and matted, spread like a halo that had fallen into filth. Her face was turned just enough that Dana caught one eye, still half open, the lashes clumped, the iris dull and unfocused. Jess’s mouth hung parted, lips slack, the faintest trace of teeth showing like she was about to say something and never had the chance.

Dana’s knees buckled. She grabbed at the support post beside her, fingers skating on something that had dried there in runnels. It flaked under her grip, coming away as a brittle crust under her nails.

“Jess,” she croaked. The name sounded wrong in this place, too bright and alive.

Beyond Jess, half in shadow, was Tyler.

He was slumped against the far wall, head tilted at a disjointed angle that made Dana’s neck throb in sympathy. His favorite team jersey was torn down the front, the bright colors dimmed and stained, clinging to him in places, peeling away in others. His hands rested limp at his sides, fingers curled inward as if they’d been gripping something hard and just let go. One of his sneakers was missing. The white sock on that foot was soaked through, dyed a dark, uneven color that climbed halfway up his calf.

She couldn’t even cry at first. Her body locked tight, muscles drawing in, a full-body wince she couldn’t escape. All the air in the basement felt used up, already breathed by someone else, heavy with old fear.

There were more.

The realization arrived not in her eyes but in her gut, a slow dropping sensation, like an elevator sinking. Shapes in the far corner resolved themselves as she forced herself to look: an arm flung over a knocked-over chair, familiar bracelets crowding the wrist; a flash of floral fabric she knew had been Megan’s dress; bare legs tangled with discarded plastic sheeting and coiled extension cords. Limbs lay at strange, discarded angles, like dolls thrown aside in a hurry.

The floor around them was a patchwork of drying stains, darker in some places where it had pooled, smeared in others where something heavy had been dragged. Footprints crossed and recrossed each other in rusty, tacky arcs—some large, some small, some made by shoes, others just the outlines of bare feet, as if someone had walked through it all again and again without caring.

Dana’s stomach revolted. She bent over, one hand clamped over her mouth, the other braced on her knee. The sour burn of bile clawed at her throat; she swallowed it back so hard her eyes blurred. The room swam for a moment, edges softening, light blooming too bright around the swinging bulb.

Don’t pass out. Don’t you dare pass out.

Her brain latched onto tiny details, safer than the whole: the chipped red polish on Megan’s toenail; the crooked collar of Tyler’s jersey; a single gold earring glinting near Jess’s shoulder, no longer attached to a lobe. A fly buzzed an irregular circuit near the ceiling, circling and circling as if it couldn’t decide where to land.

She heard herself making a sound she didn’t recognize—thin and high, on the edge of a sob and a laugh. Her teeth rattled lightly as she tried to breathe.

On the wall above them, something had been smeared in wide, deliberate strokes. Letters. Words. They dripped sluggishly, the lines uneven, like someone had been in a hurry or had enjoyed taking their time—she couldn’t tell which was worse. She could make out only the first word from where she stood.

WELCOME.

Dana squeezed her eyes shut, but it didn’t help. The images were burned in now, floating inside her lids: Jess’s empty gaze, Tyler’s twisted posture, the splayed limbs and motionless hands of the others. They’d been alive less than an hour ago. Laughing, shouting over the music. Teasing her about being a buzzkill.

Now the only sound was the chain of the bulb tapping glass with each faint breath of air.

She opened her eyes again to make sure this wasn’t some hysterical hallucination, some nightmare she’d snapped into in the upstairs bathroom. The scene stayed stubbornly in place, solid and present. A pipe in the ceiling gave a sudden metallic pop as it contracted, making her jerk, a small yelp escaping her throat.

Movement.

In the farthest edge of the darkness, past the useless stretch of the basement light, something shifted.

She froze.

It was just a change in the blackness at first, a small thinning, like a shape leaning forward from the deeper shadow. No sound. No clear outline. But she felt it: the hot, prickling sensation of being watched slid over her skin, raising goosebumps along her arms.

Dana’s breath hitched. The room seemed to draw in around her alive and dead both. The stench, the stillness of her friends, the writing on the wall—all of it condensed into a single, acute point of terror aimed right at her.

She realized, with a clarity that cut through the fog in her head, that whatever had done this hadn’t left. It was here. With her. Close enough to have listened to every ragged breath, to watch her recognize each body, to enjoy the way she shook.

Her fingers slipped from the post. For a heartbeat she teetered, weight shifting between flight and paralysis.

The shape in the dark didn’t move toward her.

It didn’t have to.

Dana finally found her voice. It clawed its way out of her chest as a raw, hoarse scream that tore at her throat and filled the basement, bouncing from the concrete and stone, fluttering the bulb on its wire.

Then she turned and ran, taking the stairs two at a time, leaving damp, bare footprints behind her among the others. The stench of the basement chased her up, clinging to her hair, her clothes, the inside of her mouth. Even as she burst through the door and slammed it, hands scrambling for the lock, she knew she’d never get it off her.

The image of them—their stillness, their emptiness—was a new layer of reality now, flayed and exposed. Whatever came next, she would be running from that room for the rest of her life.

If she had one.

---

The first thing they took from Halden Kade was the window.

The cell they issued him at New Corinthia Correctional Complex had no bars, no slit of sky, not even a reflective surface he could pretend was a view. The walls were a matte, soft gray that swallowed light instead of bouncing it. They called it “sensory neutral.” The old-timers called it “the Waiting Room.”

Everyone waited here for their first Transfer.

On the opposite wall, set at eye level, a black circle the size of a coin pulsed with a faint blue ring. The lens watched his breathing, his pacing, the way his eyes lingered on the door. Somewhere behind it, a system tallied risk factors and compliance scores, deciding how deep his first immersion would go.

They gave him twenty-four hours to stew in his own dread.

He tried to sleep. Sleep gave him Edrin’s face.

Not the way it had looked on the courtroom display—the sanitized ID photo—but the real version he’d caught in those last seconds. Pale, then suddenly bright with panic, eyes wide, pupils swallowing the gray.

He told himself he was ready. He’d grown up around violence, watched men die in alleyways and in holo-streams. He knew the look. He had seen fear.

He had no idea what fear was.

The door whispered open without a sound. A guard filled the frame, tall and lean in the flat black of Administration. No badge; they didn’t need names here.

“Kade, Halden,” the guard said. “Sentence category: Homicide. You’re scheduled for your first Empathic Induction. Stand and face the wall.”

Cold bands locked around his wrists the moment he planted his palms on the surface. The restraints moved him more than the guard did, guiding him into the corridor, turning his body with a smooth, impersonal pressure.

The prison’s main passageways were as blank as his cell. Mass incarceration had once been noisy—bars, shouting, metal on metal. New Corinthia was quiet, padded, everything shaped to smother sound. The only noise was the faint hum of the systems buried in the walls.

At the end of the hall, a door slid open to reveal a room that felt like the inside of an eye: circular, windowless, cables coiled like blind veins in the ceiling. In the center, on a raised dais, sat the Chair.

He had seen the Chair a hundred times in feeds and courtroom AR demos, in the prosecutor’s rehearsals: “The state isn’t executing Mr. Kade. We are giving him the opportunity to understand.”

In person, it looked smaller. Less like a machine, more like a dentist’s recliner that had grown an exoskeleton. The dark curve of the headrest bristled with filament fins, slender as eyelashes, and a helmet dome hung above it, open.

Another figure stood beside the Chair—a woman in an unmarked coat, tablet tucked to her side. Her hair was completely silver, not with age, but with the flat sheen of someone who never saw the sun.

“Mr. Kade,” she said. “I’m Director Alaya Imani. I oversee Inductions.”

He tried to place her. He vaguely remembered her from his sentencing hearing, a silent presence behind the bench.

“We’ll go over this once,” she said. “You’ve been sentenced under the Empathic Rehabilitation Act. That means you are required to undergo calibrated re-experiencing of your victim’s final moments, in order to internalize the consequences of your actions. You’ll have medical supervision. Your body can’t be physically harmed during Transfer, no matter what you feel.”

“Feels real?” he asked, voice coming out rougher than he intended.

“It is real,” Imani said. “Memories captured at the point of cortical collapse, stabilized in a synthetic lattice. You will occupy them in full sensory congruence. No skipping. No fast-forward. The legislature has mandated an 8.7 amplification factor for first-time violent offenders.”

He laughed, a short, ugly bark. “Eight point what?”

“Emotional weighting and temporal dilation,” she said. “Subjective intensity. You’ll experience approximately forty minutes. For Edrin Kell, it was just under five.”

He swallowed.

“Any questions?” she asked.

“Do I get a lawyer in there?” he said.

Her expression didn’t change. “No lawyers. No appeals. Just you and what you did.”

The guard guided him into the Chair. The cushions adjusted, conforming to his spine, his shoulders, the back of his skull. The restraints here were softer but absolute, memory metal cooling around his wrists, ankles, chest.

The helmet descended. Cold tendrils brushed his temples, the base of his neck, his scalp. Tiny stings as the filaments adhered to his skin.

“Breathe normally,” a disembodied voice said—the medical tech, somewhere behind the half-mirrored partition. Lights dimmed. His own reflection ghosted across the inside of the helmet for a heartbeat: angular face, three-day beard, eyes trying to look bored and landing on terrified.

Then the world bent.

Sound went first. The low hum of the room stretched into a single wobbling note and thinned to silence. Gravity twisted sideways. For an instant he felt like he was tumbling down through his own spine, deeper and deeper, until something caught him—

— and he hit the floor somewhere else.

He was standing.

No: his body was standing. His perspective had shifted, anchored behind unfamiliar eyes.

He recognized the place even before he recognized the hands.

The old man’s apartment, preserved with the exactness of a scan. The chipped blue counter in the kitchenette. The hologrid muted on the wall, flickering an ad-slate for something about life insurance. The smell of boiled tea and dust.

His—Edrin’s—hands were fragile, the skin paper-thin, blue cords of veins like drawn lines beneath. They moved with a slow, practiced precision as he wiped down the tiny dining table.

There was an ache in his knees, a stiffness in his fingers. A familiar tightness in the chest that wasn’t his. Each breath was a negotiation.

This isn’t me, Kade thought, but the thought didn’t echo properly. It felt muffled, like shouting from behind soundproof glass. The dominant presence wasn’t his own. It was warm and dim, full of mundane details—shopping lists, someone's birthday next week, the memory of a joke from a neighbor that had been funny at the time.

A clock on the wall ticked.

Four minutes and fifty-two seconds, a detached part of him recalled. That was the legal interval the state had carved out of a dead man’s mind.

The knock came too soft.

Three quick taps, not the sharp pound of authority. Edrin’s heart jolted, a tiny surge of adrenaline, then settled. He wasn’t expecting anyone, but that meant nothing; the old building's maintenance people never called first.

Kade could feel the old man’s thoughts forming around that assumption, the familiar little irritation at inconvenience. He set down the cloth, wiped his hands on his faded trousers, and moved toward the door.

Each step was heavier than Kade thought it should be. His—Edrin’s—feet ached in their worn slippers. The hallway light seeped in under the door, a hard white line.

Somewhere under that, under the ordinary grumble about creaky stairs and forgetful landladies, there was a completely different life: a son who lived two districts away, hadn’t visited in months; the taste of a wife’s cooking who’d died ten years ago; the feel of small fingers gripping his thumb decades earlier. They sat in Edrin’s chest like folded papers in a drawer, unseen but present.

Kade felt them all at once, like weight adding to weight.

His hand closed around the latch.

He opened the door.

Kade remembered this moment from the outside: the way Edrin had appeared in the frame, surprise flaring, his mouth shaping a word that hadn’t gotten past the first consonant.

From the inside, it was nothing like memory.

The hallway seemed to shove itself forward. The fluorescents overhead hummed harshly, buzzing louder than they had any right to. At the far end, past the peeling paint and the fire door, someone shouted something indistinct, a scrape of conversation he’d never registered on the night. All of it came in as if the world had lunged.

And there, in the doorway, stood a man.

Him.

But not as he saw himself—no mirror arrogance, no practiced tilt of the head. Edrin saw a shape first: broad shoulders filling the space, the bulk of a jacket, a hood casting his features in shadow. The sense of threat came not from any one detail but from the outline, the intrusion.

Every primitive sensor in the old man’s body spiked.

The smell of the hallway—damp plaster, old pipework, faint piss from the stairwell—seared into his nose. The air seemed to thicken. The unfamiliar figure eclipsed the light.

“Yeah?” Edrin said. His voice sounded thin.

Kade knew what he’d said. He knew his own answer, the lie he’d prepared about being from the power company, an inspection, some nonsense. But in this lattice there was only Edrin’s side of the exchange, one channel recording.

There was an edge to the intruder’s stance, a tautness along the shoulders Edrin’s brain, running on seventy-odd years of learned caution, cataloged and struggled to interpret. Something’s off, something’s wrong.

He didn’t understand it fast enough.

Movement: sudden, stepping in. A push.

The world lurched backwards as the intruder slammed into him—not a slow shove, not a warning, but all at once, the force of a body far stronger than his. The back of his head clipped the wall inside, a bright ringing shock that shattered his earlier assumptions.

This is not a maintenance man.

This is not a mistake.

Terror didn’t arrive as a scream. It arrived as a collapse.

Every other thought in his mind—tea on the stove, the show he’d been half watching, the list of medicines he had to remember—fell away in a single cascading instant, like a shelf’s worth of books knocked to the floor. What remained was a raw, animal question:

Am I about to die?

In that question, in the space of a few seconds, an entire lifetime compressed.

He saw the intruder’s hand, gloved, moving toward his pocket—toward the tool Kade refused to think about too closely in this retelling. He saw the other hand clamp on his shoulder, fingers digging into frail muscle. The grip was vice-strong, impersonal.

Kade had remembered this as clumsy, chaotic. Here it was horribly clear.

“Please,” Edrin heard himself say, the word ripped out of him without planning. “Please, don’t.”

The sound of his own plea was a shock. He had never heard that tone in his own voice before: high, frayed, stripped of all the small dignities he allowed himself. Dignity was gone, knocked from his hands along with balance.

He stumbled. The intruder pushed harder. The room refused to hold still. Corners stretched, the walls seemed to sway. The clock above the counter suddenly roared loud in his ears, each tick a hammer blow.

Time thickened.

Later, in his cell, Kade would try to describe this part and fail. The techs called it dilation: the brain, flooded with stress hormones, sampling reality at an obscene resolution. A second became an ocean. Every droplet of sound, every shimmer of light on the countertop, every creak of floorboard under his dragging slippers expanded until it filled the whole sky of his mind.

He could feel his heartbeat not as a thump but as a series of distinct stages: the tight wind of the muscle, the squeeze, the bitter metallic rush of blood through narrowing vessels. Each pulse carried a message: You are in mortal danger. You are in mortal danger. You are in mortal danger.

His breath went shallow, then shallower, not through choice but because his chest had locked. Air scraped in. His mouth tasted of copper and old fear, memories of childhood nights hiding under a table while drunk voices shouted in the next room. That same ancient helplessness bloomed, but this time it had teeth.

“Kaden, Edrin,” the medical file had said. Hypertension. Arrhythmia. A heart that had survived grief, poverty, decades of strain. Now it bucked in his ribcage like something trying to escape.

The intruder spoke. Edrin heard only fragments, swallowed by the roar of his own adrenalized senses. “—wallet—quiet—don’t—”

Don’t what? Move? Scream? Look at his face?

But he looked. He couldn’t not. His eyes found the shadowed hood, the glint of eyes beneath it. For an instant, the intruder’s features came into focus.

It wasn’t the mouth or the nose that lodged in his memory. It was the flatness.

No rage, no froth of passion. Just a concentration as dull and lethal as a brick.

The crushing weight arrived then, fully.

It wasn’t a physical blow, though others followed. It was the sudden, absolute understanding that the person in front of him had made a choice. That this was not a mistake, not a flared temper that might cool, but a deliberate crossing of a line.

I am not a person to him, Edrin thought, and that thought rang through his whole being, a bell-strike of horror. I am an obstacle. I am a wallet. I am—

The word never fully formed. It didn’t need to. The realization was complete without language, a free-fall through a void where his own life, his own intricate collection of days, meant nothing to the one with the power.

All the years he had accumulated—every morning he had woken, every small decision—suddenly showed themselves to him like glass stacked on a shelf. He saw his late wife’s smile lit by the cheap bulb over their first kitchen table. He saw his young son’s hair sticking up in the back after a nap. He saw the street he’d grown up on before they paved it over, heard the distant shout of boys playing ball. He felt the ghost of warm sun on the back of his neck in some long-ago summer.

They piled up, higher and higher, a dazzling, fragile tower of moments.

And then he understood that in the space between one heartbeat and the next, all of it could vanish at the whim of another person’s hand.

The terror squeezed his world to a pinprick. It wasn’t just fear of pain; it was fear of erasure. Of everything he’d been becoming nothing, as easily as flipping a switch.

The world tilted.

He hit the floor.
