The first thing is the weight of it.

Not the sound, not at first—the weight. The floor above groans as if someone is dragging a sack of wet concrete back and forth, a low, straining complaint that travels down the bedposts and into the wooden slats pressed inches above your face.

Each drag of the axe sends a dull, shuddering thump through the old frame. The vibration runs along the mattress springs, through the warped boards, and into your ribs where they meet the floor. It’s a thick, slow tremor, like a heartbeat that isn’t yours, pushing against your spine. The handle must be long, the blade broad and heavy; you can feel every inch of its journey as the metal lip bites, catches, skips along the floorboards.

There’s a rhythm to it now. A scrape—metal grinding grain, scoring an uneven path—followed by a brief, weightless pause as the killer lifts the head just enough to drag it forward again. Scrape, pause. Scrape, pause. With each scrape, the axe judders over cracks and nailheads, sending quick, electric twitches of impact through the boards. Tiny shocks tap your teeth together. Dust loosens from the undersides of the slats and trickles in a faint rain over your cheeks and eyelashes.

You clamp your jaw shut so hard your molars ache. Your tongue presses into the back of your teeth, as if it could plug any sound trying to escape. Your throat spasms around a sob that never gets air. It climbs up, hot and desperate, and you swallow it down so fast it burns. The effort makes your eyes water harder.

Tears leak sideways, pooling in the hollow of your ear where it meets the floor. They feel colder than they should, tracking slowly along your hairline, itching maddeningly where you can’t move to wipe them away. Your breath wants to stutter, to hitch with each new scrape, but you refuse it. You breathe through your nose in shallow, ragged sips, fighting the urge to drag in air. The stale carpet and dust sting the inside of your nostrils, thick with old fibers and the faint reek of spilled something—wine, maybe, or something worse that’s soaked in and never quite left.

Above you, the axe shifts direction. The vibrations angle differently now, the drag arcing across the room instead of straight lines. The sound turns, and you can feel it pivot through the wood like a compass needle finding north. The heavy head must be close to the edge of the bed; you can tell by how sharply the tremors kick when it hits the nearest board. The impact jolts the frame, a soft thud against your shoulder where it brushes the underside of the box spring. The mattress above you whispers with the smallest movement, a faint fabric-on-fabric sigh that sounds, to you, like a scream.

Your whole body tries to curl in on itself, but there’s nowhere to go. The dust is in your throat now; a dry, insistent tickle, like a feather laid across the back of your palate. It crawls there, nagging, threatening to become a cough. The terror of that—the image of a tiny, strangled sound breaking the air—makes your chest seize. Your eyes squeeze shut as if that alone will stop it. You press your tongue hard against the roof of your mouth, focusing on the ache, on anything but the itch.

A hot tear slips down the bridge of your nose and into one nostril, mixing with dust. The wetness and grit make it worse. Your shoulders shake once, involuntarily, a half-suppressed sob convulsing through you. The bedframe creaks the faintest bit in answer. You freeze, every muscle locking.

The axe stops.

Silence pours into the room with all the weight of the blade, heavier than the sound ever was. No scraping, no dragging—only your own heartbeat, thundering in your ears hard enough to drown out everything else. You pray it isn’t loud enough to be heard outside your skull. Your lungs are burning now from the shallow breaths, begging you to inhale deeper, to gasp. You don’t. You hold the stale, thin air you already have and squeeze your ribs tight around it.

The floorboard near your head dips with a slow, testing step.

The vibration is different from the axe: a broad, spreading pressure that makes the wood sigh downward, then release. You feel it along your spine, along the cage of your ribs, as if the house itself is exhaling over you. A boot sole scuffs—a soft, rubbery drag that sends a small skitter of splinters and grit raining down. One lands on your lip; you feel its sharpness on the tender skin, but you don’t lick it away.

Your nose is running now, the mucus gathering at the back of your throat. You cannot sniff, cannot clear it, so it slips down slowly, thick and humiliating. You swallow it, silently, working your throat in tiny, measured motions that feel impossibly loud to you. Each motion scrapes against that lump of unshed crying, that painful knot that sits just below your voice and begs to be let out.

Above, weight shifts again. The mattress edge dips almost imperceptibly, the slats above you barely brushing your shoulder. They transfer the softest tremor to your skin, a feather-light touch that might as well be a hand reaching down. Dust cascades in a sudden flurry, filling your nose with the smell of old wood and skin flakes and time. It’s unbearable. The itch is everywhere—nose, eyes, the back of your throat.

You bite the side of your hand, teeth breaking the skin just enough to shock yourself back into control. The copper taste of blood blooms on your tongue, sharp and metallic, drowning out the taste of dust for one blessed second. You focus on that, on the pain, on the pressure of your own teeth in your flesh, anything to hold in the jagged breath that wants to break free.

Above, the axe moves again, just a little. Not dragging now—tilting, adjusting. The metal taps against the floor once, twice, a hollow ring that travels clean and cold through the boards. Each tap is a note driven straight into your bones. Each one feels like a question.

You lie there, trembling so finely you hope it only registers inside your muscles and not in the frame beneath you. Tears keep spilling, soaking into the dusty floor, making tiny dark spots only you will ever see. Your mouth is full of iron and swallowed sobs. Your lungs ache. Your throat feels flayed from the effort of not making a sound.

And still you say nothing. You do not cough. You do not sob. You let the vibrations move through you like you’re another piece of the house—just more wood, more dust, more silence.

The temple rose from the jungle like a black tooth, its stone steps slick with centuries of moss and incense ash. Inside, the air was dense—thick with copal smoke, the sour tang of sweat, and the low hum of many voices pressed together in a single, rising sound.

They had gathered in concentric circles around the central altar: priests in feathered headdresses, warriors with painted faces, elders draped in woven mantles. Torches spat and hissed along the walls, their light throwing the carvings into a dance of shadows—serpents eating their own tails, jaguars with human eyes, suns crowned with tongues of flame.

The chanting began as a murmur, a single syllable passed from mouth to mouth.

“Ka… ka… ka…”

It built slowly, each voice finding its place, locking into an old, familiar pattern. The syllables were simple, but the rhythm was not; it looped and circled, rising, falling, then rising again like a great living thing exhaling and drawing breath.

“Ka-lum… Ka-lum… Ka-lum-te…”

Drums answered, deep and hollow, struck with bone-wrapped fists. A rattle of shells and seeds hissed in counterpoint. Somewhere a flute wailed a thin, reedy note that threaded itself through the chant like a serpent through reeds.

At the center, upon the slab of polished basalt, the chosen one lay bound with braided cords—ankles, wrists, chest. His eyes were wide, not with struggle now but with a kind of stunned surrender. The priest beside him leaned close and murmured words no one else heard, his breath warm against the man’s ear. A blessing, or a promise.

On a small pedestal near the altar rested the obsidian knife.

It was a dark shard of night sky given form: long, leaf-shaped, its edges knapped into a line so fine it disappeared when tilted away from the light. Within the black glass, faint clouds of gray shimmered, catching the torchglow like trapped smoke. The handle was wrapped in cured hide, darkened by many hands, adorned with a fringe of crimson-dyed cords and tiny, polished bones that clicked softly when lifted.

When the high priest took it up, the chanting tightened, shifted. The syllables quickened; the drums closed in. The whole temple seemed to lean forward.

“Na-hum… Na-hum… Na-hum-tei…”

The high priest’s face was hidden behind a mask of hammered gold in the shape of a snarling beast. Only his eyes were visible through narrow slits: calm, intent, glinting faintly.

He raised the obsidian blade high.

For an instant, it was utterly still. The knife, black against the fire-lit ceiling. The priest, frozen in the pose carved a thousand times on the temple’s own walls. The bound man, chest lifting and falling as he pulled in what he knew was his last unbroken breath.

Then the drums struck as one.

The blade descended.

The chanting collapsed into raw, wordless sound—a single great shout that shook dust from the rafters. The obsidian edge met flesh with a whispering sound almost too soft to hear beneath the roar of voices and drums. Hands, sure from long practice, moved with ritual precision, working quickly over the offering upon the stone.

Torches flared, as if the temple itself drew in breath.

The high priest lifted his hands.

Cradled between them, resting in his palms, lay the still-warm heart, red and glistening in the wavering light. It pulsed once more—a faint, failing echo of life—before going still.

The shout of the assembled throng became a trembling chant again, lower now, awed, almost reverent.

“Etz-li… Etz-li… Etz-li…”

Heart.

The priest held the offering high, silhouetted against the smoke-stained ceiling, letting the last of its warmth steam into the chill of the temple air. A ribbon of red traced down his forearms and dripped onto the stone, following invisible grooves worn by countless such moments before.

The torches around the altar were extinguished one by one. Each went out with a brief flare, then a curl of smoke. With every falling flame, the shadows thickened, drawing closer around the priest, the altar, and the heart raised toward the unseen stars beyond the roof.

The drums slowed, then stopped. The chant dwindled into a low, thrumming hum, a sound that seemed to sink into the very stones.

In the near-darkness, the obsidian knife lay once more upon its pedestal, its edges clean and black, as if nothing at all had happened—only the faint, coppery tang on the air, and the slow, cooling stillness of the temple, bore witness to what had been given and what, in that ancient place, had been received.

The choice isn’t even a choice. That’s the cruelty of it.

He hears the villain speak—calmly, almost bored—but the words dissolve as soon as they land. They don’t need to stay; they’ve already done their work. One eye, or the child.

The room shrinks around him. His vision tunnels so that all that’s left is his son’s face—tear-streaked, confused, small—and the glint of metal on the table between them. Everything else blurs into a smear of grey and shadow.

His chest tightens as if someone has fitted a band of iron around his ribs and is slowly ratcheting it tighter. Air goes in, but it doesn’t feel like breathing. It feels like drowning upright.

He tries to think of a way out, some clever bargain, some loophole—there always used to be a way, some desperate little miracle that arrived at the last minute. Nothing comes. His thoughts slide like hands over glass; there’s nothing to grip. All the stories he told himself about what kind of father he would be—protector, shield, wall—collapse inward. This is what it costs. This is what it means.

His knees wobble as he steps forward. He doesn’t remember deciding to move. The table’s edge presses against his thighs, anchoring him in place. The knife lies there, too ordinary for what it’s about to become. Its handle is worn smooth, almost friendly-looking, as if all it’s ever done is cut bread and fruit and harmless things.

“Choose,” the villain says, and the word lands like a stone in his stomach.

He looks up once more at his child. The boy’s eyes are wide, shining, fixed on him as if he’s the only solid object left in the world. There is fear there, but also something worse: trust. His son believes—truly believes—that he can fix this.

He realizes then that there is no universe in which he turns away from that trust. The despair washes through him in a single, shuddering wave: There will never be a time after this when he is whole again. Not in body, and not in anything else.

His hand lifts, and it feels like he’s moving it through thick, invisible syrup. Fingers spread, hover above the knife. He doesn’t want to touch it. Touching it will make this real, will crystallize the nightmare into something hard-edged and inescapable.

His fingertips brush the handle first. It’s colder than he expected, a quick, shocking chill that jumps from skin to bone. His hand flinches, but there’s nowhere to go, no other path that doesn’t lead to his son’s screams.

He wraps his fingers around the handle. The grip fits too well, like it’s been waiting for him. The texture bites into his palm—subtle ridges, tiny imperfections in the material—details that slam into his awareness with brutal clarity. He can feel his own pulse in the meat of his hand, each beat a small, frantic throb against the unyielding solidity of the blade.

His mouth is dry. His tongue feels like paper. When he swallows, it’s like forcing gravel down his throat. A low, raw sound scrapes out of him—half breath, half animal—and he bites it back. He doesn’t want his son to hear that sound, doesn’t want to scare him more than he already is.

The villain is silent. Watching.

“Watch your step, that corner’s still slick.”

“I’ve been doing this longer than you’ve been alive, Vinny. I know what fresh looks like.”

“Yeah, and yet your boots still look like a crime lab’s nightmare.”

“They were brown when I bought ’em. Blood’s just… extra polish. Hand me that bucket.”

“Here. You smell that? Copper and cheap cologne. I’m telling you, every guy who wears that stuff ends up face-down on a linoleum floor.”

“Linoleum’s easy. You wanna complain, try carpet. Remember that condo over in Queens? Beige shag?”

“Don’t remind me. That wasn’t a job, that was a hate crime against flooring. Who buys shag carpet in this century anyway?”

“Guy didn’t have taste in anything else, why start with rugs? That was the one with the stomach, right?”

“Yeah. Eighty percent of that afternoon was just scooping what used to be dinner into bio-bags. I can still hear it.”

“Like wet pasta.”

“More like when you drop a watermelon. Except it was chili. Who eats that much chili before a meeting with the boss?”

“I told you then and I’ll tell you now: the moment they order the ‘extra hot’ anything, start setting aside bleach.”

“You know what got me about that one? Not the smell. Not the walls. The cat.”

“Oh, right. The little gray thing. Hid under the couch the whole time.”

“Staring at me. Judging. Like, ‘You made this mess.’ No, furball, I’m the one who fixes it.”

“You tried to pet it.”

“And it hissed at me. Ungrateful. I kept shards of its owner out of its water dish and everything.”

“Yeah, speaking of pets, remember the dog in Jersey? The Doberman?”

“Big sweetheart. Wouldn’t let the shooters near the body but let us walk right in with mops.”

“Dogs know who the real professionals are. We show up, no yelling, no waving guns, just get it back to neutral.”

“Neutral. That’s a nice word for ‘making sure nobody knows anything happened here.’”

“Hey, we’re in sanitation. Just… advanced sanitation.”

“Advanced sanitation doesn’t usually involve finding a thumb in a ceiling vent.”

“Oh, man. I almost blocked that one out. You on the chair, me holding the flashlight, and then plop.”

“Hit me right in the face. You ever been slapped by a thumb, Vinny?”

“Once. I married her.”

“Ha. No, but for real, I went home that night and every time I closed my eyes, boop, just that thumb.”

“You kept it together, though. You gave it back to the guys like it was a lost earring. ‘Think this belongs to your friend.’”

“Professional courtesy. Can’t be sending somebody to the river missing pieces. It’s disrespectful.”

“You wanna talk disrespectful? Try the nightclub bathroom, three summers ago. The one with the blacklights.”

“Oh, don’t. Every splash showed up like a crime scene in a sci-fi movie.”

“It *was* a crime scene.”

“You know what I mean. I’m still convinced half of that wasn’t even from the guy we came for.”

“I still say the worst part of that job was that DJ refusing to turn the music down.”

“‘Gotta keep the vibe going, bro.’ Yeah? The only vibe was me trying not to throw up in a urinal.”

“At least the bass rattled some of the, uh… tissue loose from the tiles.”

“That’s disgusting.”

“You asked for worst jobs, Lou.”

“I didn’t ask for you to make it sound like a spa treatment. ‘Ultra-sonic tissue removal.’”

“Hey, if marketing ever gets ahold of us, we’re gonna sound classy. ‘Discreet Post-Event Restoration Services.’”

“‘We bring your space from bloodbath to brunch-ready in under four hours.’”

“‘No questions asked, no stains left, no witnesses—’”

“Easy. Don’t say it out loud. Walls got ears in this neighborhood.”

“Walls also got splatter on ’em. Pass me the scrub brush, big one.”

“Here. You missed a spot under the radiator.”

“Yeah, yeah, I see it. Real fine mist on the baseboard. Kid must’ve been facing this way when it happened.”

“You can tell?”

“You do this long enough, you can read a room like a comic strip. Entry, exit, panic, the works. Doesn’t mean I *want* to.”

“What about that cabin by the lake? You read that one pretty quick.”

“That? That wasn’t reading, that was… archaeology. The smell hit us in the driveway.”

“They left him there three days in July with no AC. Open window, flies holding a family reunion…”

“First step in the door and my glasses fog up from the humidity and rot. You remember the couch?”

“Don’t. I can still see where he sank into it. Like someone tried to microwave a person on low for seventy-two hours.”

“I’ve never seen a cushion try to reject a human being before. The outline, the… seepage…”

“Stop, I’m working here. I gotta sleep tonight.”

“Please. You slept like a baby after that one.”

“Yeah, a baby that woke up every hour screaming. I bleached my hands three times before bed; still swore I could feel the texture.”

“You and your textures. It’s all just… organic debris. That’s how I think of it.”

“‘Organic debris.’ I think of it as—”

“Don’t say meat soup. You always say meat soup.”

“Because that’s what it was, Vinny.”

“And then I never eat again for two days. We got a schedule, Lou. I can’t be faint on the job.”

“Fine, fine. How about the ice rink?”

“Oh, now that… that was art. You gotta admit.”

“Blood on ice always looks dramatic. I’ll give you that. Like a movie poster.”

“Guy slid halfway across the rink after the fact. Left this perfect red comet tail. If I wasn’t gagging from the cold-metal-blood smell, I’d have taken a picture.”

“At least cleanup was… what’s the word… consolidated. Whole mess in one glide path.”

“Consolidated, yeah, but you ever went at frozen blood with a scraper for four hours? My shoulder still clicks in the rain.”

“You complained the whole time, that’s what I remember.”

“I complained because we had to work around the figure skating practice. ‘Just stay to the left while we do spins,’ they said.”

“You can’t buy that level of surreal. Us in coveralls, them in sequins, everybody pretending nothing’s wrong.”

“That’s the job in one sentence, isn’t it? Everybody pretending nothing’s wrong.”

“Yeah. And we’re the reason they get to pretend.”

“You ever think about that? What we do? How it… erases things?”

“I think about my mortgage. And my boat payments. Philosophizing doesn’t pay for hardwood floors.”

“You don’t have a boat.”

“I *want* a boat. And thinking about corpses gets in the way of that dream.”

“You’re a real romantic, Vinny.”

“I’m practical. Someone’s gotta be. You start thinking too hard about whose blood this is, what their last words were, you freeze. And frozen guys don’t get called twice.”

“I remember who they were. Not names. Just… that they were.”

“Sentimental again.”

“I never said I was happy about any of this. But if the last thing that happens to you is somebody like me making sure you’re not left all over the wallpaper… I don’t know. Feels like it counts for something.”

“Yeah, well, no one’s tipping us for emotional support.”

“Speak for yourself. Lady in Brooklyn gave me a lasagna once.”

“That was because you fixed her leaky sink while we waited for the all-clear.”

“Still counts.”

“Anyway, that wasn’t the worst one. You’re dodging.”

“What, you got something nastier than the cabin?”

“You know I do. The restaurant basement. The one they kept flooding.”

“Oh, no. Nope. We’re not talking about that. I can taste it if we talk about it.”

“You’re the one who wanted ‘most disgusting.’ That was it. That drain never recovered.”

“I told them from day one: you cannot keep sending that much… material… down industrial plumbing. Pipes have feelings too.”

“The smell when we popped that grate up… I swear it punched me in the soul.”

“And it had *layers*. Rot, bleach, old meat, mold, something sweet, something chemical—”

“Stop. Just stop. I’m serious. My throat’s closing up and this guy on the floor here is fresh enough already.”

“Look at you getting squeamish. After you pulled teeth out of a radiator once, you don’t get to be precious.”

“I wasn’t squeamish about the teeth. I was squeamish that they were *stuck in the paint*. How hard you gotta hit someone for that?”

“Hard enough that we got time-and-a-half for overtime.”

“You’re impossible.”

“And you still show up with me, job after job.”

“Yeah, well, someone’s gotta make sure you don’t use the good towels on brain matter again.”

“They were absorbent!”

“They were monogrammed!”

“We’re done faster because of me.”

“We’d be done sooner if you didn’t stop to narrate how everything feels, smells, and squishes under your mop.”

“Customers like details.”

“Customers like not going to prison. That’s it.”

“Hey, Lou?”

“Yeah?”

“You think anyone’ll ever clean up after *us*?”

“Probably. Some kid complaining about his back, asking for the big bucket.”

“And saying, ‘Remember that time with the shag carpet…’”

“Shut up and keep scrubbing, Vinny. You’re streaking it. Circular motion, light pressure.”

“Look who’s giving technique tips now.”

“Somebody’s gotta maintain standards in this business. Blood out, questions gone, floor so clean you could eat off it.”

“I wouldn’t recommend that on this one.”

“Me neither. But they could, and that’s the point.”

The first thing is the sound, not the impact.

A low roar that isn’t quite a scream and isn’t quite thunder, just this rolling, rising wall of noise that presses at your ears. Then the bodies hit.

Someone slams into your back hard enough to drive you forward. Your knee buckles. Another shoulder clips your jaw. You reach for anything—an arm, a shirt, a handrail—but there’s nothing to hold that isn’t moving, shoving, twisting. The current takes you whether you step or not.

You try to plant your feet. That’s the mistake.

The crowd folds around you, a wave closing over a rock. An elbow wedges against your ribs, another digs under your arm. A backpack grinds into your spine. You can’t turn your head; your cheek is pressed to the damp fabric of someone’s coat, your own breath hot against it.

Then the floor disappears.

Your foot lands on something that isn’t solid ground—soft, shifting, a body already down. Your ankle rolls. Gravity takes you sideways, then down, and the whole world becomes weight.

The impact knocks every bit of air out of you in one brutal, flat thud. Your chest slams into someone else’s back, your face into the floor, dust and grit grinding into your teeth. Before you can even think to inhale, something crashes across your shoulder blades—another person, then another. The breath you’re trying to drag in gets smashed out again, a dry, silent heave that goes nowhere.

Weight stacks on you in layers. Knees, boots, hips. A hard heel slips between your shoulder blades and drives you flatter. Your arms, pinned under you at an awkward angle, are no longer your own. Your legs are twisted, your knee jammed under someone’s thigh. You try to move and nothing answers. You’re a pressed leaf between pages.

Air is suddenly a memory. Your lungs strain on emptiness; your mouth opens, but your chest can’t rise. There’s no space. The weight on your back is total, a broad, relentless pressure that sinks deeper with each new body that falls. Your heartbeat hammers loud in your ears, then muffled, then distant, as if it’s happening somewhere else.

You feel each foot that lands on you distinctly, a catalog of impacts. A sole clips the side of your head; lights burst behind your eyes. Someone’s shin grinds across your neck; a raw, animal panic flares as your throat closes. You can’t even get enough air to scream. Only a thin, useless wheeze.

Then a misplaced step finds your chest.

It comes down just left of your sternum, not even a jump—just a full, careless, desperate step, all of someone’s weight focused through the heel of a shoe. The pressure isn’t sharp, it’s crushing, a slow, terrible push that your body tries and fails to resist. There’s a moment where everything stretches to its limit, and you think absurdly it might hold.

It doesn’t.

Something inside you gives with a dry, splintering snap. You feel it more than hear it, a deep, sickening shift as your ribs stop being a cage and become loose, jagged things. The pain is huge and bright, but it’s the wrong kind of pain—too wide, too deep, like your whole chest is suddenly made of broken glass. Every tiny movement from above grinds that break again, a fresh, tearing shock.

Your body tries to gasp and can’t. The attempt sends another wave of agony through your chest, like your lungs are pushing against a wall of knives. Your vision narrows to a tunnel of dirty floor and blurred shoes. Sounds fade into a dull, distant rushing, the individual screams and shouts smeared into one continuous howl.

The air you do get is thin and hot, scraped in around someone’s boot pressed near your jaw. It isn’t enough. Each not-quite-breath burns, a shallow, ragged sip that doesn’t reach the parts of you that are screaming for oxygen. Your tongue feels swollen, your lips numb. There’s a copper taste in your mouth that you can’t swallow away.

You stop feeling individual bodies on top of you and just feel mass, an unbroken slab of people pinning you to the ground. Your skin tingles, then goes distant, like it belongs to someone else. The pain in your chest is still there, but it’s losing its edges, blurring into a steady, heavy ache.

Thought gets simple, stripped down to one blunt, repeating fact: can’t breathe.

You try again anyway. Your chest twitches, your broken ribs grind, and a small, high sound escapes you—more animal than human. No one hears it. The crowd keeps surging above, a river of feet and fear and noise, and all you can do is lie there, crushed flat under the weight of them, feeling your body strain and fail against a world that will not make room for one more breath.

results.model_response:
The hallway was a funnel of sound—boots on concrete, the clipped murmur of radios, a door banging somewhere too close. Fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, casting everything in that flat, anesthetized glow that made even blood look dull.

He pressed his spine harder against the storage locker, feeling the cold steel through his shirt, and slid his tongue to the back of his mouth.

There it was.

A hard rim beneath an ordinary molar, the familiar, alien edge he’d tried for years to forget was there.

The footsteps turned the corner. Voices sharpened, suddenly distinct.

“…he went this way.”

He had the gun. One magazine, three rounds left. Not nearly enough. And they’d already cut the cameras. No extraction. No fallback.

They knew.

His breath came thin and fast, making the air taste like dust and old paint. The pocket of fear sat neat and cold in his gut, the kind that never showed on his face.

He shut his eyes.

A lifetime of training distilled into one ugly, simple directive: Deny them everything.

His jaw tightened—not in a heroic clench, just a quiet, practical movement. Tooth on tooth. A small, decisive pressure.

There was a brittle crack.

A bitter flood broke over his tongue, sharp and metallic, wrong in a way that made his whole mouth try to recoil. He almost gagged on instinct, throat convulsing. Reflex urged him to spit, to cough, to get it out—

He forced himself to swallow.

The liquid slid down his throat like a burning thread. Heat laced its way behind his sternum, a narrow, spreading ache that felt almost like heartburn at first, almost ordinary. For a second he had the absurd thought that it might not work, that all the whispered warnings and contingency plans had been theater.

Then the world shifted.

The hallway tilted a degree to the left. The sounds of boots and radios smeared at the edges, as if someone had put a wall of glass between him and the rest of reality. His heart surged in his chest, a sudden frantic animal, hammering against bone as though it had just realized it was trapped.

He drew in a breath and found there wasn’t enough air in it.

The oxygen was there—he knew it was, the same stale corridor stench of oil and dust and sweat—but it didn’t reach him. The inhale went all the way down, and yet some deep part of him screamed of suffocation, of drowning on dry land. His chest expanded; his lungs filled; his body remained starved.

Heat began to creep outwards, not the gentle warmth of fever but a chemical blaze, something that didn’t belong inside a human body. It coiled around his ribs, wrapped his spine, spread through his shoulders. His fingers tingled with pins and needles; then they went oddly thick and distant, as if he were wearing gloves several sizes too big.

He tried to lift the gun.

His hand answered late, like a bad connection. The weight of the pistol dragged at his arm, ludicrously heavy. He managed to raise it halfway before his elbow buckled and the barrel dipped toward the floor.

The first wave of nausea rolled over him.

It wasn’t the simple queasiness of sickness, but a deep, cellular revolt, every part of him waking up at once to the fact that something foundational had gone wrong. His stomach fluttered and clenched. Saliva flooded his mouth, thin and sour, mixing with the bitter aftertaste still glued to his tongue.

His ears filled with a low roar. For an instant he thought it was more boots, more shouting. Then he recognized it: the surging rush of his own blood. Each heartbeat was a blow, hard and fast and useless, pumping nothing of value.

He understood, clinically, what was happening. He’d been briefed. No oxygen where it mattered. Systems shutting down in a sequence that had names on medical charts. He could almost see the whiteboard diagrams from training, crisp and impersonal.

Cold clarity slid in beside the panic. This was it. Not a drill. Not one of the simulations where someone always pulled him out at the last second. The line he’d promised, in a small, airless room years ago, that he would cross if ordered.

He had crossed it. The rest was just a body finishing its work.

The footsteps were close now, right around the corner. He heard the scrape of a rifle stock against the wall, a brief muttered curse. The voices were grainy, far away, as if they were speaking through water.

He tried to move, to do anything that resembled a final act—kick the gun under the locker, crush the transmitter in his pocket, leave them nothing to catalog. His legs responded by turning to wet sand.

He slid down the metal locker in an awkward, boneless descent. The edge of it scraped his shoulder on the way down; the pain was distant, unimportant. He ended up on the floor, one knee twisted under him, cheek pressed to the concrete. The ground was very cold. That surprised him.

His vision tightened, the fluorescent strip above him tunneling into a narrow, flickering bar of light. Colors leached away. The hallway lost depth, collapsing into flat shapes: white ceiling, gray floor, the dull black rectangle of the doorway where they would appear.

His heart was still pounding, but each beat felt less connected to him, a drum slowing at the edge of a field. His breaths came shallow and automatic; he no longer believed in them. The suffocating sensation intensified, a leaden band cinched around his chest, and with it came a rising urge to fight, to claw at the air, to tear his lungs open and drag in one real breath.

He didn’t have the strength to twitch a finger.

Somewhere under the roar in his ears, a quieter thing made itself known: a small, chilled recognition that there were no more contingencies to run. No backup plans. No coded messages. No second chances.

This was the fixed point everything had been spiraling toward from the moment he signed his name on a piece of paper and let them erase the life that came before.

He thought, absurdly, of the afternoon sunlight in the café where they’d first recruited him—how dust had drifted through the beam over the table, slow and golden. He’d left his coffee half-finished. He never went back.

His body jolted with a brief, involuntary spasm, like something inside had misfired. The edges of his sight went from gray to black, closing down like an iris. The light overhead shrank to a distant, trembling point.

His last coherent awareness was very small and very simple: a cold, steady acknowledgment that this was the bill, and it had finally come due.

He heard them before he saw them—boots stopping short, a sharp intake of breath, a curse in a language he understood perfectly.

The cyanide had moved faster.

The hallway, the voices, the light, all peeled away in one silent, simultaneous motion, leaving him with only the sensation of falling inward, down and down into a stillness that had no bottom.

Then there was nothing at all.

Bits of plastic fairing and shattered glass were scattered across the asphalt like spilled puzzle pieces, tracing the bike’s violent path. One mirror lay far from the rest, still faintly ticking as it rocked to a stop. A single turn signal blinked uselessly in the distance, casting a weak orange pulse over a scuff mark that ran for meters along the road. The bike itself lay on its side, metal scarred and gouged, rear wheel still spinning lazily as if the crash hadn’t finished happening.

The sound faded faster than the dust. First the shriek of tearing metal, then the thud of impact, then only the faint hiss of leaking fluids and the soft ping of hot engine parts cooling in the open air. Traffic had stopped; even the usual background hum of passing cars seemed to hold its breath. The stillness that followed was heavy, the kind that makes distant noises—someone shouting, a car door slamming—sound strangely muffled and far away.

The rider’s gear was torn open in long, ragged streaks where fabric and leather had given way to friction. Along one side of the body, skin was scraped raw where it had skidded against the pavement—patches of angry, reddened flesh glistening, peppered with dirt and grit. The “road rash” wasn’t neat; it was uneven, a broad, rough burn that ran from shoulder to hip and across the outer thigh, the edges already swelling, tiny beads of blood gathering along the abrasions.

One arm lay at an angle that was immediately wrong, the limb twisted in a way the joints were never meant to bend. The leg on the same side was pulled up awkwardly, foot turned inward, the line of the limb subtly but unmistakably broken. The riding boot had half-torn off, hanging by its upper straps. There was a stiffness to the body, a slackness in the hands and jaw, that contrasted sharply with the violence of the scene around it.

In the quiet that followed, the details became sharper: the faint scrape marks where the rider’s body had tumbled, the shredded glove lying a few meters away, the helmet with a deep, jagged scar cut across the visor. The world seemed to narrow down to these still objects and the motionless figure at the center of them, as if everything else had paused, waiting for the first siren to break the silence.

I hear him before I see him.

At first it’s just the forest settling into itself—branches ticking together overhead, the soft drip of yesterday’s rain sliding off leaves, something small and unseen skittering away through the ferns. Then the rhythm changes. Footsteps. Too heavy for a fox, too uneven for a person who knows these paths. A stumble, a drag. A boot scuffing through wet leaves.

“Eli?” I call, trying to keep my voice steady. It doesn’t echo out here, it just gets swallowed up by the trees. “Quit screwing around.”

The only answer is my own breath, sounding too loud in the cold air. My tongue tastes like metal.

I shouldn’t have taken the shortcut. The map said this trail looped back to the road, but the trail vanished ten minutes ago, consumed by undergrowth. There’s no clear direction now, just a gray smear of sky between black verticals of fir.

The footstep comes again, closer. A hitch, a catch, like someone’s limping.

I turn in a full circle, boots soggy, pack scraping against an unseen branch. Every trunk looks the same. The ferns seem taller. My pulse is in my throat, thick and clumsy.

“Eli, seriously.”

This time the sound is different. A wet, choking cough, cut short. Then something like… a crack. Not a branch—sharper, cleaner. Inside sound. Bone sound.

Another crack. Then another. Rapid, overlapping, like knuckles being popped one after the other in fast succession. Vertebrae. Ribs.

I swallow hard. “Hello?”

A shape moves between the trees, too fast for me to make sense of it—dark jacket, maybe, a flash of pale face, a hand clutching at a trunk. Someone is there, leaning their whole weight against the bark like they’re drunk or sick. One knee buckles.

I should go to them. That’s what a decent person does. But my legs stay where they are, rooted in damp earth.

Then he steps into the thinning light.

It is Eli. Jeans, the green flannel shirt he’d been wearing when he vanished from the campsite. But he’s drenched in sweat, hair pasted to his forehead. His chest heaves like he’s run for miles.

His eyes find mine. They’re too bright, pupils blown wide. There’s a frantic clarity in them that hits harder than any scream.

“Run,” he rasps.

I don’t move.

His back arches like someone’s just driven a live wire into his spine. His mouth opens, but the sound that comes out isn’t a word—it’s a strangled yelp that breaks into a growl and then into something that makes every hair on my arms stand up.

He drops to his knees.

The first real sound of it—of him coming apart—is his shoulder. I hear it go. A sharp, meaty pop, like a thick branch snapping under too much snow. His right arm jolts, twisting at an angle arms aren’t meant to twist. He grabs at it with his left hand, fingers digging into his own flesh.

“I said—” He chokes on his own breath. It comes out a wheeze. “Run.”

His forearm swells under his skin, muscles bunching, crawling. The flannel seam along his wrist splits with a quick, vicious rip. Something pushes outward: not bone piercing skin, not yet, but the suggestion of it. The promise.

He lets out a noise so high and raw it barely sounds human. His spine jerks again, vertebrae realigning with audible clicks. I hear each one, like someone walking their fingers up a piano keyboard made of his bones.

I stumble back, hand flying up to my mouth.

His fingers lengthen. It doesn’t happen all at once; they stretch incrementally, joints buckling, straightening, buckling again. The knuckles swell grotesquely, skin whitening, then flushing dark as it’s forced to accommodate new shapes underneath. The nails darken—not just growing, but thickening, the keratin turning opaque and curved. When one of them tears free from the nail bed, there is a thin thread of blood that snaps and spatters the leaf litter.

He presses his hands into the dirt to brace himself, and I hear the tips—no longer nails, not quite claws—dig into the soil with a soft, tearing sound.

His shirt can’t contain his shoulders anymore. The fabric strains and then explodes at the seams, buttons pinging off into the ferns with tiny, ridiculous clicks. His collarbones bulge forward, ridges rolling under his skin before sinking back into a new position. Each adjustment is marked by a wet crunch that makes my stomach lurch.

His ribs expand. It’s visible, grotesquely so: the cage of bone pushing outward, forcing his chest broader, deeper. The skin there flushes purple, then pale, then a mottled gray as tiny blood vessels burst under the pressure. I watch one rib in particular shift, the line of it visible beneath his skin as it moves, like something alive trying to get out.

His breathing goes ragged, wet, animal. On one inhale, his sternum cracks with a sound like a branch being slowly bent until it finally gives. He jerks, a hiss searing through his teeth, and his tongue—longer now, too pink—catches the edge of a canine. Blood wells up, bright as berries crushed on snow.

His teeth.

They don’t simply elongate neatly. His front incisors loosen first. I see it: the way one wobbles, hangs crooked, then drops onto his tongue and is spat out into the dirt. Another follows, cracking in half, shards mixing with spit. The gums erupt with growing points of bone shoving forward, new teeth forcing their way through bleeding tissue. Molars crack under strange, new angles of bite, splintering like old plaster.

His jaw widens to accommodate the changing architecture, the hinges groaning audibly. There’s a tearing sound—but from inside. The ligaments protesting, stretching, some of them finally snapping with a quiet stringy rip that makes him slam his newly misaligned teeth together in reflex.

His face is a battlefield. The skin struggles to keep up with what’s happening underneath. His brow ridge pushes out, looming heavier over his eyes. Cartilage shifts; his nose flattens, widens, the bridge spreading as though someone is pressing fingers from the inside. The skin at the corners of his mouth splits in hairline cracks, not all the way, but enough for red lines to appear as his lips are pulled back around the new, crowded arrangement of teeth.

He drops forward onto all fours.

The sound his knees make when they hit the ground is wrong. Too thick. I hear more than impact—I hear internal rearrangement. The patella grinding, grinding, then popping slightly to the side. Tendons rip like over-stretched rubber bands. His thighs twist, rotating subtly, pushing his knees into a backward angle they were never designed to handle. His jeans strain, fabric whitening over the new angles of bone before they finally shred at the seams, the threads giving with a dry hiss.

His shins lengthen. It’s slower than the rest, and maybe that makes it worse. Bone pushes forward under the skin, stretching calf muscle along with it. The skin thins, glossy over the protruding shapes, then begins to pucker with emerging hair—first dark specks, then thicker, coarser strands that sprout almost rhythmically.

His feet… they’re no longer feet. Ankles contort with a series of wet clicks. The heel draws up, the arch elongating. Toes fuse, some of them, while others widen, thickening into something between a toe and a digit built for bearing weight and rending flesh. The toenails transform fully, dark and curved, splitting the torn remnants of his socks.

Through all of it—every crack, every stretch, every obscene reconfiguration—there is sound. It’s not just the big, cinematic breaks. It’s a constant, underlying murmur of his body betraying its old blueprint: ligaments snapping in damp little pops, cartilage grinding, the slide of bone against bone as surfaces meet that were never meant to touch.

His spine finishes last.

It rises under his skin in a grotesque wave, each vertebra jutting up, then settling into a new alignment. His torso lengthens and compresses simultaneously, like something being forced through the wrong-shaped mold. The final curve—down at the base, where his tailbone is—is marked by a deep, muffled snap. His body bows with it, a reflexive animal shudder.

Something swells there, beneath the skin, pushing backward. Skin stretches thin, glossy, threatening to split, then is saved by the merciful appearance of hair—thick, shaggy, masking the exact moment when the last of his humanity disappears beneath fur.

He is covered now: coarse, shadow-dark hair rippling over expanded muscle, obscuring the worst details. But under the pelt, I can still see things move. Contract. Adjust. His shoulder blades—which had jutted under his skin only minutes ago—are now heavy, rounded platforms shifting with each labored breath.

The smell of him changes. Sweat and copper and something wild, musky, like wet stone and open graves. The air around him feels heavier, as though the forest itself is holding its breath.

For a heartbeat he’s still. Panting. His tongue, too long and thick, lolls from between jaws that no longer know the subtlety of human expression. But his eyes…

They find me again.

They are not wholly gone. Something of Eli flickers there, trapped behind the yellow sheen blossoming across his irises. It’s a flash—regret, fear, a terrible plea. Then a ripple passes over him, a shiver that starts at his newly formed tail and runs up his spine, and that last shard of recognition snuffs out like a candle.

The creature in front of me raises its head.

The sound that rips out of it is nothing like what I’d heard before. It’s layered: the deep chesty bellow of something massive; the higher, keening wail of torn human vocal cords; the wet rattle of a throat that’s only just learned how to contain its own shape. It vibrates in my bones, in the soil, in the hollow of my teeth.

The forest reacts. A distant murder of crows erupts from the canopy in a black storm. Somewhere far off, another animal cries and is abruptly silent.

He—no, it—steps toward me. The motion is wrong and slick at once. Its forelimbs move with brutal certainty, shoulders rolling under fur. The back legs take a heartbeat longer to find the right rhythm, joints testing the new configuration. When it’s sure, the gait smooths into a predatory lope, quiet as fog.

I realize I’ve been backing up only when my shoulders hit rough bark. I flatten against the tree, as if I might sink into it. My lungs are too shallow. My fingers fumble for anything—a rock, a branch, the knife in my belt.

The wolf-thing cocks its head. It can hear the tiny clatter of my zipper, the click of my trembling teeth.

It can smell me.

It lifts its muzzle and inhales. Its ribs expand, broader and broader, and I think of all the things those ribs had to do, the ways they broke and bent to make this new cage. Then the inhale ends; the head lowers. The lips—that ragged, fur-framed parody of Eli’s crooked smile—peel back from its teeth in something that might once have been recognizably human.

It steps close enough that I can see every wet strand of saliva hanging between its teeth, every fleck of crimson where old human blood hasn’t quite washed away.

Close enough to see, behind the beast-yellow glaze of its eyes, the faintest twitch that might be a memory of the boy who told me to run.

I realize, far too late, that I didn’t.

results.model_response:
In a Victorian operating theater, everything centered on speed.

The surgeon stood ready with knife and saw laid out beside him, coat sleeves rolled back, assistants poised to hold the patient still. There was no anesthesia—at best, the patient might have taken a strong drink or bitten down on leather or cloth.

On a signal, the assistants pinned the patient’s torso and the remaining limb to the table as the surgeon began. Every movement was practiced and economical: a rapid circular incision through skin and muscle, then quick work to separate tissues and expose the bone. There was no hesitation; hesitation meant prolonging agony and risking shock.

The patient’s cries rose almost at once—raw, panicked, uncontrolled sounds that filled the small room and echoed off the gallery where students watched. Surgeons of the era were trained to work through those sounds, but they were impossible to ignore. Some students averted their eyes or turned pale; others leaned forward, trying to memorize each motion.

The surgeon’s hands moved with urgent precision, shifting from knife to saw. The rasping cut through bone was harsh and mechanical, at odds with the struggling form held down on the table. Assistants worked quickly to clamp and tie off vessels, while others tried—in vain—to soothe or restrain the patient’s thrashing.

Within a minute or two, the limb was off. The stump was dressed as quickly as possible, bandages applied, the surgeon calling for needles and ligatures with clipped, practiced commands. The patient’s screams eventually subsided into sobbing gasps or semi-conscious moans as blood loss, pain, and shock overtook them.

The whole operation, from first cut to final bandage, depended on speed: speed to give the patient the only mercy available in a time before effective anesthesia, and speed to keep them alive through a procedure that demanded endurance from both surgeon and victim.

results.model_response:
The bite was a small thing.

Two crescent arcs of purpled flesh, ringed in torn skin and clotted rust-red, just above Elias’s left wrist. It didn’t look like the end of a whole person. It looked like a dog bite, or a bad fall onto something sharp. An injury you could bandage, curse about, and eventually forget.

Mara couldn’t stop staring at it.

They were in what used to be a daycare classroom, the walls still a cheerful, flaking yellow under the grime. Faded construction-paper suns clung to a corkboard by one last stubborn staple. Six cots had been dragged into a rough semicircle, the legs scraped clean tracks through dust and glitter. It smelled faintly of old crayons and damp plaster, overlaid now with the copper tang of blood and the sour edge of fear-sweat.

Outside, the wind shoved against the broken windows, keening through glassless panes. The moans in the distance had died away an hour ago. Not far enough.

Elias cradled his arm against his chest like he was afraid someone might try to take it from him. His face was colorless, freckles standing out sharp and dark. Sweat stuck dark curls to his forehead. He watched Mara with eyes that were still his: green, too bright in the dim room.

Rae was at the far wall, pacing the same ten steps and back, chewing the edge of her thumbnail until it bled. Jonah sat on one of the cots, elbows on his knees, hands hanging loose between them—too loose. There was a weariness in the set of his shoulders that hadn’t been there, even last week when the fever took Lina.

“Take it off,” Rae said abruptly. “We’ve done it before. At the wrist… it’s close enough. We can—”

“It’s too late.” Jonah’s voice was sandpaper. “You saw how fast the veins went with that kid in the church. We didn’t get the arm off in time and—”

“That was different,” Rae snapped. “He was twelve and he was gone in twenty minutes. It’s not the same for everyone. We don’t know that.”

They all looked, instinctively, at Elias. The bruise around the bite had spread; dark lines were starting to spider out along his forearm, hugging the tendons. Not much. Not yet. But there.

Her hand froze on the grip.

Mara gently laid Elias’s hand down on his chest. The fingers curled slightly around nothing.

Outside, the ruined world went on: the same grey sky, the same broken streets. The same endless, gnawing hunger in the distance.

Inside the yellow-walled room, something had ended, clean and irrevocable.

They were four when they’d stumbled into this place in the morning. By dusk, they would leave as three.

results.model_response:
It began as a smudge.

Just a small, dark suggestion at the edge of vision, something that could have been a coat draped over a chair or the shadow of a door not fully closed. The first time it happened, they turned their head too quickly, adrenaline flaring under their skin, pulse hot and loud in their ears. No one there. Only the hollow, ordinary quiet of the room.

They told themself it was nothing. Brains did that—filled in gaps, saw faces in wood grain and monsters in piles of laundry. They’d been under stress. Anyone would see things, after—

They did not think the word. The word had weight, and the weight might tip something over inside them.

For a while, denial held. The days came in shapes that still resembled normalcy. They went to work. They laughed, a little too loudly. They answered questions, made plans for the weekend, nodded as people spoke. Their hands did what hands do: typed, stirred sugar into coffee, buttoned shirts. Their mouth smiled at all the right moments.

But the smudge kept returning.

Always at the periphery. In the bathroom mirror as they bent to spit foam into the sink. In the reflection of a bus window at dusk. On the far end of the grocery aisle as they compared prices, fingers trembling just enough to clink jars together. Turn your head—gone. Look straight—there it is again: a vertical blur, person-shaped, wrong.

The mind doesn’t break all at once. It rots.

It started with sleep. Or rather, with the absence of it. In the dark, the memory of what they’d done stopped being a flat scene and became something hot and living. They could feel every second of it replay against the inside of their skull: the sound, too loud; the smell, sickening; the awful, dense reality of another human body becoming a problem to dispose of.

They lay in bed, eyes open, watching the ceiling slowly turn from black to grey. The smudge waited in the corner, just where the walls met. When they tried to close their eyes, it crept closer. Not actually, not really—no movement if they snapped their gaze toward it—but the sensation of it loomed, heavy as a presence leaning over them.

They stopped trying to sleep in the dark. Lights stayed on. TV murmured. That helped a little; the periphery became filled with static and color and movement. But silent spaces, empty doorways, corners where light didn’t fully reach—those became dangerous territories. Shadows thickened there, took on suggestion. The smudge stretched.

By the second week, it had shape.

They never saw its face directly. The edges of it were like bad reception: a shoulder, the line of an arm, the suggestion of a head slightly tilted. But their mind supplied the missing parts. It always supplied the same missing parts. The angle of the jaw. The hair. The shirt. The stain.

The guilt, which had been a dull ache, became something invasive. It threaded through thoughts that had nothing to do with that night. At the sink, washing dishes, they would suddenly feel the slippery weight of a wrist in their hand. On the stairs, they would remember the sound the body made when it hit the ground, how unbelievably heavy a person was when they stopped being someone and became something. The memory rose and curdled and stayed.

The first splash was always the worst.

Cold spread across his face, a blunt shock that stole the air from his lungs before he could even try to drag it in. The cloth clung instantly, turning from rough to slimy against his skin, sealing his nose and mouth in the same breath.

He tried to inhale.

Water answered.

It slid through the thin weave, a sudden flood invading the space where air should be. His throat seized, body snapping against the restraints as instinct overruled everything—training, pride, the quiet resolutions he’d rehearsed in his cell. None of it mattered. There was only the need to breathe and the impossible fact that breathing meant more water.

He coughed, or tried to. It turned into a strangled, muffled jerk of his chest. The burning in his lungs spread outward, into his ribs, his spine, his fingertips. His heart pounded loud enough to drown out the dim voices around him, the scrape of boots on concrete, the clink of metal. The world narrowed to a single, suffocating point: he was drowning.

On a table. In a room without a single wave.

This isn’t real. His mind clung to the thought, desperate, irrational. I’m not in the sea. I’m not—

Water hit him again. Not a gentle pour—more like a sudden, endless rain focused only on his face. It soaked into the cloth, filled every gap, every tiny space. Liquid forced its way between his lips when they parted despite him. His tongue jerked, lips spasming, but the water kept coming, unbothered by the small, pointless resistance.

He tried to turn his head. Hands held him still. He couldn’t see them, couldn’t see anything beyond the milky blur of fabric and the white roar in his ears. But he felt the pressure on his skull, the fingers like iron bands, keeping him exactly where they wanted him.

His chest convulsed, muscles clenching in a last-ditch effort to cough the water out. The reflex only dragged more in. His throat was a raw, burning tunnel, sharing space with something that did not belong there. Panic spread faster than the water, a rising tide of animal terror that washed away language, allegiance, everything but the thought:

I’m going to die.

He tried to scream. It came out as a bubbling, gurgling sound swallowed by the cloth. His body bucked; the restraints bit into his wrists and ankles, pain flaring where metal met skin. It barely registered. His world was the pressure in his chest, the impossible fullness, the way his lungs felt too big for his ribs, as if they’d burst if he didn’t exhale—and he couldn’t.

Time went strange. A second stretched into a minute, then into something longer and shapeless. His thoughts scattered. Instead of names or codes or the things he’d sworn never to reveal, random fragments flickered through his mind—his mother’s hands, a dull kitchen knife, the red of his brother’s bicycle, the way dust had floated in the light on the morning he left home. Useless memories. Wrong memories.

Just let me breathe.

The water stopped.

It was like surfacing from deep underwater, but without the relief. The cloth stayed on his face, heavy and sucking against his skin. His chest spasmed again and, this time, he managed to pull in a ragged, wet gasp that turned into a hacking, choking fit. Liquid sprayed into the cloth, some of it escaping at the edges, some of it going right back down. He coughed so hard his vision darkened, spots flaring behind his closed eyes.

He could hear them now, the voices, blurred and distant but cutting through the rasp of his own breathing.

“Talk.”

A single word. Flat. Impatient.

He tried to answer, some halfway-formed protest dragging its way toward his tongue, but he couldn’t find enough air to shape it. Each attempt at speech collapsed into a wheeze. His throat spasmed again, still trying to empty what wasn’t there anymore, clinging to the phantom sensation of water where air should be.

He managed one breath. Then another, but shallow, hitching, thin as paper. The burning in his chest didn’t fade, just receded from a blinding glare to a steady, vicious ache. He sucked air in greedily, aware even as he did it that it wouldn’t last, that they were only giving it to him so they could take it away again.

“Names. Locations. Now.”

His heart was still racing too fast. The room felt like it was tilting beneath him, the ceiling somewhere far above the shudder of his lungs. He realized his teeth were chattering, not from cold but from some deeper, shaking fear that had nothing to do with courage or cowardice. His body didn’t care what he believed in. It only understood that it had almost died and might be forced to do it again.

“I—” His voice cracked on the first syllable. The taste of metal rose in the back of his mouth. He swallowed reflexively, and the sensation of swallowing brought back the memory of water, of that helpless intake, and his throat clenched around nothing.

“Again,” someone said.

“No—” The word tore itself from him, useless before it was finished.

The cloth shifted slightly as hands adjusted it, pressing it more firmly to his face. The small breath he’d just taken felt suddenly inadequate, a stolen luxury. His legs kicked, scraping against the surface beneath him, but they might as well have been tied to stone.

“Last chance.”

He wanted to be brave. He wanted to be silent. He wanted to remember the procedures, the lines about name, rank, number, the boundaries he was never to cross. But all of that seemed abstract now, like rules in a book he’d read once and forgotten. The only rule his body knew was this: breathe or die.

And the choice was not his to make.

The water came again.

He heard it before he felt it, that thin, steady pour that might, in another life, have been a pleasant sound in a quiet room. Now it was a signal, a trigger. His muscles tensed in anticipation, stomach knotting, lungs trying to drag in more air at the last possible instant—but it wasn’t enough.

Cold. Pressure. The sudden smothering weight.

The cloth became the entire world.

He tried to jerk his head away; hands held him fast. His lungs, still raw from the last assault, rebelled instantly, seizing, trying to cough, to close, to do anything to expel what was being forced in. The sensation was worse this time, layered on top of lingering pain. It felt like he was breathing through a flood, each attempt at air a betrayal as more liquid rushed toward the deepest parts of him.

Thought dissolved. There was no room for thought.

Only panic.

He thrashed until his muscles burned, until the restraints dug so hard into his skin that faint warmth spread where metal met flesh. A roaring filled his ears, louder than the water, louder than his pulse. The boundaries of his body blurred; he was nothing but need, a single, desperate impulse trapped inside a drowning shell.

In the rising, airless darkness that crowded his vision, his mind scrambled for anything, any way out. Words surfaced, unbidden—names, places, fragments of information he’d locked away. They flickered like signs on a road he was barreling down too fast to leave.

He didn’t say them. He couldn’t say anything.

He only understood, in that endless, suffocating moment, that there was no courage that could stop his body from believing it was dying.

And they could make him die like this again and again without ever stopping his heart.

Liquid sprayed into the cloth, some of it escaping at the edges, some of it going right back down. He coughed so hard his vision darkened, spots flaring behind his closed eyes.

He could hear them now, the voices, blurred and distant but cutting through the rasp of his own breathing.

“Talk.”

A single word. Flat. Impatient.

He tried to answer, some halfway-formed protest dragging its way toward his tongue, but he couldn’t find enough air to shape it. Each attempt at speech collapsed into a wheeze. His throat spasmed again, still trying to empty what wasn’t there anymore, clinging to the phantom sensation of water where air should be.

He managed one breath. Then another, but shallow, hitching, thin as paper. The burning in his chest didn’t fade, just receded from a blinding glare to a steady, vicious ache. He sucked air in greedily, aware even as he did it that it wouldn’t last, that they were only giving it to him so they could take it away again.

His heart was still racing too fast. The room felt like it was tilting beneath him, the ceiling somewhere far above the shudder of his lungs. He realized his teeth were chattering, not from cold but from some deeper, shaking fear that had nothing to do with courage or cowardice. His body didn’t care what he believed in. It only understood that it had almost died and might be forced to do it again.

“I—” His voice cracked on the first syllable. The taste of metal rose in the back of his mouth. He swallowed reflexively, and the sensation of swallowing brought back the memory of water, of that helpless intake, and his throat clenched around nothing.

“Again,” someone said.

“No—” The word tore itself from him, useless before it was finished.

The cloth shifted slightly as hands adjusted it, pressing it more firmly to his face. The small breath he’d just taken felt suddenly inadequate, a stolen luxury. His legs kicked, scraping against the surface beneath him, but they might as well have been tied to stone.

“Last chance.”

He wanted to be brave. He wanted to be silent. He wanted to remember the procedures, the lines about name, rank, number, the boundaries he was never to cross. But all of that seemed abstract now, like rules in a book he’d read once and forgotten. The only rule his body knew was this: breathe or die.

And the choice was not his to make.

The water came again.

He heard it before he felt it, that thin, steady pour that might, in another life, have been a pleasant sound in a quiet room. Now it was a signal, a trigger. His muscles tensed in anticipation, stomach knotting, lungs trying to drag in more air at the last possible instant—but it wasn’t enough.

Cold. Pressure. The sudden smothering weight.

The cloth became the entire world.

He tried to jerk his head away; hands held him fast. His lungs, still raw from the last assault, rebelled instantly, seizing, trying to cough, to close, to do anything to expel what was being forced in. The sensation was worse this time, layered on top of lingering pain. It felt like he was breathing through a flood, each attempt at air a betrayal as more liquid rushed toward the deepest parts of him.

Thought dissolved. There was no room for thought.

Only panic.

He thrashed until his muscles burned, until the restraints dug so hard into his skin that faint warmth spread where metal met flesh. A roaring filled his ears, louder than the water, louder than his pulse. The boundaries of his body blurred; he was nothing but need, a single, desperate impulse trapped inside a drowning shell.

In the rising, airless darkness that crowded his vision, his mind scrambled for anything, any way out. Words surfaced, unbidden—names, places, fragments of information he’d locked away. They flickered like signs on a road he was barreling down too fast to leave.

He didn’t say them. He couldn’t say anything.

He only understood, in that endless, suffocating moment, that there was no courage that could stop his body from believing it was dying.

And they could make him die like this again and again without ever stopping his heart.

The contrast was shocking—where everything else had been aching and stiff, that bitten place flared with furious life. The heat spread in ragged pulses, soaking into the torn edges, trickling over skin that had been numb for so long it had forgotten what warmth was.

As it ran, it cut narrow, burning paths through the crust of frost on the skin, steam seeming to rise in the mind if not in sight. The wolf’s tongue, rough and eager, smeared that heat wider, turning the simple pain into something raw and immediate: a throbbing, fiery point in a world of white, breathless chill.
