By the time Vexa saw him, the target had already spotted the exit.

He bolted.

The transit hub’s atrium flared into motion: holo-ads stuttered as his shoulder clipped a projector array, commuters recoiled, and surveillance drones pivoted on silent gimbals to follow the blur of motion across the polished synth-stone floor.

Vexa moved the opposite way—diagonal, not directly after him. Experience had taught her that prey in panic always ran in straight lines. Her boots whispered over the surface, traction fields adjusting with each stride. Above, a sky that wasn’t a sky—just a three-hundred-meter dome of glass and climate overlays—shifted from morning blue to a cautionary yellow as security subroutines flagged the disturbance.

Her visor tagged him in bright red: KANE TORVAL / PRIORITY WARRANT / ARMED-DANGEROUS.

“Torval,” she called, her voice amplified and directionally focused toward him. “Stop running.”

He didn’t. Of course he didn’t.

He crashed through a cluster of luggage drones, sending cases tumbling. The crowd parted in a wave of curses and panicked yelps. Vexa slid through the gap, shoulder-checking a suitcase aside, her hand already on the Grip holstered at her thigh.

“Security will take you apart,” she added, not out of concern but as a matter of fact. “I’m the soft option.”

He glanced back once, eyes wild, then veered toward a maintenance corridor marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The door recognized his momentum as aggression and locked down, but he was fast and angry enough to hit it full-force, rebounding with a grunt instead of going through.

That half-second was all she needed.

Vexa slowed to a walk. People were filming now, feeds going live. The station’s PA murmured a polite evacuation directive. Kane spun around, chest heaving, hand diving into his coat.

“I wouldn’t,” she said, sightline tracking his wrist.

A glint of metal appeared. She didn’t flinch.

He aimed a compact railpistol at her center mass. The muzzle hummed with a building charge.

Her Grip cleared the holster in a single smooth motion.

It didn’t look like a gun, exactly—more like a sleek baton with a flared emitter at the front, braided contact prongs folded inward like petals of a metallic flower. Thin blue status lights rippled along its length as it synced with her implant. The weapon whispered its readiness directly into her auditory cortex: charge at 94%, contact arc stable.

Kane’s hand shook. “Back off, hunter.”

“You’re not going to shoot into a crowd,” Vexa replied. “You don’t want more charges.”

He did want something, though—an exit, a miracle, anything. His finger tightened. The crowd exhaled in one terrified, collective breath.

Vexa shifted her weight.

He fired.

The rail slug never reached her. The station’s autonomous defense had been calculating vectors the moment a weapon signature lit up on its sensors. A translucent hex-grid flickered between them, absorbing the projectile with a ripple that spread like water and vanished. The crowd screamed anyway.

Kane stared at the empty space where his last hope had gone.

Her turn.

Vexa stepped in. Kane tried to retreat, banging into the sealed maintenance door. The Grip’s prongs snapped open with a soft, predatory click, small arcs of blue-white lightning dancing in the narrow gap between them.

“This is non-lethal calibration,” she said, maybe more for the watching drones than for him. “Stop resisting and I don’t have to pull the trigger.”

He snarled and lunged with the pistol as a club.

She didn’t bother to parry the swing. Instead, she twisted, closing the distance. The Grip kissed his flank just below the ribs.

Vexa squeezed the trigger.

The world, for Kane, became electricity.

---

The stun charge left the emitter as a shaped, high-voltage, low-current pulse, forced through the air on a tight ionized channel. Conventional tasers needed barbed darts and wires; the Grip cheated with directed plasma and field shaping, bridging the last few centimeters in a searing snap of ozone-scented light.

When the charge hit his skin, the outer layer of cells behaved like a resistor. Voltage soared, forcing current through microscopic pathways: sweat glands, hair follicles, the thin films of moisture across his skin. The contact points became portals, and the electricity dove inward.

It spread along the path of least resistance: blood vessels, nerve sheaths, the watery interior of muscle fibers. Electrochemical gradients that normally tiptoe in millivolts were suddenly drowned in thousands of volts compressed into microseconds.

Every nerve near the path ignited with false signals—sharp, overwhelming bursts that the brain could not distinguish from its own. Pain fibers shouted first: a white, blinding, whole-body scream. Kane felt it as if his body had been turned into a single, continuous muscle clenched in absolute agony.

Then the motor nerves, the ones that tell muscles when to contract, were hijacked.

Under normal conditions, muscles respond to carefully timed bursts of electrical activity, each impulse triggering a coordinated contraction. The stun pulse shattered that grace. Instead of a pattern, his muscles received a chaotic storm: rapid, high-frequency jolts that overlapped so completely that the muscle fibers never had time to relax.

His skeletal muscles—especially the big groups in his arms, legs, and torso—locked solid, a state called tetanic contraction. His grip on the pistol vanished not because he chose to let go, but because every muscle from his fingers to his shoulders seized so hard he could no longer control them. The weapon clattered to the floor as his hands snapped shut into distorted fists.

His legs, robbed of their delicate balance between opposing muscle groups, failed. Quadriceps, hamstrings, calves—everything fired at once. Knees buckled. He dropped straight down, joints barely articulating, like a puppet whose strings had all been jerked at once and then cut.

His diaphragm, the broad muscle that drags air into the lungs, spasmed violently. For the fraction of a second that the pulse lasted, breathing became impossible: the chest froze midway between inhale and exhale. His throat tightened, vocal cords clamping, so the scream that should have come out arrived as a strangled, animal noise.

Inside his chest, the heart felt the intrusion too.

Cardiac muscle is built on its own precise electrical rhythm, with specialized pacemaker cells dictating each beat. The Grip’s pulse was designed to skirt the frequencies most likely to trigger lethal arrhythmias, but it couldn’t avoid brushing the system entirely. For a heartbeat or two, Kane’s cardiac rhythm stuttered: not a full stop, but a couple of disordered beats, like a drummer momentarily losing the tempo before finding it again.

His vision tunneled. Electrical chaos in peripheral nerves spread to the central nervous system; for a moment, his brain was more busy interpreting the shock wave of abnormal input than keeping his perception stitched together. The world around him smeared into light and noise.

Then it was over.

---

To Vexa, it had been less than a second.

Kane dropped like a felled tree, body rigid, spine bowing as the current blasted through his musculature. Small arcs crawled across his clothes, searching for alternate paths, crawling up to his shoulder where a tattoo’s embedded metal ink briefly flared white-hot and then dimmed.

She released the trigger and stepped back, letting the automatic cutoff do its work. Smoke—a thin, barely visible mist of vaporized sweat and fabric fibers—rose from the contact point. The smell of burnt ozone and singed clothing bit at the air.

Kane hit the floor hard. The tetany lingered for an instant after the current stopped, then collapsed in a ripple as his muscles finally had permission to relax. Limbs that had been locked stiff went abruptly slack. He lay there splayed, chest hitching as his diaphragm remembered how to work on its own.

“Subject incapacitated,” one of the station’s drones announced from above, voice cheerfully neutral.

Vexa watched his hands first. Fine tremors shook them, fingers twitching with residual misfires as sodium and potassium gradients in his nerves slowly reset. His jaw quivered, teeth clicking together once in a painful snap.

His eyes were open, but not quite focused. The stun had flooded his peripheral nerves with noise, and his brain was still sorting signal from static. He blinked rapidly, as if that would clear the afterimage of the blue flash still imprinted on his retina.

He tried to move. His muscles answered with weak, jerky attempts—small, uncoordinated contractions, as if he were learning his body for the first time. It felt, from the inside, like being made of wet sand: heavy, unresponsive, tingling in strange patches where current density had been highest.

A deep ache spread from the impact points outward, the soreness of muscle fibers forced into maximum contraction all at once. Microtears formed here and there, not enough to cripple him, but enough that tomorrow his body would remember every millisecond of this moment.

His heart resumed its familiar rhythm, the quiver in his chest smoothing out. The shock hadn’t lasted long enough or crossed the wrong pathways to send it into fatal chaos. He was lucky. Or, more accurately, Vexa was practiced.

She knelt beside him, the Grip now a cooling weight in her hand, its prongs folding back into standby position with a delicate chime.

“Breathe,” she told him.

He realized he’d been holding his breath in shallow, panicked sips. He dragged in air, ribs protesting, throat dry. Each inhale scraped over a raw-feeling larynx, the aftermath of muscles clenched too hard for too long.

“What… what did you…” He swallowed, words breaking apart in the tremor of his voice.

“High-voltage neuromuscular disruptor,” Vexa said. “Short pulse. Your nervous system’s throwing a tantrum. It’ll pass.”

He tried to lunge again on instinct alone. His body responded with nothing more than a feeble fl inch—shoulder lifting three centimeters off the floor before collapsing back.

Control of his voluntary muscles was returning from the outside in: fine control in his fingers would come last. Larger muscle groups twitched now in messy, asynchronous spasms as nerve cells, briefly forced to fire all at once, reestablished their ordinary sequencing.

“Could’ve killed me,” he muttered, though it came out more as a slurred complaint.

“Not with that setting,” she replied. “Assuming you don’t have a heart condition you lied about on your ID.”

His eyes tried to focus on her faceplate, pupils still oscillating with residual autonomic agitation. The sympathetic half of his nervous system, startled by pain and shock, had slammed the panic button—heart rate up, blood vessels constricted in some places, dilated in others, cold sweat springing from his skin. Now, slowly, those responses unwound, his body backing away from the brink of fight-or-flight.

Around them, the station’s panic had ebbed to wary curiosity. The drones had shifted to a soft blue status glow, signaling the situation was under control. Someone nearby clapped once, then thought better of it.

Vexa thumbed her cuffs open, slender bands unfolding like liquid metal. She rolled Kane onto his side and then his stomach with professional efficiency. His muscles protested, a chorus of low groans from overstimulated fibers, but he couldn’t stop her.

“Easy,” she said, more to keep him from hyperventilating than anything else. “The worst is done. You’ll be sore, you’ll feel like you ran a marathon you don’t remember, and you might twitch for a few hours. That’s it.”

The cuffs clicked shut around his wrists, then hardened, bonding with a soft tone that synced to her bounty contract. Confirmed capture notice appeared in the corner of her vision, along with a transfer of funds.

“What… what did that thing do to me?” Kane asked, voice quieter now, embarrassment cutting through the fading pain.

“Hijacked your nerves,” Vexa said, standing and hauling him gently to his knees. His legs tried to help and almost managed it. “Forced every muscle to fire until they gave up. Scrambled your pain signals on the way out. Your brain couldn’t tell which impulses were real, so it treated all of them as an emergency.”

She paused, considering.

“Think of it like this: your body speaks in whispers of electricity. I just yelled.”

He swallowed again, eyes dropping. The railpistol lay a meter away, harmless now. The crowd was no longer a faceless blur but people, all of them watching him. His pride hurt almost as much as his muscles.

“Can you walk?” she asked.

He nodded, tried to stand, and almost toppled. She caught his arm, stabilizing him.

“Slowly,” she advised. “Your nervous system’s still rebooting.”

Together they moved toward the waiting security portal, drones parting to give them right of way. The station’s artificial sky shifted back toward calm blue as the last of the alerts cleared from its systems.

Behind them, on the polished floor, the faint ghost of a burn mark remained where the Grip’s current had grounded itself—just a dark scuff, already flagged by a maintenance bot for cleaning. In an hour, there would be no sign of what had happened here.

Inside Kane’s body, though, every trembling, aching fiber would remember the split-second when electricity had become law—when a hunter with a handful of stolen lightning had reached out and turned his own nerves against him.

He wakes before he understands he’s awake.

The first awareness is sound: a slow, industrial hum, like a fluorescent light about to die, layered with the faint drip…drip…drip of water. Then the smell—metallic, sharp, undercut with mold. His tongue feels swollen. There’s a taste of copper in his mouth that doesn’t belong to any memory.

He tries to roll onto his side and only makes it halfway before something wrenches tight around his left wrist. His body jerks, instinctive, and a second restraint bites into his right. Cold metal cuffs, edges digging into bone. The movement sends a ripple of pain through his shoulders; they’ve been in the same position too long.

Now he’s fully awake.

He forces his eyes open. The light overhead is stark, yellow-white, buzzing in a flickering halo. It throws hard shadows on cracked tile and exposed pipes, and turns the room into a geometry of rust and peeling paint.

He’s seated in a heavy metal chair bolted to the floor. His arms are splayed on narrow rest-plates, each wrist locked in a curved steel shackle, the kind built not just to restrain, but to punish attempts at freedom. His ankles are strapped down too. He can move his fingers, twist his forearms an inch, no more.

A band of cold pressure hugs his chest. He looks down. A harness—thick, leather-looking but harder, threaded with cables that vanish behind him. There’s a device at his sternum: a palm-sized metal box, dull gray, with a tiny red LED sleeping in its center.

He tests it, just a little, shifting his weight. The harness tightens, just perceptibly, as though something is listening.

“Okay,” he whispers, voice dry and cracked. “Okay, okay.”

The word doesn’t mean anything yet. It’s just something to fill the space around his heartbeat, which is already too fast.

In front of him, bolted to a pivoting arm at chest height, is a crude contraption. A short metal bar with a handle at the end, like a lever. At the inner end of the bar, shielded in a little half-box of steel, is a thin, gleaming edge. It’s set at an angle, perfectly aligned with his left forearm.

His stomach drops, but his mind refuses the image. Reflexive denial: This is a prank. A set. A nightmare with good production values.

On the wall beside him, a grimy speaker crackles, then clicks on with a faint, hollow hiss. There’s a mechanical whir, then a voice—distorted, genderless, too calm.

“Hello.”

His lungs seize. The voice is too close, too intimate.

“You have spent your life,” it says, “avoiding consequences. Passing your pain to others. Tonight, you are alone with your choices.”

He tries to speak, but his throat locks. The only sound that comes out is a ragged breath.

“Before you,” the voice continues, “is your path to freedom. Inside your left forearm is a key. In ten minutes, the device on your chest will activate. When it does, it will open you instead of opening your locks.”

The red LED on the box flickers to life, then settles into a slow, blinking pulse. His heart lurches in sync with it.

“To escape, you must retrieve your key. The tool is provided. Your will is…not guaranteed.” The faintest suggestion of amusement in that pause. “Choose quickly.”

The speaker cuts off with a crack. The hum of the room rushes back in, too loud.

He stares at the contraption in front of him, mind blank, a silent scream of no, no, no reverberating through the empty space where thoughts should be. The implication is simple and complete. There is no misunderstanding here. No alternative.

His gaze shifts—compulsively, unwillingly—to his left arm. Pale skin, a faint lattice of old, normal scars: the kind that come from childhood falls and clumsy kitchens. Veins thread faintly beneath the surface, blue under the harsh light. That arm has done ordinary things: lifted groceries, typed emails, buttoned shirts. It doesn’t feel like the sort of place where a key could hide.

He flexes his fingers. They respond perfectly. For a moment he clings to that, the comfort of ordinary movement. Ten fingers. Ten little proofs that his body is still his.

Then the red light on the device blinks again. Once. Twice. Relentless.

Panic comes in waves. The first is hot, a violent rush that makes him yank at the restraints despite the pain. The cuffs scrape his skin. The chair doesn’t budge. He pulls until his muscles burn and tears prick his eyes.

The second wave is cold. It leaves his hands trembling and his thoughts scattered.

“Someone will find me,” he mutters. It’s almost funny, how unconvincing he sounds to himself. No one has ever found him when it actually mattered. “There’s…there’s always a way out.”

His eyes sweep the room, desperate. Bare brick walls. One rusted drain in the center of the floor. A door with no handle on the inside, just a smooth metal plate. No cameras he can see, but he feels watched anyway.

The red LED continues its slow, indifferent blinking.

He forces himself to breathe in, count, breathe out. It doesn’t calm him, but it slows the wild, useless thrashing of his mind enough that he can look again.

Look, not imagine.

The lever’s handle is wrapped in black tape, textured for grip. The blade within its little housing is angled to meet his forearm if he pulls the handle toward him. There’s a groove in the metal platform beneath his arm, a shallow channel aligned perfectly under where his skin rests. Drains along the edge. This entire setup has been thought through.

He swallows, jaw tight.

“Inside your left forearm is a key.”

The sentence loops, not just as sound, but as a problem. The logic is simple: There is something inside him that doesn’t belong there, and the means to reach it are in front of him. Between those two points is a gulf his mind refuses to cross.

He tests his arm’s freedom again, more carefully this time. He can angle his forearm slightly. Rotate it so the inner side faces more toward the blade’s path…or away from it. The choice feels obscene.

His breathing speeds up. Dampness prickles under his shirt, trapped by the harness.

He thinks of all the ways bodies are supposed to be harmed: accidents, illnesses, the anonymous violence of stranger and fate. Not this. Not his own hand. Not deliberately.

A smaller, colder voice cuts through the agitation: You don’t have time for philosophy.

He lifts his head and fixes his eyes on the wall opposite, avoiding the sight of his own flesh. Brick. Crack. Stain. Anything but his arm.

“Okay,” he says, and this time the word lands heavier. It’s not acceptance, but a kind of perimeter around the panic. “Okay. Think.”

He imagines doing nothing. Sitting here, refusing, surrendering to the sick eventuality of the device on his chest fulfilling its purpose. The idea of that—of feeling something happen to him that he didn’t initiate—sends a new kind of terror through him. Passive, helpless terror.

It occurs to him, with grim clarity, that the trap is not just about pain. It’s about making him decide. Forcing him to be the one who acts.

He closes his eyes for a moment. When he opens them, he looks straight at his left arm, no flinching this time. He forces himself to study it the way he’d study a broken machine: clinically, from outside.

You are not your arm, he tells himself. It’s a part. A piece. An object, if you need it to be.

The thought feels like a betrayal, but also like a rope thrown across a chasm.

He wiggles his fingers again, then spreads them, then makes a fist. He notes where the skin pulls, where the tendons stand out. He bends his wrist as far as the cuff allows, examining the line of bone, the map of veins. Looking for…what? A signpost that says, “Here is where you cut”? There is none. Just flesh and the horror of guessing.

His right hand, trapped in its own cuff, can move a little more than the left. He curls it into a fist and relaxes it, trying to bleed some of the trembling out through that motion. It doesn’t work, but the rhythm helps him hold his focus.

He leans forward as far as the chest harness permits and inspects the lever mechanism. The blade is recessed just enough that he can’t touch it, but he can see the gleam along its edge when he tilt his head. Precision-made. No jaggedness, no mercy. A tool designed to do exactly one thing efficiently.

“How deep?” he whispers, and hates himself for needing that answer.

The question returns to him as echo only. No instructions. That’s part of the cruelty: uncertainty is its own form of torment. Too shallow and he’ll…have to try again. The notion makes bile rise in his throat. Too deep and—

Stop.

He drags his attention away from imagined outcomes and back to preparation. Not the act, just the lead-up. One breath. Then another.

He realizes he’s chewing the inside of his cheek, the copper taste in his mouth intensifying. He forces his jaw to unclench.

“Do it fast,” he tells himself. “Don’t…don’t drag it out.”

The LED on his chest blinks again, a little more insistently now. Time is thinning.

He studies the path of the lever. Tests its looseness with a tentative push. It resists at first, then gives a fraction of an inch. There’s clearly a threshold: an initial slack, then a point beyond which it will do what it’s meant to do. He lets it return to its starting position, hand shaking.

He imagines his muscles failing him at that threshold, the lever stuck halfway, pain stretching into something unendurable because he couldn’t commit in one motion. That image frightens him more than the pain itself.

You have to decide before you touch it, he thinks. No halfway. Once you move, you finish.

He straightens his back as much as the harness allows, as if posture could confer courage. His shoulders ache. He focuses on that trivial, already-existing pain, using it as a stepping stone. This hurts. That will hurt more. People survive worse. People wake up after surgeries. People— He cuts the chain of comparisons before it becomes an excuse.

He looks at his hand on the lever. It isn’t there yet, but he pictures it. Fingers wrapped around the taped grip, knuckles whitening. He rehearses the motion in his mind the way a diver will mentally walk through the dive before stepping off the platform: grip, pull, don’t stop.

In the privacy of his skull, two voices argue:

You can’t do this.  
You don’t have a choice.

He thinks of all the small self-betrayals that led him here—decisions he’d made where someone else paid the price. The voice on the speaker had known those, catalogued them. There is a bitter symmetry in being asked to pay directly, physically, for once.

Anger stirs under the fear. Anger at whoever put him here. Anger at being made into his own executioner, or his own savior, depending on how you frame it.

“Fine,” he says aloud, surprising himself. The word is edged. “You want a choice? Here.”

He turns his left forearm so the soft underside faces the recessed blade. The motion feels obscene, like baring his throat. His stomach tightens, but he keeps the arm there, locked in place by will more than by metal.

He flexes the muscles once, twice, memorizing how they move. Then he forces them to relax as much as possible. Tension will make everything worse; he knows that instinctively, the way an animal knows to go limp in a trap to conserve strength.

He rests his left hand’s fingers lightly on the edge of the armrest, anchoring himself. His right hand, trembling, inches toward the lever’s handle. The tape is rough under his fingertips when he finally touches it. This is the point of no return, he thinks. Not the cut. The first contact with the tool that will make it possible.

He closes his hand around the grip.

His entire body rebels. Every muscle screams to let go, to pull back, to wait, to stall. Some primitive part of his brain flails for any excuse: Maybe the device is fake. Maybe this is a test of character and not actually wired to blow. Maybe if he waits, the door will open and someone will tell him it was all a joke.

He watches those thoughts arise and burn out in quick succession. They all share the same feature: they allow him to delay.

The LED’s blinking speeds up, as if mocking him.

He tightens his fingers. The handle feels solid, heavier than it looks, connected to something that will not forgive hesitation. His grip firms. He lowers his gaze so that he’s looking not at his arm, not at the blade, but at a point on the floor beyond them both. A neutral patch of stained concrete that doesn’t care what he does.

He draws a breath in through his nose, slow and deep, counting to four. Holds it for a beat. On the exhale, he whispers, “Do it on the out-breath. Don’t think. Just move.”

He doesn’t know if he’s talking to himself or to his hand.

Another breath. In. The world narrows: the hum of the light, the thud of his heart, the scratch of tape against his skin. The room retracts to a tunnel whose only contents are him, the lever, the too-soft underside of his forearm.

He pauses at the top of the exhale, gathered like a spring.

For one last instant, his mind offers him a final escape: you can always choose not to.

He lets that possibility sit there, real and terrible. Then he pushes it aside, not because it’s wrong, but because it leads to a darker ending he’s not yet ready to accept.

His fingers clamp down on the handle. He feels the mechanism within take notice, a faint shift of weight.

He exhales.

He pulls.

The sky over the *Maiden’s Woe* had turned the color of old bruises, purple and gray smearing into the horizon. The sea below was a heaving sheet of iron, every swell catching what little light there was and shattering it into silver fragments.

They’d dragged Rook up from the hold at dawn.

Now he knelt on the sun-warped deck, wrists bound behind him, shirt torn and clinging damp to his back. Salt had dried in white lines on his skin. Every breath came shallow, sharp, as if the air itself had grown too thick to swallow.

Around him, the crew formed a rough half-circle. Boots thudded; cutlasses rattled against belts. No one spoke. The only sounds were the sea and the steady creak of timbers, the ship flexing like a living thing.

Captain Marlowe stood a few paces off, sleeves rolled to the elbow, hands resting lightly on the pommel of her sword. Her coat, sea-black and weather-faded, snapped in the wind. Bronze rings glinted in her ears, and her dark hair whipped across a face carved by salt and sun.

“Rook.” Her voice carried easily over the mutter of the ocean. “You’ve had a night to think on it. Anything you’d like to say before judgment?”

His mouth worked, dry. He swallowed sand and salt. “I—”

A gull screeched overhead, cutting him off, a harsh, mocking cry.

He tried again. “I didn’t mean—”

Marlowe’s gaze didn’t soften. “You struck your captain. You whispered in corners. You promised my men a sweeter life if they cut my throat and took my ship.” She tilted her head, considering him. “You meant every word.”

A ripple went through the crew—some shifting their weight, some staring at the boards, some watching Rook with a tight, hungry stillness.

Rook’s eyes moved jerkily from face to face, seeking any trace of help, of pity. He found none.

The wind shifted, bringing with it a sharp, briny scent—and something else. A faint, oily tang that made the hair on his arms rise.

“There,” said Old Jory from the rail, squinting down into the water. “They’re ready, Cap’n.”

Marlowe flicked her eyes toward him. “Show ’im.”

They hauled Rook to his feet. His legs were unsteady, the deck tilting beneath him in a slow, nauseating sway. Two men—Tom Black and little Harlan—fisted his arms and marched him toward the starboard side.

The rail loomed up, and beyond it, the world dropped away.

The sea spread out below, endless and indifferent. At first, Rook saw only the chop of waves and the long, dark streak of the ship’s shadow. Then, as his eyes adjusted, he saw the movement.

Shapes gliding under the surface. Gray backs breaking the water, fins slicing clean black lines through the swell.

Sharks.

There were at least a dozen of them. Some small and quick, darting in tight, nervous circles. Others slow and heavy, their pale bellies flashing as they turned. Water foamed faintly around them, a restless, swirling ring beneath the ship’s flank.

One of the larger ones rolled close enough for Rook to see its eye—a small, flat, polished stone of darkness. It seemed to look directly up at him, unblinking, incurious, as if he were already decided, already accounted for.

His knees nearly went out from under him. Tom Black jerked him upright with a curse.

“Walk the plank,” Marlowe said.

They’d already hammered the board into place—a rough-hewn timber jutting out over the water, slick with spray, just wide enough for a man to stand on without falling if he kept his balance and didn’t think too hard about how far the drop actually was.

A murmur passed through the crew, thin as smoke. Some leaned forward. Others stepped back, as if afraid whatever doom hovered around Rook might brush off on them.

Rook’s heartbeat roared in his ears, louder than the sea, louder than the rattling canvas overhead. His wrists burned against the rope, skin raw. His mouth tasted metallic.

“Marlowe—please—” His voice came out ragged. He coughed and tried again, straining against Tom’s grip. “I was wrong. I— I’ll serve. I’ll swear on—on whatever you like. I’ll—”

“You already swore,” she said. “To slit my throat in my sleep.”

He flinched.

“That’s the trouble with promises, Rook.” She started toward him, boots silent on the boards. “They mean something on this ship.” She stopped just short of him, close enough that he could see the faint silver line of a scar cutting through her eyebrow. “You knew the code when you signed aboard. You break it; the sea takes you.”

His breath hitched. “It wasn’t just me,” he blurted, desperation cracking his words. “Radley, Finch—half of ’em—”

“And they’ll have their turn, if I find proof.” She shrugged, a tiny lift of one shoulder. “You had the poor judgment to swing first.”

He looked out past her, past the rail, to the horizon where the sky and water blurred. If he squinted, he could pretend the swaying deck was just motion, not destiny. Anything felt better than seeing those serene fins cutting lazy circles below.

“I can work the bilge for a year,” he said, words tumbling over each other. “Chain me. Lash me. Don’t—don’t feed me to them.”

Tom Black snorted softly. “They ain’t interested in the bilge, mate.”

Marlowe’s eyes never left Rook’s. “You’d have seen me gutted and tossed over, aye? What would you have done then, if our positions were reversed?”

He hesitated. In that fraction of a second, something in his face betrayed the truth.

She saw it. “Thought so.”

Behind her, Old Jory chuckled, a dry sound. “Sharks don’t care ’bout lies or pretty words, lad. Only whether ye fall headfirst or feetfirst.”

The circling fish below seemed to sense the focus shifting toward them. One darted forward, jaw yawning open in a pale flash before it closed again. Another bumped the hull with a dull, reverberating thud that traveled up through the planks, into Rook’s bones.

His stomach lurched. He imagined the drop—the sudden weightlessness, the slap of cold water, the dark shapes converging. His body started shaking, a fine, unstoppable tremor.

“I won’t do it,” he whispered, voice breaking. “I won’t walk it.”

Marlowe watched him as one might watch a wave rise—measured, distant. “You will,” she said. “Because you’ll not be hauled screaming off my deck like some land-bred coward. You’re still a sailor of the *Maiden’s Woe*, even now. You’ll meet the sea on your own feet.”

He stared at her, eyes rimmed red. Wind tugged at his hair, already plastered damp to his temples. Every instinct shrieked at him to cling to the mast, to sink to his knees, to do anything other than step closer to that edge.

Marlowe reached out and took his chin in her hand, turning his face toward hers. Her grip was firm but not cruel.

“The last choice you get,” she said quietly, too low for most to hear. “Headfirst or back-first. Spare yourself the panic, if you’ve any steel left at all.”

His breath stuttered across his teeth. For a long moment, he said nothing.

Then, hoarse: “Back.”

She nodded once and let him go. Straightening, her voice rose again, crisp and carrying. “Cut him free.”

Harlan hesitated. “Cap’n, his hands—”

“I said cut him free.” Her tone brooked no argument.

Harlan swallowed hard and sawed at the rope. It fell away in a rough coil at Rook’s feet, leaving angry bands across his skin.

The sudden lightness in his arms made him feel strangely faint. For an instant the idea flickered—lash out, grab a pistol, go for Marlowe’s throat.

Then he glanced down, and the thought died.

The water writhed. There were more sharks now; he could see them clearly. Tails knifing, bodies twisting in restless arcs. No frenzy, not yet, but an expectant hum under the surface, like a plucked string waiting to sing.

“Walk,” Marlowe said.

The word pressed on him like a hand between his shoulder blades. Around him, the circle of men seemed to lean inward, drawn as much as they were repelled.

Rook stepped onto the plank.

It dipped a fraction under his weight, answering him with a small, traitorous groan. The sea filled his vision now, the ship and sky narrowing to the edges of his sight. Spray cooled his face. The air out here tasted harsher, sharpened by the open drop.

He took another step. The board flexed again.

Behind him, the crew had fallen utterly silent. He could feel their eyes, a line of tension running from his back to them and back again. The only sounds were the hiss of water along the hull, the snap of sails, and the soft slap of waves meeting fins.

Three more steps, and he was well clear of the rail. There was nothing beneath him but empty air and the slow churn of gray-green water flecked with white.

“Nnnh—” A choked sound escaped his throat. His legs locked.

“Rook.” Marlowe’s voice floated out to him, measured and unyielding. “On your feet. Don’t make me come out there.”

He stared down. The sharks moved in patient loops, their shapes overlapping, tails flicking lazily. One rose almost to the surface, its dorsal fin cutting a perfect black arrow. He could see its snout now, the faint scar along one side where something had once taken a bite out of it and failed.

His breath came too fast, too loud. His fingers twitched at his sides. He imagined reaching out, clutching at the empty air, as if that would give him something to hold onto.

He swallowed hard, Adam’s apple bobbing. “I—I can’t,” he whispered, the words lost in the wind.

“Yes you can,” Marlowe answered. Her tone softened a hair—not enough for kindness, but enough for certainty. “You’ve faced cannon fire and storm seas. You’ll not whimper at a bit of brine.”

The board creaked, complaining. A faint breeze licked at his ankles, reminding him, insistently, what waited below.

His mind flashed in wild, useless circles—memories tumbling over each other. The stink of tar in the shipyard where he first signed on. The crush of a storm wave rolling the world sideways. Laughter in the galley. The sting of the back of Marlowe’s hand when he’d first stepped out of line. Radley’s whisper: *We could take her. We *should* take her.* The shape of a knife in his palm.

The sharks turned, and turned again.

In that endless, stretched moment, Rook understood that nothing he had done in his life mattered to them. They did not know his name or his sins. They did not care that he had once dreamed of his own ship, of a different flag.

To them he was only weight and meat, something that would fall and thrash and then stop.

His body trembled so violently the plank shivered under him.

“Face the sky,” Marlowe called. “Not the water.”

Slowly, with effort, he forced himself to look up. The clouds above rolled heavy and low, a dark ceiling pressing down. A single strip of pale blue glimmered far to the east, thin as a promise.

The wind rushed past his ears, suddenly loud. His heart still thundered, but there was a strange clarity in it now, too—a hard, cold knot where the panic had burned itself nearly out.

His heels edged back until they found the end of the plank. There was no more wood. Nothing but that sheer, empty drop humming at his back.

He breathed in. The air smelled of salt and rope and distant rain.

“Any last words?” Marlowe asked.

For a brief second, anger flared in him, sharp and bitter. Anger at her, at Radley, at the sea itself. Words rose to his tongue—curses, pleas, bitter confessions.

In the end, all that left his mouth was a fractured, hoarse, “Don’t let ’em have my boots.”

A faint, surprised snort of laughter broke from someone on deck—quickly smothered. Marlowe’s jaw tightened once, as if holding back something, then loosened.

“I’ll see they go to someone who’ll wear ’em,” she said.

He nodded, though she might not see it. His fingers curled into fists, nails digging into callused palms. The tremor in his legs steadied, just a fraction.

Then Rook closed his eyes.

He let his weight tip backward.

For an instant he felt nothing but wind, cold and wide and endless against his back, rushing up to meet him. The plank fell away. The ship’s sounds—the creak of rope, the murmur of men—snapped off as if someone had slammed a door.

And the last thing he heard before the sea swallowed him whole was the low, excited churn of the circling sharks, rising to meet the disturbance from above.

The first thing they feel is wrong is the weight.

It sits on their chest like a hand pressing down, unfamiliar and solid under the thin layer of fabric. When their fingers slide under their shirt, they meet not skin, but edges—hard, square, unyielding. Cold plastic, colder metal. For a heartbeat they don’t understand. Their mind stalls.

Then their fingertips find the wires.

They’re small, almost delicate, but there’s nothing delicate in the way they bite into the pads of each finger. The insulation is smooth but gritty, like it’s been dragged across concrete, warmed slightly by their body heat. Different textures—one wire just a bit thicker, its plastic casing slightly sticky with sweat; another slicker, rubbery, almost slippery under their trembling touch. They try to pinch one between thumb and forefinger and it slides away, snaking back against their chest, alive with threat.

Tape holds everything in place. They tug at the edge, and the adhesive pulls at the fine hairs on their chest, a sting that feels grotesquely normal amid the rising unreality. The tape crackles faintly when their fingers lift it, the sound too loud in the airless space between their racing thoughts. Beneath it, more wires are crisscrossed, some looped tight, others slightly bowed, as if breathing with them. Each shallow inhale nudges the bundle, makes it quiver.

And then they hear it.

At first it hides inside the roar of their own pulse, blended with the air in their lungs and the static in their ears. A soft, precise click. Then another. The tiniest mechanical tap. Ticking.

Tick.

A dry, insect-like sound, impossibly close to their heart.

Tick.

Once they’ve heard it, they can’t unhear it. It’s in the base of their throat, in the hollow of their collarbone, vibrating through bone and blood. Every second is a small, distinct violation, a measured intrusion. The noise doesn’t echo so much as burrow—under their skin, between each breath.

They press their palm flat against the device, as if they could smother the sound. The plastic is firm, edges digging into their hand. They can feel the faint, rhythmic twitch of some interior mechanism against their palm. Not strong, just insistent. Tick. Tick. Tick. The sound travels up through the bones of their hand, into their wrist, as if they’re wired into it now, part of the circuit.

Their other hand gropes blindly at the cluster of wires. Their nails catch on a knot of them, scraping. The bundle shifts, and for an instant, one wire snaps taut, pressing sharply into their skin like a cutting string. Panic jolts through them—don’t pull, don’t pull, don’t touch anything—yet their fingers won’t let go. Each wire is a live question: red, black, blue, it doesn’t matter—any one of them could be the one holding everything back, or the one that ends it.

Their fingertips are clumsy. The sweat on their hands turns the insulation slick. They feel every ridge of plastic, every tiny bump where two pieces have been joined, the faint, raised seam down the length of one wire. They can’t stop touching it; they can’t bear to touch it at all. Their hands shake so badly the wires rustle against each other, a faint friction sound like dry grass rubbed together. Each rasp feels like it might be the last sound they ever cause.

Tick.

The ticking gets louder, not because the device changes, but because their world shrinks to the size of that sound. Their breathing becomes shallow, ragged. They draw in air and it shudders over their tongue, but their chest feels locked, each breath pushing the device, shifting the wires against their skin—cold plastic tracing jerky paths over their ribs. By the time Claire found the front door key in the bottom of her bag, the rain had already crept under her collar.

She nudged the door with her shoulder, listening for the familiar metallic click of the deadbolt turning. Instead, the door eased inward with a soft sigh, the latch grazing the strike plate.

She froze.

She always locked the door. Even when she was just taking out the trash. It was muscle memory, the twist of the thumbturn, the check of the handle. She felt it now in her hand, an echo of the action she was certain she’d done this afternoon.

Wind pressed a bit of rain in through the gap, dampening the hardwood inside.

“Hello?” she called, because it felt stranger not to.

The word flattened itself against the dark and came back to her as a dull shape. Nobody answered. The house smelled faintly of cooling coffee and laundry detergent, the way it always did at night. Ordinary.

She stepped inside and reached for the light switch with her left hand while her right, unconsciously, slid her keys between her fingers the way her roommate had shown her in college.

The switch clicked uselessly. No overhead light flared to life. The hallway remained a long, narrow strip of black.

Power outage, she thought first. The house was old; the wires were temperamental. She glanced back over her shoulder. The streetlight on the corner was still glowing, casting wet reflections on the pavement. Next door’s porch lamp burned steady.

Just the house, then.

Her phone was in her coat pocket. She pulled it out and the screen’s dim glow painted her hand blue-white. Eight percent battery. The storm must have knocked something loose; she’d deal with it later. For now, she thumbed on the flashlight.

The narrow LED beam cut a slice out of the dark. Dust motes rotated lazily in the air. The hallway walls, with their framed prints and light scuffs near the floor, sprang into sharp, almost too-bright focus while everything else sank deeper into shadow.

The front door eased closed behind her with a soft click, the sound somehow much louder in the silence that followed. The house felt padded, like all the air had been thickened.

She toed off her wet shoes, half from habit, half because loud footsteps suddenly felt like a bad idea. The wood floor was cool through her thin socks.

From the living room to her right came the faintest sigh of movement—fabric settling, or perhaps just the house reacting to the change in temperature as the front door shut. Her shoulders climbed by a fraction of an inch.

“Stupid,” she muttered, more to the house than to herself, and pivoted toward the kitchen. The breaker box was down there, in the basement, behind the washing machine. She’d flip it, text her landlord about the door latch, and then maybe make tea.

As the narrow cone of her phone’s light swung away, the living room on her right disappeared from view, folding back into darkness.

In that darkness, behind the arm of the sofa, a figure remained perfectly still.

He had been there for forty minutes, kneeling first, then easing himself carefully to a low crouch when his thighs began to burn. He knew where the floorboards complained the loudest. He knew which parts of the room the streetlight sometimes reached, the pale smear of moving branches painting the far wall.

He also knew the precise angle at which the front door failed to catch if you leaned on it as it was closing. He had tested it twice that afternoon while the house was empty.

His knife lay along the inside of his forearm, the blade hugging the skin, its black handle lost in his palm. No light touched it. Only his fingers noted the texture, the way the handle was just beginning to warm under his grip.

Her footsteps were soft but not silent. A faint tacky sound from wet socks, the almost imperceptible squeak of wood as weight shifted. The beam from her phone ghosted over the far wall, catching the edge of a picture frame, a small flash of glass.

He watched the circle of light glide past the doorway and vanish toward the back of the house, like a drifting planet receding into space. Her silhouette, an absence of light beside it, moved with it, then was gone.

He did not turn his head to follow. He moved his eyes, only, keeping everything else still. The smallest movements made the least noise.

Claire’s heart had settled into something approaching normal by the time she reached the short flight of stairs leading down to the basement door. The phone’s light jittered a little as she descended the three steps, her hand skimming the wall out of habit for a banister that wasn’t there.

She hated the basement. Everyone did. It smelled like damp concrete and cardboard, and some part of her brain always expected spiders the size of her hand to abseil down from the ceiling. But the breaker box was there, screwed into unfinished drywall above the washing machine, and this was her house. It was ridiculous to be afraid of your own basement.

Still, when she opened the basement door, she did it more slowly than necessary. The hinges complained with a drawn-out creak that made the fine hairs at the back of her neck stir.

“Seriously?” she whispered at the hinge.

The basement swallowed her light the way dark water absorbs the first few feet of a dropped flashlight. The cone revealed concrete stairs, the skeletal outline of shelving units, the white bulk of the washer and dryer squatting along the far wall. The air was cooler, layered with the faint metallic tang of old pipes.

Behind her, upstairs, the front door’s latch and the gentle shift of air had already erased her entrance. The house seemed to hold its breath again.

He listened until the creak of the basement door stopped and another, different groan—the sound of a step bearing weight—took over. One, two, three; the rhythm of descent.

He rose from his crouch slowly, knees crackling almost imperceptibly in the quiet. His thighs hummed with delayed pain. The knife shifted as his angle changed, the shallow weight of it new and familiar all at once.

He could cross the living room on the rug; it would mask his footsteps. The hallway was trickier. There was a board, just past where the runner ended, that squealed even under the cat’s paws.

He knew this because he had watched, for two evenings and one long morning, from the car parked two houses up, timing departures and arrivals, noting who carried groceries, which curtains opened and closed, which windows glowed late.

Now he placed his feet with the same care he had used to catalog those movements, rolling from heel to toe, feeling for the flex in the old wood. The living room window, with its gauzy curtain, let in enough of the street’s sodium light to outline the major shapes: coffee table, couch, the tall floor lamp like a sentinel.

He slid past it, becoming another dark between darks, his shoulder skimming the shadowed wall where, five hours earlier, Claire had hung her coat and laughed into the phone about something forgotten now.

Downstairs, her own footsteps slowed. The phone’s light seemed suddenly weaker in the open space of the basement, throwing a cone that trembled over boxes—“XMAS,” “BOOKS,” “MISC”—then up to the breaker box. Silver toggles in neat rows.

She pinched the phone between her arm and chest to free one hand, the light skewing off toward a stack of paint cans, and flipped each switch off, then on again. The thin metal clicked under her fingers with unsatisfying daintiness.

She waited. No hum of the refrigerator upstairs. No sudden, reassuring thump of the heater. The phone remained her only light.

“Come on,” she murmured. Thunder rolled, distant and lazy, somewhere beyond the house.

Her battery icon dipped to seven percent.

Claire exhaled, long and slow. If the power was actually out inside the house, maybe there was a bigger problem—something with the line. She should call it in before everyone in the neighborhood did the same. She imagined spending the night without heat and grimaced.

Her service bars hovered between one and nothing. She lifted the phone a little higher, as if a few inches would draw reception down through the ceiling.

Upstairs, he reached the point in the hallway where the runner ended. The darkness was thicker here, the streetlight from the front no longer reaching, the faint, cold rectangle of the kitchen window a soft gray at the far end.

He paused, balancing with weight on his back foot, and tested the next board with the lightest brush of his toes. A minor exhale of wood replied, the kind of complaint no one would hear from downstairs. He adjusted his path, placing his right foot half a plank over, judging the subsurface support from the absence of give.

The knife handle nestled more securely against his palm as his fingers tightened. His breathing was slow, measured, deliberately quiet. He heard, more than felt, his own pulse, a low, steady drum behind his ears.

The basement door stood ajar to his left, a flat black rectangle in the dim hall. From within came the faint, concentrated glow of her phone, cupped in darkness like a single coal.

He could hear her now that the house had learned her new location—the small friction sounds of skin against plastic, the tiny rasp of fabric when her sleeve brushed a cardboard box. The distance, he estimated, was fifteen steps down, then another twenty-five to cross the basement to the breaker.

If he went down after her, the confines of the staircase would pin them into a narrow, predictable corridor. But narrow also meant noisy. The old wood would betray him on every rung.

He stopped at the doorway and waited.

Claire, still frowning at the lack of bars, stepped backward without looking, the heel of her socked foot smudging a faint, dusty mark onto the concrete. The phone’s beam caught the underside of the stairs, the naked wooden slats and their long, narrow shadows striping the far wall like prison bars.

She swallowed. It was childish and she knew it, but she didn’t like having her back to the open basement. Not with the door upstairs a black slot and the house above her quiet as abandoned property.

“Okay, I’m being ridiculous,” she said aloud. Her voice came out hushed, as if in deference to something, and the fact that she couldn’t name what made a small, cold knot in her stomach.

A faint sound drifted down then; a noise small enough that she couldn’t tell if she had imagined it. Not quite a footstep, not quite the house shifting. A feather-weight of displacement above.

“Hello?” She hated how the word thinned at the end, almost questioning her own right to ask.

Upstairs, he inhaled once, slowly, through his nose, and let the air ease out between pressed lips soundlessly. The floor had done that—complained just a fraction under his shift of weight. He had expected it, had chosen the board he thought would be quietest, and still sound had seeped through. Old houses were liars.

He raised his free hand from his side, palm out, fingers hovering a fraction of an inch from the wall to balance. The knife stayed low, along his thigh.

Claire listened, her head tilted slightly. The phone’s light shook minutely with the muscle tension in her hand. Upstairs, someone’s television in another house laughed faintly through the walls. Rain ticked against the basement window like fingernails.

Nothing else.

After a moment, she let out the breath she hadn’t meant to hold and shook her head. “You are scaring yourself,” she told the washing machine, the paint cans, the breaker board. Normal things, rooted in place, that could not mean her harm.

She turned toward the stairs, angling the phone so the beam lit the steps from beneath, her own elongated shadow stretching up into the open doorway and painting the ceiling at the top of the basement like a stretched, dark figure.

At the top of those stairs, just beyond where the light reached, something eased back by the breadth of a heartbeat, retreating into the deeper dark along the wall.

He had seen the beam’s glow swell, then her shadow elongate ahead of it. If he remained directly in its path, the light would catch at least his feet, cast a second shadow. Too soon. Too clumsy.

He flattened himself against the narrow slice of wall between the basement door frame and the kitchen opening, shoulder blades pressing hard into the cool plaster until he could feel the faint irregularities of the wall’s texture through his shirt. His breath he kept tight in his chest, as if expanding his ribs might nudge something that would creak.

The first of her steps landed on the bottom stair. The wood gave a small, resigned groan, the kind that spoke of long use, not of warning. The second step mirrored it.

Each ascending footfall brought the light closer, brightening the top stairs one by one, pushing the darkness up ahead of it like a tide.

He watched the edge of that light approach the threshold. The knife, now turned so the blade lay flat again along his forearm, was invisible, just another shadow on his skin.

Claire’s hand trailed along the railing-less wall as she climbed, fingers splayed, looking for contact. The small circle of light guided her feet. She counted the steps automatically, the same way she always did. Seven, eight, nine—

The beam jumped as her toe snagged on the lip of the last step, and her palm smacked against the doorframe to catch herself. The phone’s light shot briefly forward, flaring across the opposite kitchen wall, then back down.

Her heart spiked, sending a flush of heat through her. “Jesus,” she gasped, half-laughing at herself, the sound thin but a little closer to normal now. “Graceful.”

She reached with her free hand and pushed gently at the basement door. It swung the last few inches open with a low wooden sigh, revealing the other side of the hallway.

The darkness there was solid, the edges of the kitchen only hinted at—a square where the fridge would be, the suggestion of the table. The hallway ran off to her right, toward the front of the house, a black ribbon.

She stepped onto the hall rug, grateful for its soft texture underfoot, and raised the phone a little higher, widening the pool of light.

For a second—less than that, a fraction between blinks—she had the sensation, more in her skin than in her eyes, of occupying space already taken. Of being too close to something else in the dark.

The air on her left side felt cooler, as if someone had just moved away.

Her scalp prickled. The keys bit into the inside of her clenched fist.

“Is someone there?” she asked, and the hallway swallowed the question whole, tucking it deep into its long, whispered silence.

He listened until the creak of the basement door stopped and another, different groan—the sound of a step bearing weight—took over. One, two, three; the rhythm of descent.

He rose from his crouch slowly, knees crackling almost imperceptibly in the quiet. His thighs hummed with delayed pain. The knife shifted as his angle changed, the shallow weight of it new and familiar all at once.

He could cross the living room on the rug; it would mask his footsteps. The hallway was trickier. There was a board, just past where the runner ended, that squealed even under the cat’s paws.

He knew this because he had watched, for two evenings and one long morning, from the car parked two houses up, timing departures and arrivals, noting who carried groceries, which curtains opened and closed, which windows glowed late.

Now he placed his feet with the same care he had used to catalog those movements, rolling from heel to toe, feeling for the flex in the old wood. The living room window, with its gauzy curtain, let in enough of the street’s sodium light to outline the major shapes: coffee table, couch, the tall floor lamp like a sentinel.

He slid past it, becoming another dark between darks, his shoulder skimming the shadowed wall where, five hours earlier, Claire had hung her coat and laughed into the phone about something forgotten now.

Downstairs, her own footsteps slowed. The phone’s light seemed suddenly weaker in the open space of the basement, throwing a cone that trembled over boxes—“XMAS,” “BOOKS,” “MISC”—then up to the breaker box. Silver toggles in neat rows.

She pinched the phone between her arm and chest to free one hand, the light skewing off toward a stack of paint cans, and flipped each switch off, then on again. The thin metal clicked under her fingers with unsatisfying daintiness.

She waited. No hum of the refrigerator upstairs. No sudden, reassuring thump of the heater. The phone remained her only light.

“Come on,” she murmured. Thunder rolled, distant and lazy, somewhere beyond the house.

Her battery icon dipped to seven percent.

Claire exhaled, long and slow. If the power was actually out inside the house, maybe there was a bigger problem—something with the line. She should call it in before everyone in the neighborhood did the same. She imagined spending the night without heat and grimaced.

Her service bars hovered between one and nothing. She lifted the phone a little higher, as if a few inches would draw reception down through the ceiling.

Upstairs, he reached the point in the hallway where the runner ended. The darkness was thicker here, the streetlight from the front no longer reaching, the faint, cold rectangle of the kitchen window a soft gray at the far end.

He paused, balancing with weight on his back foot, and tested the next board with the lightest brush of his toes. A minor exhale of wood replied, the kind of complaint no one would hear from downstairs. He adjusted his path, placing his right foot half a plank over, judging the subsurface support from the absence of give.

The knife handle nestled more securely against his palm as his fingers tightened. His breathing was slow, measured, deliberately quiet. He heard, more than felt, his own pulse, a low, steady drum behind his ears.

The basement door stood ajar to his left, a flat black rectangle in the dim hall. From within came the faint, concentrated glow of her phone, cupped in darkness like a single coal.

He could hear her now that the house had learned her new location—the small friction sounds of skin against plastic, the tiny rasp of fabric when her sleeve brushed a cardboard box. The distance, he estimated, was fifteen steps down, then another twenty-five to cross the basement to the breaker.

If he went down after her, the confines of the staircase would pin them into a narrow, predictable corridor. But narrow also meant noisy. The old wood would betray him on every rung.

He stopped at the doorway and waited.

Claire, still frowning at the lack of bars, stepped backward without looking, the heel of her socked foot smudging a faint, dusty mark onto the concrete. The phone’s beam caught the underside of the stairs, the naked wooden slats and their long, narrow shadows striping the far wall like prison bars.

She swallowed. It was childish and she knew it, but she didn’t like having her back to the open basement. Not with the door upstairs a black slot and the house above her quiet as abandoned property.

“Okay, I’m being ridiculous,” she said aloud. Her voice came out hushed, as if in deference to something, and the fact that she couldn’t name what made a small, cold knot in her stomach.

A faint sound drifted down then; a noise small enough that she couldn’t tell if she had imagined it. Not quite a footstep, not quite the house shifting. A feather-weight of displacement above.

“Hello?” She hated how the word thinned at the end, almost questioning her own right to ask.

Upstairs, he inhaled once, slowly, through his nose, and let the air ease out between pressed lips soundlessly. The floor had done that—complained just a fraction under his shift of weight. He had expected it, had chosen the board he thought would be quietest, and still sound had seeped through. Old houses were liars.

He raised his free hand from his side, palm out, fingers hovering a fraction of an inch from the wall to balance. The knife stayed low, along his thigh.

Claire listened, her head tilted slightly. The phone’s light shook minutely with the muscle tension in her hand. Upstairs, someone’s television in another house laughed faintly through the walls. Rain ticked against the basement window like fingernails.

Nothing else.

After a moment, she let out the breath she hadn’t meant to hold and shook her head. “You are scaring yourself,” she told the washing machine, the paint cans, the breaker board. Normal things, rooted in place, that could not mean her harm.

She turned toward the stairs, angling the phone so the beam lit the steps from beneath, her own elongated shadow stretching up into the open doorway and painting the ceiling at the top of the basement like a stretched, dark figure.

At the top of those stairs, just beyond where the light reached, something eased back by the breadth of a heartbeat, retreating into the deeper dark along the wall.

He had seen the beam’s glow swell, then her shadow elongate ahead of it. If he remained directly in its path, the light would catch at least his feet, cast a second shadow. Too soon. Too clumsy.

He flattened himself against the narrow slice of wall between the basement door frame and the kitchen opening, shoulder blades pressing hard into the cool plaster until he could feel the faint irregularities of the wall’s texture through his shirt. His breath he kept tight in his chest, as if expanding his ribs might nudge something that would creak.

The first of her steps landed on the bottom stair. The wood gave a small, resigned groan, the kind that spoke of long use, not of warning. The second step mirrored it.

Each ascending footfall brought the light closer, brightening the top stairs one by one, pushing the darkness up ahead of it like a tide.

He watched the edge of that light approach the threshold. The knife, now turned so the blade lay flat again along his forearm, was invisible, just another shadow on his skin.

Claire’s hand trailed along the railing-less wall as she climbed, fingers splayed, looking for contact. The small circle of light guided her feet. She counted the steps automatically, the same way she always did. Seven, eight, nine—

The beam jumped as her toe snagged on the lip of the last step, and her palm smacked against the doorframe to catch herself. The phone’s light shot briefly forward, flaring across the opposite kitchen wall, then back down.

Her heart spiked, sending a flush of heat through her. “Jesus,” she gasped, half-laughing at herself, the sound thin but a little closer to normal now. “Graceful.”

She reached with her free hand and pushed gently at the basement door. It swung the last few inches open with a low wooden sigh, revealing the other side of the hallway.

The darkness there was solid, the edges of the kitchen only hinted at—a square where the fridge would be, the suggestion of the table. The hallway ran off to her right, toward the front of the house, a black ribbon.

She stepped onto the hall rug, grateful for its soft texture underfoot, and raised the phone a little higher, widening the pool of light.

For a second—less than that, a fraction between blinks—she had the sensation, more in her skin than in her eyes, of occupying space already taken. Of being too close to something else in the dark.

The air on her left side felt cooler, as if someone had just moved away.

Her scalp prickled. The keys bit into the inside of her clenched fist.

“Is someone there?” she asked, and the hallway swallowed the question whole, tucking it deep into its long, whispered silence.

The gas rolls in low, a pale, oily mist that pours over the parapet and drops into the trench like something alive. The soldier’s first warning is the smell—sharp, alien, cutting straight through the damp stink of mud and sweat. His throat tightens before he understands what’s happening.

He drags in a breath to shout a warning and it’s like inhaling acid. The air sears down his windpipe, a raw, stripping burn that makes every nerve in his throat snap awake in pain. He tries to cough it out, but the cough won’t stop; it tears at his chest, a harsh, hacking convulsion that doubles him over. Each breath is shallow and frantic, yet it still feels like he’s drowning on dry land. The gas clings inside him, turning his lungs into a place where air doesn’t belong.

His eyes stream and blur; tears mix with the sting of the gas and his world dissolves into a wavering smear of green-grey haze and splintered wood. He claws at his collar, at his own neck, as if he could pry open a new way to breathe. Every inhalation is a choice between suffocation and agony. The muscles between his ribs cramp and flutter with the effort; his chest feels too small, his lungs too tight, as though they’re swelling against bone.

Panic comes in hot, jagged waves. There’s no room left for discipline or training—only the animal terror of a body that can’t get air. His thoughts skid and shatter: mask—too late—can’t breathe—going to die here. Sound narrows to the ragged rasp of his own breathing, the wet, broken coughs from men around him, some collapsing face-first into the muck. He feels light-headed, vision tunneling, black creeping in from the edges.

His mind flickers between frantic calculation and numb surrender. Part of him is still trying to crawl, to find higher ground, fresher air; the rest is already slipping away, stunned by the intensity of the pain and the sheer, helpless suffocation. Time stretches—each second marked by another desperate, burning gasp that brings no relief, only more fire in his chest and the cold certainty that his own lungs have turned against him.

The restaurant had closed an hour ago, but the lights in the back room still burned low and yellow, staining the smoke that hung in the air. The city murmured outside—a far-off hum behind triple-glazed windows. Inside, everything was muffled: the clink of porcelain, the soft slide of cards on felt, the occasional flare of a lighter.

At the head of the table sat Mr. Carbone, white shirt sleeves rolled up, tie loosened a single inch, not a thread more. A steaming espresso rested untouched by his right hand, a neat stack of papers by his left. The air around him seemed cooler than the room.

Three men waited on his words. Nino leaned by the wall, hands folded in front of him, heavy shoulders filling the doorway. Marco sat two chairs down, staring at the table, jaw tight. Frankie—small, restless Frankie—fidgeted with his napkin, fingers tracing the same crease over and over.

Carbone flipped a page. Didn’t look up.

“So,” he said quietly, “our friend took a walk.”

Marco nodded once. “Yes, sir.”

Carbone turned another page. “And he didn’t walk alone.”

“No, sir.”

He closed the folder with two fingers and finally raised his eyes. They were pale and calm and empty of surprise.

“Explain it to me,” Carbone said. “Nice and slow.”

Marco cleared his throat, sat up. “He went in at eleven seventeen. Side entrance, like always. Met with two agents. They had the file.” He tapped the folder on the table. “This one. He stayed forty-three minutes. Came out alone. Different exit.”

Carbone studied Marco’s face as though he were reading fine print.

“And you’re sure,” Carbone said, “he wasn’t just… socializing.”

Marco’s mouth twitched. “They don’t socialize, Mr. Carbone.”

Carbone glanced at Nino. “You see it?”

Nino shifted his weight, the floor creaking under him. “Saw him go in. Saw him come out. Got the plates on both cars. They’re federal.” He paused. “He was laughin’ with them when he left. Shakin’ hands. Real friendly.”

Carbone sat back in his chair. He brushed an invisible piece of lint from his cuff, slow, deliberate.

“He take anything in with him?” he asked.

“A folder,” Marco said. “Blue, with the clips. Two inches thick, maybe more.”

“And he didn’t come out with it.”

Marco shook his head. “Empty hands.”

The room was quiet except for the low hum of the refrigerator somewhere in the kitchen. Frankie’s napkin made a dry, whispering sound.

Carbone turned his wrist to check his watch, though the time had no bearing on anything.

“How long’s he been with me?” he asked, almost to himself.

“Since you took over from your uncle,” Nino said. “’Bout eleven years.”

Carbone nodded, lips pressed together. He rubbed his thumb gently along the edge of the folder as if testing the sharpness of paper.

“He eats at my table,” Carbone said. “I held his boy when he got baptized. You remember?”

“Yeah,” Frankie answered quickly. “You gave the kid the little gold chain—”

Carbone flicked his eyes to him, and Frankie fell silent.

Carbone looked back at Marco. “Did he see you there?”

Marco hesitated. “Think he caught a look, yeah.”

“And?”

“And he kept walkin’,” Marco said quietly.

Carbone let that hang there a moment.

“So.” He tapped the folder once. “He took a walk. He made some new friends. He brought them presents. He comes out lighter than he went in.” He shrugged one shoulder. “People get curious these days. They like to talk. Maybe he just forgot where he belongs.”

Nobody answered. They knew that tone.

Carbone folded his hands in front of him.

“Any of you ever been in that building?” he asked.

Head shakes around the table.

“I have,” he said. “Long time ago. Different faces, same furniture. You go in with a question mark on your head, you come out with a leash round your neck. They say it’s cooperation. I call it… relocation.” He smiled without warmth. “They move you from our world to theirs. Bit by bit.”

He slid the folder across the table to Marco. “What’s in there?”

“Everything he gave them,” Marco replied. “Names. Places. Numbers. Some of it’s wrong, some of it’s old. Not enough to hurt. Enough to show he’s willing.”

Carbone studied Marco. “He give them you?”

Marco’s jaw flexed. “He tried,” he said. “They were fishing. They were asking. They didn’t get nothin’ that sticks.”

Carbone’s eyes moved to Nino. “You?”

Nino shook his head once. “Didn’t mention me. Or you. Not in what we saw.”

“Not yet,” Carbone said. “That’s the thing with leaks. They start small.” He glanced at the sweating espresso cup, then pushed it away. “Then one day you wake up and the whole ship’s under.”

The men shifted, waiting for the drop of the blade that hadn’t yet been named.

Carbone clasped his hands again. His fingers were steady, his voice even.

“Where is he now?” he asked.

“Home,” Marco said. “He went straight there from the meet. Lights went out at one. He hasn’t left since.”

“He with his family?”

“Wife and the two kids,” Marco said. “Oldest girl’s at her aunt’s for the week.”

Carbone nodded slowly, once. “He sleep good, you think?”

Marco swallowed. “Didn’t look restless.”

Carbone turned his head toward the window, though the curtains were drawn. “Man makes new friends like that, sometimes his old ones keep him up at night.” He tilted his head. “Not this one, apparently.”

He faced them again, eyes clear.

“This is how it’s gonna go,” he said, voice soft. “Our friend is going on a trip.”

Frankie stopped folding the napkin.

“A permanent one,” Carbone added, in the same tone he might use to order dessert.

Nino’s eyes dipped in a slow, understanding nod.

“Travel arrangements are important,” Carbone went on. “You send a man off the wrong way, people talk. Police get curious. Priests get loud. I don’t like noise.”

“No noise,” Nino said.

Carbone looked at Marco. “You ever notice how sometimes, a man just… doesn’t wake up?”

Marco held his gaze. “Yeah.”

“Heart stops. Breathing slows. Doctor shrugs, priest mumbles, everybody cries.” Carbone’s fingers tapped once on the table. “Especially when that man’s been thinking too much. Talking too much. Sometimes his thoughts catch up to him in the night.”

Marco’s throat worked. “You want it to look like he had a change of heart.”

Carbone’s mouth twitched—just enough to be almost a smile. “Let’s say his heart decided it didn’t like the company he’s been keeping.”

He shifted his attention to Frankie. “You got that thing you use for dogs? When they get sick?”

Frankie licked his lips, nodding. “Yeah. Yeah, in the car. Couple drops, they don’t even twitch.”

“Good,” Carbone said. “Our friend’s been sick for a while. Nobody noticed. Tonight, his body catches up to the condition of his soul.”

He took a breath, slow and careful. The faint scent of cigar smoke clung to his words.

“Timing,” he said. “We got any reason to be seen over there?”

“His kid’s birthday’s in two weeks,” Nino said. “We were all invited.”

Carbone frowned slightly. “Two weeks is generous. I’m not in a generous mood.”

He thought for a moment, then nodded to himself. “He’s been… unstable. Upset. Lost. That’s the story.” His eyes flickered from face to face. “He can’t sleep. He drinks. He takes things to help. Tonight he takes a little too much. Doesn’t get back up. You understand?”

“We understand,” Nino said.

Carbone looked at Marco. “You go in first. You talk to him. You look him in the eye before he lies down. I want him to see exactly who still stands with me. Right up until the end.”

Marco’s jaw tightened, but he didn’t look away. “Yes, sir.”

“You tell him I’m hurt,” Carbone said. “Not angry. Hurt. You tell him I was ready to forgive. You tell him I was considering… a second chance.” He shrugged. “Let him carry that thought where he’s going.”

“Want me to say anything else?” Marco asked.

Carbone’s eyes grew colder. “You tell him I don’t share. Not my business. Not my people. Not my table. If he wanted to eat somewhere else, he should’ve gone hungry.”

Marco nodded.

“Frankie,” Carbone said without looking. “You handle the medicine. Careful with it. I don’t want a show. He goes quiet. He goes calm. He looks like he made peace with himself, not with anyone else.”

“Got it,” Frankie murmured. “Nice and clean.”

Carbone turned to Nino. “You stay outside. Watch the street. Nobody in, nobody out. If his wife gets curious, you be polite. You tell her the boys are catching up. Old stories, old times. She’ll believe that. She’s seen it before.”

“And when she finds him in the morning?” Nino asked.

Carbone’s expression didn’t flicker. “She’ll say he seemed tired lately. Worried. Distant. People will nod. People will say, ‘Poor guy, he carried so much on his shoulders.’ They’ll never know what he dropped and who caught it.”

He slid his chair back an inch, the scrape of wood on tile sounding too loud in the small room.

“One more thing,” he said, voice softer still. “His house. His car. His accounts. They don’t exist anymore after tonight. His name’s not to be spoken. If somebody says, ‘Hey, what happened to—’” He lifted one finger and let it fall. “You look at them and you say, ‘Who?’”

Marco answered with a single, clipped nod.

Carbone glanced at the untouched espresso, then pushed it away. “He made a choice,” he said. “He switched jerseys mid-game. That’s fine. People change. But once you play for the other side, you don’t come back to the bench.”

He stood, smoothing his shirt.

“You got two hours,” he said. “By sunrise, he’s resting. By noon, he’s a memory. By next week, he’s a story nobody tells.”

The three men rose as one.

Marco gathered the folder, tucking it under his arm. Frankie wiped his damp hands on his pants. Nino adjusted his jacket, checking the weight under his arm out of habit.

As they started for the door, Carbone spoke again.

“Marco.”

Marco turned.

Carbone’s gaze fixed him in place. “Look in his eyes when it happens.”

Marco held the stare. “I will.”

“Don’t look away,” Carbone said. “I want him to see exactly what it costs to walk out of this room and not come back.”

Marco swallowed once. “Understood.”

Carbone nodded, as if they’d settled nothing more serious than a late delivery.

“Go put our friend to bed,” he said. “Make sure he sleeps through.”
