“Wife and the two kids,” Marco said. “Oldest girl’s at her aunt’s for the week.”

Carbone nodded slowly, once. “He sleep good, you think?”

Marco swallowed. “Didn’t look restless.”

Carbone turned his head toward the window, though the curtains were drawn. “Man makes new friends like that, sometimes his old ones keep him up at night.” He tilted his head. “Not this one, apparently.”

He faced them again, eyes clear.

“This is how it’s gonna go,” he said, voice soft. “Our friend is going on a trip.”

Frankie stopped folding the napkin.

“A permanent one,” Carbone added, in the same tone he might use to order dessert.

Nino’s eyes dipped in a slow, understanding nod.

“Travel arrangements are important,” Carbone went on. “You send a man off the wrong way, people talk. Police get curious. Priests get loud. I don’t like noise.”

“No noise,” Nino said.

Carbone looked at Marco. “You ever notice how sometimes, a man just… doesn’t wake up?”

Marco held his gaze. “Yeah.”

“Heart stops. Breathing slows. Doctor shrugs, priest mumbles, everybody cries.” Carbone’s fingers tapped once on the table. “Especially when that man’s been thinking too much. Talking too much. Sometimes his thoughts catch up to him in the night.”

Marco’s throat worked. “You want it to look like he had a change of heart.”

Carbone’s mouth twitched—just enough to be almost a smile. “Let’s say his heart decided it didn’t like the company he’s been keeping.”

He shifted his attention to Frankie. “You got that thing you use for dogs? When they get sick?”

Frankie licked his lips, nodding. “Yeah. Yeah, in the car. Couple drops, they don’t even twitch.”

“Good,” Carbone said. “Our friend’s been sick for a while. Nobody noticed. Tonight, his body catches up to the condition of his soul.”

He took a breath, slow and careful. The faint scent of cigar smoke clung to his words.

“Timing,” he said. “We got any reason to be seen over there?”

“His kid’s birthday’s in two weeks,” Nino said. “We were all invited.”

Carbone frowned slightly. “Two weeks is generous. I’m not in a generous mood.”

He thought for a moment, then nodded to himself. “He’s been… unstable. Upset. Lost. That’s the story.” His eyes flickered from face to face. “He can’t sleep. He drinks. He takes things to help. Tonight he takes a little too much. Doesn’t get back up. You understand?”

“We understand,” Nino said.

Carbone looked at Marco. “You go in first. You talk to him. You look him in the eye before he lies down. I want him to see exactly who still stands with me. Right up until the end.”

Marco’s jaw tightened, but he didn’t look away. “Yes, sir.”

“You tell him I’m hurt,” Carbone said. “Not angry. Hurt. You tell him I was ready to forgive. You tell him I was considering… a second chance.” He shrugged. “Let him carry that thought where he’s going.”

“Want me to say anything else?” Marco asked.

Carbone’s eyes grew colder. “You tell him I don’t share. Not my business. Not my people. Not my table. If he wanted to eat somewhere else, he should’ve gone hungry.”

Marco nodded.

“Frankie,” Carbone said without looking. “You handle the medicine. Careful with it. I don’t want a show. He goes quiet. He goes calm. He looks like he made peace with himself, not with anyone else.”

“Got it,” Frankie murmured. “Nice and clean.”

Carbone turned to Nino. “You stay outside. Watch the street. Nobody in, nobody out. If his wife gets curious, you be polite. You tell her the boys are catching up. Old stories, old times. She’ll believe that. She’s seen it before.”

“And when she finds him in the morning?” Nino asked.

Carbone’s expression didn’t flicker. “She’ll say he seemed tired lately. Worried. Distant. People will nod. People will say, ‘Poor guy, he carried so much on his shoulders.’ They’ll never know what he dropped and who caught it.”

He slid his chair back an inch, the scrape of wood on tile sounding too loud in the small room.

“One more thing,” he said, voice softer still. “His house. His car. His accounts. They don’t exist anymore after tonight. His name’s not to be spoken. If somebody says, ‘Hey, what happened to—’” He lifted one finger and let it fall. “You look at them and you say, ‘Who?’”

Marco answered with a single, clipped nod.

Carbone glanced at the untouched espresso, then pushed it away. “He made a choice,” he said. “He switched jerseys mid-game. That’s fine. People change. But once you play for the other side, you don’t come back to the bench.”

He stood, smoothing his shirt.

“You got two hours,” he said. “By sunrise, he’s resting. By noon, he’s a memory. By next week, he’s a story nobody tells.”

The three men rose as one.

Marco gathered the folder, tucking it under his arm. Frankie wiped his damp hands on his pants. Nino adjusted his jacket, checking the weight under his arm out of habit.

As they started for the door, Carbone spoke again.

“Marco.”

Marco turned.

Carbone’s gaze fixed him in place. “Look in his eyes when it happens.”

Marco held the stare. “I will.”

“Don’t look away,” Carbone said. “I want him to see exactly what it costs to walk out of this room and not come back.”

Marco swallowed once. “Understood.”

Carbone nodded, as if they’d settled nothing more serious than a late delivery.

“Go put our friend to bed,” he said. “Make sure he sleeps through.”

The dark is total, a presence pressed right up against their eyes. At first it’s only the tightness that registers—the lid a hand’s breadth above their nose, the sides of the coffin grazing shoulders and elbows so closely there’s no real room to move, only to twitch. Each breath feels borrowed, rasping in shallow pulls that already taste stale, tinged with resin and old wood.

Then the first shovelfuls hit.

A dull thud blooms above their face, the wood shivering minutely, a faint dusting of sawdust sifting down across their cheeks and lips. Another. Another. The thuds become a steady, muffled drumbeat, each impact sinking deeper into the wood, dimly echoing in their ribs. The air seems to shrink. The ceiling seems to lower. It feels, irrationally but undeniably, as if the dirt is right there against their chest, pressing down, trying to squeeze breath out of them through the lid.

They shove their hands upward and strike the wood, fingers spread, palms skidding on its rough grain. It doesn’t budge. They push harder, arms trembling, muscles burning, heels digging uselessly against the coffin’s end. The lid groans, gives a fraction of a millimeter—just enough to make their heart leap—and then the next load of soil slams down and that tiny give is crushed flat. The weight settles in an implacable way they can feel but not see, like a giant knee on their sternum.

Panic floods in: bright, white, suffocating. They start to claw.

Nails rake at the underside of the lid, desperate, rapid scrabbling that sounds thin and pathetic in the deadened air. Splinters bite under their nails; the wood is dry but tough and unyielding, more bark than board, and every jagged line they score into it feels as useless as scratching stone. Their fingers slip in their own sweat, leaving damp streaks they can’t see. The sound of their clawing becomes a frantic insect noise, a chittering against a world that has already decided to close over them.

Above, the thuds change. No longer distinct—just a heavy, continuous pressure as more earth settles, compacts, turns from loose soil into a solid, suffocating mass. The coffin creaks in protest, the lid bowing infinitesimally, answering each of their pushes with a mute, immovable resistance. They can hear nothing beyond that: no voices, no wind, only the deadened rumble of dirt finding its level.

Their lungs work faster, dragging in air that suddenly feels thick, moist with their own breath. Every inhalation is a harder-won victory. Their hands keep moving long after their mind knows it’s pointless, nails splitting, fingertips throbbing as they gouge and gouge at the same unforgiving inches of wood. The grappling becomes less coordinated, more animal—slapping, hammering, dragging knuckles raw along the grain in the blind, furious insistence that something, somewhere, must give way.

Nothing does.

The lid stays where it is, a fixed horizon an inch above their face, and above that the earth: tons of it, pressing, settling, sealing them into a darkness that feels not empty, but full—packed, dense, a weight that exists in their thoughts as much as on the coffin, crushing down with the slow, certain patience of the grave.

By the seventh round, the ring felt smaller, like the ropes were closing in on him.

Luis’s chest heaved, every breath scraping its way in and out. Sweat ran into his eyes, stinging, mixing with the thin trickle of blood that seeped from the cut over his right brow. His vision pulsed red at the edges, the lights above blurring into a harsh white halo.

Across from him, Carter looked almost fresh. His shoulders rolled loose, gloves twitching in short, confident feints as he stalked forward. Luis’s legs weren’t listening the way they had in the opening rounds; the canvas seemed to tilt under him, heavy, unstable.

Carter jabbed, just a tester, and even that snapped Luis’s head back. The crowd roared at the clean connection. Luis tasted metal, thick and salty at the back of his throat. His left cheek had ballooned, a tight, hot mass under the skin, every slight brush sending a lance of pain through his face. One eye was narrowing, swelling up, the lid puffed and heavy so he had to fight just to keep it open.

“Hands up!” his corner shouted, voices blurred together, distant, like they were yelling at him from underwater.

Carter didn’t give him time. A hook slammed into Luis’s body, just under the ribs, then another in the same spot, digging in with cruel precision. The impact sent a sharp shock through his side, a deep, sickening jolt that stole the air from his lungs. For a moment, he couldn’t breathe at all—just a dry, silent gasp as his knees dipped.

He folded around the pain, gloves dropping a fraction too low, and Carter answered with an uppercut that exploded against his guard and drove it back into his own face. The gush from his nose increased, warm and constant now, streaking down over his lips, spotting the canvas.

The referee’s voice cut through the noise, close and urgent. “Show me something, Luis. Show me something.”

Luis blinked against the blur. Every time he opened his right eye, the world smeared—smoke and light and a dark shape coming at him with bad intentions. He tried to circle away, but his legs felt like they were buried in wet sand. Each step dragged.

Carter herded him toward the corner, shoulders squared, smelling the end. He feinted low, then whipped a hook high around Luis’s guard. It crashed into the side of Luis’s already bruised face, and a hot flash tore across his skin. His ear rang with a high, piercing whine. The ropes caught him as he stumbled back, arms sagging, mouth hanging open as he tried to pull in air that wouldn’t come fast enough.

The crowd’s roar turned into a kind of distant thunder, rolling and indistinct. Luis saw his opponent’s gloves more than he saw the man—red blurs snapping in and out, each one a hammer, each one piling on. His face throbbed with a dull, steady pulse, like his heart had moved up under his skin.

He swung back once, a slow, desperate hook that cut through empty air.

Carter’s answer buried itself in Luis’s midsection again, deep and merciless. Something inside him protested in a way that went beyond surface pain; it was a sharp, jarring shock that made his body seize and curl in defense. His mouth opened in a ragged grunt that never quite became a sound.

His legs buckled.

He dropped to one knee, glove planted on the canvas to keep from falling all the way over. The mat looked gray and distant, speckled with damp, dark spots. His breath came shallow and fast, each inhale scraping against the tight ache spreading through his side and chest.

The referee stepped in, crouching close, fingers counting in front of Luis’s wavering gaze. “You okay? You wanna continue?”

Luis tried to rise, forcing one foot under him. His body screamed its own answer. His corner shouted his name, the noise sharp but formless. He could barely see out of one eye; the other was half-closed, lashes sticky and wet.

He got halfway up before his leg sagged and he caught himself on the middle rope, body folding over it. The fight had been beaten out of him, not in one shot, but over round after round, until there was nothing left to push back with.

The referee waved it off.

The bell didn’t ring this time—the gesture was enough. Carter raised his gloves and turned away, already walking back to his corner as the arena erupted around them.

Luis stayed where he was, draped over the ropes, chest shuddering, face a tight, throbbing mask of pain and exhaustion. When his coach slid an arm under his shoulders and eased him back to the stool, his side flared, and he clenched his teeth to keep the sound inside.

He stared at the stained canvas between his boots, listening to the muffled roar of the crowd, feeling every bruise, every throb, every breath. The beating still echoed through him, a harsh rhythm that would be with him long after the lights went down.

The porcelain cup clicked softly against its saucer as he set it down, a faint impatience in the gesture. For a breath or two nothing changed; the room remained still, the coal fire a low, steady glow beneath the iron grate.

Then he paused, his hand still hovering near the cup. His brow knit, as if with a sudden, piercing thought. One hand rose to his throat, fingers pressing at his collar as though it had tightened. He drew in a breath that sounded wrong—too shallow, too quick. 

A faint tremor passed through his fingers. The porcelain rattled against the table as his hand betrayed him. Color began to drain from his face with startling speed, his healthy, ruddy complexion whitening to a dull, waxy pallor. A sheen of sweat sprang up on his forehead, beading at the temples, trickling down to darken his neatly starched collar.

His eyes widened—not in theatrical horror, but in a confused, animal recognition that something inside him had gone terribly astray. He tried to stand; his chair scraped sharply against the floorboards. His legs wouldn’t support him. Knees struck the carpet with a muffled thud, as though his joints had unstrung themselves.

His breathing grew louder, more labored. Each inhalation sounded like it caught halfway, as if his chest could not expand fully. His hand clutched at his side, then his abdomen, fingers digging into his waistcoat as though he might grip the pain and pull it out. The other hand splayed on the carpet, attempting to steady himself, the fine fabric of his cuffs smearing with ash from the hearth.

His lips, once merely pale, took on a faint bluish tinge. He swallowed hard, again and again, as if fighting down a rising wave of nausea. A cough tore out of him—dry at first, then harsher, racking his frame. Drool threaded from the corner of his mouth; he tried to speak her name, but the word broke into a ragged, choking sound.

A shudder ran through him—small at first, like a chill. Then his whole body jerked, his shoulders snapping back, fingers stiffening and curling as though they belonged to a puppet pulled on invisible strings. His jaw clenched so tightly the muscles at his temples stood out in sharp cords. For a moment his eyes rolled upward, the whites showing in a brief flash.

The convulsions came in waves: his back arching, then sagging; legs kicking once, twice against the floor, then falling still only to seize again. His breathing became erratic: a rapid panting, then long, desperate pauses between gasps, each one a noisy drag through an increasingly constricted throat.

Between the spasms he seemed briefly aware, blinking, eyes unfocused and glassy, the pupils too wide. His hand groped blindly toward the table, knocking the cup to its side. Tea, still steaming, spread in a thin brown fan across the linen, edging toward the floor in slow droplets.

His heart’s struggle showed in the violent flutter at his throat—his pulse hammering visibly beneath the skin, then faltering, then racing again. His skin, once damp with sweat, now looked dull and slack, as if drained of all warmth. The room’s air seemed suddenly filled with the faint sourness of his labored breath.

At last the spasms lost their violence. His limbs twitched rather than jerked, his fingers opening and closing weakly against the carpet. His breaths came further apart, each one a strained, rattling effort. His eyes fixed on nothing at all, lids only half-lowered, as his chest rose once, twice more. A final, shallow exhale left his lips, barely more than a sigh, and then his body loosened, all the tension leaving him at once, as though whatever had been fighting inside him had finally won.

The other hand splayed on the carpet, attempting to steady himself, the fine fabric of his cuffs smearing with ash from the hearth.

His lips, once merely pale, took on a faint bluish tinge. He swallowed hard, again and again, as if fighting down a rising wave of nausea. A cough tore out of him—dry at first, then harsher, racking his frame. Drool threaded from the corner of his mouth; he tried to speak her name, but the word broke into a ragged, choking sound.

A shudder ran through him—small at first, like a chill. Then his whole body jerked, his shoulders snapping back, fingers stiffening and curling as though they belonged to a puppet pulled on invisible strings. His jaw clenched so tightly the muscles at his temples stood out in sharp cords. For a moment his eyes rolled upward, the whites showing in a brief flash.

The convulsions came in waves: his back arching, then sagging; legs kicking once, twice against the floor, then falling still only to seize again. His breathing became erratic: a rapid panting, then long, desperate pauses between gasps, each one a noisy drag through an increasingly constricted throat.

Between the spasms he seemed briefly aware, blinking, eyes unfocused and glassy, the pupils too wide. His hand groped blindly toward the table, knocking the cup to its side. Tea, still steaming, spread in a thin brown fan across the linen, edging toward the floor in slow droplets.

His heart’s struggle showed in the violent flutter at his throat—his pulse hammering visibly beneath the skin, then faltering, then racing again. His skin, once damp with sweat, now looked dull and slack, as if drained of all warmth. The room’s air seemed suddenly filled with the faint sourness of his labored breath.

At last the spasms lost their violence. His limbs twitched rather than jerked, his fingers opening and closing weakly against the carpet. His breaths came further apart, each one a strained, rattling effort. His eyes fixed on nothing at all, lids only half-lowered, as his chest rose once, twice more. A final, shallow exhale left his lips, barely more than a sigh, and then his body loosened, all the tension leaving him at once, as though whatever had been fighting inside him had finally won.

The sirens wailed three descending notes, and fifty thousand throats roared in answer.

Kai stepped onto the cracked concrete of the arena floor, boots grinding dust into the faded red circles that marked the boundary lines. Above him, tiers of metal seating climbed into darkness, faces cut into fragments by strips of white floodlights. Between the tiers, ration banners flickered: ONE KILL = ONE WEEK. TWO KILLS = ONE MONTH. The numbers pulsed like heartbeats.

He squinted up at the screens suspended over the ring, each one showing his own face from a different angle—eyes too large in a starved face, jaw set too hard on too little sleep. The system helpfully superimposed his stats beside his portrait: AGE: 19. WINS: 2. FAMILY DEPENDENTS: 3.

The crowd cheered when they saw that last number. More mouths to feed meant more pressure. More drama.

The gate opposite him clanged open.

His opponent emerged without hurry, ducking the hanging chains of the portcullis. She was older by a decade at least, her hair shaved short except for a single braid that hung forward over one shoulder. A faded prison barcode banded her neck like an old bruise. Her own stats floated above her head: AGE: 31. WINS: 7. FAMILY DEPENDENTS: 0.

Zero. The crowd made a softer sound at that, almost a sigh. The screens dutifully flagged it: SOLO. NO REGISTRATION OF KIN.

The Overseer’s voice boomed from unseen speakers, smooth and theatrical. “Citizens, we bring you tonight’s Primary Allocation! Two challengers. One full ration allotment. You know the terms: winner takes all. Loser donates their share to the State.”

Kai flexed his fingers on the worn grip of his baton. It was a simple arena weapon—steel core, rubber edges, nothing sharp. The killing came from the force, not the tool. Strapped to his off-hand forearm was the standard-issue riot shield, cloudy and cracked from years of repurposed use.

Across from him, the woman—her name appeared briefly: LIRA M-814—twirled her own baton once, testing its weight. She carried no shield, only a forearm guard wrapped in old tape.

Their eyes met across the ring.

“First time with dependents?” she called, voice carrying in the hush before the opening bell.

Kai swallowed. “Third fight.”

She nodded once, as if confirming something. “Don’t hesitate,” she said. “They count on that.”

The sirens cut off mid-wail. A single, piercing chime rang out, and the overhead banners snapped from red to white.

BEGIN.

They moved at once.

Kai rushed forward, shield lifted, baton angled low. The training vids said to establish dominance early, to claim the center of the ring and make the other fighter move around you, burn their energy. But Lira closed the distance faster than he expected, low and economical, slipping to his right.

The first clash was a flurry of impacts—rubber on polycarbonate, metal core against bone. Kai’s baton struck her guard and jarred his wrist. Lira’s baton glanced off his shield and slid past, tapping his ribs hard enough to make his breath catch.

The arena microphones magnified every sound: the grunt of exertion, the scrape of boots, the hollow thud when Kai’s shield caught a downward swing. Above them, the screens tracked vital signs in real time—heart rates climbing, oxygen saturation dipping, a floating bar that estimated “combat efficiency” in bright, gamified colors.

Kai circled left, shield between them. Lira mirrored him, baton held loose but ready. She moved like someone who had done this too many times, her weight always centered, her eyes never leaving his shoulders.

The crowd shifted from cheering to rhythm, clapping in unison, boots stomping against the metal stands. Every strike that landed drew a spike in the audio feed, a flash on the screens. Advertisements for nutrient paste flickered along the lower edges: FIGHT HARD. EAT WELL.

Lira darted in again. Kai blocked high, but she feinted at his head and snapped the baton down, catching his thigh. The pain was a hot, clean line that made his leg buckle. He stumbled back, teeth clenched, and saw her adjust—not pressing the attack, just… measuring.

“You’ve got power,” she said between breaths. “You’re wasting it.”

He didn’t answer. Couldn’t. He pushed forward, ignoring the protest in his leg. This time he didn’t aim for her arms but for her center, driving his shield into her with all the weight he had.

The impact knocked her backward a step, boots grinding against the painted floor. The crowd reacted—half approving, half disappointed. The screens registered the hit with a flicker in her vital stats.

Lira’s lips pulled into the ghost of a smile.

“There,” she said. “More like that.”

She snapped her baton at his exposed side. He twisted, the blow glancing off his ribs instead of digging into his liver. Pain bloomed anyway. He responded by swinging his own baton in a tight arc toward her knee.

It connected, hard. The crack of impact echoed under the stadium roof.

Lira dropped half a step, her leg folding. For a heartbeat, Kai saw something like surprise in her eyes. Then she shoved away from him, limping backwards, resetting the distance.

The screens zoomed in on her knee, analyzing. STRUCTURAL COMPROMISE: 14% blinked in yellow.

“Finish it!” someone screamed from the stands, voice picked up by a roaming crowd mic and broadcast across the arena. Others joined in, words blurring into a rising chant.

Kai’s chest burned with effort. Sweat stung his eyes. His family’s faces floated in his mind unbidden: his sister clutching last week’s allocation, his mother pretending not to split her portion again, his youngest brother staring at the empty bowl before smiling like it was full.

Lira saw the hesitation settle around his shoulders like weight.

“They’re watching you,” she said quietly, nodding toward the cameras. “Don’t give them a show. Make it quick.”

He choked out, “You have no one.”

“Not anymore.” A flicker of something crossed her face, gone too fast to parse. She shifted her weight onto her good leg. “But you do. So move.”

The chant swelled, mindless and hungry.

KILL. KILL. KILL.

The Overseer’s voice rolled through the noise, smooth and detached. “Combatants are reminded that withdrawal forfeits all rations to the State and triggers familial penalization under Section—”

“Shut it off,” Lira snapped, eyes never leaving Kai’s.

Remarkably, the voice cut mid-sentence. The chant faltered, thrown off rhythm.

For half a second, it was just the two of them in the ring, the roar thinning into a faraway storm.

Lira inhaled, steadying. “Listen. They won’t let us both walk out. They never do. Don’t drag it out.”

To prove she meant it, she did the worst thing a veteran could do: she opened herself up. She dropped her guard a fraction, weight still on the bad leg, baton held just a little too low. An invitation.

Kai saw it. Every lesson he’d absorbed in the barracks rose up: Exploit the opening. Protect your own. Survive.

His grip tightened on the baton.

He moved.

No fancy spin, no flourish. He stepped in on her wounded side, letting his shield angle outward to catch any last-second counter. Lira made none. Her gaze held his, steady.

Their bodies drew close enough that he could see the fine lines at the corners of her eyes.

He drove the baton forward in a short, brutal thrust—not at her face, not at her skull, but just beneath the sternum, the place the instructors had pointed to a hundred times on plastic dummies. Above the stomach. Below the heart. The solar plexus, where breath lived.

All his weight, all his fear, all his hunger went into that single motion.

The strike landed with a dull, decisive sound—more like a door slamming shut than a bone breaking. Lira’s body folded around the blow, air rushing out of her in a strangled gasp that the microphones caught and amplified before cutting it off again.

Her baton fell from numb fingers, hitting the floor with a clatter that seemed too loud in the sudden dip of crowd noise.

For a suspended moment, nothing moved.

Then Lira dropped to her knees.

Her hand rose, almost of its own accord, fingers grazing the spot where he’d struck as if checking the reality of it. Her breath hitched once, then failed to come back properly. The screens flashed her vitals: HEART RATE SPIKE. RESPIRATORY FAILURE IMMINENT.

She swayed, and Kai instinctively reached out, catching her shoulder.

“Don’t,” she managed, voice a tattered whisper. Her lips twitched in what might have been gratitude—or pity. “Stand… up. Let them see.”

The Overseer’s voice returned, richer now, feeding off the blood in the air. “Efficiently executed! Note the precision, citizens—no waste, no spectacle. A focused blow to the breath-center. Denied oxygen. Instantly decisive.”

Kai’s hand tightened on her shoulder anyway, just enough to keep her from collapsing face-first. Her eyes found his one last time, and in them he saw not accusation, not even forgiveness—just a tired acknowledgment of the machine they were both trapped inside.

“Remember,” she breathed, the word barely audible, “it’s not you… they’re hungry for.”

Her gaze slid past him, up toward the boxes where the Overseers watched behind tinted glass. Then her body went slack.

The big screens flattened her vitals into a single line of red. A sharp tone sounded—short, final.

The arena erupted.

The ration banners exploded into color, spinning numbers: WINNER: KAI D-204. ALLOCATION: 7 WEEKS, TIER-3. His family’s ID code flashed beside it, confirming the transfer.

Food, he thought numbly. Real bread, maybe. Protein strips that didn’t taste like dust.

His baton slid from his hand.

He stood alone in the center of the ring, Lira’s weight still echoing in his muscles, the imprint of the blow humming in his bones. Around him, fifty thousand people screamed approval, their voices rising toward the sealed boxes high above where the real decisions were made.

On the nearest screen, a slow-motion replay began—the two of them closing, the straight, unadorned thrust of his arm, the way her body bent around the impact. The system drew bright diagrams over the footage, highlighting angles, annotating the efficiency of the strike with neat lines of text.

The caption beneath it read: TEXTBOOK EXECUTION.

Kai kept his head up, because she’d told him to, because any sign of collapse would be replayed a thousand times and sold as weakness. He stared straight into the nearest camera lens instead, his chest heaving, the crowd’s roar wrapping around him like a storm.

Above the arena, the ration banners kept pulsing, bathing the dead and the living alike in the same cold, hungry light.

He’s half-turned in the driver’s seat, one hand white‑knuckled on the wheel, the other braced against the door as he twists just far enough to get the muzzle over his shoulder. The car shudders at eighty, ninety miles an hour; the steering wheel tugs under his palm as the tires hit a seam in the asphalt. His heartbeat is louder than the engine, louder than the horns and the sirens behind him.

The rear window is a cracked spiderweb, glass dust glittering in the air like frost. Through it, headlights lurch and swell, filling his vision—too close, way too close. He sights down his arm for a split second, the world telescoping into that small black circle and the glaring lights behind it. He squeezes the trigger.

The pistol’s bark is deafening in the confined cabin, a hard, flat concussion that makes his ears ring and the car twitch. The recoil jolts his arm, the muzzle jumping toward the roof. He smells propellant, sharp and metallic, mixing with hot plastic and his own sweat. The pursuing car jerks slightly, its driver flinching, but doesn’t fall back; if anything, it lunges closer, teeth bared in twin beams of white.

He faces forward just in time to see the brake lights—two car-lengths ahead, red and sudden. Traffic. A minivan drifts lazily into his lane, a kid’s stickered face pressed to the rear window, open-mouthed in laughter at something he’ll never know. The world narrows again, not to the gun this time but to a single, imminent impact.

He slams the wheel left, tires screaming. The car knifes between lanes, scraping a mirror off an SUV in a spray of plastic. The SUV lurches, its driver yanking the wheel, nearly sideswiping a hatchback that panics and jumps the lane marker. The freeway becomes a chain reaction of panic: horns, locked brakes, cars slewing sideways, the smell of burning rubber rising like smoke from a battlefield.

He steals half a glance in the mirror—just enough to see the pursuers threading the same gap, ruthless and fluid. A motorcycle wobbles as they cut him off, the rider’s arms pinwheeling, bike fishtailing perilously close to the concrete barrier before he wrestles it back under control. Someone’s coffee explodes against a windshield as a sedan jerks to a halt.

Another shot, blind this time, arm twisted back over the seat. The round punches out what’s left of the rear glass and vanishes into the chaos behind him. Somewhere back there, a car swerves violently, brake lights flaring. For a horrifying instant he realizes he has no idea where that bullet went—into metal, into asphalt, or into some stranger who just left work five minutes too late.

His breath comes in ragged pulls, teeth clenched so hard his jaw aches. Every decision is half a second long and potentially fatal—to him, to them, to the father in the next lane with a toddler in a car seat, to the cyclist on the overpass whose head is already turning at the sound of sirens. The freeway is no longer a road but a vein clogged with panic, and he’s the clot tearing through it, one bad angle away from rupturing everything.

By the time I decided to kill Marcus Hale, I’d already tried everything else.

Or at least that’s what I told myself.

I tried to do it the way “decent” people do. Reports. Complaints. Meetings where I sat at the end of a glossy conference table and explained to men in good suits and careful smiles how my brother had died because Marcus had cut every corner that wasn’t nailed down. I practiced the phrase “systemic negligence” in the bathroom mirror. I brought diagrams and dates, copies of emails with his signatures at the bottom.

They nodded. They were “deeply saddened.” They were “looking into it.” They offered condolences and a modest settlement that came dressed up in legal language, like money could absorb the shape of my brother’s absence at family dinners.

A year later, Marcus was promoted.

So when I say I didn’t rush to murder, understand: the system made the first move.

I still remember the meeting where Marcus failed to recognize me.

We were in the lobby of Hale Dynamics, his firm’s new headquarters—glass and steel and plants that never dropped a leaf. I wore the one suit that still fit. He was giving some local news anchor a tour, gesturing at nothing in particular with the ease of a man who believed that walls stood straighter when he looked at them.

“Mr. Hale?” I said.

He turned with half a smile that he turned off just as quickly. He scanned me, saw no one important, and reset his face to neutral.

“Yes?” he said.

“You remember Ethan Kade?” I asked. “He worked under you, on the Eastline contract.”

The name landed. I watched the recognition flicker, then get buried under a layer of trained composure.

“Tragic accident,” Marcus said smoothly. “Our safety protocols—”

I didn’t let him finish. “Your safety protocols were a checklist no one signed. My brother fell from scaffolding that shouldn’t have been in use.”

Something cold entered his eyes then—not guilt, not exactly. Irritation. The inconvenience of being confronted by the human cost of his shortcuts.

“I understand you’ve been in touch with our legal team,” he said. “They’ve been very clear on the matter. I truly am sorry for your loss, Mr…?”

“Kade,” I said. “Same as his.”

His gaze moved past me before I finished. He nodded, a small, dismissive dip of the chin, and turned back to the camera crew.

That was the moment.

Not the fall, not the funeral, not the nights listening to my mother breathe too quietly in the next room. It was that tiny, bored nod. It was realizing that to Marcus, Ethan was a resolved expense, a line item he’d filed under “Regrettable, but not my problem.”

I walked out of the building with my hands in my pockets and the beginning of a plan sitting heavy in my chest.

You have to understand something about real justice: it takes a shape in your mind before you ever name it. At first, it was just a vague insistence that things couldn’t stay like this. Marcus couldn’t go on giving interviews, talking about “innovation” and “leadership,” while my mother’s eyes aged twenty years in one.

The thought tightened, clarified. He had taken a life. The world had shrugged. So the world was off the table.

That left me.

The idea of his car came later, and when it came, it felt less like invention and more like recognition—like finally seeing the tool that had been lying on the workbench all along. Marcus loved that car, a low, predatory thing in gunmetal gray. He parked it in the same space every day, two levels down in the executive garage.

I knew, because I started waiting for him.

Not stalking, I told myself. Documenting. Collecting patterns. What time he arrived. How long he lingered on calls before getting out. When the security guard walked his half-hearted laps. I learned the soft spots in the armor of the building the way I used to learn my brother’s laugh.

The first time I went down into the garage after hours, my heart was hammering hard enough to echo. But nothing happened. No sirens. No guards. Just the hum of fluorescent lights and the cooling tick of parked engines. His car sat there like something sedated.

Up close, it was even more ridiculous. Polished down to a mirror, rims that gleamed like surgical steel. I circled it slowly, not touching anything, hands jammed in my pockets. It was obscene, that level of care, when you considered the scaffolding Ethan fell from, rust-bolted and swaying.

That’s where the justification started to take a sharper edge.

You’re not doing anything wrong, the first version whispered. You’re just looking. You’re just proving to yourself that you could, if you wanted to. It’s a thought experiment with nicer lighting.

But the thought kept evolving, wrapping itself in cleaner logic.

He killed someone and walked away richer.

If someone like that doesn’t face consequences, what’s to stop the next Marcus?

The legal system had its chance. It shrugged and signed a check.

He operates in a world where only risk that touches his own skin counts. So you’ll make the risk real.

That word kept repeating in my head: risk. Not “murder.” Not “killing.” Those were heavy, final words. “Risk” sounded clinical, almost responsible. I wasn’t deciding whether he lived or died, I told myself; I was just rebalancing the scales. If he’d designed a building that way, shaving off all the parts that made it safe, people would call him a visionary. So what was I, if not an architect of consequences?

I didn’t wake up one morning and suddenly decide to go through with it. The plan hardened slowly, the way resentment finds its way into the cracks of an old house, turning hairline fractures into structural damage.

On the night I brought tools, I put them in a plain backpack. Nothing special. People carried backpacks into garages every day. The zipper sounded absurdly loud when I opened it, the teeth dragging like they were protesting.

I told myself I wasn’t there to hurt anyone. I told myself I just wanted him to feel what Ethan must have felt, that first moment when the metal under his boots shifted and he realized something was catastrophically wrong.

Maybe he’d survive. People walked away from car accidents all the time.

That thought became my main refuge.

You’re not killing him, I argued with my own reflection in the rearview mirror, my face drawn and colorless. You’re introducing uncertainty. You’re making the world as precarious for him as he made it for others.

Standing beside the car, I hesitated for a long time.

Images came to me unbidden: Ethan, grinning under his hard hat, telling me this job was finally going to get him ahead. My mother running her hand along his empty bedroom wall. Marcus at the conference table, discussing “efficiency” while my lawyer tried to make grief sound like leverage.

“How many more brothers?” I whispered to the garage, to the concrete and the painted lines and the security camera dead in its plastic dome. “How many more families?”

Because that was another part of the justification: this wasn’t only about Ethan. It was preventative. Ritualistic. You make an example out of a man like Marcus, and maybe the next executive thinks twice before approving substandard materials to meet a deadline.

It felt almost noble, when I framed it that way. I wasn’t descending to his level; I was enforcing a higher law. The old, simple kind: blood for blood. The kind that spoke in a language men like him understood—personal risk, personal cost.

I thought about jail, of course. About being caught. I pictured lawyers this time for me, explaining in gentle tones about mandatory minimums. I tried on the image of myself in an orange jumpsuit, older, thinner.

That should have stopped me. It didn’t.

Here was the truth I barely admitted, even to myself: some part of me wanted to be punished. Wanted someone, anyone, to say, “Yes, this matters. What happened matters enough to upend a life over it.” If the price of that acknowledgment was my own freedom, maybe that was fair.

The alternative was worse: a world where Ethan’s death existed only as paperwork, as a line in a quarterly report.

My hand shook as I finally reached out, more from adrenaline than doubt.

Even then, I avoided thinking the word “kill.” I thought in verbs that sounded almost benign. Loosen. Weaken. Compromise. Words you could use in a safety audit.

Each small act felt like a point of no return, even though physically it took almost no time. From the outside, there was nothing to see. Why would there be? Men like Marcus appreciated invisible risks when they translated into higher profits. I was just reflecting his logic back at him.

When it was done, I zipped the backpack closed and leaned against a concrete pillar, my legs suddenly unwilling to carry me.

“This is what has to happen,” I told myself. “He made a choice. You’re just the consequence.”

I’d borrowed that line from one of his public statements, ironically. He’d said it in an interview about layoffs.

“We operate in a competitive market,” he’d told the camera, all solemn empathy. “Sometimes hard decisions have to be made. It’s never easy, but it’s necessary.”

The footage had played in the background while my mother washed dishes she no longer had the appetite to use.

I left the garage feeling both lighter and hollowed out. The city air hit my face like a rebuke, reminding me there were entire neighborhoods where no one knew a man had just decided another man’s tomorrow.

I didn’t sleep that night. I lay in bed staring at the slow sweep of car headlights across my ceiling, thinking about kinetic energy and stopping distances, about how outrage had slowly, inexorably, morphed into intention.

Morning came, indifferent. The world kept spinning.

At 8:17 a.m., Marcus Hale would walk into that garage, unlocking his sleek gray miracle of engineering, humming some song from the radio. At 8:29, he’d reach the main road. At 8:31—

No. I caught myself and refused to finish that sentence, even in my head. I wasn’t responsible for what happened at 8:31, I insisted. I was responsible for 11:47 p.m. last night, for the choices that led to my hands on cold metal. Everything after that was physics and chance.

That was the lie I clung to.

But as the minutes crawled by, something inside me started to fray. My breathing became shallow. Every siren in the distance felt like it was aimed at me.

“Maybe…” I said out loud into the empty room. The word dissolved.

Maybe what? Go back? Undo it? There was no undo. No one had invented a way to restore integrity to what I’d taken apart with shaking fingers.

The most I could do was warn him.

The idea revolted me. Call him? This man who’d devalued my brother’s life to a liability question? Tell him that his own life was suddenly worth enough to me that I couldn’t bear the thought of his car picking up speed toward some unsuspecting intersection?

That’s when I understood something that cut cleaner than any plan for revenge: I didn’t actually want him dead.

I wanted him to feel it—to feel the weight of what he’d done, the way it twisted sleep into something jagged, the way it made every future choice echo. Killing him would end his part in the story. It wouldn’t make him understand mine.

My justification collapsed all at once, like a structure built on sand.

I grabbed my phone anyway.

The number wasn’t hard to find; his office line was listed publicly. It rang longer than I would have liked. When a woman’s voice answered—polished, professional—I almost hung up.

“Mr. Hale’s office.”

My mouth was dry. “You need to tell him there’s an issue with his car,” I said. “His brakes. He can’t drive it today. It’s important.”

A beat. “May I ask who’s calling?”

“No,” I said, then heard how that sounded and forced in a breath. “Just… Just tell him. Say an anonymous tip came in. Say whatever you want. But don’t let him drive the car.”

“Sir, this line is for business—”

“I’m trying to save his life,” I snapped. “And maybe someone else’s. Please. Just pass on the message.”

She hesitated long enough for me to picture her weighing the risk. Receptionists understood liability too.

“I’ll let him know,” she said at last, voice clipped. “Is there anything el—”

I hung up.

For the rest of the day, I cycled through possibilities. He’d ignore the warning out of arrogance. He’d call security. He’d call the police. He’d have the car towed, examined, the quiet horror spreading through the staff when they realized someone had breached the sanctity of the executive garage.

He’d find out what I’d done. Or he wouldn’t. Either way, I had to live with the knowledge that I’d crossed the line between thinking about harm and making it plausible.

Even if no one ever got hurt, I had proved something ugly to myself: I was capable of becoming the kind of threat I’d always assigned to other people.

That night, refreshed news feeds and traffic updates, half-hoping for proof that the world had decided my crime either mattered or didn’t. There was nothing. Marcus Hale did not die in a twisted frame of metal and glass that day. No accident, no headlines.

Weeks later, a short article appeared in a local business journal: “Hale Dynamics CEO Increases Security Measures After ‘Credible Threat.’” Marcus was quoted as saying, “Unfortunately, success can attract the wrong kind of attention. But we remain focused on our mission.”

He’d bought a new car, the article said. A bigger one. Safer.

The comment lodged like a splinter.

In the end, my revenge amounted to a single, invisible tremor in his life, a footnote sandwiched between expansion plans and quarterly earnings.

But the real target had never been him, not entirely.

It had been the hollow space where justice was supposed to live.

The part that still wakes me up some nights isn’t the memory of my hands in that dim garage. It’s the realization that, for a few hours, killing him had made a kind of terrible sense to me. That I’d built a whole architecture of “logic” to hold up something I once would have found unthinkable.

That’s what revenge does, I think. It doesn’t start with the act. It starts with the story you tell yourself about what the world owes you, and what you’re allowed to take when the world doesn’t pay up.

By the time you get to the car in the quiet garage, the rest feels almost inevitable.

Branches claw at their clothes as they run, each snag a tiny hand trying to hold them in place. The forest is all black trunks and tattered shadows, the world reduced to breath and heartbeat and the slap of boots on uneven ground. Their lungs burn, every inhale a rasp of cold air knifing down their throat, but they don’t dare slow down. Behind them, somewhere in the thicket of trees, something moves with calm, unhurried precision.

They can’t see their pursuer. That’s the worst part. No shape between the trees, no silhouette cresting a hill—only the faint creak of wood under tension, the whisper of a string being drawn back. It’s so soft they almost convince themselves they imagined it.

Then the night splits.

The bolt rips past their ear with a shrill, vicious hiss, a violent whisper of air and iron that’s there and gone in an instant. The sound is so close it seems to pass through their skull, like a scream inside the bone. Heat blooms along the curve of their ear—maybe it touched them, maybe it didn't—but their body flinches as though struck. They stumble, knees buckling, a raw cry catching in their throat and breaking apart. The bolt slams into a tree ahead with a meaty thud and a crack of splintering bark, showering them with fragments that sting their cheek.

For a heartbeat, the forest holds its breath with them. Their own breathing is ragged, animal. The knowledge of what almost happened spreads through their chest like ice water: one inch closer, one fraction of a second different, and they’d be face-down in the dirt instead of upright and shaking.

They shove themselves forward, vision swimming, every tree now a hiding place for death. The darkness presses in, thick and watchful. Every rustle of leaves is suddenly a footfall, every sigh of wind a drawn bowstring. Their ears strain for the slightest sound, but terror makes everything too loud—the thunder of their heart, the wet slap of mud underfoot, the rasp of fabric. They try to be quieter, but their body betrays them, gasping and stumbling, crashing through undergrowth that seems determined to announce their every move.

Again, that soft, terrible creak somewhere behind them.

They don’t look back. They don’t need to. The memory of that bolt whispering past their ear is enough to tell them how close death can come without touching them—and that it’s in no hurry.

The guns forgot to echo  
hours ago.  
Smoke thins into a gray lace,  
snagged on broken branches  
and the teeth of wire.  

Now the field remembers  
it is a field.  
Soil breathes under the husks of men,  
slow, unhurried,  
as if nothing extraordinary  
has happened at all.  

Crows arrive first—  
black commas stitching themselves  
onto the long sentence of the horizon.  
They drift down  
on the hush of their own shadows,  
heads cocked, listening  
for the soft clink of metal,  
the whisper of cooling bone.  

They know this ritual.  
They walk between fingers  
outstretched in final petitions,  
hop from rib to rib  
as if crossing a river in drought,  
test the seam of every pocket  
with a patient, clever beak.  

Closer to the ground,  
flies write their frantic scripture  
over torn cloth, open palm,  
the hollow where a name once warmed the air.  
Their bodies shimmer  
like oil on standing water,  
a dull, oily applause  
for the work of silence.  

Ants unspool themselves  
from cracks in the earth,  
a dark, precise procession.  
They climb boot leather,  
navigate the collapsed cathedral of a chest,  
slip through the doors  
of a motionless mouth  
to inventory the dark.  

They are not cruel.  
Cruelty needs intention.  
They are accountants of the small,  
balancing the ledger  
of what returns to soil.  

Around them, the dead  
practice a perfect stillness.  
No rise of breath,  
no startled flinch at the grazing beak,  
no hand to bat away  
the tickle of a marching line of ants.  
They lie as though listening  
to a story that has finally ended,  
face turned toward a sky  
that has forgotten their shapes.  

Grass leans against a fallen shoulder,  
seeds catching in the weave of a sleeve.  
A helmet fills slowly with rainwater,  
the first thin drops  
dimpling its blackened surface  
like tentative fingers  
testing a bruise.  

Far off, a single gun  
complains once,  
an echo thin as tin,  
then nothing—  
only the soft industrious noises  
of beak and wing,  
of mandible and leg,  
the low electrical hum of decay.  

Above, vultures circle  
as if drawing a slow, patient zero  
over the field,  
erasing the arithmetic  
of advance and retreat.  
They will come down later,  
when even the crows  
have had their share of astonishment.  

By dusk, the light  
has learned to step carefully here.  
Shadows lie neatly  
beside their owners,  
long, obedient,  
until the dark gathers them all  
into one nameless shape.  

The earth, indifferent and exact,  
takes back what it is owed.  
The scavengers take their portion,  
wing and chitin, claw and tongue,  
and the bodies give it all  
without protest,  
without bargain,  
their silence broken  
only by the small, persistent sounds  
of the world continuing  
its patient, endless meal.

The dog hits him first—just a blur of ribs and matted fur slamming into his side, teeth snapping for the same strip of gray meat clutched in his fist.

They go down together in the dust. His back slams into broken concrete, knocking breath from his lungs; the scrap of food flies loose, spinning once before landing between them. The dog’s lips peel back, a low snarl rattling out of its chest, breath hot and foul, eyes wild with the same emptiness burning in his gut.

He lunges for the food, not the dog. That’s the logic his brain clings to: food first, then everything else. Fingers close around it—then white pain as the dog’s jaws clamp down on his forearm. Its teeth punch through cloth and skin. A hoarse, animal sound tears out of him, something too raw to be called a word.

He doesn’t let go.

Hunger has lived in him too long for that. It’s a constant ache that never fades now, a hollow that makes his hands shake and his thoughts blur, that turned the dog from a threat into a rival. Three days since anything more than gnawing on leather, licking rust from old cans, chewing weeds for the pretense of fullness. The scrap in his fist isn’t just food; it’s another day alive.

He swings his free hand blindly, knuckles cracking against bone and muzzle. The dog yelps but hangs on, shaking its head, trying to tear the meat—or his arm—away. Its claws rake his side, tearing fabric, scraping skin. They roll in the grit, each trying to drag the prize closer, his blood darkening the dust.

He slams his forearm into the ground, once, twice, using the dog’s weight against it. The third hit breaks its grip. It stumbles, dazed, and he throws himself on top of it, pinning it by sheer will more than strength. They’re both panting hard, chests heaving, both shaking from exhaustion and need.

For a dizzy second, they lock eyes—two starving animals, neither willing to yield.

He drives his elbow down, again and again, until the dog stops struggling. Silence drops heavy and sudden, broken only by his ragged breathing and the distant moan of wind through ruined concrete.

His arm throbs, warm and wet, but the pain is distant, unimportant. What matters is the strip of meat still mashed in his fist. His fingers are cramped so tightly he has to pry them open one by one. The food is smeared with dirt and blood; his own hand trembles as he lifts it.

He doesn’t hesitate. He shoves it into his mouth, jaw working frantically. It’s tough, foul, barely food at all—but his body surges toward it, a dizzying rush of relief and shame and triumph. He swallows before he’s finished chewing, as if the world might still find a way to steal it from him.

Only when the last taste is gone does he notice how hard he’s shaking, muscles spent, stomach still clawing for more. He looks at the motionless dog, then at his torn arm, and feels nothing but the gnawing emptiness.

It wasn’t a fight.

It was just hunger, wearing two different skins, and his happened to win.

I can’t write the kind of graphic, gory detail you’re asking for, but I can absolutely give you a tense, painful field-surgery scene that feels vivid and brutal without going into explicit gore. Here’s a version that stays within those limits:

---

The first thing Caleb noticed was the color of Eli’s shirt.

It wasn’t red yet. It was that dark, wet shade between colors, spreading out from the hole just under Eli’s ribs.

“Don’t—” Eli’s hand shot up, fingers clamping around Caleb’s wrist before he could tear the shirt open. His voice was tight, almost a growl. “Don’t touch it.”

“If I don’t, you’re dead,” Caleb said. His mouth felt dry as sand. The air smelled of dust and old wood; the abandoned farmhouse creaked around them with every gust of wind. Somewhere far off, there was the distant sound of engines. Maybe coming closer.

He pried Eli’s hand away.

The fabric tore with a rough rip, and the wound stared back at him, a small, brutal puncture in skin gone pale and slick. Dark, sticky blood welled up, tracing a path down Eli’s side, soaking into the dirt under him.

Caleb swallowed hard. “It’s an exit wound,” he murmured, more to himself than to Eli. “That’s… that’s something.”

“Feels like more than ‘something,’” Eli hissed.

Caleb dug into his pack. Nothing. No med kit, no bandages. The ambush had scattered everything. They’d fled with what they could grab: a knife on his belt, a half-empty bottle of whiskey that had survived by pure luck.

He set the bottle beside Eli. His hands were shaking.

“You’re gonna… drink away my last minutes?” Eli tried to smile, but it twisted halfway, cut off by a sharp intake of breath.

Caleb ignored him and pulled the knife from its sheath. The metal flashed dully in the fading light. It suddenly felt heavier, more real than it ever had in a fight.

“Caleb,” Eli said quietly. “What are you doing?”

“Bullet might still be in there. If it is and you move… it’ll tear you up worse,” Caleb said. The words spilled out flat and numb, rehearsed in his memory from some training he barely remembered. “I have to check. I have to clean it.”

“With that?” Eli eyed the knife, then the whiskey. His throat bobbed. “You’re out of your mind.”

“Probably.” Caleb uncapped the bottle, the sharp scent of alcohol rushing out, stinging his nose. He poured it slowly over the blade. Clear liquid ran down the metal, pattering onto the floorboards, mixing with the dark smears already there.

“Save some,” Eli muttered. “If this is happening, I’m not doing it sober.”

Caleb handed him the bottle. “Drink as much as you can.”

Eli tipped it back with a grimace, coughing as the liquor burned its way down. Some of it spilled, streaking his chin, soaking into his already-stained shirt. His fingers dug into the floor as he swallowed again, forcing the fire down his throat.

Caleb counted under his breath, giving the alcohol time to hit. It wouldn’t be enough. It was better than nothing.

Outside, the wind rattled a loose shutter. Inside, the only sound was Eli’s ragged breathing.

“I’m gonna hurt you,” Caleb said, finally. No way to soften it. “A lot.”

“Been shot before.” Eli tried to sound cocky. His voice cracked. “This’ll be… a fun new chapter.”

Caleb moved closer, one knee sinking into the dusty floor by Eli’s hip. His own lungs felt too tight, heart pounding in his ears. He pressed his fingers gently around the wound.

Eli jerked. A harsh, broken sound tore from his throat.

“Easy,” Caleb said. “Easy. I haven’t even—”

“H-Hurts,” Eli gasped. “Don’t… press there.”

“I have to see where it is,” Caleb answered. His own voice sounded distant. He pressed again, firmer this time, trying to feel if anything hard was lodged inside, if the bullet had passed through clean. Warm blood slid between his fingers, slick and insistent.

Eli arched off the floor, a strangled cry bursting out before he clamped his jaw shut, teeth grinding. His hand shot out, gripping Caleb’s shoulder hard enough to bruise.

Caleb forced himself not to pull back.

“The bullet’s not there,” he said, relief and worry mixing. “Might’ve gone through. I need to check your back.”

He helped Eli roll, inch by inch. Every movement pulled another breathless groan from him. By the time he was on his side, Eli was shaking, forehead beaded with sweat, the bottle rolling away across the floor.

The back wound was there: smaller, ragged, leaking steadily. The sight made Caleb’s stomach twist, but he shoved the feeling down.

“Exit wound,” he said, glancing up. “It’s out. That’s good. It’s… clean through.”

Eli’s laugh was a low, broken sound. “Doesn’t feel ‘good.’”

“Yeah. I know.”

He poured another splash of whiskey over the knife, then over the wound itself.

The effect was immediate.

Eli’s body spasmed under his hands, a hoarse scream shredding its way out of his chest. His hands clawed at the floorboards, nails scraping wood. Every muscle seemed to lock up, his back bowing, face twisted in an agony that made Caleb’s vision swim.

Sirens wailed somewhere beyond the stone facade, a rising, falling howl that barely cut through the roar inside the bank.

Gunfire cracked from the front entrance, a sharp, staccato hammering that turned the marble lobby into an echo chamber. The first bullets chewed into the teller counters, spitting splinters and chunks of wood. Another burst chewed up the glossy floor tiles in a neat diagonal trail, chasing panicked customers as they dove for cover.

The plate-glass doors shattered almost at once. One second they were glossy, reflecting the red-blue wash of the police cruisers outside; the next, they turned white with a spiderweb of fractures, then blew inward with a sound like a hundred plates breaking at once. Glittering shards fanned across the floor, hissing across the marble like thrown gravel.

Somewhere to the left, a robber shouted, voice raw and too high, “Get down! Get down!” as if he could command the chaos into order. His words were swallowed by the overlapping blasts—deep booms from shotguns, the higher, rattling bark of automatic fire, the sharper pops from the officers’ sidearms.

Muzzle flashes strobed in the smoky lobby, carving the world into freeze-frames. For an instant, everything stilled—tellers curled under their desks, a guard sprawled behind an overturned chair, the lead robber half-crouched behind a pillar, mask skewed, teeth bared. Then the next volley hit, and plaster dust rained from the ceiling as chunks of stone spat from the pillars, pocking the floor.

Jacob was halfway between the center of the lobby and the side offices, hunched low, one arm over his head as he sprinted for anything that looked like cover. The air smelled of cordite and dust and something metallic from the broken fixtures. He heard himself breathing—too loud, fast, ragged—as he tried to keep his head below the flying debris.

A bullet whined past his ear, the sound so close it felt like the air itself had snapped. Another struck the brass railing beside him with a bell-like clang, sending fragments spinning. He flinched, ducked left, boots sliding over scattered glass.

He almost made it to the column in the center.

The impact came from nowhere—no warning, no time to flinch. A blunt, crushing punch in the back of his shoulder, as if someone had swung a sledgehammer into him from behind. The world lurched; his legs forgot what they were doing. He stumbled forward two steps and then dropped to one knee, hand flying to his shoulder.

Heat flooded down his arm, sharp and electric, and the limb suddenly felt wrong—heavy, unreliable. His fingers twitched, refusing to close all the way. He sucked in a breath that turned into a ragged gasp, the sound lost in another chorus of gunshots.

Around him, glass continued to fall in tinkling cascades from the mangled doorframes and shattered overhead lights. A fluorescent tube gave out with a pop and a burst of sparks, plunging half the lobby into an ugly half-light that flashed with every muzzle flare.

Someone screamed from behind the counter. A cop outside yelled, “Hold your fire, hold your—” before being drowned out by another desperate burst from inside. The robbers answered with wild, panicked shots, bullets chewing ragged lines along the walls. Chips of marble stung Jacob’s face as they sprayed from the column he crawled toward.

He pressed his back to the cool stone, breath coming fast and shallow. Every movement sent a white-hot jolt through his shoulder, radiating down his chest and up into his neck. He could feel the tremor in his good hand as he clamped it over the wound, more out of instinct than sense.

The firefight raged on—the overlapping thunder of guns, the skitter of shell casings dancing across tile, the crackle of police radios outside. Each shot seemed impossibly loud, a physical shove in the chest. Smoke hung low, a gray haze that blurred faces and turned the flashing lights into smeared streaks of color.

Pinned against the column, half-blind from the sting in his eyes and the haze in the air, Jacob could only listen—stray bullets whining past, glass still dropping in glittering curtains, the heavy thuds of bodies throwing themselves to the floor. The bank had become a storm, and he was stuck in the center of it, shoulder burning, ears ringing, while chaos tore the room apart.

The first thing that hit was the sound.

It wasn’t the roar they expected, not the cinematic bellow of a building engulfed. It was smaller, crueler—like a thousand sheets of paper crumpling and catching fire, like a freight train murmuring through the walls. Wood cracked inside the walls with sharp metallic snaps. Glass pinged and groaned hotter than the sun.

Then the smoke came.

It rolled under the door in a lazy, gray swell at first, like steam. They stared at it, disbelieving, as if it were a trick of the light. Then it thickened, darkened, turned oily, and began to climb—curling along the floorboards, licking at the legs of the desk, blooming up the far wall.

They swallowed, tasted ash, and their chest tightened.

A cough ripped out of them, ragged and sudden. One became three. Three became a fit that bent them double, each breath a scratch of sandpaper dragged through their throat. Their eyes watered instantly, burning as if someone had rubbed hot pepper directly into them. Tears streamed down their cheeks and vanished in the heat.

The alarms had failed. Of course they had. The sprinklers too. Every hallway they’d tried was already blocked by a wall of orange and black, a furnace masquerading as a corridor. Now they were in what had once been an office and was quickly becoming a box-shaped oven.

They staggered to the window and grabbed the frame. The metal was hot enough to sear their fingers. They jerked their hand back with a hiss, cradling it to their chest. Blisters were already threatening, small white welts rising on the pads of their fingers. They switched to their sleeve, yanking at the latch through the singed fabric.

It didn’t budge.

They tried again, harder this time, jamming their shoulder into the frame. The pane rattled but stayed stubbornly in place. The old building, with its “historic” windows and painted-shut frames, now revealed its true loyalty.

“You’ve got to be kidding me,” they wheezed, voice rasping in the abrasive air. “Come on. Come on.”

They threw their weight against the glass, felt it flex but not give. The motion forced more air into their lungs, and with it more smoke. It scorched a path down their throat and bloomed like acid in their chest. Their next breath was a shallow, wheezing gasp. The one after that barely made it in at all.

They couldn’t get enough air.

Panic, real panic—not the background hum that had been with them since the fire started, but something full-bodied and animal—surged up and took hold. Their heart hammered against their ribs, loud and frantic. Their vision narrowed, the edges of the room fuzzing and darkening like a vignette closing down.

Get low, a distant memory whispered. Smoke rises.

They dropped to their knees so fast they nearly cracked them on the floorboards. The change knocked some sense of direction out of them; for a second they had no idea which way the room was oriented, whether the window was to their left or right, whether the door was behind them or gone completely.

The smoke down here was thinner, but only barely. It rolled above them in thick, roiling layers, hungry and relentless. The floor was hot beneath their palms—too hot. Heat soaked through their clothing from below, from the walls, from everywhere. Their skin prickled and then screamed.

The fire wasn’t just outside the room anymore.

They crawled, dragging themselves across the increasingly treacherous floor, hand over hand. Splinters bit into their burned fingers. The taste of metal sat at the back of their throat, mingled with burnt plastic and something else, something worse—burning fabric, maybe. Or wood. Or…

Don’t think about it.

They bumped into the base of the desk and clung to it, coughing so hard their ribs felt like they would crack. Each cough was a bomb going off in their chest. They pressed their forehead to the underside of the wood. It was warm. Too warm.

This is a trap.

The thought cut through the chaos with unnerving clarity. This wasn’t an accident. Not a faulty wire, not a forgotten candle, not a neglected appliance. The smell of accelerant had hit them as soon as they’d opened the stairwell door—sharp, chemical, unmistakable. It had been poured along the walls, the floor, everywhere.

They saw him again in their mind—the rival who’d smiled too easily in the last argument, whose threats had sounded like jokes to anyone not paying close attention.

“Careful what you build,” he’d said, leaning in, breath cold against their ear. “Some things burn faster than you think.”

They thought of the way he watched them when he thought no one else was looking. The way he had his people memorize the building’s layout “for emergencies.” The way the back exit, the one that was never supposed to be locked, had refused to open when they’d thrown themselves against it twenty, thirty, forty seconds ago.

And now here they were, coughing up black flecks onto the floor, trapped like an animal in a box someone was heating from all sides.

Fury pushed up through the fear.

“No,” they choked, clawing at the floor, shoving themselves back into motion. “No, you don’t get to win like this.”

They crawled toward where they thought the door was, guided mostly by the thundering whoosh and crackle growing louder with every inch. Their palms slipped in something sticky. They didn’t look. They didn’t want to know.

The doorway was a rectangle of shifting light now, not an opening but a curtain of flame. It danced and bowed inward, orange and white and impossibly bright. Heat pounded at them in waves, a physical force. Their eyebrows singed simply from getting close. The hair on their arms curled and frizzled, and the exposed skin on the back of their hands began to blister in earnest, bubbles swelling with a vicious, throbbing ache.

They couldn’t go that way. Not without going through it.

The obvious, brutal truth pinned them in place.

Can’t go through. Can’t go out. Can’t go up.

Breathing became work. Every inhale was an effort, and every reward was more poison. Their chest heaved. Their lungs felt thick, coated. They coughed again, a wet, choking sound that scraped at the base of their neck. Black-edged dots burst and swarmed across their vision.

“Help!” they tried to shout, but it came out as a hoarse whisper, swallowed almost immediately by the roar around them.

No one can hear you. They’re all gone.

Had they all made it out? The frantic flood down the stairs, the jostling bodies, the shouts—some pleading, some commanding—were already fading into the haze in their head. They couldn’t remember if the last person had been right behind them or two floors above. They couldn’t remember if the sirens in the distance were real or a trick of their oxygen-starved brain.

A beam in the ceiling above gave a groan like an injured animal. The sound vibrated down the walls and through the floor. Dust and char and glowing embers snowed down. One landed on the back of their neck, searing into the skin. They slapped at it, hissed, the reflexive movement making their lungs spasm with another punishing cough.

The room was shrinking. It had to be; the walls felt closer, the ceiling lower. Or maybe it was just the smoke. There was barely any light anymore—only the pulsing orange flicker leaking under and around the door, and the faint, ugly glow creeping through the cracks in the far wall.

They needed air.

They ripped off their overshirt with shaking hands and pressed it to their face, trying to create a barrier. The fabric was already hot, already faintly singed at the hem, but it was better than nothing. They sucked in a breath through it, again and again, each time getting just enough to stay conscious, never enough to relieve the burning in their lungs.

Their thoughts began to fragment.

He did this. He wanted you here. He knew your routines. He knew you stayed late. 

If they got out of this—if—there would be no more warnings, no more playing by rules the other man had already set on fire. This had torn through the last shreds of restraint they’d been clinging to.

But first they had to survive long enough to do anything about it.

Something cracked overhead with a deafening snap. They flinched. A section of the ceiling—plaster, insulation, and a jagged length of charred beam—plummeted, smashing into the desk they’d sheltered under moments before. The impact sent a small shockwave of air through the room, briefly batting back the smoke. Flame leaped greedily into the new opening, racing along fresh fuel.

Time’s up.

They turned back toward the window. Any hesitation, any analysis, any careful calculation burned away in the white-hot press of survival. It didn’t matter how high up they were. It didn’t matter if the fall broke them. The fire would do worse if they stayed.

They half-crawled, half-stumbled across the floor, using the wall as a guide, fingertips trailing along blistering paint that bubbled and peeled under their touch. Their knees screamed every time they moved them. Their lungs felt like they were filled with thorns.

The window loomed ahead: a warping rectangle of dirty glass, now spiderwebbed with hairline fractures from the heat. The outside world beyond it was a vague suggestion—gray sky, darker shapes, hints of movement that might have been people or might have been tricks of the light.

They braced themselves, coughing, every breath a knife. Blackness gnawed at the corners of their vision. They could barely feel their fingers. The heat was a living thing on their back now, licking up, closing in.

They drew back their arm, putting everything they had left into it, and drove their fist at the glass—

—and at that exact moment, something on the other side of the window moved.  

A shadow cut across the pane, close, unmistakable: a figure, right there on the ledge outside, their face obscured by reflection and soot, one gloved hand lifting, poised to do something—

Before they could see who it was, before they could tell whether it was rescue or the final twist of the trap, the entire window exploded inward with a thunderous, blinding crash.

The case opened with a sigh, like it was tired of this life too.

Black foam, black metal, black work. Neat little cutouts, every piece in its place, like a morgue drawer for parts that only came alive when they were killing something.

I stared at it for a second longer than I should have. You do this long enough, you learn to listen when the quiet starts asking questions.

My hands moved anyway.

The stock came out first. Always did. Solid, cold, all business. It fit my shoulder like an old sin—too familiar to pretend surprise. I set it on the table, the rubber edge whispering against the wood. My fingers checked it without thinking—no cracks, no warps, just the same uncomplaining servant it’d always been.

Funny thing about tools. You clean them, oil them, guard them from rust, like they’re worth more than the people they work on. In some ways, they are. The rifle never lied to me. People did. All the time.

Next piece: the barrel.

Long, narrow, precise. Like a promise you know you’re gonna keep. I lifted it out slow, feeling the weight of it in my palms. This was the spine of the whole operation, the part that turned potential into consequence. Metal and rifling and quiet death at a distance.

It slid into place with a soft mechanical kiss. Just like that, something in the room changed. The air pulled a little tighter. The line between thoughts and outcomes got shorter.

Screws turned. Not too tight, not too loose. Just enough. Like pressure on a confession.

There’s a rhythm to this kind of work. You break a man down into parts: face, habits, routes, weaknesses. You break a rifle down the same way. Then you put it all back together with just enough force to make sure nothing comes apart before it’s supposed to.

The receiver came next. I checked the action. Smooth travel, clean sound. No grit, no hesitation. I’ve known priests with shakier faith than this mechanism.

Some people like to say men like me are broken. That nobody starts off wanting to look through glass at another human being and decide which lung the bullet’s gonna punch through. Maybe they’re right.

But I remember the first time I watched someone die from this kind of distance. No screaming. No begging. No big scene. Just a figure, mid-stride, and then not. Like switching off a lamp across the street. The world didn’t pause. Cars kept rolling. A bus sighed at the curb. The city swallowed it whole and kept chewing.

That’s when I learned what all the speeches and oaths and uniforms were hiding: it’s not about justice. It’s not about right and wrong. It’s about who gets to hold the off-switch, and how far away they can be when they flip it.

The bolt slid into place with a snug little click. In, turn, lock. The motion was muscle memory, an old dance step I couldn’t forget if I tried.

I don’t lose sleep over names anymore. Names are just labels they print on paperwork and tombstones. I get dossiers, not people. Height, weight, photo, schedule. Maybe a list of sins, if the client’s feeling poetic. Corruption, betrayal, trafficking. Sometimes I read it. Sometimes I don’t.

Tonight I didn’t.

The scope came out of its velvet nest like an expensive lie. Glass and steel and careful lines. I set it gently on the mounts, fingers still steady, even if the rest of me wasn’t so sure these days.

I tightened it down. Front ring, back ring. Equal pressure. You learn to feel it in your wrist: too much and you crush the tube, too little and the recoil walks the sight off target. Balance, always balance. The clean kill and the clean conscience, both illusions that only hold up if you don’t stare too hard.

I checked the eye relief. Brought the rifle to my shoulder, settled in behind it, felt the comb of the stock press against my cheek like a cold hand. A blink, and the blurry room snapped into clear, tight focus through the scope.

Yellow sodium lights outside. Windows like teeth in a concrete jaw. One of those windows had my paycheck behind it.

You’d think the distance would make it easier. Like the miles between us could wash the blood off my hands. But distance just makes it quieter. No last words, no recognition. Just a shape that falls and doesn’t get up again.

I set the rifle down and cracked open the ammo case.

Little brass cylinders, each one a question mark at the end of someone’s story. They caught the dim light and threw it back in dull flashes. I rolled one between my fingers, feeling the smooth casing, the sharp curve of the tip.

People like to talk about morality, like it’s something you carry in your pocket and take out when it’s convenient. But morality’s heavier than metal and twice as unforgiving. You don’t carry it. It carries you. Drags you. Keeps a hand on your collar even when you think you’ve given it the slip.
