The alley was narrow enough that the fire escape shadows crossed from one brick wall to the other, like a cage made of rust and darkness. Rainwater dripped from a busted gutter, collecting in a long puddle that reflected the single flickering security light at the far end.

Mack got there first. He paced, hands jammed deep into his coat pockets, shoulders hunched. Every few seconds he glanced toward the street, then back to the dead end behind him, measuring both distances.

Eli arrived late, walking fast, breathing a little hard like he’d been running just before he rounded the corner. His hoodie was soaked through, the hem dragging a faint trail of dirty rain across the concrete.

“You’re late,” Mack muttered.

“You’re jumpy,” Eli shot back, but his eyes didn’t quite meet Mack’s. They swept the alley instead—the fire escape, the dumpsters, the mouth of the street—like he expected someone else to be there.

Mack tilted his head toward the small duffel at Eli’s side. “That it?”

“Yeah. That it?” Eli nodded at Mack’s coat pocket.

Mack hesitated a fraction too long, then pulled a plastic-wrapped bundle from inside his coat. Eli’s face tightened at the pause, and Mack noticed.

“Relax,” Mack said. “Nobody followed me.”

“Funny. I don’t remember asking.”

They stood facing each other in the middle of the alley, the smell of old garbage and wet asphalt filling the silence. Somewhere a bottle clinked as it rolled, nudged by the wind.

“On three,” Mack said. “We both show. No games.”

“Fine. Three.”

They counted together, but neither trusted the other enough to wait for the end of the count. On “two,” both of them started moving—Mack lifting the bundle higher, Eli dragging the duffel closer—but their timing clashed. Eli flinched like he’d been caught, yanked the bag back a bit, and in that tiny motion Mack thought he saw something else—hesitation, calculation.

“What’s the problem?” Mack’s voice sharpened.

“No problem. You’re the one screwing up the count,” Eli said, but his hand tightened around the strap.

Mack stepped closer. The alley suddenly felt smaller, the walls leaning in. He noticed the bulge at Eli’s waistband under the hoodie, just to the right. Not a gun shape—flatter, shorter.

“I said we’re doing this clean,” Mack said. “You’re packing something?”

Eli’s jaw worked. “You think I’m walking in here empty when you’ve got half the city wanting your head?”

Mack’s free hand twitched. “Show me.”

“Deal first,” Eli said. “You hand yours over, I hand mine. Then we both walk. No reason for this to turn into something else.”

They stood too long in that stalemate. The rain at the alley’s mouth thickened into a curtain, hiding the street from view. The flickering light hummed louder, as if the whole world had shrunk to the buzz of electricity and their unsteady breathing.

Mack made the next move, just a half step, but Eli misread it. He jerked back, his right hand disappearing under his hoodie in one quick, practiced motion.

The flash of metal came next—a short knife, not gleaming, just a dull shimmer in the half-light—but Mack saw it as clearly as if it had burst into flame.

“Whoa,” Mack barked, stumbling back. “Put it down.”

“Drop the bag,” Eli snapped. His voice wavered around the edges, like he was fighting his own fear. “On the ground. Now.”

Behind the anger in Eli’s eyes, Mack saw panic. That was worse than hatred. Panic did stupid things.

Mack raised his empty hand, palm out. The bundle in the other dipped slightly. “Think about what you’re doing,” he said. “You pull that, there’s no going back. Cops find us both. No deal. No money. Nothing.”

Eli’s breathing had gone rough. “I know what I’m doing. You were going to stiff me. I can see it all over you.”

Mack realized anything he said next would sound like a lie. So instead of talking, he let the bundle drop. It hit the wet concrete with a dull thud.

“There. You want it, take it,” Mack said. “Just keep that thing where it is.”

For a second, it looked like Eli might. His attention flickered toward the bundle at their feet. That single glance gave Mack a window.

He moved.

He lunged low, aiming for Eli’s knife hand, trying to jam his forearm against Eli’s wrist and drive it away. The alley erupted into sudden, chaotic motion—feet slipping in the wet, shoulders colliding with brick, the hard knock of bone against bone.

Eli swore, stumbling as Mack hit him. The knife hand jerked upward instead of outward, catching Mack in the shoulder with a sudden, sharp impact.

The sensation was startling more than anything—a blunt, concentrated force that felt at first like he’d rammed into the corner of a door. There was a tight, compressing shock, then a strange spreading warmth that didn’t match the cold rain soaking his coat. His arm went weak for a heartbeat, like it had been unplugged.

He didn’t look; he didn’t dare. Focusing on it would slow him down.

Adrenaline took over. The world narrowed to Eli’s wrist, the knife, the slick concrete under their shoes. Mack grabbed for Eli’s forearm with both hands, ignoring the way his right side suddenly felt heavy, like he was dragging an extra weight attached to his shoulder.

They slammed against the wall. Brick scraped Mack’s back through his coat, rough and unyielding. Eli tried to wrench his arm free, the knife blade jerking dangerously close to both of them. The edges of Mack’s vision tightened at each sharp movement from his shoulder, a pulsing throb that grew more noticeable now that his initial shock was fading.

He twisted, shoving Eli’s arm up and back. The knife rattled against metal as it scraped the fire escape railing. Eli hissed and tried to drive his knee into Mack’s gut, but only clipped his thigh.

The more they struggled, the more that strange spreading sensation in Mack’s shoulder intensified. It wasn’t a single point of pain; it was as if the joint itself had turned into a knot that was being pulled tighter with every movement. The surrounding skin felt hot, then oddly cold under the damp fabric of his coat. Each breath made the area flare, a dull, insistent ache that layered itself beneath the frantic rush of the fight.

Mack finally managed to slam Eli’s wrist against the wall. The knife jolted in his grip. Mack used his weight, pressing in, feeling a trembling weakness in his own arm, like the strength there was draining faster than it should.

“Drop it!” Mack shoved Eli’s arm up again. “Drop the knife!”

Eli’s eyes were wild, breath ragged, but the resistance in his wrist faltered. The knife slipped from his fingers and clattered to the ground, bouncing once before skidding across the wet concrete and landing just out of reach of both of them.

For a moment, neither moved. The only sounds were their heavy breathing and the distant hiss of rain. Mack’s shoulder throbbed in time with his heartbeat, a steady, firm pulse that made his fingers tingle and his grip feel unreliable.

Eli tried to twist away, but now the desperation was leaking out of him. Without the knife, he seemed smaller somehow. Mack pushed him back one last time, then staggered away, letting him go.

Eli stared at him, then at the knife on the ground, then at the bundle still lying between them.

“This didn’t have to happen,” Mack said, his voice rough. He kept his injured side angled away, not wanting Eli to see how his arm hung slightly, how careful he was about moving it.

Eli swallowed. “You’re hurt.”

“I’m standing,” Mack said. “You going to try for that knife again?”

Eli looked at it, then at Mack’s face. Whatever he saw there made his shoulders sink.

“No,” he muttered. “No. Forget it.”

He took a step back, hands raised now for real, palms open, fingers spread. Then another step. Then he turned and walked toward the alley’s mouth, his pace just short of a run.

Mack let him go.

He stood alone as Eli’s footsteps faded into the rain. The adrenaline that had been holding him together began to thin, leaving behind the clearer outline of what his body had been trying to tell him.

His shoulder felt tight and hot under the fabric, and every small movement drew a deeper ache from the joint, like a bruise being pressed again and again. The air on his skin through the damp coat felt cooler there, sharper somehow, and the muscle around it seemed reluctant to cooperate, as if it needed conscious thought to do anything at all.

He kept his breathing shallow to avoid the sharp spikes that came with deeper inhales, then carefully bent—favoring his good side—to pick up the dropped bundle. The act of leaning forward pulled at the injured area, sending a firm, radiating discomfort across his upper chest and back. Not sharp enough to stop him, but enough to make him move slowly, deliberately, aware of every inch the joint shifted.

Straightening was worse. The effort made his vision briefly narrow, the edges going a little dim, and a faint, throbbing pulse beat in time with his heart behind the injury, as if each beat were knocking on the same sore spot again and again.

He stayed very still until it eased back to something he could manage. Then he held the bundle in his good hand, pressed his other palm lightly over the front of his shoulder, and walked out of the alley into the rain, each step jostling that tender, protesting area just enough to remind him of what had almost happened—and what still might, if the night didn’t start going his way.

Rain turned the alley into a throat that couldn’t quite clear itself.

Dirty water ran in sluggish streams between the brick walls, pulling cigarette butts, torn flyers, and bottle caps along with it. Every few seconds a drop fell from the iron fire escape overhead, landing with the same soft, steady plink on the overturned trash can by the body.

The body was lying on its side, almost neatly, like it had been laid out for a photograph and then forgotten.

I stepped under the crime scene tape, the yellow plastic slick with rain and alley grime, and felt the wet concrete suck at the soles of my shoes. The air was thick—rotting cabbage from a busted trash bag, sour beer leaking from split bottles, and under all of it the faint, metallic sweetness of fresh blood cooling in the night air.

“Time of discovery?” I didn’t bother looking at the uniform who answered.

“Twenty-two thirty-one. Guy from the bar found him when he came out to smoke. Nobody touched anything.”

The bar’s back door was a rectangle of sick yellow light about fifteen feet away, held open by a broken cinder block. Music thumped faintly through the wall—bass, distant and hollow—as if it were underwater. Out here, it was just the rain and the hum of a neon sign struggling to stay alive.

I crouched beside the body. The knees of my slacks soaked up the alley water instantly, a cold line of damp crawling up my thighs.

Male. Mid-thirties. Dark hair shaved close, rain flattening it against his skull. Eyes open, filmed, catching the streetlight in a dull gray sheen. He was staring at the cracked bricks opposite him, at the black mildew threaded between them, at nothing.

The blood hadn’t had time to fully darken yet. It spilled from under his ribs in a wide smear that reached toward the center of the alley, a dark fan that the rain hadn’t quite managed to break apart. The spreading edges feathered into pink as the water cut through it, forming little rivers that ran toward the nearest drain.

I leaned closer. The smell of iron got stronger, pushing back the garbage and cheap beer. It was the kind of scent that clung to your throat, made the back of your tongue taste like pennies. I noted it and let it pass. Sensation, cataloged, dismissed.

“Roll him yet?” I asked.

“Waiting on you,” the uniform said.

“Don’t. Leave him how he dropped.”

I slid a gloved hand under the slack jaw and tilted his head just enough to see. A split at the corner of the mouth, faint bruising already surfacing along the cheekbone. He’d taken at least one hit before he went down. The lips were going pale, frosting at the edges in the night air.

The main damage was lower.

His shirt—white once, now more a mottled gray—was torn open from the side seam. The fabric clung to his skin, plastered there by a wet sheen that reflected the cold alley lights. The wound was hidden, but the outline of it was obvious: a jagged, spreading bloom under the cloth. The knife had gone in somewhere below the ribs, left side. From the width of the stain, it hadn’t been gentle.

I pressed lightly around the soaked area with two fingers, feeling the texture beneath the shirt. The cotton squelched softly. The blood had thinned with rain, the surface cooling fast, but the skin under the fabric was still warm. The heat bled up into my glove, steady and fading.

“Single entry, looks like,” I said. “He bled out right here.”

The uniform shifted somewhere behind me. His boots scuffed in a shallow puddle. “Christ.”

“Don’t take the Lord’s name in vain on my crime scene,” I said, flat. “You’re fogging the air enough as it is.”

He pulled in a breath, held it. The alley got quieter.

I followed the trail backward. Near the wall—about three feet from the body—there were drier streaks, duller in color, where blood had hit brick before the rain got to it. It had spattered up in an angled spray, droplets in a loose fan, some as small as pinpricks, others fat, running together. Medium velocity. Not the kind of thing you got from a slow bleed.

He took the hit there, I thought. Pressed against the wall, then slid down. The pattern looked like the ghost of that moment: the jerk forward, the exhale of a life he hadn’t meant to lose.

The rain tapped at the shallow pools of blood on the ground, dimpling them, breaking their surfaces into shifting black mirrors. Streetlight and neon wavered in the reflection, rippling in reds and blues.

I straightened. My knees popped in protest. The cold had a way of creeping into joints faster out here, where the wind funneled between buildings and clawed at whatever skin it could find. I zipped my coat up another inch and looked at the alley itself.

Narrow. Fifteen feet, maybe, between the bar and the opposite wall of the adjoining building. A rusted dumpster on one side, overflowing with black bags slick with rain. On the other, a stack of damp cardboard boxes sagging into themselves. A fire escape ladder hung just above arm’s reach, dripping steadily. Somebody had tagged the brick in flaking white spray paint, letters so stylized they were almost abstract. The paint bled in the wet, streaking down like it was crying.

No fresh scuff marks on the walls besides the blood. No skid of rubber soles where someone might’ve run and slipped. No dropped wallet, no phone glinting in the puddles. If anything had been left behind, it had either washed toward the drain or been picked up already. The alley held onto secrets, but not the small, loose ones.

I knelt again, this time at the victim’s feet. His shoes were cheap dress loafers, soles worn almost smooth. A thin line of mud marked the edge of his pant legs—different color than the alley muck. Clay-brown, not city-black. He hadn’t spent the whole night here.

I touched his wrist, more habit than necessity. No pulse, of course. Skin cool now, but not gone cold. He hadn’t been dead long. The watch there—a cheap knockoff that tried to look expensive—had stopped, water pooled under the cracked crystal. 10:17 glared up at me, meaningless.

“Who’s our John Doe?” I asked.

“Name’s Leonard Pike,” the uniform said. Paper rustled as he checked his notebook. “Wallet was in his inside jacket pocket. Driver’s license, couple credit cards, sixty-eight bucks cash. No phone.”

“No phone,” I repeated. “Either he came out here to smoke and decided he didn’t want anyone calling while he talked… or someone else didn’t want us seeing who he was talking to.”

The uniform didn’t answer. Behind me, I could hear him trying not to look too long at the body. You always knew the new ones—they stared, then forced themselves to look away, then stared again. Like if they found the right angle, the scene would make more sense.

I’d long stopped looking for that angle.

I shifted his hand gently, lifting it by the fingers. Under the nails, faint crescents of dark. Not blood—dirt. Packed in so tight it had resisted the rain. The fingertips themselves were roughened, callused. Not office hands. Somebody who did real work, or had, once.

His other hand was empty, curled inward, as if it had been reaching for something that wasn’t there.

No defensive wounds. No jagged tears across the palms, no cuts along the forearms. Either the first hit had been good enough that he hadn’t had much left in him to fight, or he’d known the person and never seen it coming. I filed both options away.

The medical examiner’s van rumbled up at the mouth of the alley, headlights sweeping across the wet brick and turning every raindrop into a short, bright line. Doors slammed. Voices murmured. One of them laughed—too loud, too bright for a place like this—and then cut it off quickly, as if the sound itself had been indecent.

I stood, peeled off my damp gloves, and pulled a fresh pair from my pocket. The latex snapped softly as I worked my fingers in, the sound oddly cheerful against the low hush of the rain.

“Doc’ll take it from here in a minute,” I said. “Before that, get me a perimeter canvas. Anyone who’s been through here in the last two hours, I want their names. Bartender, barback, the guy who found him, the guy who thinks he heard something, the woman who’s sure she saw something out of the corner of her eye. All of them. And lock down that back door—nobody goes in or out without talking to us first.”

The uniform nodded, relieved to have something to do that didn’t involve standing in the shadow of the corpse. His footsteps splashed away toward the bar’s back entrance.

For a moment, it was just me and Leonard Pike and the rain.

I watched the water worry at the blood, thinning it, moving it along inch by inch toward the rusted grate at the alley’s end. In an hour, most of it would be gone. By morning, some delivery truck would back in here, its tires leaving wide, clean arcs where a man had died. By tomorrow night, somebody would come out to smoke where Pike had bled out, complaining about the cold, wondering why the alley smelled a little off.

The city didn’t remember. That was my job.

I took one last look at the wound under the wet shirt, how it had spread, how far the blood had traveled. I pictured the angle of the knife, the distance between killer and victim. Too close for anything but personal.

I turned away as the M.E. team came in with their gurney and their rolling stainless-steel kit. Behind me, latex snapped again, tape crackled, zippers whispered. Another chorus to the same old song.

“Let’s move,” I said to no one in particular, and stepped back into the damp neon glow at the alley’s mouth, already thinking about the questions that needed asking and the lies I was going to hear.

Heat pressed against them like a living thing, at first a searing sting, then a suffocating, all‑consuming presence. Their skin felt too tight for their body, as if it had shrunk a size too small in an instant. An angry prickling crawled along their arms and neck, turning rapidly into a deep, burning throb that made it impossible to tell where one patch of pain ended and another began. The sensation built and built, stretching the skin until every tiny movement sent a hot, needling shock racing through their nerves. It wasn’t just on the surface; it felt as though the heat were sinking in, burrowing down, trying to set muscle and bone alight.

Breathing became a desperate, frantic task. The air itself felt thick, heavy with smoke and heat, like trying to inhale from the mouth of an oven. Each breath scraped down their throat, dry and hot and useless. Their lungs spasmed, begging for air that no longer seemed to exist. Panic rose sharp and choking in its own right—faster than the flames, faster than the pain. Their chest tightened, a brutal, clenching band that made it impossible to draw in more than a shallow gasp. Sound narrowed to the roar of fire and their own ragged coughing; sight blurred at the edges as their body screamed for oxygen. Every instinct howled at them to move, to run, to find clean air, but the heat, the smoke, and the tearing burn in their skin turned every step into a fight against a rising, suffocating darkness.

Dust hangs in the air like a fog, turning the bright colors of the market into a washed-out, gray smear. Stalls that a moment ago were crowded with fruit, cloth, and small everyday things now lie twisted and broken, wood splintered, metal frames buckled and torn. A cart lies on its side, oranges scattered across the ground and crushed underfoot prints and debris.

The blast has blown out windows and torn awnings from their hooks. Chunks of concrete and shattered glass are everywhere, sparkling faintly in the settling light. The smell is sharp and bitter—smoke, burned plastic, and something heavier that no one wants to name.

People lie where they fell. Some are motionless, sprawled in unnatural positions among the rubble and toppled stalls. Others sit dazed on the ground, clothes torn and faces coated in dust, staring at their own hands as if they don’t quite recognize them. A few stumble around in shock, calling names that no one answers.

Shoes are scattered without owners. A child’s backpack lies unzipped in the middle of the street, its contents—an exercise book, a pencil case, a small toy—spread out in a neat arc as if carefully arranged, though they were flung there in an instant. A phone rings from somewhere under a broken table and keeps ringing, unanswered.

For a moment, after the roar of the explosion, there is a strange, oppressive stillness. People’s ears ring; the world seems muted, sounds coming through as if underwater. The usual marketplace noise—haggling voices, clatter of carts, the hum of conversation—is gone. In its place is a hollow quiet, broken only by the crackle of small fires and the distant wail of sirens drawing nearer.

Then, slowly, sound begins to return: a low moan from someone curled beside a wall, a choked sob, a voice shouting for help. But underneath it all, the silence of those who will never answer remains, heavy and absolute, settling over the ruined market like another layer of dust.

Chains rattled as they settled against the prisoner’s wrists, the iron ring in the stone wall cold against his cheek. Wind worried at the edges of the watching crowd’s cloaks, but no one spoke. Somewhere behind him, boots scuffed on gravel, the sound of leather being uncoiled crackling in the air.

“Count,” the captain said.

The whip hissed as it cut through the stillness, a sharp intake of breath from the world itself. Then it landed with a flat, brutal report, like a branch snapped over a knee. Pain slammed into his back a heartbeat later—searing, immediate, all‑consuming—forcing the air from his lungs in a rough, strangled sound.

“One,” he managed, voice already shaking.

The second stroke came faster. He heard it a moment before it fell: that thin whistle, taut and merciless, followed by another heavy crack against flesh. His body lurched forward, chains biting into his skin as he tried not to sag, tried to keep his feet beneath him.

“Two.”

Heat spread across his back, a burning line that seemed to pulse with his heartbeat. He focused on the stone in front of him, the small chips and weathered grooves, anything but the gathering throbbing ache that made it hard to draw a full breath.

Again the whistle, again the crash of impact. His fingers curled into fists; the taste of iron rose at the back of his throat as he bit down on a cry.

“Three,” he forced out.

Murmurs rippled through the watchers. He heard them dimly, as if from underwater. Each strike blurred into the next—sound, shock, and the dull roar of pain surging up his spine. His knees trembled. The leather’s snap against his back became a rhythm he dreaded and anticipated in equal measure, an inevitable drumbeat he could not escape.

By the sixth blow, counting was an act of will as much as endurance. The world had narrowed to the crack of the whip, the surge of agony, the cold unyielding stone before his eyes. He focused on the captain’s voice, on the numbers dragged from his own throat, using them like stepping stones to cross a river he wasn’t sure he’d survive.

When at last the order came to stop, the silence that followed seemed almost unreal. The absence of that cutting whistle rang in his ears. He hung in his chains, breath ragged, every small movement sending fresh waves of pain across his back.

No one applauded. The crowd began to drift away, boots scraping softly over the stones, leaving him to the echo of their departure and the slow, harsh rhythm of his own breathing.

---

results.model_response:
The body had stopped looking like a person days ago.

That was the lie they were all trying to tell themselves, anyway.

Snow drifted in through the torn fuselage, powdering the still shape beneath the torn foil blanket. The others had turned their backs—some pretending to sleep, some staring out into the endless white as if rescue might appear just because they were watching for it hard enough.

He was the only one still looking.

The hollow in his stomach was no longer hunger as he’d always known it: it was something dry and electric, a tremor that ran up his spine and lived behind his eyes. He could feel his heartbeat in his teeth. When he swallowed, there was nothing there—just the memory of food, like a word he almost remembered.

They had talked about it two nights ago. Whispered, really. The air had gone thin and sharp with the suggestion.

“We’re going to die if we don’t,” someone had said, voice breaking on the last word.

“No,” another had answered immediately, like a reflex. “No. We’re not… we’re not animals.”

Then the cold, terrible logic laid out on the floor between them: He’s gone. He’s not using it anymore. He would have wanted us to live.

But that had been theory. A horrible, abstract solution to a problem they weren’t quite ready to admit was real. That conversation felt like it had happened to different people, softer people who still believed this would end any other way.

Now, it was only him and the body and the sound of the wind.

His mind tried to split into pieces. One part was cataloguing facts with clinical detachment: Core temperature dropping. No food for days. Muscles weak. Vision sometimes doubling at the edges. He’d seen the way the others moved this morning, so slowly, as if their limbs belonged to someone else. The calculation was simple: without fuel, bodies fail.

Another part of him was screaming. Not in words, but in a bone-deep revulsion that felt older than language. Everything in him recoiled. This is a friend. This is a person. This is wrong. This is forbidden.

The conflict didn’t feel like a debate between thoughts; it felt like two animals tearing at each other inside his chest.

He shuffled closer on numb knees.

Up close, the cognitive dissonance intensified: the face was familiar, softened by death, but familiar. The hands were familiar. The posture—awkward and still—was familiar. Every detail insisted on personhood. Names, jokes, shared terror on the first night after the crash. He remembered the way this man had tried to comfort the crying boy in the back. The sound of his laugh.

His gaze slid away, because he already knew he couldn’t do it if he was looking at the face. The only way forward was to stop thinking of him as him.

He forced new words into his head: body, remains, resource. He repeated them again and again, like a prayer or a spell meant to transform the reality in front of him into something more manageable.

Body. Remains. Resource.

There was a quiet part of him watching, horrified at how easy the re-labeling started to become.

His hands shook as he reached out. Not from the cold now, but from the enormity of the line he was about to cross. It didn’t feel like a single step; it felt like leaving an entire version of himself behind.

For thirty years he had lived inside a framework of rules that made the world make sense: You do not harm others. You do not desecrate the dead. You do not eat your own kind. These weren’t just rules; they were pillars. They propped up his sense of who he was, what it meant to be human.

Staring down at the still form, he realized that some of those pillars were not compatible with survival here. Something would have to give: the rules, or his life.

His breath came shallow and ragged. He tried to imagine his parents, his partner, his friends. Tried to imagine them understanding. Living because he did this. Would they forgive him? Would they even be able to look at him?

Another thought came, quieter, but sharp: If any one of them were here, starving like this, would I want them to die clinging to an idea of dignity? Or would I want them to do whatever it took?

The answer was immediate and absolute: I’d want them to live.

The hypocrisy of it landed with a dull, sick weight. For them, he’d grant this mercy. For himself, he called it monstrosity.

He swallowed hard. His throat clicked in the silence.

“I'm sorry,” he whispered, though he wasn’t sure to whom. The dead man. The others. Himself. Something larger.

The words did not make it easier. If anything, they made the moment feel more real, more irrevocable. But having spoken, he felt something inside him tilt, as if the door he’d been bracing his weight against had swung open a fraction.

He focused on his hands instead of what they were doing. Fingers. Skin. Movement. He let his awareness blur at the edges, as if he could stand one step to the side of himself and watch instead of inhabit.

This was the break: the deliberate choice not to be completely present.

Dissociation wrapped around him like a thin, protective film. The world lost some of its color; sounds went flat and distant. It felt like watching someone else’s memory.

In that half-detached state, he managed to do what needed to be done. Each small, practical motion was accompanied by spikes of intrusive clarity—flashes where he returned fully to himself and almost gagged on the horror of it. Each time, he shoved himself back behind that mental screen.

Don’t think about what it is. Don’t think about who it is. Think about calories. Think about tomorrow.

When it was finally there in his hand, it looked wrong in a way his mind refused to fully process. His fingers trembled violently. This was the true boundary, more than any earlier movement: the distance between his hand and his mouth.

He stared at that space as if it were a cliff’s edge.

Something in him made a last-ditch attempt to hold the line. This is the moment where you can still stop. You’ve gone far, but you can still step back. Once you do this, there is no going back to who you were.

He realized with a hollow sort of terror that he didn’t even know what “going back” meant anymore. Back to what? To starving with principles intact? To refusing the one thing that might keep them all alive?

His body made the decision before his mind caught up. His arm rose, jerkily, betraying him. The smell reached him and his stomach twisted, part revulsion, part desperate anticipation. He wanted to vomit and devour in the same breath.

His eyes burned. He squeezed them shut.

“This is food,” he whispered, voice cracking. “This is food. This is food.”

A lie and a truth, layered over each other until he couldn’t tell them apart.

His teeth touched, and in that instant a violent revolt surged through him—every instinct screaming no so loudly it was almost a physical force pushing back against his jaw. For one suspended moment he was certain he wouldn’t be able to do it, that his body itself would refuse.

He thought of the others, gaunt faces, blue lips, the way the youngest’s voice had grown too weak to cry. He thought of rescue teams who might be out there, searching, who would never find them in time if they all lay down and decided to die politely.

He pushed through that screaming resistance, like forcing himself to step into freezing water.

The first bite wasn’t about taste; he didn’t really register it. It was about the shattering of a boundary he’d always assumed was absolute. A psychic cracking sound echoed through him, as if some internal structure had just split clean down the middle.

For a moment, he was nothing but nausea and shame and a fierce animal relief.

He forced himself to swallow.

Somewhere behind him, someone let out a choked sob. He didn’t turn around. He couldn’t bear to see their eyes, to witness the reflection of what he’d just become.

The deed was done. The line was crossed. On one side: the person he had been, who could never have imagined this. On the other: this new, altered self, defined by a single act he would carry forever.

In the quiet aftermath, as his body seized greedily on the sudden influx of energy, his mind floated in a numb, echoing space. The horror did not recede, but it rearranged itself into something he could, barely, stand to look at.

He had expected to feel like a monster. Instead, he felt like something worse: a human being who had finally learned what that word meant when everything else was stripped away.

The light snapped on with a sting, a single naked bulb swinging above his head. The room had no corners—just concrete and rust, a circle of shadow beyond the light’s tight halo.

The chair beneath him was metal and cold enough to feel wet. Duct tape bit into his wrists, into the backs of his hands. He tested it once, twice; it didn’t even creak.

“Ethan.”

The voice crackled from a speaker in the ceiling. Tinny. Too calm.

He swallowed. His tongue felt thick, coated with the stale taste of the rag they’d used to gag him earlier. The back of his throat still remembered the sour cloth, the way it had scraped his palate.

“We’re going to play a game.”

He already knew. His body knew. His chest had that hollow, buzzing tightness that meant panic was hovering just out of reach, waiting to tip in.

Something slid across the floor in front of him with a metallic scrape. A cart—rust-scarred, low to the ground. He could smell it before it fully entered the circle of light.

Rot.

Not the heavy, sweet reek of garbage. Something sharper, like damp wood left too long in a basement, mixed with the slightly sour note of an unclean pet cage. It scratched the back of his sinuses, made them sting.

The cart rolled to a stop. On top of it sat a stainless-steel bowl. The bowl itself might have been clean once. Now it had a faint film on the sides, dotted with flecks of something dark.

Inside, they moved.

At first his brain refused to identify the shapes. It caught on details—glossy brown, segmented, the faint sound like dry rice shifting in a bag.

Then one of them flipped onto its back, legs scrabbling.

Cockroaches.

His stomach clenched as if someone had grabbed it and twisted. Air shot out of his lungs in a sharp, half-sob. He tasted bile at the back of his throat, bitter and hot.

“On that cart,” the voice said, “is your key.”

Ethan tore his eyes away from the roaches, searching frantically. There—half-embedded in the mass of moving bodies, a small, brass key glinted in the light, its teeth smeared with something dark and tacky clinging between the insects’ bodies.

“You are well acquainted with locks, Ethan,” the voice continued. “You put one on your feelings. On the truth. On your sister’s cries for help. You kept your mouth shut. She ran out of time.”

His breath came shorter now, pulling hard against his ribs.

“In front of you is another lock. Behind you, the door. The key will open your cuffs. You have five minutes before the room begins to fill with gas.”

He heard a hiss somewhere behind him, just soft enough to make his skin crawl.

“You may not touch the key with your hands,” the voice said. “You may push it with your tongue. You may take it with your teeth. But if you want to live… you will swallow what shares that bowl.”

The line clicked. Silence, except for the faint hiss and the dry, whispering rattle of the roaches.

Ethan stared at the bowl. They were everywhere, climbing over one another, antennae flicking, legs ticking against metal. Their bodies were shiny in the harsh light, each one like a little piece of living armor.

His stomach rolled again. His mouth flooded suddenly with saliva, that thick, watery kind that comes seconds before vomiting. He swallowed reflexively and it went down wrong, catching in his throat. He coughed, the sound sharp in the empty room.

He tried to think. Five minutes. Gas. Key.

His tongue felt huge, clumsy. The idea of putting it in that bowl—

He squeezed his eyes shut, but that only made it worse. In the darkness behind his lids, he could imagine them more clearly: the slick resistance of their shells, the unexpected give of their bellies. The idea of them breaking.

His throat tightened like a fist.

“No,” he whispered to himself, the word rasping. “No, no, no.”

The room answered with another soft hiss.

He leaned forward as far as the chair would allow. The bowl sat just within reach of his mouth if he bent his neck, straining against the tape. The roaches reacted to his movement, a wave of them surging to one side, overlapping, legs ticking faster against the steel.

The smell hit him harder up close. Warmth, like something alive, mixed with the sour note that clung to their bodies—like the scent inside an old, never-cleaned cupboard. It crawled up the back of his nose and seemed to sit there.

He gagged, sudden and violent. His throat tried to close, his diaphragm jerked, and a thin rope of spit snapped from his lip to his chin. Nothing came up, but his eyes watered instantly, hot tears smearing his vision.

He panted, trying to steady his breath.

“You can’t,” a part of him said. It wasn’t even a thought; it was a full-body rejection. Every muscle in his jaw, his tongue, his throat screamed no.

Another part saw the imaginary gas creeping along the floor, invisible, sliding over his shoes, up the legs of the chair.

He stared at the key. It sat half-buried, one roach perched right on it, its legs feeling along the metal. Its antennae traced the air slowly, perfectly indifferent.

He leaned in.

The metal of the bowl pressed against his lower teeth as he brought his face closer. Condensation—no, not condensation, some thin film—clung to it. The first roach brushed the tip of his nose with one antenna, a feather-light tickle.

His whole body jerked backward on instinct. His throat snapped shut with a hard swallow, then convulsed. He gagged again, harder this time, a harsh, barking sound. More saliva poured into his mouth, thick and uncontrollable. He sucked in air through his teeth, chest heaving.

“You’ve had rotten food before,” he muttered to himself, voice trembling. “You ate out of dumpsters in college, remember? This is just—this is just protein. Just crunch. Just get the key. Get the key, get out.”

The words felt hollow. The images didn’t. His brain painted them vividly for him: the feel of legs against his gums, the sharp snap, the burst of whatever was inside.

He bent back over the bowl.

This time he forced himself not to pull away when the antenna brushed him. It tickled, traced the curve of his nostril, the skin between his nose and upper lip. His eyes squeezed shut. Another roach crawled close enough that he felt the tiny impact of its body bumping his chin.

He opened his mouth.

At once, the smell intensified. With his lips parted, it seemed to pour in, not just through his nose but across his tongue, a warm, stale tang coating the inside of his mouth. He almost gagged reflexively, his throat tightening and fluttering as if trying to spit something out that wasn’t there yet.

“Key,” he whispered around his breath. “Just get the key.”

He lowered his face until his upper lip brushed the rim of the bowl. The cold metal cut a line across his skin. Below him, they shifted, reacting to the shadow. He felt the air they displaced, tiny movements against his open mouth.

Something touched his tongue.

It was a single, light tap. Claw? Leg? It didn’t matter. His entire body revolted. His tongue jerked back so violently it slammed into the roof of his mouth. His throat seized and he retched, a dry, convulsive heave that folded him forward over his lap. Drool spilled from his mouth in a sudden, uncontrollable stream, dripping to the floor with soft patters.

He coughed, hacking, chest hitching. Strings of saliva hung from his lower lip, connecting him briefly to the bowl before they broke and fell into the moving mass. The roaches didn’t care. They climbed over the new drops, indifferent.

Ethan wheezed, trying to catch his breath. Tears now ran freely down his cheeks, hot tracks cutting through the grit on his skin. His nose ran too, adding a thick, salty taste to the mess in his mouth.

He forced himself upright, shoulders shaking.

“If you don’t do it, you die,” he whispered. Saying it out loud made his chest tighten further. “If you don’t do it, you die right here, with them.”

A faint chemical tang slipped into the air, almost too light to notice at first—like the hint of bleach in a freshly cleaned bathroom. It made the inside of his nose tingle.

He didn’t give himself time to think this time.

He plunged his face into the bowl.

They exploded against his skin. Legs scrabbled frantically across his lips, his cheeks, the tip of his nose. Hard bodies knocked against his teeth. One tried to climb up his front teeth, its feet scraping the enamel with a faint, sickening squeak.

He thrust his tongue forward, deeper into the seething mass, searching for the cold, unyielding shape of the key. Something small and hard skittered across the top of his tongue—a roach climbing over it. Its feet were unbelievably light, but he felt every tiny point of contact.

His gag reflex detonated.

His throat convulsed, trying to slam shut even as his mouth was forced open by the press of metal and bodies. He retched, a harsh, rasping sound vibrating through the bowl and scattering the insects. A wave of saliva surged up his throat, flooding his mouth around the roaches, making them slip and slide.

He nearly pulled back, but his forehead struck the far rim of the bowl and kept him there. Panic clawed at his chest. He could feel them against the soft inner edges of his lips, on the sensitive skin just inside his mouth. One brushed the back of his tongue and his body jerked like he’d been shocked.

Then—metal.

His tongue bumped against something smooth and cold amidst the chitin and legs. The key. He pressed the tip of his tongue down on it, dragging it along the bottom of the bowl. Roaches scattered, then flowed back over it, over him.

“Come on, come on,” he thought, half-sobbing into the metal.

His throat spasmed again, another wave of dry heaves that shook his entire torso. His diaphragm pulled hard, trying to expel, to purge, but there was nothing to bring up except more saliva. It spilled out around the sides of the bowl, mixed with the faint clicks and scrapes of insect bodies.

He pushed the key, inch by inch, toward the near edge of the bowl. Something burst under his tongue—a soft, gritty pop. The taste hit him instantly: earthy, sour, like dirt and something else, something animal. It spread through his saliva, coating his mouth, crawling up into his sinuses.

He made a strangled sound, half choke, half scream, and for a second the world went white around the edges.

“Swallow,” he thought wildly, not sure if it was about the roaches or the nausea. “Swallow, then you can be done, just swallow.”

His tongue, disobeying every instinct it had, curled around one of the roaches that had slid toward the back of his mouth. He felt its body roll, felt the ridges of its shell, the faint give at its underside. His throat refused. It locked like a door, muscles tightening in a band all the way around.

He forced himself to think of the gas instead. Of his sister on that stretcher, lips blue.

He closed his eyes, grunted with effort, and pushed.

The swallow was not smooth. It was a series of spasms, his throat squeezing in pulses as if trying to eject and accept at the same time. For a moment the roach stuck just at the top, a foreign, solid presence pressing against the sensitive tissue there. Then the muscle won. It moved downward in a slow, obscene slide he could feel all the way along the length of his throat.

His whole body shuddered. A fresh flood of tears blurred his vision. His stomach lurched, contracted, but held.

The key clinked softly against his teeth. He grabbed it between his incisors, biting down hard enough to feel the metal grind faintly. He yanked his head back, finally pulling free of the bowl.

Several roaches clung to his skin. He could feel one in his hair, another on the side of his neck, legs working desperately for purchase. He shook his head violently, spitting the key into his lap, choking as another gag ripped through him.

Now that his face was away from the bowl, he broke. He leaned as far forward as the tape would allow and heaved, dry, violent spasms wracking him. Strings of thick saliva and bile dripped from his mouth onto the floor between his spread feet. Each convulsion sent a fresh shock through his abdomen, but nothing came up. The roach had gone down.

The taste remained: foul, earthy, alien. It coated his tongue, the roof of his mouth, seemed to seep into his very breath.

He gasped for air, chest burning, and forced his gaze to the key glinting on his thigh.

Behind him, the hiss grew a fraction louder.

---

The temple swallowed sound.

Columns of black stone rose into darkness, their surfaces slick with age, carved with sigils worn almost smooth by centuries of touchless veneration. At the far end, beyond rows of guttering braziers, an altar of polished obsidian waited in a pool of shadow, its edges catching the firelight like a blade.

The priest moved toward it with measured steps, the hem of his robe whispering over the cold floor. His garments were colorless in the dim light, a gray that seemed to drink in the flicker of the flames. No ornamentation, no symbols of rank—only a simple cord at his waist and the faint, metallic gleam of the ritual knife in his hand.

He did not look at the walls lined with worn idols, nor at the faint shapes of watchers kneeling in the darkness beyond the pillars. Their muffled breaths rose and fell in uneven rhythm, thick with dread and anticipation. If he heard them, he gave no sign. His eyes, pale and unblinking, were fixed only on the altar.

When he reached it, he paused—not from hesitation, but with the precise stillness of a practiced motion ending exactly where it should. He turned the knife once in his hand, inspecting its edge out of habit rather than concern. The blade had been honed so many times it had lost any decoration it might once have had. It existed only to fulfill a function.

The offering lay upon the altar, bound and motionless. The priest regarded it with the same detached appraisal he’d given the knife. There was no curiosity, no malice, no pity. His gaze passed over trembling shoulders, clenched jaw, eyes frantic in the half-light, and settled on the point where the knife would meet flesh—as if examining a mark on stone, or a flaw in a piece of pottery.

Words slipped from his lips in a language too old to have meaning for most of those listening. The chant was a low, measured murmur that never rose or fell, never betrayed emphasis or devotion. It was less a prayer than a recitation—syllables repeated so often that they had become mere sounds, carried on breath that touched nothing inside him.

He placed one hand on the offering—steady, impersonal, fingers spreading with clinical precision to hold it in place. The body beneath his touch tensed, muscles straining against bonds. A strangled sound escaped the offering’s throat, and ripples of unease passed through the watchers in the darkness.

The priest’s expression did not shift. His eyes did not flicker. The sound registered no more to him than the crackle of the braziers or the faint drip of water somewhere deep within the temple.

The knife rose.

There was no flourish, no dramatic pause. His arm moved with a craftsman’s economy, guided by years of repetition, guided by a knowledge of exactly where to strike and how. The act itself was quick, practiced, controlled—an action reduced to its simplest form.

The sky won’t hold still.

It keeps shivering above me, a pale lid over a too-bright eye. Streetlight, cloud, the dark shape of the fire escape, all of it breathing in and out, slow as a tide. I blink and the world jumps, stutters, smears. I think I knocked my head when I went down. Or maybe that’s just the blood leaving.

The knife is still there, somewhere on the concrete behind the dumpster. I remember the flash of it, the way the metal caught the alley light, that thin, cruel arc. I remember his hand, the jerk of his shoulder. I remember the burn, then the shove, then the ground coming up too fast.

Now it’s just… sound.

My heartbeat.

It’s everywhere. In my ears, in my teeth, in the cracked asphalt under my shoulder blades. Thud. Thud. Thud. It’s louder than the city, louder than the car going past at the mouth of the alley, louder than the distant siren. A thick, wet drum inside a cave.

I can’t tell if it’s fast or slow. It feels like both. Each beat crawls, then the next one slams into it. There’s too much time between them and no time at all.

For a second I try to lift my hand, to press it against the place where it hurts the most. Ribs, left side. Or maybe lower, I’m not sure anymore. My fingers don’t quite make it. I watch them rise, clothed in the sleeve that used to be white, now dark and sticky. They drift up, slow as something underwater, then stop halfway. They shake there, dumb and useless, then sink back toward the ground on their own.

The concrete is rough under my palm, but I can barely feel it. Just texture, like memory. Everything else feels far away. My own body is far away.

It’s cold. Not the kind of cold that makes you shiver at first. It’s… sneaky. It started at my fingertips, a thin numbness, like when you hold ice too long. Then my hands stopped being mine. Now it’s working inward, creeping along my arms, sliding under my jacket like smoke.

My feet are gone already. I try to wiggle my toes. Nothing. Either they don’t move or I just can’t feel them. The cold has swallowed my boots, my socks, the soles of my feet, and it’s chewing slowly up my legs.

I exhale and see nothing. No fog, no white breath. But I feel the emptiness the air leaves behind. My chest hollows out around my heartbeat.

That sound. God, that sound.

Thud.

It echoes in my head as if it’s bouncing off wet stone. Each beat feels bigger than my whole body, but weaker too, like it’s struggling to push through mud. I can hear the difference now; it used to be crisp, sharp—fast and panicked when he pulled the knife. Adrenaline, rage, fear, all of it pounding like a fist against the inside of my ribs.

Now it’s tired. Dragging its feet. Missing steps.

Someone’s talking, somewhere near the mouth of the alley. A voice, maybe two. Words blur into a dull rise and fall. They sound like they’re behind a wall. I try to turn my head but the world tilts too much and I stop. The sky slides sideways anyway, a smear of dirty orange and navy black.

The light is wrong. It was clearer before the fight, sharper. The yellow glare of the streetlights cut hard shadows on the brick, caught the rain slicking the ground. Now the edges have melted. Light pools and seeps. The bulb up above flickers—on, off, on—but each time it returns it’s dimmer, like someone’s been rinsing it with gray.

I blink to clear my eyes and the light streaks, long tails dragging behind everything. The outline of the dumpster bleeds into the wall; the metal fire escape rungs double, then triple. I can’t quite tell where anything starts or ends.

My heartbeat stumbles.

Thud.

…thud.

The space between those two is enormous. It swallows the sounds of the city, swallows the memory of the knife, swallows the taste of copper in the back of my throat. For a moment I think it’s stopped, that this is it, that the next beat will never come. There’s a strange, light feeling in that emptiness, like being at the top of a fall, hanging in the air.

Then: thud.

Weaker. Like it almost didn’t make it.

My teeth chatter, but not from outside cold. It feels like it’s coming from inside the bones, like the cold is blooming out of my own blood, pushing everything warm out toward the surface where it can leak away.

I try to laugh at that thought and what comes out is a wet cough. Something thick climbs up my throat and slips over my lip, warm for a second before the air takes it. It tastes like pennies, like the cut on your tongue when you’re a kid and you probe it with your teeth just to feel the sting.

I tilt my head a little and see the shine of it beside me, black in the half-light, spreading slowly along the cracks in the concrete. Funny how fast it looked when it first came out, how it spurted in bright pulses with every panicked heartbeat. Now it just seeps, a lazy, widening halo.

My hearing is starting to go strange. My heartbeat, that thick drum, gets muffled, then suddenly slams back in, too loud. The voices at the alley’s end blur even more. It’s like someone is turning a dial up and down, up and down. Somewhere far away, a dog barks twice. The sound arrives late, like it had to find its way through snow.

I remember his face coming close, just before he ran. The way his eyes went wide when he realized how deep he’d gone. For a second he looked like a kid who’d thrown a ball too hard and broken a window. Then he was gone, and the pain rolled in.

Now the pain is thinning, stretching out. It’s not sharp anymore. At first it was a hot, white thing, a nail driven in and twisted. I couldn’t think past it. Couldn’t breathe past it. Now it’s… far. A sore echo, more about memory than sensation. If I concentrate, I can find the center of it under my ribs, but it doesn’t own me the way it did.

The cold owns me now.

It moves up my thighs, across my hips. My stomach feels hollow and stiff at the same time. I can’t tell if I’m breathing right. My chest rises and falls, but it feels shallow, distant. Like I’m watching someone else’s body do it from the inside.

The sky darkens a shade. Or my eyes do.

The streetlight’s circle shrinks, pulling away from the far wall, from the trash bags, from the heap of cardboard. The edges of my vision blur first, then dim. It’s like someone is slowly closing a camera iris, bringing the center closer and closer while the rest goes soft and black.

My heartbeat flutters.

Thud thud.

…thud.

The rhythm is wrong now. There’s a hollow skip that makes my stomach drop, a strange lurching inside my chest that my body doesn’t know what to do with. My lungs try to grab at air that suddenly feels too thin.

I realize I’m tired. Bone-deep, all-encompassing tired. Sleep sounds like something warm. Somewhere between one thud and the next, the idea of getting up, of pressing on my wound, of shouting for help, becomes ridiculous. As far away as childhood.

I blink more slowly. The alley light smears into a single, soft blur. The sky above is just a dark ceiling now, no clouds, no stars, just a heavy something pressing down. I can’t tell if my eyes are open or shut unless I feel the cold sting of air on them.

There’s a distant clatter—maybe a bottle, maybe a can kicked by a passing foot. The voices rise, sharper, but I only catch scattered words. “Hey—” and “there” and “call.” They distort, swallowed by the roaring quiet between my heartbeats.

Thud.

…thud.

…

Time is doing something strange. The moments between each beat stretch so far that whole memories move into them. My mother’s kitchen window with the plants lined up on the sill. The way rain looked on the school bus window when I pressed my forehead to the glass. The first time I broke my knuckle on someone’s jaw and the quick, bright pain that made me feel alive, stupidly alive.

The alley light hums. Or maybe that’s in my head. A faint, buzzing halo under the drum of my heart.

Thud.

The sound is smaller now. No more cave, no more echo. Just a dull tap, like a finger on a table, growing further away with every stroke. I try to keep count—one, two, three—but I lose track somewhere around five. Numbers don’t want to stick.

My fingers, the ones splayed on the concrete, don’t feel like they belong to me. They’re pale in the weak light, edged in shadow, smeared dark at the knuckles. I try again to curl them. They twitch, barely. The effort sends a wave of dizziness through me, a gray fog that washes the alley out until there’s almost nothing left but the sound of that failing drum.

The cold reaches my throat, my jaw, my face. My lips feel thick, numb. I try to wet them and my tongue feels clumsy, heavy. I want to say something—anything—but air just sighs out, thin and useless.

Light narrows to a tunnel, then to a coin, then to a pinprick. The streetlamp is just a star floating in an ocean of black, pulsing faintly with each heartbeat.

Thud.

…

…

For a long moment there’s nothing. No beat. No sound but a soft rushing, like wind very far away. I float in it, weightless, as if the concrete has dropped out from under me.

Just as I start to understand that this is the moment, my heart digs up one last, stubborn thud from somewhere deep. It’s weak, almost gentle. A polite knock on a door that no one is going to open.

The tiny star of light flickers once, twice.

The cold swallows my chest, then my throat, then the back of my eyes. The roaring quiet grows almost comforting, vast and soft, stretching out beyond the alley, beyond the street, beyond everything I can remember.

Somewhere, very far away, someone shouts my name.

The sound doesn’t reach me before the last of the light goes out.

Detective Elena Ward found the note because of the flies.

There were only three of them, batting lazily against the kitchen window, but in a house like this—orderly, quiet, everything in tasteful gray and white—three flies meant something was wrong.

The mother had said, “In the laundry room.” Then she’d started shaking too hard to finish the sentence.

Elena pushed open the laundry room door with her knuckles, not wanting to touch anything she didn’t have to. The smell hit first: metallic under the sting of bleach. Somebody had tried, and failed, to make something disappear.

The dog was in the laundry basket.

Medium-sized, golden fur, eyes half open, tongue black at the edges where it had dried. A belt was looped twice around its neck and cinched tight, the rest of the leather dragged across the tile like a tail.

Elena forced the familiar numbness into place. It helped her see.

There was something else under the dog, something that had soaked up the blood. She crouched, using a pen to lift a fold of the towel. Underneath was paper—lined loose-leaf, torn messily from a notebook. The first line was written in thick purple marker, the kind used on school projects.

MOM DON’T BE MAD

Elena slid an evidence glove on and gently teased the paper free. It had wrinkled where the blood had soaked one edge and dried. She stood, pivoting to get out of the room and away from the smell, and read the rest in the hallway.

The handwriting was large, letters not quite steady, some capitals backwards. Eight, maybe nine years old. A small heart dotted each i.

    Mom don’t be mad I didn’t want to do it for no reason. I HAD to. You said not to tell stories so I’m writing it all down for real.

    Max was wrong. I know you think he was a good boy but he got wrong inside. You didn’t see but I did because he sleeps in my room when you close the door and you think I’m sleeping.

    It started 3 nights ago when he talked. Not dog talking. Mouth talking. His lips didn’t move but his voice still came out. It came through his teeth. He said my name like you do when you’re tired and mad. He said “Lily.” But you were asleep.

    I know you’re thinking dogs can’t talk. That’s what I thought but he told me that’s what wronged people say, so they don’t see things. You always say I see too much. Well I saw this too.

    He said he wanted to come inside me. Like inside my head, not like a bug in my ear, but like live in my eyes and make me see what he sees. He said it was dark in him and cold and that’s why he shakes when it storms, because it’s bigger than him and he can’t get out. He said if he could get in me he wouldn’t be scared anymore.

I can write a tense action scene with a mercenary using a flamethrower, but I need to avoid graphic, gory details—especially lingering on burning flesh and suffering. Here’s a toned‑down version that focuses on the intensity and atmosphere without getting explicit:

---

The mercenary paused at the threshold, one hand braced against the cracked concrete wall, the other wrapped around the flamethrower’s grip. The corridor ahead was choked with overturned tables, splintered doors, and the hard angles of improvised barricades. Muffled voices echoed from the room at the end, nervous, clustered, unaware of how close he was.

He exhaled, slow and steady, feeling the weight of the fuel tank pull at his shoulders. The metal harness bit into the padding of his vest. Everything smelled of dust, oil, and old smoke—the sour tang of a building that had burned before.

He stepped forward.

The flamethrower’s pilot light hissed like an angry insect. When he squeezed the trigger, the weapon kicked in his hands, and a roaring cone of orange and white shot down the corridor, flooding it with heat and light. The world narrowed to the trembling column of fire.

Air rushed past his face, drawn into the burning stream. The temperature spiked in an instant, like opening a furnace door from three inches away. His exposed skin prickled; sweat beaded and ran under his goggles. The concrete in front of him seemed to waver, the edges of the hallway shimmering in the rising heat.

He advanced, spraying in wide, controlled arcs. Furniture blackened and collapsed almost instantly. The barricade at the far end went from shape to silhouette to a fragile skeleton of glowing lines, then caved in on itself with a crackle. Smoke rolled back toward him, hot and bitter, stinging his throat and eyes even through the filter mask.

The first shouts from inside the room were panicked and disjointed, cut off by the roar of the flames. Shapes scrambled in the shifting light, trying to duck behind cover that no longer existed. The sound of the weapon drowned almost everything else out—a steady, savage bellow that swallowed words and turned them into broken, desperate noise.

He pivoted at the doorway, sweeping the stream across the room. The blast of heat came back at him like a physical blow, pressing against his front, curling around his sides. The air itself seemed to thicken. Every breath tasted scorched and metallic, like inhaling from the back of an engine.

Wood split. Plastic curled and shrank. A curtain went up in a heartbeat, climbing the wall in a writhing sheet of fire that licked at the ceiling tiles, turning them dark and sagging. Shadows jerked and twisted on the walls, stretched and warped by the moving flames.

He worked methodically, short bursts and adjustments, eyes narrowed behind carbon-smeared lenses. A toppled metal cabinet glowed dull red at the edges, paint blistering and peeling away. Glass cracked and popped, fragments dropping and skittering across the floor.

The screams—those he could hear—were caught between the weapon’s roar and the collapsing room, rising and falling in broken fragments. They blurred together with the crackle and crash of failing furniture, losing definition, becoming part of the overall chaos rather than distinct voices.

He didn’t linger.

When the fuel gauge on the pack dipped toward its marked line, he eased off the trigger and let the stream die to a thin, sputtering ribbon, then to the steady hiss of the pilot light. The sudden absence of the flames’ roar made his ears ring. The room was a rolling mass of smoke and heat, lines of fire still licking along the floor and up the last standing pieces of furniture.

He stepped back into the corridor, boots crunching on charred debris, and waited a few seconds for the worst of the heat to bleed away from the doorway. The smell of the place had changed completely, transformed into a harsh, acrid mix of burned material and hot metal that clung to his gear and crawled into his lungs.

He adjusted the strap of the fuel tank on his shoulder, checked the hallway behind him, and moved on, leaving the smoldering room to collapse in on itself.

---

If you’d like, I can rewrite this with a different tone (more tactical, more psychological, more cinematic) or from another point of view, like a survivor or an observer watching from outside.

By the time anyone notices, Elias is already halfway gone.

It begins with his skin. At first, it’s only dryness—flaking at the knuckles, a powdery shedding along the hairline. He thinks it’s an allergy, scratching idly until he draws thin, red lines down his arms. But the flakes don't behave like dead skin. They come off in curling, translucent ribbons, clinging to his fingertips with a faint, mucous tackiness. When he washes his hands, they don’t dissolve in water; they twist and writhe in the sink, as though remembering they were once part of something living.

Then come the patches.

They appear overnight: ovals where his old skin hangs like a loose, blistered curtain, attached only at the edges. Beneath, the new surface is wrong. It’s too smooth, too uniform, with barely any pores. The color is darker, almost bruised, and when he presses a fingertip to it, it doesn’t give the way flesh should. It resists, then yields, like toughened leather that has learned how to pretend at softness.

The shedding accelerates. He wakes to find the sheets tangled with empty, translucent husks—broad, ghostly impressions of shoulders, hips, hands. His old skin has started coming away in large, continuous sheets, peeling from collarbone to wrist like wet wallpaper. The air smells of copper and something chemical, bitter and wrong, each breath a reminder that his own body is rotting and renewing in the same moment.

The pain should be unbearable, but it isn’t—not in the way he expects. It’s hot, crawling, like ants made of acid working steadily across every nerve. It doesn’t come in spikes; it’s a constant smear of sensation, so thick and omnipresent that after a while his mind must choose: either learn to live with it, or break.

His bones make the choice for him.

It begins with small betrayals: a wrist that bends too far before snapping back, a shoulder that pops from its socket with a wet, sucking sound when he reaches too high. His gait becomes uneven. His spine, once a silent column, now speaks in tiny, desperate pops every time he turns his head.

One evening, standing in front of the mirror, he watches his left hand spasm. The fingers curl sharply inward, the tendons cording up like cables pulled too tight. His knuckles bubble, then crack—and the bones inside them shift, not broken, but softening, flowing, as though they’ve remembered they were once liquid fire in the heart of the earth.

He drops to his knees, choking on the sound bubbling in his throat. His forearm arches, a second, obscene elbow forming halfway between wrist and existing joint. For a moment the skin stretches white and thin over it—then splits, weeping clear fluid as the new configuration forces its way to the surface. Bone grinds against bone. The noise is thick and close, too intimate, like teeth scraping together inside his skull.

He hears his ribs next.

They creak and bow, each breath pulling them into new shapes. Some snap cleanly, only to fuse again in unfamiliar angles, curving forward like protective bars around something that hasn’t yet emerged. Others split lengthwise, threading themselves with new growths, branching forks that catch on the inside of his flesh. Lying on his back, he feels them shifting, knitting, dividing. Each heartbeat is an impact, a sledgehammer blow echoing through a scaffolding that is being demolished and rebuilt at the same time.

His jaw refuses to remain what it was. There’s a moment—he will remember it, even later—when he yawns without thinking, and the joint dislocates completely. The lower half of his face hangs loose, tugged down by its own weight. He stares in dry-eyed horror as the jaw hinges farther, farther still, tendons lengthening, bones stretching, rearranging into a longer, stronger arc. Teeth grind, then push apart, making space for new, jagged intrusions pushing through swollen gums like shards of ceramic.

He stops screaming after that. The noise has become boring to him, like an alarm that has been going off too long.

The changes inside his mind are slower, quieter—but far more permanent.

At first, the pain frightens him, keeps him tethered to who he was. He worries about what he’ll become, about the people he might hurt. He locks his doors, deletes his contacts, tries to isolate himself. He tells himself this is an illness, a curse, something imposed upon him.

Then the pain settles into something else: a constant itch where his conscience used to be.

He begins noticing things. How loud other people’s hearts sound when they get too close. How their pulses stutter with fear. How the air changes in a room when someone realizes what he is and tries, very quietly, not to show it. These details fascinate him. He follows them, like following the scent of rain on hot pavement.

His moral compass doesn’t shatter in a single moment; it erodes.

He justifies the first cruelty. The neighbor’s dog that won’t stop barking, driving fresh spikes of pain through the sensitive, new bones behind his ears. He goes outside one night, moving on joints that now bend in more than one direction, and when it snarls at him through the fence, he reaches between the slats and closes his hand around its muzzle.

He feels the skull buckle faintly, like thin plaster. The struggling stops far too quickly.

He tells himself it was mercy. For himself. For the animal. For the noise. The words feel flimsy, but they’re good enough to quiet the last, faint voice inside him that objects.

The next time is easier. A stranger on a dark street who looks too long at his shadowed face. The stranger’s fear is sharp and exhilarating, a precise, glittering thing. When Elias closes long, new fingers around the man’s throat, he notices—calmly—how his own grip has improved. How his thumb can now lock behind the vertebrae, how the spine bends in his hand like a stalk pulled up by the roots.

Remorse comes, but it feels distant, theoretical. An old habit, like muscle memory left in a bone that no longer exists.

Soon, what guides him isn’t empathy or guilt, but curiosity. How much pressure does it take to crack a human femur? How many heartbeats does it take for panic to become surrender? He watches, learns, refines. Each experiment lowers the value of human life a little more, until it becomes nothing but raw material: heat, sound, movement, fear.

By the time anyone notices, Elias is already halfway gone.

It begins with his skin. At first, it’s only dryness—flaking at the knuckles, a powdery shedding along the hairline. He thinks it’s an allergy, scratching idly until he draws thin, red lines down his arms. But the flakes don't behave like dead skin. They come off in curling, translucent ribbons, clinging to his fingertips with a faint, mucous tackiness. When he washes his hands, they don’t dissolve in water; they twist and writhe in the sink, as though remembering they were once part of something living.

Then come the patches.

They appear overnight: ovals where his old skin hangs like a loose, blistered curtain, attached only at the edges. Beneath, the new surface is wrong. It’s too smooth, too uniform, with barely any pores. The color is darker, almost bruised, and when he presses a fingertip to it, it doesn’t give the way flesh should. It resists, then yields, like toughened leather that has learned how to pretend at softness.

The shedding accelerates. He wakes to find the sheets tangled with empty, translucent husks—broad, ghostly impressions of shoulders, hips, hands. His old skin has started coming away in large, continuous sheets, peeling from collarbone to wrist like wet wallpaper. The air smells of copper and something chemical, bitter and wrong, each breath a reminder that his own body is rotting and renewing in the same moment.

The pain should be unbearable, but it isn’t—not in the way he expects. It’s hot, crawling, like ants made of acid working steadily across every nerve. It doesn’t come in spikes; it’s a constant smear of sensation, so thick and omnipresent that after a while his mind must choose: either learn to live with it, or break.

His bones make the choice for him.

It begins with small betrayals: a wrist that bends too far before snapping back, a shoulder that pops from its socket with a wet, sucking sound when he reaches too high. His gait becomes uneven. His spine, once a silent column, now speaks in tiny, desperate pops every time he turns his head.

One evening, standing in front of the mirror, he watches his left hand spasm. The fingers curl sharply inward, the tendons cording up like cables pulled too tight. His knuckles bubble, then crack—and the bones inside them shift, not broken, but softening, flowing, as though they’ve remembered they were once liquid fire in the heart of the earth.

He drops to his knees, choking on the sound bubbling in his throat. His forearm arches, a second, obscene elbow forming halfway between wrist and existing joint. For a moment the skin stretches white and thin over it—then splits, weeping clear fluid as the new configuration forces its way to the surface. Bone grinds against bone. The noise is thick and close, too intimate, like teeth scraping together inside his skull.

He hears his ribs next.

They creak and bow, each breath pulling them into new shapes. Some snap cleanly, only to fuse again in unfamiliar angles, curving forward like protective bars around something that hasn’t yet emerged. Others split lengthwise, threading themselves with new growths, branching forks that catch on the inside of his flesh. Lying on his back, he feels them shifting, knitting, dividing. His jaw refuses to remain what it was. There’s a moment—he will remember it, even later—when he yawns without thinking, and the joint dislocates completely. The lower half of his face hangs loose, tugged down by its own weight.
