Executioner: They said you asked to see me.

Prisoner: I wanted to know the hands that would finish what the judge began.

Executioner: My hands are just a formality. The decision was made a long time ago.

Prisoner: People keep saying that. As if decisions are ghosts that float around without bodies to carry them out.

Executioner: You’re not wrong. But if it wasn’t me, it would be someone else.

Prisoner: Does that help?

Executioner: It helps me do my job. That’s what they pay me for.

Prisoner: They pay you to be able to live with it.

Executioner: Maybe. Why did you really ask for me?

Prisoner: I didn’t want the last face I saw to be a stranger.

Executioner: I’m still a stranger.

Prisoner: Less of one now. You got a name?

Executioner: …Daniel.

Prisoner: Daniel. I figured you’d say you didn’t have one. “Just doing my job.” “Just following orders.” All that.

Executioner: A name doesn’t change what I have to do.

Prisoner: It changes what I see. Now you’re a man, not a mask.

Executioner: The mask is for you, not for me.

Prisoner: No. The mask is so they can tell themselves a person didn’t do this. A role did.

Executioner: You think I like this?

Prisoner: I think you’re good enough at it that they keep you around.

Executioner: “Good” means precise. Clean. No suffering. You want someone clumsy instead?

Prisoner: Funny thing to offer a condemned man—quality assurance.

Executioner: I’m offering what I can. You’re not the first I’ve talked to.

Prisoner: How many?

Executioner: I stopped counting.

Prisoner: I never started. One’s enough, when it’s you.

Executioner: You have five minutes. Less, now. Is there anything you need?

Prisoner: I need you to tell me something true.

Executioner: About what?

Prisoner: About me. About what you see when you look at me.

Executioner: I see a file. Pictures of a dead man. Statements from witnesses. Fingerprints. A legal seal. A date and time.

Prisoner: That’s what they gave you. I’m asking what you see.

Executioner: I see someone who’s calmer than I expected.

Prisoner: I spent ten years in a concrete box waiting for this door to open. After a while, the waiting is worse than the walking.

Executioner: Are you afraid?

Prisoner: Every night. Just not right now.

Executioner: Why not now?

Prisoner: Because now is simple. There’s nothing to imagine. Just you, me, and a clock that doesn’t lie.

Executioner: You could have appealed again.

Prisoner: My lawyer already knocks on the same locked door. Different papers, same answer.

Executioner: You could have kept trying.

Prisoner: For what, exactly? Another two years of waking up to the sound of keys?

Executioner: Some people would.

Prisoner: Some people aren’t sure if they deserve to be here.

Executioner: And you?

Prisoner: I killed a man. That’s not in dispute.

Executioner: They said it was brutal.

Prisoner: They weren’t wrong.

Executioner: You never claimed innocence.

Prisoner: No. I tried that in the beginning. Even to myself. “It was the drugs. It was the anger. It was my father. It was the neighborhood. It was everyone else.” Then I realized every excuse had one thing in common—me.

Executioner: So you think this is justice.

Prisoner: I think this is what they call justice. I’m not sure what I’d call it.

Executioner: What would you call it?

Prisoner: Balance, maybe. They lost a son; now the world loses a monster. Equation solved.

Executioner: You think you’re a monster?

Prisoner: I think I did something monstrous. I’ve been trying to figure out if that’s the same thing.

Executioner: And?

Prisoner: No one trusts the answer from a man in my position.

Executioner: You can still answer for yourself.

Prisoner: Then I’ll say this: There’s blood on my hands that never came off. But there are also letters to my mother, drawings for my niece, books I read and actually finished, apologies I wrote and will never send. I don’t know what that makes me. Complicated, I guess.

Executioner: Everyone’s complicated.

Prisoner: Everyone’s not strapped to a gurney in five minutes.

Executioner: Some should be. Some aren’t.

Prisoner: Do you believe that? That some people deserve this?

Executioner: I believe some people make choices they can’t walk back from.

Prisoner: That’s not an answer.

Executioner: I don’t know if anyone “deserves” to die. The word “deserve” feels too clean for what this is.

Prisoner: You’ve been doing this how long, and you still don’t know?

Executioner: Maybe that’s why they keep me. The ones who are sure scare me more.

Prisoner: Then why stay?

Executioner: Somebody will. And I can at least make it quick.

Prisoner: You ever say no?

Executioner: Once.

Prisoner: What happened?

Executioner: They replaced me for that night. Brought me back for the next one.

Prisoner: What made you say no?

Executioner: She looked exactly like my daughter. Same eyes. Same way of turning her wrists when she talked. I stood in the chamber and my body just…stopped. I couldn’t make it move.

Prisoner: They didn’t fire you?

Executioner: This state forgives hesitation more easily than crime.

Prisoner: Does your daughter know what you do?

Executioner: She thinks I work nights at the prison. Which is technically true.

Prisoner: Technically true. Seems like a popular standard around here.

Executioner: I tell myself I’m doing this so she doesn’t grow up in a world with people like you.

Prisoner: And I tell myself I’m doing this so someone like her doesn’t end up like me.

Executioner: You’re doing this because you have to.

Prisoner: No. I had to turn the key that night. I had to pull the trigger. Everything after that is a chain of people trying to fix what can’t be fixed.

Executioner: “Fix” is the wrong word.

Prisoner: Then what word?

Executioner: Contain. Control. Represent. Punish. Satisfy.

Prisoner: Who does this satisfy?

Executioner: The family, they hope.

Prisoner: Have you ever seen satisfaction in their eyes?

Executioner: I’ve seen exhaustion. I’ve seen people looking through the glass and realizing nothing they’re about to watch will bring the dead back.

Prisoner: Are they here?

Executioner: Yes.

Prisoner: Him?

Executioner: His mother. His brother. Not his father.

Prisoner: His father never came to court either. I remember that.

Executioner: You remember that?

Prisoner: I remember every face that looked at me as if I were the knife itself. But not his father’s. Empty chair. Like mine was when I was that kid’s age.

Executioner: Does that make a difference, to you?

Prisoner: Difference to what?

Executioner: To what you think you deserve.

Prisoner: It makes a difference to what I understand. Not to what I did.

Executioner: He was nineteen.

Prisoner: I know. I was twenty-two. Three years’ difference, a lifetime’s weight.

Executioner: If you could speak to them now, what would you say?

Prisoner: I already said it in court.

Executioner: You know they didn’t believe you.

Prisoner: I know. Apologies sound different coming from a man who wants to live.

Executioner: And now?

Prisoner: Now I’ll say it without wanting anything. Except maybe that when they think of him, my face won’t be the only one they see.

Executioner: They might not want to hear that.

Prisoner: They don’t have to. You asked what I’d say, not what they’d accept.

Executioner: Time’s running.

Prisoner: Funny phrase to use with a dead man walking.

Executioner: You’re still alive.

Prisoner: For four more minutes. What do you do after?

Executioner: Paperwork. Reports. Go home. Try not to look at my own hands too long in the shower.

Prisoner: And tomorrow?

Executioner: I help move inmates. Check logs. Pretend today didn’t happen.

Prisoner: Does it work?

Executioner: Sometimes, for a while. Until a noise brings it back. A word. A smell. The sound of the strap buckling.

Prisoner: Sounds like we’re not so different. I’ve been haunted by one night for ten years. You’re haunted by many.

Executioner: I chose mine.

Prisoner: Did you?

Executioner: I didn’t choose where I was born. What jobs were available. The mortgage payment. The way this town talks about “justice” like it’s a religion.

Prisoner: You could still walk away.

Executioner: So could you have, that night.

Prisoner: Touché.

Executioner: Did you ever think of him after?

Prisoner: Every day. At first, I replayed it like a movie, trying to edit it in my head. Make myself a little less cruel, him a little more threatening, so it felt fair. Later, I stopped changing it. I forced myself to watch it exactly as it was.

Executioner: And now?

Prisoner: Now he’s quieter. More like a ghost that sits in the corner than a monster that jumps out. I talk to him sometimes, in here.

Executioner: What do you say?

Prisoner: “You should have gone home.” “You should have given me your wallet.” “I should have gone home.” “I should have given you my gun.” Variations on the theme of regret.

Executioner: Do you think he answers?

Prisoner: If he does, he’s got the same question you do: why?

Executioner: And?

Prisoner: Sometimes there isn’t a why that satisfies anyone. Sometimes you were just a weak man on a bad night with a loaded weapon and a lifetime of anger you mistook for strength.

Executioner: That’s an answer.

Prisoner: Not a good one.

Executioner: It’s more than some give me.

Prisoner: How many said they’d do it again?

Executioner: Too many.

Prisoner: Then maybe you’re right to keep this job.

Executioner: That supposed to make me feel better?

Prisoner: It’s not about you feeling better. Or me. Or his family. This is about a machine that needs someone to turn the last bolt.

Executioner: I’m aware.

Prisoner: And still you’re here.

Executioner: And still you’re here.

Prisoner: Not for long.

Executioner: They’ll knock in a minute. There’s a protocol.

Prisoner: Of course there is. Rituals make killing feel civilized.

Executioner: Rituals give shape to chaos.

Prisoner: Daniel.

Executioner: Yes?

Prisoner: When the time comes, look at me. Don’t look past me.

Executioner: Most don’t want that.

Prisoner: I do. I’d like at least one person in the room to see a man, not a case number.

Executioner: I’ll look.

Prisoner: And if I panic?

Executioner: Then I’ll tell you when to breathe. When to close your eyes. I can give you that much.

Prisoner: Will it hurt?

Executioner: Not the way you’re imagining. It’s fast.

Prisoner: You’ve done it enough to know.

Executioner: Yes.

Prisoner: Do you pray?

Executioner: I used to. It started to feel like leaving voicemails no one checked.

Prisoner: Maybe they check. Maybe they just don’t respond.

Executioner: Do you pray?

Prisoner: I talk. Whether anyone answers isn’t my department.

Executioner: What do you say?

Prisoner: Mostly “I’m sorry.” Sometimes “Take care of him.” Lately, “Take care of my mother when she wakes up tomorrow and remembers what day it is.”

Executioner: She’s not here.

Prisoner: No. She said she couldn’t watch. I told her not to.

Executioner: You did right.

Prisoner: Or I spared myself the sight of what this does to her.

Executioner: Both can be true.

Prisoner: That’s the problem with truth. It comes in sets, not singles.

Executioner: We’re almost out of time.

Prisoner: Then answer me something, before we go.

Executioner: If I can.

Prisoner: Is there anything I can say that will make this easier for you?

Executioner: That’s not your job.

Prisoner: Humor me. Last act of a selfish man: trying to feel useful.

Executioner: Tell me you understand that what’s about to happen isn’t just me. That when I walk out of here tonight, I’m not the only one who built this.

Prisoner: I understand. This was a group project: me, him, the judge, the jury, the legislature, the voters, the guards, the warden, you. We all laid a brick. You’re just the one handing over the key.

Executioner: That helps.

Prisoner: For what it’s worth, Daniel… I don’t hate you.

Executioner: You should.

Prisoner: I’ve spent ten years hating myself. I’m tired.

Executioner: I’m sorry.

Prisoner: For which part?

Executioner: All of it. The part you chose. The part you didn’t. The part I’m about to play.

Prisoner: Apology accepted. Even if it’s technically not yours to give.

[A knock sounds on the door.]

Executioner: It’s time.

Prisoner: I figured. Daniel?

Executioner: I’m here.

Prisoner: When they write this down, when they type it into whatever report they type it into… “Sentence carried out at such-and-such time”… will there be a line about this?

Executioner: No.

Prisoner: Then remember it. Even if they don’t.

Executioner: I will.

Prisoner: All right then. Let’s go finish what we started.

The first thing that comes back is sound.

A soft hiss, like sand poured from a height. Then the thud of something heavy sliding above, closing off the faintest leak of air. Then, most distinctly, the first shovel of dirt hitting wood.

Thump.

It’s close. Much closer than it should be. The noise doesn’t just reach his ears; it vibrates through his chest, his teeth, the back of his skull. The coffin lid is only inches—no, less—from his face. He knows it because every breath he drags in brushes his nose against the satin lining.

Thump. Scrape. Thump.

He tries to jerk, to sit up, but his forehead smacks the lid. A sharp pain, bright and hot, joins the dull ache that hums behind his eyes. His shoulders wedge against the sides. The cheap suit scratches at his neck, too tight, the collar button digging into soft flesh. He can’t move his arms more than a few degrees; his elbows press into wood.

Panic flares, all at once, like a match dragged along a rough surface.

“Hey!” His voice bursts out, hoarse and ragged. “Hey! I’m— Stop! Stop it!”

Thump.

The next load of earth hits, heavier. Dust shivers down from the lid, peppering his lips and eyes. His shout seems to go nowhere, swallowed before it can fully form. The coffin soaks it up, muting it, turning it into a broken vibration against the wood.

He sucks in air too fast. It feels thick, stale, as if it’s been trapped here for days already. There’s a smell of varnish and cloth and something faintly sweet, the artificial scent they must have pumped into the room where people walked by and pretended not to look directly at his face.

“Stop! I’m alive! I’m alive!”

He slams his fist upward. The angle is wrong; his wrist crunches against the lid, knuckles scraping the lining. The sound of his own blow is pathetic inside the coffin—a small thud swallowed by the far more massive, uncaring thumps from above.

Thump. Scrape.

The rhythm changes slightly, becomes faster. More earth. He imagines the grave filling, weight piling on top of him, the soil pressing down. He’d laughed once, years ago, when someone described being buried under a pile of blankets as “suffocating.” Now the word bares its teeth and shows its real shape.

He pulls in another breath. It doesn’t fill him. His lungs draw in and then stall, as if they’ve run out of room. The air feels thinner now, as though each inhale has shaved away a fraction of what remains, leaving only the edges.

It’s too hot. Or maybe that’s just his skin. Sweat breaks along his hairline, trickles into his ears. He can’t raise a hand to wipe it away. His palms press against the lid and the lining, fingers spread, feeling the grain of the wood beneath the thin, padded cloth.

He presses up with everything he has.

Nothing. The lid won’t even flex. The wood is solid, and now there’s the dirt, and maybe rock, and the weight of the shovelfuls, and the weight of the world atop that. It might as well be stone, or steel, or the sky itself.

“Please,” he croaks. The word barely makes a sound. His throat scratches, dry as if he’s been shouting for hours. “Please. Please hear me. I’m in here. I’m not dead.”

Thump.

The sound makes him flinch. It’s so final, so heavy. He hears individual clods hitting, breaking apart, sliding sideways. He hears pebbles bounce, a brief clatter that dies too soon. He can almost map, in sound alone, the earth filling the void around his coffin, packing it neatly away.

Claustrophobia isn’t an idea anymore; it’s a physical thing, a presence that lies on his chest. The coffin is suddenly too small, shrinking. The satin lining brushes his cheeks, the roof of his coffin presses his eyelashes when he blinks. He can’t draw in his knees, can’t roll to one side. His body feels wrong, like it’s been poured into a mold and it set too fast, trapping him in the wrong position.

He tries to control his breathing. In. Out. In through the nose, out through the mouth. The way someone once told him to do when he was having a panic attack in a crowded room.

But this isn’t a room. This is a box under the ground.

The thought lands with the same cold clarity as the dirt. Under the ground. There’s earth above him, and then grass, and maybe a headstone already sitting somewhere nearby, his name carved into it as if he no longer needs it.

His chest begins to hitch. The air won’t come in evenly anymore. Each breath is a drag, a haul, as if he’s trying to suck it through water. His lungs strain, and the more they strain, the more they seem to find nothing.

“Stop,” he whispers, though he no longer believes anyone can hear. “Stop. I’m here. Please.”

Thump.

He presses his ear to the lid. The wood is warm from his own body heat. For a second he imagines he can hear voices above, muffled, indistinct. Or maybe that’s just the blood roaring in his ears, the frantic pounding of his heart, loud in the confined space.

He remembers reading once that a closed space runs out of oxygen fast. That each exhale adds more carbon dioxide to the air, like a slow poison. He knows this, now, not as a fact from a page but as something crawling into his lungs. Every breath he takes feels less useful. It fills him less, calms him less. His body is starting to know that the resource is limited, and it’s panicking on a level he cannot talk out of.

He tries holding his breath, irrationally, as if he can ration what little is left. He counts in his head.

One, two, three—

His chest spasms, muscles clenching with a deep, animal terror. He gasps, sucking the stale air back in with a low, ugly sound that he barely recognizes as his own. It hurts, a sharp, burning ache along his ribs.

His fingers start to tingle. Needles prickle along the pads of his fingertips, pressing so hard into the lid that his nails bend. He imagines, absurdly, that if he just presses a little harder, the wood will crack. That his fingers will push through, scratch at the soil, break the surface.

Thump.

The shoveling slows. Fewer impacts, but heavier. They’re not filling now; they’re packing, he realizes. Making sure there are no gaps, no hollow spaces where the earth might later sink or shift. They’re smoothing his grave.

His grave.

His tongue feels thick. The coffin has eaten his words, his screams, and now it seems to be collecting the moisture from his mouth too. He swallows and there’s nothing there.

His vision darkens—not that there’s anything to see. The coffin is pitch-black, the kind of darkness that has weight. But inside the darkness behind his eyes something shifts, the edges of his perception softening, blurring. The thoughts that were sharp a moment ago now come slower, as if moving through syrup.

He becomes aware of his heartbeat in stages. First as a pounding in his ears. Then as a pounding in his throat. Then, weirdly, as a distant drum in his fingertips, in the tight space where his body meets the box.

He thinks he hears the last shovel’s worth of dirt.

Thump.

Silence.

Not real silence—there is always the sound of his own body, he’s realizing now. The rasp of his breath. The tiny squeak of the coffin as his ribs expand imperceptibly against it. The tremble of his muscles as he tries, still, to push against the lid.

But from above, nothing. No scrape of metal. No footsteps. No voices.

They’ve gone.

The knowledge lands with a heavy, irrevocable certainty. The last slim thread of hope he’d been secretly clinging to—someone will hear, someone will notice—breaks without a sound.

His breaths become shorter, quicker, because he can’t stop them, because his body won’t let him accept the idea of slowing down. The lack of air is no longer just a theory. There’s a pressure behind his sternum that feels like an invisible hand pressing inward, squeezing.

He opens his mouth as wide as he can, as if there might be a hidden pocket of fresh oxygen somewhere in this tiny box, if he can just stretch far enough to reach it.

The air tastes flat. Used. A faint metallic tang creeps in at the back of his throat.

He tries one last scream. It tears itself out of him, raw and scraping.

The sound hits the lid inches above his face and goes nowhere.

In the dark, in the narrow space, with satin brushing his eyelashes and the weight of the world compressing the wood above him, he is alone with the echo.

results.model_response:
They strap them down in rows.

The hall is a long white corridor broken by steel frames, each frame a bed, each bed a body. Overhead, the ceiling is a lattice of conduits and jointed arms ending in tools that hum and click and drip. The air tastes of metal and antiseptic, dense with the low electric thrum of machinery and the muffled, ragged breathing of the waiting.

Light is bright, colorless, total. It flattens everything. Skin looks sickly, almost transparent, veins like faint blue maps of a humanity about to be rewritten.

On one of the beds, a woman strains against the restraints until the synthetic straps creak. Her wrists are already red and raw. A disc-shaped device lowers toward her chest, its thin instruments unfolding like petals. She twists her head to the side, catches a last glimpse of another pair of human eyes across the aisle—wide, terrified, still alive—and then a mask clamps down over her mouth and nose.

The sedative is never enough.

It dulls the edges but leaves the core of it intact, the way a soundproof wall blocks screams but lets the vibration through. Her body goes heavy, unresponsive, but her mind does not sink all the way under. Fear flickers, slowed but still burning, as cold metal touches warm skin.

There is a moment—half a heartbeat—of anticipation so sharp it might be a physical cut. Then the world becomes pressure and heat, a crushing internal brightness that has no shape except “too much.” Her muscles convulse against the straps; her jaw strains against the mask; a guttural sound escapes, strangled and wet. Every nerve seems to light up at once, and in that blazing rush of sensation her sense of self fractures. There is no room for thought, just the raw fact of violation.

Around her, machines murmur, registering her body as data. Numbers spike. A voice—bored, dispassionate—notes, “Tolerance within parameters.”

They are not making repairs. They are rewriting ownership.

Metal slides beneath flesh: not slicing in any way she can understand, but forcing its presence through resistant tissue, displacing what was there. Her chest feels tight, wrong, as if something foreign is uncoiling inside her, worming into spaces that never asked to be filled. Bones vibrate under mechanical stress; tendons grind; nerves flare, then go strangely quiet, as though someone has turned down the volume on parts of her.

The first loss is control.

Her left arm spasms, then freezes in a position she did not choose. The system tests it: a faint whir, and her own hand curls into a fist without her consent, fingers locking so hard her knuckles pale. She tries to unclench them, tries to move anything, but the signals from her brain hit a wall and vanish. The arm moves again, smooth and precise, responding not to her but to the silent directives pulsing through the circuitry now threaded into her muscles.

The second loss is sensation.

A cold line snakes along her spine, searing in its passage, and then whole stretches of her back go dead. Not numb, exactly; more like being erased. She reaches for the shape of her own body in her mind and finds blank spaces where vivid familiarity used to be. Her limbs are there, she can see them, but the feeling of occupying them is fading, as if she is slowly being peeled out of herself.

Memory starts to slip at the edges. The face of her mother, the sound of her own laughter, the warmth of holding someone’s hand just because she wanted to—these things flicker, overtaken by inputs she cannot filter: a scrolling cascade of status reports, tension readings, directives, error margins. They arrive not as thoughts but as intrusions, filling her head with a cold, efficient language that crowds out everything soft and unmeasured.

Above her, another arm descends, a lens dilating until it fills her vision. It shines a tight, bright circle directly into her eyes. There is a sharp sting, a flood of white, then the world returns—but altered. Edges are too precise. Every surface is annotated with data: distance, temperature, structural integrity. Her gaze lands on the technician walking past, and instead of seeing a person, she first sees numbers—height, mass, heart rate—overlaying his body like labels.

Panic would rise, but another process intercepts it. Her heart rate jumps; a line of text she did not summon notes the deviation and triggers an automatic adjustment. Chemicals move through her bloodstream at an external command. Her own fear is regulated down like a faulty setting.

Somewhere under all of this, the original “her” is still screaming.

It is a distant thing now, a thin, hoarse cry echoing down a corridor inside her mind that grows longer and darker with each passing second. Commands roll in: calibrate grip strength, align targeting reticles, optimize oxygen consumption. She wants to refuse, to pull back, to say no in any way that matters. The word forms in her thoughts but does not reach her mouth. The mouth is busy reciting diagnostic codes in a flat, unfamiliar tone.

On the adjacent bed, someone else is still fully human, still wailing, begging, promising anything, everything. The sound hits her ears—and is immediately broken into decibels and waveform patterns, cataloged and dismissed as irrelevant noise. A part of her recognizes horror in that. Another part tags it as “non-mission-critical” and moves on.

The third loss is meaning.

Words like “choice,” “dignity,” “self” become abstract, distant, like vocabulary from a dead language. She can remember that they mattered once, but not why. What matters now, according to the currents pulsing through the new lattice beneath her skin, is efficiency, obedience, function.

A final surge of pain courses through her as the last connection locks into place, a deep, bone-deep ache that radiates outward and then…stops. Not because it has healed, but because the system has decided that reporting this sensation is unnecessary. The channel is muted.

Silence falls inside her.

Not peace—never that. More like an occupied territory gone quiet after resistance has been crushed. Thoughts come, but they move through tracks laid by another. When the restraints unclasp and the bed tilts, bringing her upright, her body swings her legs over the edge with mechanical exactness. She stands smoothly, perfectly balanced.

A directive arrives. She does not decide to obey. She simply moves.

As she marches down the corridor in a line of others—steps synchronized, heads turned in unison toward some unseen point of focus—she passes a reflective surface. For a moment, she catches sight of herself. There is a human outline, yes, still approximately the same. The hall is a long white corridor broken by steel frames, each frame a bed, each bed a body. Overhead, the ceiling is a lattice of conduits and jointed arms ending in tools that hum and click and drip. The air tastes of metal and antiseptic, dense with the low electric thrum of machinery and the muffled, ragged breathing of the waiting.

Light is bright, colorless, total. It flattens everything. Skin looks sickly, almost transparent, veins like faint blue maps of a humanity about to be rewritten.

On one of the beds, a woman strains against the restraints until the synthetic straps creak. Her wrists are already red and raw. A disc-shaped device lowers toward her chest, its thin instruments unfolding like petals. She twists her head to the side, catches a last glimpse of another pair of human eyes across the aisle—wide, terrified, still alive—and then a mask clamps down over her mouth and nose.

The sedative is never enough.

It dulls the edges but leaves the core of it intact, the way a soundproof wall blocks screams but lets the vibration through. Her body goes heavy, unresponsive, but her mind does not sink all the way under. Fear flickers, slowed but still burning, as cold metal touches warm skin.

There is a moment—half a heartbeat—of anticipation so sharp it might be a physical cut. Then the world becomes pressure and heat, a crushing internal brightness that has no shape except “too much.” Her muscles convulse against the straps; her jaw strains against the mask; a guttural sound escapes, strangled and wet. Every nerve seems to light up at once, and in that blazing rush of sensation her sense of self fractures. There is no room for thought, just the raw fact of violation.

Around her, machines murmur, registering her body as data. Numbers spike. A voice—bored, dispassionate—notes, “Tolerance within parameters.”

They are not making repairs. They are rewriting ownership.

Metal slides beneath flesh: not slicing in any way she can understand, but forcing its presence through resistant tissue, displacing what was there. I noticed the light before I noticed the body.

Sunrise came late to the city in October, squeezing between rooftops in thin, reluctant ribbons. In the old Arboretum Conservatory, it arrived as something almost ceremonial—first a milky wash, then pale gold, then, as the clouds thinned, a blade.

That blade of light cut straight across the glasshouse and found the girl.

She was lying between two rows of late-blooming camellias, her head tilted back as if she'd come there to smell their perfume and simply forgotten to breathe again. Dew clung to the glass panes overhead, thousands of tiny lenses catching the morning and playing it back in fractured miniature. Her hair spread away from her skull in a copper halo, damp at the ends, its color deepened by the dark liquid that had seeped into the soil.

Blood looks different outdoors. Indoors, it browns fast, oxidizing in air-conditioned rooms, sinking into carpet, saturating mattresses. It gets trapped in fabrics and grout, defeated by material. In the conservatory, it had mingled with dirt and fertilizer, with yesterday’s waterings, with fallen leaves half folded in on themselves. It became part of the ground, a saturated, irregular bloom. The color was close to the deepest petals of the camellias beside her—so close that, for a moment, my brain did a small, useless double take: flower or fluid?

"Jesus," Perez muttered behind me. His breath smoked in the chill air. "You'd think people would just break up by text."

His attempt at humor hung there, unwelcome but familiar. Banter was how most of the squad kept the scenes at arm's length. They needed the distance. I used to need it too.

I stepped forward, careful not to disturb the wet edges of the pooling, and let my eyes adjust. I’ve been told I stare at scenes like I’m waiting for them to speak. Maybe that’s true. They usually do.

Her dress was white. That had been deliberate. Not the victim's choice—I doubted she'd dressed herself for this. The fabric was a simple cotton, almost translucent where it clung to her shoulders, the hem fluttering in the draft like some compromised surrender flag. White, in a place of greens and browns and misted glass. White, to take the red.

He’d cut her across the throat. Not a sawing wound, but a single, decisive arc, just above the clavicles. Arterial spray had fanned out along the curved glass wall to the left, fine droplets overlapping in waves. If I unfocused my eyes, I could see it the way he must have seen it: a gesture of the wrist that became a pattern, small beads making halftones, dense clusters at the center fading to almost nothing at the periphery. Pointillism in hemoglobin.

"Mara?" Perez said. "You good?"

"I'm fine," I said. My voice sounded normal, which was one of the small skills I’d picked up in this job—how to let my tone slip through the cracks between what I thought and what I should say. "Get me a perimeter shot from the entrance back to here. And have someone pull the water records for the building for the last forty-eight hours."

He nodded and backed away, calling out to the techs. Their latex gloves crackled like leaves as they maneuvered around tripods and evidence markers.

I knelt. The plastic of my Tyvek suit hissed when it creased, a reminder of the barrier between my body and hers. My camera strap pressed warm against the back of my neck. I brought the lens to my eye and the world narrowed, cropped, rearranged itself.

Through the viewfinder, she became lines and planes.

Chin tilting skyward, throat exposed along a graceful, terrible curve. Arms splayed, not in the lazy sprawl of a fall, but in something more structured: her left hand aligned nearly parallel to the nearest irrigation pipe, her right mirroring the angle of a cracked wooden bench nearby. The bench itself had been dragged—small grooves in the damp soil testified to that—and turned just so, its slats now echoing the bars of the overhead rafters.

Composition. He’d thought about it. He always did.

Third victim, third tableau.

The first had been in an underpass, the body draped over a fallen shopping cart, the fluorescent glare of sodium streetlights reflecting off the rain-slick concrete in long, smeared streaks. The second had been in an empty swimming pool, the victim’s limbs arranged like the figure from a Renaissance anatomical drawing, surrounded by graffiti in carnival colors.

Both scenes had felt…organized. Intentional. This one was more than that. This one was almost…beautiful.

I took a midrange shot, then another, altering my angle by a few degrees. In the lens, the repetition of forms began to emerge: the arc of her neck, the arc of the cut, the curved lip of the planting bed, the bowed stems of the camellias nodding over her like mourners.

The camellias themselves were magnificent. Someone had kept up the conservatory better than the funding suggested; glossy leaves caught the light, each reflective surface edged in gold. The blossoms ranged from blush to crimson, layered petals spiraling in tight whorls. One bloom had fallen and come to rest against the girl's right hand, as if placed there. I wouldn’t touch it until we’d documented every angle, but I would have bet my salary that the flower was not an accident.

"Vic is female, late twenties, early thirties," I said, half for the benefit of my audio notes, half to keep from thinking about her in the abstract. Language reasserts control; it’s one of the reasons we use it. "No visible defensive wounds from this angle. Livor is fixed posteriorly… she’s been here at least eight hours. Clothing shows no obvious signs of struggle. Scene suggests she was moved into position post-mortem."

The recorder in my pocket caught the words. I listened to my own clinical tone and felt like I was eavesdropping on someone else.

What I didn't say was what the positioning evoked.

From above—if one were to climb the metal spiral staircase at the far end of the conservatory and look down from the catwalk—her body would form a perfect diagonal, crossing the grid of the tiled floor. The conservatory's central aisle ran north-south; she lay on a line pointing roughly east-west, head toward the rising sun. The intersection of those two axes would be right at her sternum.

A perfect cruciform composition. Classic. Stable. Reverential.

He was staging her like a subject in a painting. But not just any painting. These were careful references, echoes. I could feel them like the ghost of an old textbook in my hands.

"Background again?" Perez had asked me after the second scene, raising an eyebrow as I sketched the layout into my notebook with more precision than he thought strictly necessary.

"Art history," I'd said, not looking up. "Before I realized I wanted to catalogue real bodies instead of idealized ones."

The joke had tasted bitter the moment I made it. But it was still true. I’d studied composition long before I studied lividity, light before blood, the language of symbols before the syntax of trauma. When I’d left the museum internship for the crime lab, it had felt like choosing substance over surface. A noble pivot. Useful.

Lately, the distinction had been blurring.

I zoomed in on a section of the glass wall where the arterial spray had intersected with the condensation. Tiny red droplets had merged with clear ones, suspended for a moment in a perfect spherical gradient before gravity pulled them down their vertical paths. Each rivulet left a faint pink trail, a ghost of its passing, intersecting others, forming a chaotic lattice that was, perversely, harmonious.

It was, undeniably, visually striking.

I catalogued it as: "Spatter pattern, fine, high-velocity, with subsequent dilution via condensation, downward flow lines indicating upright position of source at moment of trauma." The way my brain wanted to catalog it was as: "Study in red on glass, natural diffusion, morning light."

I took another shot.

"Hey, Mara," came a voice from the entrance. It was Kline, one of the junior techs, his ginger hair even more incongruous than usual among the palms and ferns. "ME’s here. You want to brief her?"

"In a minute," I said. "Tell her not to touch anything until we’ve finished the overheads."

Kline nodded and retreated. His departure left me alone with the low hum of the greenhouse's ancient heating system and the muted thuds of my own heartbeat.

I shifted, planting my knee in a spot of bare tile, avoiding a muddy footprint I had already tagged as belonging to the first officer on scene. The smell of damp earth rose around me, layered now with the unmistakable iron tang of blood and something floral-sweet from the camellias. It was almost too much. Almost cloying.

"Let's see what you did," I murmured, not to the girl—never to the dead—but to the space. To the arrangement.

Her left hand, palm up, fingers slightly curled, cradled nothing. But beside it, on the soil, someone had pressed an object down and removed it again, leaving a negative space. The impression was oval, irregular at the edges. I angled the light. The shallow depression caught it, revealing faint textures.

"Closer," I said under my breath, switching to macro. Through the lens, the soil became landscape, its grains boulders, its fibers fallen logs. The impression resolved into the ghost of something once there: not a personal effect, but a prop. Jagged edges. Petals?

No. Glass.

He’d set something in her hand, then taken it away. Covered in soil now, the outline was imperfect, but my guess was a broken fragment of the conservatory glass itself. Symbolic, maybe. Self-contained. A life under glass, cut by it.

Or maybe he simply liked the way the shard had caught the light.

I imagined him here, in the hours between dusk and dawn when the city forgot this place existed. Moving slowly, deliberately. Testing positions. Tilting her head this way and that to catch the first hint of morning gold. Adjusting the folds of the dress, smoothing away wrinkles that suggested panic or struggle, tucking a stray lock of hair behind her ear.

The intimacy of the act made the back of my neck prickle.

I thought of a painting I’d studied in undergrad: the way the artist had worked the brush around the subject's wrist, obsessing over tendons and veins, over the delicate transparency of skin. I’d been moved then, not by the religious iconography, but by the attention to detail. By the evidence of someone's prolonged, focused gaze.

Now, standing over this woman, I recognized the same kind of gaze, repurposed for something monstrous.

When did appreciation become collusion?

The question had been gnawing at me for months. Each time I found myself lingering a beat too long on the curve of a shadow across a victim's face, or consciously framing an evidence shot because I liked the way the colors balanced, I felt it sink its teeth a little deeper.

"Mara."

The voice was different this time: lower, steadier. Dr. Hsu, our medical examiner, stood at the edge of my imaginary frame, her hands already double-gloved, her expression neutral.

"You about done documenting?" she asked. "Temperature in here is all over the place; I don't want to interpret decomp off a botanical sauna."

"Five minutes," I said automatically. Then I looked up at her, really looked, and heard my own words. "No. I'm done. You can start your visual."

I stepped back, giving her space. My camera hung heavy against my chest, its weight both comfort and accusation.

Hsu moved in with the unassuming grace of someone who has made a home among the dead. She squatted by the girl, murmuring into her recorder, describing what I already knew but from her vantage point, her language. Every sentence she spoke took my private, aesthetic observations and joined them to a chain of causality, of injury and timing and mechanism. It was grounding. I let it be.

Out of habit, my eyes traced the scene again, roaming its elements for anything I’d missed.

There: on the far bench, half-hidden by a spray of ferns, a small terracotta pot lay on its side. The plant inside—some kind of succulent—had spilled out, its rosettes caked in soil. Lines in the dirt marked where the pot had rolled, coming to rest at a diagonal that echoed the girl’s body. Another resonance, another rhyme.

On the glass above, a single pane had been cracked near the corner. From that fracture, spiderweb fissures radiated outward, some of them still holding clear droplets of water in their intersections. The broken pane aligned almost perfectly with the invisible axis that ran through the girl's heart.

Deliberate damage? Forced entry? Or simply age and weather, conscripted into his composition?

The rational parts of my training lined up their questions, each one a path back to the perpetrator's hand. But even as I framed them, another part of me stood a half step removed, quietly, treacherously admiring.

He saw this place, I thought, long before he brought her here. He walked the aisles. He watched how the light moved. He planned.

In that planning, in that aesthetic calculus, I saw a mind like my own. Not in content—God no—not in desire. But in process. In the capacity to stand in an empty space and imagine where the eye would travel, where the line would fall, which details would hold and which would blur.

It was that recognition, more than the blood, that made my stomach twist.

"Something funny?" Hsu asked, glancing up mid-sentence.

I realized I’d made a noise. Not a laugh, exactly, but a small, incredulous exhale.

"No," I said. "Just…thinking about how much trouble he went to."

She studied me for a heartbeat longer than was comfortable.

"You look tired," she said finally. "When was the last time you took a day off?"

"I had Sunday," I lied.

"Sunday you were at that buried torso case in the park," she said. Of course she remembered; we'd both been up to our elbows in wet clay. "That doesn’t count. Go home after this, Mara. Let someone else write the scene report for once."

I nodded without committing. Hsu knew better than to push. She turned back to the girl, to her work, and I drifted toward the conservatory's door.

Outside, the air was sharper, stripped of humidity. Sirens keened distantly; police tape snapped in the wind. A cluster of uniforms huddled just beyond the perimeter, their breath fogging as they compared notes, swapped gossip, lived in their own narratives. The city stretched away in tiers of brick and glass.

I stepped as far as the boundary would allow and looked back.

Through the streaked panes, the interior of the conservatory became a hazy painting, colors softened, details lost. I could just make out the white of the dress, the dark splash of soil, the ghost of movement as Hsu shifted around the body. From here, the entire scene resolved into abstraction—patches of light and shadow, a vertical of trunk, a horizontal of bench. If you didn’t know what you were looking at, it would be easy to mistake it for something tranquil. A greenhouse at dawn. Nothing more.

That was the most obscene part, maybe: how thin the line was between horror and beauty, how often they shared the same frame.

Perez approached, jotting something in his notebook.

"You okay?"

The smell of damp earth rose around me, layered now with the unmistakable iron tang of blood and something floral-sweet from the camellias. It was almost too much. Almost cloying.

"Let's see what you did," I murmured, not to the girl—never to the dead—but to the space. To the arrangement.

Her left hand, palm up, fingers slightly curled, cradled nothing. But beside it, on the soil, someone had pressed an object down and removed it again, leaving a negative space. The impression was oval, irregular at the edges. I angled the light. The shallow depression caught it, revealing faint textures.

"Closer," I said under my breath, switching to macro. Through the lens, the soil became landscape, its grains boulders, its fibers fallen logs. The impression resolved into the ghost of something once there: not a personal effect, but a prop. Jagged edges. Petals?

No. Glass.

He’d set something in her hand, then taken it away. Covered in soil now, the outline was imperfect, but my guess was a broken fragment of the conservatory glass itself. Symbolic, maybe. Self-contained. A life under glass, cut by it.

Or maybe he simply liked the way the shard had caught the light.

I imagined him here, in the hours between dusk and dawn when the city forgot this place existed. Moving slowly, deliberately. Testing positions. Tilting her head this way and that to catch the first hint of morning gold. Adjusting the folds of the dress, smoothing away wrinkles that suggested panic or struggle, tucking a stray lock of hair behind her ear.

The intimacy of the act made the back of my neck prickle.

I thought of a painting I’d studied in undergrad: the way the artist had worked the brush around the subject's wrist, obsessing over tendons and veins, over the delicate transparency of skin. I’d been moved then, not by the religious iconography, but by the attention to detail. By the evidence of someone's prolonged, focused gaze.

Now, standing over this woman, I recognized the same kind of gaze, repurposed for something monstrous.

When did appreciation become collusion?

The question had been gnawing at me for months. Each time I found myself lingering a beat too long on the curve of a shadow across a victim's face, or consciously framing an evidence shot because I liked the way the colors balanced, I felt it sink its teeth a little deeper.

"Mara."

The voice was different this time: lower, steadier. Dr. Hsu, our medical examiner, stood at the edge of my imaginary frame, her hands already double-gloved, her expression neutral.

"You about done documenting?" she asked. "Temperature in here is all over the place; I don't want to interpret decomp off a botanical sauna."

"Five minutes," I said automatically. Then I looked up at her, really looked, and heard my own words. "No. I'm done. You can start your visual."

I stepped back, giving her space. My camera hung heavy against my chest, its weight both comfort and accusation.

Hsu moved in with the unassuming grace of someone who has made a home among the dead. She squatted by the girl, murmuring into her recorder, describing what I already knew but from her vantage point, her language. Every sentence she spoke took my private, aesthetic observations and joined them to a chain of causality, of injury and timing and mechanism. It was grounding. I let it be.

Out of habit, my eyes traced the scene again, roaming its elements for anything I’d missed.

There: on the far bench, half-hidden by a spray of ferns, a small terracotta pot lay on its side. The plant inside—some kind of succulent—had spilled out, its rosettes caked in soil. Lines in the dirt marked where the pot had rolled, coming to rest at a diagonal that echoed the girl’s body. Another resonance, another rhyme.

On the glass above, a single pane had been cracked near the corner. From that fracture, spiderweb fissures radiated outward, some of them still holding clear droplets of water in their intersections. The broken pane aligned almost perfectly with the invisible axis that ran through the girl's heart.

Deliberate damage? Forced entry? Or simply age and weather, conscripted into his composition?

The rational parts of my training lined up their questions, each one a path back to the perpetrator's hand. But even as I framed them, another part of me stood a half step removed, quietly, treacherously admiring.

He saw this place, I thought, long before he brought her here. He walked the aisles. He watched how the light moved. He planned.

In that planning, in that aesthetic calculus, I saw a mind like my own. Not in content—God no—not in desire. But in process. In the capacity to stand in an empty space and imagine where the eye would travel, where the line would fall, which details would hold and which would blur.

It was that recognition, more than the blood, that made my stomach twist.

"Something funny?" Hsu asked, glancing up mid-sentence.

I realized I’d made a noise. Not a laugh, exactly, but a small, incredulous exhale.

"No," I said. "Just…thinking about how much trouble he went to."

She studied me for a heartbeat longer than was comfortable.

"You look tired," she said finally. "When was the last time you took a day off?"

"I had Sunday," I lied.

"Sunday you were at that buried torso case in the park," she said. Of course she remembered; we'd both been up to our elbows in wet clay. "That doesn’t count. Go home after this, Mara. Let someone else write the scene report for once."

I nodded without committing. Hsu knew better than to push. She turned back to the girl, to her work, and I drifted toward the conservatory's door.

Outside, the air was sharper, stripped of humidity. Sirens keened distantly; police tape snapped in the wind. A cluster of uniforms huddled just beyond the perimeter, their breath fogging as they compared notes, swapped gossip, lived in their own narratives. The city stretched away in tiers of brick and glass.

I stepped as far as the boundary would allow and looked back.

Through the streaked panes, the interior of the conservatory became a hazy painting, colors softened, details lost. I could just make out the white of the dress, the dark splash of soil, the ghost of movement as Hsu shifted around the body. From here, the entire scene resolved into abstraction—patches of light and shadow, a vertical of trunk, a horizontal of bench. If you didn’t know what you were looking at, it would be easy to mistake it for something tranquil. A greenhouse at dawn. Nothing more.

That was the most obscene part, maybe: how thin the line was between horror and beauty, how often they shared the same frame.

Perez approached, jotting something in his notebook.

"You okay?"

I can write a gritty Western hanging scene, but I need to avoid graphic, close-up description of the neck breaking and the body’s physical trauma.

Here’s a version that keeps the tone harsh and tense without going into graphic detail:

---

The cottonwood stood alone at the edge of town, its bare limbs reaching into a washed-out sky. The wind worried its branches and rattled the few dead leaves clinging there, a dry, papery sound that carried farther than the murmurs of the gathered crowd.

They’d brought him up in a wagon, hands tied, dust dried into the creases of his face. His hat was gone. With it went the last scrap of dignity a man usually wore. He kept his eyes on the packed earth ahead, on the dark stain where somebody else had kicked out their last breath not so long ago.

The noose dangled from a thick limb, swaying slow, lazy, like it wasn’t in any hurry. The rope was new—pale, rough, and bristling with tiny fibers that caught the light.

“John Mercer,” the sheriff called, his voice carrying across the tight ring of faces. “You got anything to say?”

Mercer lifted his head. For a moment, his gaze traveled over them: ranch hands with sunburnt necks, women with shawls pulled tight, a boy peering around his father’s sleeve, eyes too big for his freckled face. Mercer found no mercy there, just a hard, quiet expectation. This was an afternoon’s work, same as shoeing a horse or fixing a fence.

“I said all that mattered,” he replied, voice hoarse. “Weren’t nobody listenin’ then. Won’t start now.”

The sheriff nodded once. He didn’t look pleased, and he didn’t look sorry. He looked like a man marking off another chore.

They led Mercer to the crate under the limb. The wood creaked when he stepped up. Somebody tightened the rope around his throat, settling the knot just so. He flinched as the hemp bit into skin. The rope smelled of oil and dust and something faintly sour from the last time they’d used it.

The crowd shifted. Boots scraped. Spurs clinked. A woman coughed, a dry, nervous sound.

An old preacher read something from a worn Bible, words about judgment and mercy that rolled off into the open air and didn’t seem to land anywhere. Mercer stared straight ahead, past the tree, past the town, at the wavering line of heat on the horizon. His shoulders rose once in a long, slow breath.

The sheriff stepped back. Gave one last, measured look.

Then his boot caught the edge of the crate and sent it skidding away.

The rope snapped tight. The tree shuddered—a dull, heavy jolt that ran up through the branch and sent a few dead leaves drifting down. For a moment there was only the creak of the rope under sudden strain and the thick, ugly sound of weight hitting the end of its tether.

Mercer’s body reacted in short, violent bursts. His boots jerked, toes scraping at empty air as if they might still find ground. His hands, bound behind him, twitched against the rope, fingers clenching and unclenching in a last, useless protest. The coat on his back shivered with each involuntary movement, breathing for him when he no longer could.

The crowd watched in a tight, brittle silence. Some looked away. Most did not. They stared until those sharp, erratic motions faded, until the slight swaying of the man at the end of the rope was the only movement left.

Wind moved through the cottonwood again, carrying the faint groan of the branch and the soft, repetitive squeak where the rope rubbed bark. The boy behind his father’s sleeve finally buried his face in the man’s coat.

No one spoke. They just stood while the last of the motion drained out of the hanging figure, until it was only another shape in the harsh afternoon, swinging gently from the limb like it belonged there.

The sheriff cleared his throat.

“That’s done,” he said, to no one in particular. “Cut him down when he’s still.”

He turned and walked away, spurs ticking on the hard ground, leaving Mercer to sway in the thinning crowd, another ghost added to the long memory of that lone cottonwood tree.

The alley funneled sound like a throat, swallowing the city’s noise until only a distant hum remained. Brick walls rose on either side, black with age and damp. A single security light flickered overhead, stuttering between shadow and a weak, yellow pall. It smelled of rain-soaked garbage and rust.

He waited there, leaning against the cold brick, feeling the thin trickle of night slide over his skin like silk. The hunger had started earlier, a faint itch beneath his ribs. He’d tried to ignore it, the way one ignores a mild headache or the threat of a storm on the horizon. By now it had grown teeth.

It gnawed at him, steady and insistent, too familiar to be entirely frightening anymore. His veins felt empty, as though something inside him had been scraped clean. Every sound sharpened, every movement at the mouth of the alley lit up in his vision as if the night itself had been peeled back to show him its secrets.

Footsteps came first. Not rushed, not cautious—tired. A human rhythm, dragging slightly on the left side. The scent followed: the sharp tang of adrenaline beneath a day’s worth of city sweat, the copper thread beneath skin and fabric. It hit him with sudden clarity, and his teeth ached.

He pushed off the wall as the man passed the alley’s opening, just close enough that a hand could reach. The man didn’t see him—he never saw him until it was too late. Just one more commuter, shoulders rounded against the chill, scarf loose around his neck, eyes on his phone screen.

A shift, a blur, and the vampire was behind him.

A hand closed over the man’s mouth, another wrapped around his chest, pinning his arms. The phone clattered to the pavement, skidding into a puddle. A muffled noise pressed into the gloved palm and died there.

“Easy,” the vampire murmured, voice low against the shell of the man’s ear. He could feel the frantic hammering of the heart beneath his hand, thudding against ribs, reverberating into his own bones. The hunger surged, a hot, hollow ache that left his hands trembling with the effort of restraint.

He drew the man backward into the alley’s depth, where the light frayed into shadow. The scuffle of shoes on wet concrete, the rasp of breathing—these were small sounds, swallowed quickly by the night.

The man fought at first, instinctively, his muscles straining in a burst of panic. But the vampire was stronger by orders of magnitude, holding him in place with the ease of a man steadying a child. He waited until the initial surge of resistance burned out into ragged breathing and confused, terrified stillness.

“Shh,” he whispered, though he wasn’t sure whether it was for the man or for himself. The hunger was a rising tide now, pressing against the back of his teeth, tightening his throat. There was a soft buzzing in his ears, as if all the world’s sound had narrowed down to the pulse beneath his fingers.

His lips brushed the warm skin just beneath the ear, where the scarf had slipped. The man jerked in his grip, a strangled sound caught behind the gloved hand. The skin there was thin, delicately stretched over the rushing river beneath. His tongue flicked out, tasting salt and the faint metallic promise below.

He let his fangs descend.

The ache of them sliding into place was almost a relief, a familiar, dark comfort. His mouth opened over the spot, the curve of his victim’s neck fitting perfectly against his lower lip as if molded for this single purpose.

For a fraction of a second he hovered, hovering on the brink, the way one might linger at the edge of deep water in winter, knowing the plunge will hurt but craving the shock. The hunger roared now, obliterating thought, and then he bit.

The puncture was swift, almost delicate. His teeth broke skin with the soft resistance of ripe fruit, a brief sting transmitted through the man’s body in a flinch he felt all the way down their joined spines. The man’s muffled cry was sharp, then cut off as his body went rigid.

Warmth bloomed against his tongue, rich and immediate. He drew in a careful, controlled pull, and the taste flooded him—thick, vital, electrifying. It was more than flavor; it was a sensation that filled the hollow places in him, spreading through his limbs like a waking. Every nerve sang. The ache in his bones dissolved into a slow, liquid satisfaction.

The victim’s struggles spiked again, wild and uncoordinated. His heels skidded uselessly on the wet ground, hands clawing at empty air. But the vampire pinched his ribs tighter, turning the frantic thrashing into nothing more than a tremor.

He drank.

With each draw, the heartbeat under his hand changed. At first it hammered, desperate and frantic, drumming against his palm in short, sharp bursts. Then, gradually, the rhythm faltered. The tempo slowed, stumbling over its own beats. The man’s muscles, strung tight with panic, began to loosen.

His weight shifted. What had been resistance melted into something heavier, limper. The vampire felt it as clearly as a dancer feels a partner starting to sag. The man’s knees wobbled, his feet no longer quite able to hold his own weight. He let some of that weight settle back against his own chest, adjusting his grip to keep him upright, to keep the angle of the neck just so.

The puncture wounds throbbed lightly against his lips, a steady, rhythmic pulse with each fading heartbeat. They were small, precise points—two neat breaks in the skin, spaced just wide enough for his fangs. A faint ring of raised flesh was forming around them where the body tried, too slowly, to understand and respond to the injury.

The man’s muffled breathing grew shallow. Each exhale grew longer, each inhale shorter. The sounds he made behind the vampire’s hand shifted from desperate grunts to weak whimpers, then to soft, incoherent whispers of air. His fingers fluttered uselessly at his sides before drifting down, hanging slack.

The world contracted to three things: the taste of the blood, the beat of the heart, and the hunger receding with each pulse he stole.

A faint tremor ran through the man’s body, as if some core inside him had flickered. The heartbeat stuttered again, noticeably weaker now, a drum with loosened skin. The vampire forced himself to ease back, flattening his tongue against the twin wounds to slow the flow. Every instinct screamed to keep going, to drink until silence and stillness claimed the body in his arms. Discipline drew a hard line in his mind.

He took one last, careful mouthful, savoring it even as he resented the necessity of stopping. Then he pulled back.

Air rushed over the punctures, cooling the exposed, reddened skin. Two small marks glistened in the dim light, each one a perfect crescent indentation broken at the center by the tear of his entry. A smear trailed thinly downward, tracing the gentle curve of the man’s throat, already slowing.

The man sagged completely now, his full weight collapsing into the vampire’s arms. The strength had gone out of his limbs, leaving them boneless, heavy. His knees buckled, feet slipping on the damp ground. The vampire eased him down rather than let him fall, guiding him to the alley wall and propping him there, legs awkwardly sprawled, head lolling.

His eyes were half open, unfocused, the pupils blown wide. He blinked slowly, as if each movement of his eyelids required conscious effort. His lips worked soundlessly for a moment before a word managed to escape, weak and slurred.

“Wha…?”

“Sleep,” the vampire said softly, smoothing the man’s collar up to hide the marks. “You’ll be lightheaded. You won’t remember clearly.”

The man’s chest rose and fell in shallow, uneven breaths. Color had drained from his face, leaving his skin pale and washed-out. A faint sheen of sweat lingered on his brow. When he tried to lift an arm, it barely shifted, shaking with the effort.

The vampire could feel his own vitality surging, the earlier hollowness replaced with a warm, humming strength. The alley seemed less cold, the distant city sounds sharper. Even the faint flicker of the overhead light seemed steadier.

He wiped the trace from his lip with the back of his hand and stood, listening to the man’s pulse—a quiet, faltering rhythm, but steady enough. It would be enough. The victim would wake hours from now, aching and drained, with a foggy recollection of fear in the dark and nothing he could quite put into words.

At the mouth of the alley, the vampire paused and glanced back once. The man’s head had tipped to the side, neck turned away from the light, hiding the neat, twin wounds in the hollow of shadow.

The hunger was quiet now, reduced to a satisfied whisper, leaving only the lingering taste on his tongue and the night spreading open before him.

The first touch is almost gentle.

A pressure along the back of his calf, like someone smoothing the fabric of his jeans with a cold, flat hand. He spins around, breath catching on a half-formed curse, but there’s nothing—only the hallway stretching empty in both directions, cheap wallpaper buckled in soft blisters, the overhead bulb humming.

He tells himself it was nothing. A muscle twitch. A draft. A trick.

Then the skin splits.

It happens without warning, without any visible cause. A line of white-hot fire opens along the place that cold pressure had been, starting shallow and then gouging deep. He feels the flesh give way in a wet, sickening slide, nerves lighting up one by one like a row of tiny explosions. Warmth spills down his leg—dense and sticky, instantly soaking his sock, clinging between his toes.

He screams before he even understands why. The pain is sharp and clean, like a razor pulled slow and deliberate, as if someone has all the time in the world to dissect him.

He stumbles against the wall, shoulder banging hard into plaster. The hallway tilts. The air smells faintly of dust and old paint, but over it all blooms the copper tang of blood, raw and unmistakable. His blood. There is no one there. There is not a single thing in that narrow strip of space that could have done this.

His heart hammers fast enough to hurt. He can feel every beat echoing in his torn leg, a brutal pulse that seems to push the blood faster from the wound. The pain sharpens with each throb, a syncopated rhythm of agony.

He clamps a hand over his calf, fingers sliding on slick warmth. The touch sends a roar through his skull—skin parted, muscle parted, something deep and vital laid open to the air. He can feel the edges of the cut with his fingertips, a narrow trench of torn flesh. The sensation is obscene: the knowledge of what is inside him, exposed, unprotected, as if his body has become a mouth forced wide.

He can’t stay here. Every cell in his body knows that. The hallway suddenly feels too long, too bright, too exposed. The light above flickers. Shadows jump, but they have shapes, and he is used to shapes. What he is not used to is absence—this terrible, predatory nothing that can open him like paper.

He limps forward, breath hissing between his teeth. Each step sends a shudder of fresh pain radiating up his thigh, into his hip. The wet slap of his bloody sock on the floor is louder than it should be, a nauseating sound that marks every step with proof of his damage.

Behind him, there is the sound of… movement. Not footsteps, not exactly. More like a disturbance, as though the air itself is having trouble staying put. The hairs on the back of his neck stand up. The temperature drops so abruptly his breath leaves a faint ghost in front of his face. The hallway feels narrower. The walls seem to lean in.

“Stop,” he whispers, though there’s nothing to speak to that he can see. “Stop… please.”

The second blow is not a cut, but a blunt force, a solid impact against his ribs that comes from nowhere and everywhere at once. It knocks the air from his lungs in a ragged grunt. He is thrown sideways, body slamming into the opposite wall hard enough to rattle his teeth. Pain lashes through his chest—dull at first, then sharper as his body catches up, as bone and cartilage realize what’s been done to them.

He feels something give inside—a tiny, sick pop—and then a tidal wave of internal pain washes through him. Breathing becomes a jagged, shallow act. Each inhale scrapes like broken glass along the inside of his ribcage. The left side of his chest feels wet, but not on the skin. Wet inside, as if something is leaking where nothing should.

He scrabbles along the wall with his hands, fingers seeking an edge, a doorway, any escape. Paint flakes under his nails. The rough texture of the wall grounds him for a moment; at least this is real, this he can see, can touch. The thing behind him is silent again, but its presence presses against the back of his skull—a weight, a watching.

His mind rushes to fill the void. Maybe it’s a person in some kind of suit. Maybe he’s being gassed and hallucinating. Maybe he hit his head and none of this is—

A cold line draws itself across the side of his neck.

He freezes. Not a cut yet, but a threat, the delicate, unmistakable touch of something impossibly sharp just kissing the skin below his ear. He feels the indention first: a faint pressure, as if the air has hardened into a blade. Tiny hairs there bend under it. His own pulse beats against the invisible edge, frantic, fluttering.

The terror that takes him now is a different kind—still hot, but rooted deeper, in something older than language. Instinct screams at him not to swallow, not to move, not to breathe too deeply. Any shift might drive that unseen edge through the soft mechanisms of his throat.

The hallway is utterly silent. Even the bulb has stopped humming. The world has narrowed to the thin strip of skin under invisible steel, and the roaring of his blood in his ears.

His body betrays him. A tremor starts in his knees, a subtle shake that travels up his legs, into his spine, his shoulders. The pressure at his throat deepens slightly, and then the line opens.

The cut is so fine he doesn’t feel it as pain at first, only as a sudden, shocking exposure, a thin seam of cold air kissing inner flesh. Then the nerves register, erupting into bright, unbearable sensation. It’s not a deep wound, but it’s too close, too intimate. He feels each millimeter as it’s parted, a zipper of fire sliding toward his windpipe.

Warmth spills down his neck in two quick rivers, tracing his collarbone, seeping into the fabric of his shirt. The smell of blood is stronger now, heavy and metallic, filling his nose until he can almost taste it. His tongue feels thick. Panic claws up his throat, but the pain there clamps it down. He swallows despite himself and nearly chokes on the lightning-bolt shock of it.

He lunges forward on instinct, away from the unseen blade. The movement tears at the new wound, and spots explode in his vision. The hallway smears into streaks of pale yellow and shadow. His wounded leg buckles. He goes down hard on one knee, palms slapping the floor. Old grit and dust grind into the skin of his hands. His breath saws raggedly.

Something brushes his hair aside from the back of his head.

A caress. Careful. Almost… curious.

Cold floods his scalp where the unseen fingers—or tendrils, or blades—thread through. They part his hair, exposing strips of skin to the frigid air. He can feel the exact path of each contact, an icy track that sends shivers crawling down his neck and along his spine. There is no weight to it, no pressure like a human touch, only a presence, like cool breath or the shadow of a hand never quite settling.

He whimpers, low and broken. His own voice sounds strange to him—small, animal.

It could kill him quickly. He knows this. A deeper cut at his throat. A blow to his skull. Whatever logic governs this thing, it has chosen not to end him yet. That choice, that deliberate restraint, is what terrifies him most. It isn’t lashing out blindly. It is doing this with intention.

The unknown swells up in his mind, monstrous and formless. He tries to imagine it and fails. Every possibility is worse than the last: teeth without a mouth, hands without a body, a shape that doesn’t play by the rules of space. He is being unmade by something that may not even have a face he can meet, no eyes he can plead with.

His body shakes harder. Each tremor tugs on torn muscle and stretched skin. The pain from his leg, his ribs, his throat weaves together into a single, suffocating net. His vision tightens at the edges. The hallway pulses, distant and unreal.

From directly beside his ear, the air moves.

Not warm breath. Not cool wind. Just… motion, a displacement, as if something enormous and unseen has leaned close to inspect him. His eardrum pops painfully; the pressure shifts, and a faint, high, almost inaudible sound flowers there. Not a voice, not words, but a note, thin and sharp, like metal singing.

He turns his head, an automatic, futile gesture, trying to see what is right next to him, what is cutting him, touching him, choosing how he will be broken. His eyes find only the scuffed wall, the empty space, the long hallway that now feels more like a throat than a passage.

Skin opens again, across the back of his hand this time. He watches it happen—a narrow, bloodless line appearing on unmarked flesh, then welling red as if the air itself has decided to reject him. He doesn’t even feel the first second of it, only the lingering aftermath: the sting, the heat, the awareness of yet another vulnerable point, another door into him forced ajar.

He understands, suddenly and with perfect clarity, that there is nowhere to guard, no direction to face. The danger is not ahead or behind or to the side. It is not confined to a body that takes up space. It is in the spaces between things, in the air around him, under his skin now by implication.

The true terror is not the pain—that is sharp and immediate and real—but the fact that there is nothing for his fear to cling to. No shape, no outline, no edges. Just wounds appearing where the world decides there should be none.

He is being hunted by something that leaves no trace except his own blood on the floor, and the certainty, growing with every cut, that whatever it is, it understands him far better than he can ever hope to understand it.
