results.model_response:
They lined them up beneath the hanging lights.

Four chairs, four sets of tied wrists, four faces he knew better than his own. The warehouse smelled of oil and dust and something acid that burned the back of his throat. A concrete floor, an iron beam overhead, shadows like bars slanting across everything.

Marcus stood alone in the cleared space, knees trembling so badly he could feel the fabric of his jeans quiver. His hands were empty. That felt wrong. Usually when they were together—game nights, road trips, stupid bar crawls—his hands were full of something: a beer, a controller, a steering wheel. Now they just hung at his sides, as useless as he was.

“You understand the terms,” said the man behind him.

Marcus didn’t turn. He knew the voice. Calm, steady, professionally uninterested. The kind of voice that belonged to emails marked “regret to inform you.” The kind that never really had regret in it.

“If you don’t choose,” the man continued, “we execute all four. If you choose one, the other three leave with you. I’m not asking for a speech, just a name.”

Just a name.

The light above them buzzed. It flickered in that way that made everyone look sick. Pale. Dead already.

“Marc.”

It was Elise. Third chair from the left. Her blond hair was stuck to her face in places, sweat glistening along her hairline. Her lip was split. A thin line of dried red traced down from the corner of her mouth to her chin. Her eyes were wide, but he recognized something there: the flint at her core. She’d broken her wrist in college punching a guy twice her size for grabbing her friend. That same stubbornness stared at him now.

“Marc, look at me,” she said, voice ragged. “Hey. Hey.”

He forced his gaze to focus on her. Not on the zip ties cutting into her wrists, not on the bruise spreading across her collarbone. Her eyes. Just her eyes.

“It’s okay,” she said. “We’ll figure this out. There has to be—”

“There isn’t.” Devon’s voice, from the far left. He sat slumped, his dark curls wild, his glasses crooked. There was a smear of blood along one lens, turning his left eye into a warped red blur. He tried to straighten, winced. “This is what they want. He chooses or we all die. That’s the game.”

“Don’t call it a game,” Joanna snapped from the second chair. She jerked against her restraints, the metal legs scraping loud on the concrete. Angry to the last second, of course. Joanna didn’t bend. She’d once argued with a traffic cop for twenty straight minutes and somehow walked away without a ticket.

Now there was a purple shadow along her jawline and one eye swelling, but she still glared like she could rip the roof off the building with her bare hands.

“You can’t make him do this,” she spat at the shadows behind Marcus. “You hear me? You cowards. You want to kill us, kill us. But you don’t get to play with him like he’s—”

“Jo,” Mateo said quietly. Fourth chair. Almost directly in front of Marcus. “Stop. Please.”

Mateo looked the worst of them, and somehow the most composed. Dried blood crusted along his hairline, disappearing into his black curls. His shirt was ripped at the shoulder, exposing a bloom of bruises like ink spreading beneath his skin. His hands were twisted awkwardly behind the chair, but his posture was straighter than the others. He kept his eyes trained on Marcus, steady, dark, unreadable.

Marcus’s chest clenched so hard it felt like someone pressing an iron bar through his ribs.

“Time is limited,” the man behind him said. “We have other matters to attend to.”

Marcus swallowed. His tongue felt too big, his throat too dry.

“There has to be another option,” Marcus said. The words came out hoarse. “Use me. Trade me. I’ll—take my—”

“It’s not negotiable,” the man said. “Your life isn’t worth as much as theirs to the people who hired me. That’s why you’re the one standing.”

The way he said it hit harder than a slap.

Worth. As if his best friends’ lives had been tallied, invoices filed, and somewhere on a spreadsheet his name had ended up in the wrong column.

“I can’t,” Marcus whispered. It felt like speaking against a knife edge. “I can’t pick one of them.”

“Then we kill them all,” the man said. “And you live with that. Or you die too. It makes no difference to me.”

A silence fell that wasn’t really silence. It was breathing and the hum of lights and the faint metallic clink each time one of them shifted and the rope or plastic bit a little deeper into flesh.

“Marc.” Devon squinted at him through his cracked glasses. “Listen. Statistically, one life for three is—”

“Shut up, Devon,” Joanna snapped. “You’re not a spreadsheet.”

“It’s math,” Devon said, looking from her to Marcus. “If one of us dies, the rest live. That’s the best outcome in this mess. We all know that. It’s—” His voice wobbled. “It’s basic game theory.”

“Not helping,” Joanna muttered, though her gaze flicked to Marcus with something like fear flickering under the anger.

“Marc.” Elise again, voice breaking on his name. “Don’t do it. Don’t let them make you a part of this. If we all go, we all go. Together. They don’t get to turn you into—into—”

“Into what?” the man behind him asked mildly. “A survivor?”

Marcus spun then, unable not to. The man stood in the shadows, face half-lit by the low yellow light. Ordinary. That was the worst part. No scars, no missing eye, no cinematic villain markers. Just a man with a gun at his hip and gloves on his hands and a watch that ticked audibly each second it took Marcus to breathe.

“Why me?” Marcus forced out. “Why not just pick somebody and do it? Why do you need me to—”

“Because the people who hired me are angry,” the man said. “And hurting you is part of what they’re paying for. This way, you’ll never know if you picked right. You’ll never know if the one you saved will forgive you, or if the ones who die would have forgiven you more. It’s efficient, in its way. Psychological leverage. It lingers.”

His watch ticked once, twice.

“Name,” he said.

Marcus turned back to them. His vision had sharpened somehow, colors too bright. Joanna’s black hair looked almost blue under the harsh light. Mateo’s hands fisted behind the chair were shaking. Devon’s chest rose and fell too fast. Elise’s eyes shone wetly, tears catching the light on her lashes.

The thought stabbed him—this might be the last time he saw any of their faces alive. How small everything else became in the shadow of that.

“We’re not letting you choose,” Joanna said, as if sheer will could make reality back down. “Look at me, Marc. You’re not doing this. We’re not playing. They can’t make—”

“Jo,” Mateo said again, more firmly.

“No! I’m not going to sit here and—”

“Jo.” Mateo’s voice cut through hers, quiet but hard. He looked at her, then at Devon, then Elise. Then he lifted his chin toward Marcus.

“Marc. Listen to me.”

Marcus could barely breathe. “Don’t, T. Don’t you dare.”

“You’re going to say a name,” Mateo said, each word measured. “You’re going to say mine. You’ll walk out of here with them, and you’ll live, and you’ll carry me with you. Okay? That’s how this goes.”

Elise made a strangled sound. “No. No, Mateo, don’t—”

“Shut up, Lis.” Mateo’s eyes never left Marcus. “I’m serious. Of all of us, we know it should be me.”

“When did we vote on that?” Devon demanded, his voice breaking. “Nobody talked to me about—”

“You have a kid coming,” Mateo said, cutting him off. “You think I forgot? You showed us the ultrasound, remember? Week before all this started. You think I’m going to let your daughter grow up without you because Marc couldn’t—”

“Stop talking like this,” Elise hissed, tears spilling now. “You always do this, you always—throw yourself under things. You’re not a—”

“I don’t have anyone,” Mateo said, still looking only at Marcus. “Not like you three do. No partner, no kid on the way, no family that isn’t already barely holding their own. Of the four chairs, my absence will tear the smallest hole. That’s just fact. So. You’re going to say my name.”

Marcus pressed his palms against his thighs, as if he could hold himself together with friction alone. His vision blurred, sharpened, blurred again.

“Mateo…” The name came out like a wound.

He heard the sound again on a Tuesday.

It was a soft, deliberate thud that seemed to crawl through the beams of the duplex and into Daniel’s bedroom wall. Not the creaks of old wood or the cough of the boiler—he knew those by now. This was different: a weight set down with care, followed by the whisper of something being dragged across concrete.

He checked the clock: 1:17 a.m.

For weeks, he’d tried to ignore the sounds from the other side of the thin wall he shared with his neighbor, Mr. Harlan. At first it was just footsteps late at night. Then the scraping started. A muffled clink, like metal on stone. The hum of some machine. Once, he’d smelled something strange in the hallway—sharp and sweet, like chemical cleaner trying to smother something else.

He’d told himself all the rational things. It’s an old house. People keep odd hours. Harlan’s just…eccentric. The man was quiet, polite, with neat gray hair and a habit of wearing pressed shirts even when checking the mailbox. A man who collected old books. A man who smiled, but only with his lips.

The thud came again, faintly rattling the picture frame above Daniel’s bed.

He sat up, heartbeat tapping at his ribs. The wall between them was thin enough that sometimes he could hear the neighbor’s TV. Not tonight. No glow of moving images flickering under the shared baseboards. Just quiet, and that…sound.

He swung his legs off the bed and stood there in the dark, listening. There—a shuffle, then another drag, longer this time. It came from below.

The basement.

He grabbed his phone and tiptoed to his bedroom door. The hallway outside was unlit, washed in a gray that made the world feel like it had been emptied out. He cracked open his front door and peered out. Across the narrow landing, his neighbor’s door was closed. No movement under the threshold.

The basement door was at the end of the hall, between the two units. It was supposed to be shared, though Daniel had never really used it. When he’d moved in three months ago, the landlord had said, “Basement’s mostly his stuff. You got a storage cage down there, but neighbor’s already got it pretty occupied. Best to stay out of his way.” Then a shrug, a smile that didn’t reach his eyes. “He’s been here a long time.”

Daniel padded barefoot down the hallway. The floorboards under his toes were cold. The smell met him before he reached the door: a faint bite of bleach and something underneath it, stale and metallic. He swallowed, hand hovering over the knob.

Don’t. Go back to bed.

The next sound wasn’t a thud. It was a soft, breathy grunt from somewhere below, followed by the muted screech of metal hinges.

He turned the knob.

The basement door opened with a low sigh. A draft of cold air slid up the narrow stairwell, brushing his face. It carried that smell more strongly now—chemical, sharp, masking something he didn’t want to identify.

A single bare bulb glowed somewhere below, faint and yellow.

“Hello?” His voice sounded thinner than he meant it to. He cleared his throat. “Mr. Harlan?”

No answer.

He told himself he should stop. That normal people didn’t sneak into basements at one in the morning. But the sounds, the smells, the way his chest felt tight every time the walls shook at night—they all pressed at him until not knowing felt worse than whatever he might find.

He took the first step down.

The wood groaned under his weight. He froze, listening. Nothing changed below. No footsteps, no sudden rush of movement. Just the hum of that bulb and the quiet pulse in his ears.

He descended, one step at a time.

The basement unfolded itself as he went lower, the air growing colder, damper. The light resolved into a single bulb hanging from a cord in the middle of the ceiling, swinging almost imperceptibly, throwing slow, sickly arcs of shadow across rough stone walls.

At the bottom of the stairs, the concrete floor was stained in wide, irregular patches, as if something had repeatedly spilled and been scrubbed away in frantic circles. The bleach smell was stronger here, making his eyes prickle.

He hesitated, then stepped forward.

The basement was larger than he expected. Rows of old wooden beams carved it into crude aisles. On one side, he saw the usual clutter: cardboard boxes, a rusted bike, a sagging couch. On the other, where the light didn’t quite reach, sat a row of metal shelving units. Above them, something glinted.

“Mr. Harlan?” he called again, softer now. “You down here?”

His voice was swallowed by the room.

No answer. No sound of another breath.

He thumbed his phone awake, turned on its flashlight. The clean white beam cut through the yellow haze and slid over concrete, pipes, shadows. He moved toward the shelves.

At first, it looked like a workshop. Tools hung with care on pegboard—wrenches, pliers, saws, arranged in precise rows. Jars lined up by size. A thick plastic tarp folded neatly on a table, the surface scored with long, shallow marks.

Under the table, something dripped once, faintly, into a bucket. The echo of that single tap of liquid against metal made his skin tighten.

Sirens drowned out the first screams.

They wailed from every corner of the block—shrill, metallic, rising and falling in jagged pulses that made the concrete seem to vibrate. Flashing red beacons spun along the ceilings, washing everything in violent, stuttering color: walls, faces, uniforms, all painted in frantic red, then stripped back to dull gray, then red again.

The tier doors were half-open, some jammed, some hanging askew on twisted hinges. Inmates poured out in a flood—orange and brown jumpsuits, white T-shirts, makeshift bandanas pulled tight over faces. The air was thick with the sharp sting of pepper spray and the heavier, sour smell of sweat and adrenaline.

A metal food tray clanged off a guard’s helmet and spun wildly across the floor. Another guard went down under the weight of three bodies at once, his baton torn from his hand and disappearing into the swarm. Shouts overlapped—orders, threats, pleas—hammering against the unyielding walls.

“Back! Back!” a sergeant roared, his voice tearing at the edge. He swung his baton in tight, brutal arcs, connecting with shoulders, arms, ribs. An inmate lunged at him with a broken broom handle, jabbing again and again. The sergeant staggered, caught another blow to the side, and fell against the railing, arms flailing for balance.

On the upper tier, two inmates grappled with a guard for his shield. One man locked his arms around the guard’s neck from behind, hauling him backward while another drove fists into his ribs. The shield slipped from the guard’s hands and skidded along the walkway. A third inmate scooped it up and thrust it forward like a battering ram, smashing into another officer who’d rushed in with a Taser raised. The officer crashed into the bars, knees buckling.

One of the guards turned toward the movement, too slow. A punch caught him at the side of the head, spinning him. His helmet flew off and clattered across the floor, kicked and shoved until it disappeared under the mass of feet.

The din built and built: metal on concrete, hoarse shouting, coughs and gasps, the thud of blows landing, the barked commands of officers fighting to impose order on a place that had ruptured into open war. Lights flickered as someone somewhere ripped at wiring. A sprinkler head sheared off above the central aisle, releasing a hard, misting spray that rained down over everyone, plastering shirts to skin, turning the concrete slick.

In the middle of it all, a fallen guard lay on his side, arms wrapped over his head as a circle of inmates closed around him. Boots rose and fell. Each impact drew another grunt, another muffled cry. One inmate paused, chest heaving, then stepped in again, driving his heel down with furious, relentless rhythm.

Somewhere beyond the riot line, a heavy door clanged open. The sound cut briefly through the uproar. The inmates nearest the back of the block faltered, turning their heads toward it. More guards were coming—shields, helmets, batons, shotguns loaded with less-lethal rounds. The riot wasn’t over. It was just beginning to meet its answer.

The sirens continued to howl, unbroken, as if they were trying to tear the roof off the prison itself.

The carpet was the color of old tea and still damp in a few spots where the shower steam had rolled under the bathroom door. Cheap curtains glowed orange from the city lights outside, turning the bland hotel room into a kind of dim aquarium.

Lena sat cross‑legged on the bed, a hotel towel spread in front of her, parts of a pistol arranged in a neat constellation. The slide rested by her ankle; the frame lay bare in her hands. She ran a cloth along the rails, movements methodical, almost meditative.

On the small desk by the window, Rafe worked on a folding knife, hinge open, a bottle of oil at his elbow, the overhead lamp catching on the steel each time he turned it.

The TV was on with the sound off, some reality show flickering over their faces in bright, meaningless drama.

“Still your favorite?” Rafe asked without looking up.

“What,” Lena said, “these?” She lifted the pistol frame a few inches, the metal dull in the lamplight.

“Guns. Distance. Bang, done, cash.” He dabbed oil onto a cotton swab and ran it slowly along the inside of the handle. “Always figured you for a change‑it‑up type.”

She gave a small snort. “You say that like this isn’t changing it up. Last month I spent three weeks pretending to be a yoga instructor just to get a guy to drink the right tea.”

Rafe smiled. “How was that?”

“Terrible. Everyone wants to talk,” she said. “Favorite guns, though? That’s simple. You pull the trigger, it either works or it doesn’t. Very honest relationship.”

He clicked the knife shut, listened to the sound, and opened it again. “You’re the only person I know who calls a suppressor ‘honest.’”

“I didn’t say quiet. I said honest.”

He leaned back in the chair, letting it creak. “See, that’s why I like up close. No excuses. No wind, no distance, no bad intel. Just you, them, and the last few inches.”

She set the pistol frame down and started reassembling the slide. “Right, because nothing ever goes wrong up close.”

Rafe’s grin didn’t waver. “It goes wrong less. Or, at least, if it goes wrong, I’m right there to fix it.”

“So dramatic,” Lena muttered. “Alright, fine, philosopher. Favorite way?”

He thought for a second, turning the knife over in his fingers. “Choke wire,” he said. “Nice and quiet. No mess if you do it right. And people never look up.”

“That’s grim,” she said mildly. “And you call me cold.”

He shrugged. “You asked. Besides, it’s…clean. Efficient. The moment is clear. No misunderstanding what’s happening.”

She slid the recoil spring in with a soft click. “I always thought that was the messiest. All the struggling, all that…effort.”

“If they’re fighting, you made a mistake two minutes earlier,” Rafe said. He nudged the chair back on two legs. “You ever try it?”

“Once,” Lena said. “Didn’t like the noise.”

“You mean the—”

“I mean the sounds people make when they realize it’s actually happening.” She flicked the slide stop into place, tested the movement. “Guns don’t leave as much time for bargaining.”

Rafe considered that, his eyes going to the TV where a pair of contestants were silently arguing over a plate of food. “That why you don’t like poison? That’s the longest bargaining window of all.”

“I like poison fine,” Lena said. “Controlled environment. Easy to dress up as something else. You can walk away before anything starts.”

“And miss the moment?”

She looked up at him, expression flat. “That’s the point, Rafe.”

He watched her for a beat, then nodded, accepting the line he wouldn’t cross tonight. “Okay. So rank them for me. Favorite to least.”

She smirked. “You really want a list?”

“I like to know a professional’s preferences. Helps with planning. And Christmas gifts.”

“Do not buy me a weapon for Christmas,” she said. “Customs will have a field day.”

“Fine, I’ll declare it as ‘kitchenware.’”

She shook her head, but she was smiling now. “Alright. Distance shots first. Clean, predictable. Then poison. Then…explosions, I guess.”

“Explosions?” His eyebrows rose. “Since when?”

“Since Prague. Remember the car job by the river?” she asked, checking the magazine lips with a thumbnail. “That was almost elegant.”

“It was loud,” he said.

“That’s why it was almost elegant,” she replied. “Timing, placement, no one hurt except the target and the poor mechanic who tried to overcharge him.”

“Collateral,” Rafe said.

“He lived.” She slid the empty magazine in, tested the release. “He also lowered his prices significantly afterward. Economic stimulus.”

Rafe laughed softly. “You’re a public servant now.”

“Working on my pension,” she said. “What about you? You said wire. What’s next?”

He wiped the last smear from the knife blade and admired his own reflection for a second. “Blades in general. Short, controlled. You can feel exactly how much it’s going to…matter.”

“‘Matter,’” Lena repeated. “You are insufferable.”

“You ever notice,” he went on, ignoring her, “how different people react to seeing a gun versus a knife? Gun comes out, everybody freezes or runs. Knife, they try to reason with you. Talk their way out. Whole personalities come spilling out in thirty seconds.”

“Mining people’s souls for fun and profit,” she said. “Charming.”

“I’m just saying,” he continued. “With a gun, you’re an event. With a knife, you’re a person they think they can still negotiate with.”

“And then?”

“And then they’re wrong.” He shrugged. “But they don’t know that until the end.”

Lena checked the chamber, racked the slide, and dry-fired at the wall. The tiny click was swallowed by the hum of the AC.

“I don’t like knives,” she said. “Too much margin for error. Too…personal.”

“You don’t like personal.”

“I don’t get paid extra for personal,” she corrected. “I get paid for certainty. For people who go to sleep and never wake up. For accidents caught on cameras with bad angles. For sudden illnesses that don’t trace back to anyone.”

Rafe tilted his head, studying her. “You prefer they never know?”

“If I can arrange it,” she said. “Yes.”

“Huh.” He folded the knife, thumb resting on the worn scales. “You ever wonder if it makes a difference? To them, I mean. Two seconds of awareness versus none at all?”

Lena started wiping down the outside of the pistol, her motions slower now. “No,” she said. “That part’s not my job.”

“But you have a preference.”

“That’s for me,” she said. “Not for them.”

He smiled faintly. “Fair.”

They worked in silence for a bit, the only sounds the soft rasp of cloth on metal and the murmurless drama on the TV. Somewhere down the hall, a door slammed, followed by muffled laughter.

Rafe broke the quiet. “You ever consider going back to just…threats?” he asked. “Intimidation. Roughing people up. No final step.”

“Consulting?” she said. “You want to turn freelance murder into risk management?”

“I’m aging,” he replied. “My knees don’t like rooftop chases anymore.”

“You don’t chase anyone,” she said. “You wait in their kitchen.”

“Details.”

She set the pistol down, finally satisfied, and began lining up the remaining rounds in a box. “Threats are messy. People make bad choices when they’re scared. They talk to the wrong people, hire the wrong protection. You end up coming back to finish what you should’ve done the first time.”

“And you don’t like repeat business.”

“I don’t like inefficiency,” she said.

“Explosions are inefficient,” he countered.

“Explosions are marketing,” she said. “Once in a while, people need to remember accidents can be very dramatic.”

He regarded her, thoughtful. “You know what I really like?” he said finally.

“Oh good, I was afraid you’d run out of opinions.”

“The quiet ones that never make the news,” he said. “The ones that just…slide into the paperwork. Wrong dose at the hospital. Slip in the shower. Heart that gave up at the wrong time.”

“You like those?” she asked, surprised.

“Professionally,” he said. “The artistry. It’s like they never existed as a ‘thing that happened.’ Just data. Statistics.”

“That’s more my line,” Lena said. “Careful, you’re drifting.”

He smiled. “Maybe I’m mellowing out.”

“Maybe you’re getting lazy.”

“Maybe I’m getting smart.”

She closed the ammo box and pushed it aside. “I’ll believe that when you stop carrying that family heirloom around.”

He patted his pocket where the knife sat. “One day,” he said, “you’re going to be in trouble, and you’re going to be very happy I brought this instead of a spreadsheet.”

“If I’m in trouble,” she said, “it’s because you started a knife fight in a hallway with terrible lighting.”

He opened his mouth, considered, then shrugged. “Statistically possible.”

“Statistically guaranteed,” she corrected.

Outside, a siren wound up somewhere in the distance, then faded. Rafe got up, flicked the TV off with the remote, and the room fell into a gentler, more honest dimness.

“You ever think about what you’d do if the work dried up?” he asked, stretching his back until it popped.

“Learn to code,” she said instantly.

He snorted. “You’d last ten minutes in an office.”

“I lasted three weeks as a yoga instructor,” she reminded him. “I can fake whatever I need to.”

“That’s different. That had a conclusion.”

She slid her gun into the waiting foam of her case. “That’s the real reason I like this over all your wires and blades,” she said.

“What, the travel perks?”

“The finality,” she said. “There’s a moment where the job is just…done. No lingering. No wondering. Clean cut from one life to the next.”

Rafe leaned against the wall, folding his arms. “You like the full stop,” he said.

“Exactly.”

“And you think a bullet is a better full stop than a wire?”

“I think,” she said, closing the case with a precise snap, “that when it works, there’s nothing to argue about. No room for stories. Just cause and effect.”

He nodded slowly. “Me, I like the part right before that. The last sentence, not the period.”

“That,” she said, “is why you’re the one who gets recognized on the street sometimes and I don’t.”

He grinned. “You noticed that?”

“People remember drama,” she said. “They don’t remember…accounting.”

He chuckled, pushing off the wall. “You’re not accounting. You’re…infrastructure.”

“That’s worse,” she said, but she didn’t sound offended.

He picked up his knife, slid it into his pocket with a familiar, practiced motion. “So,” he said, “call time?”

She checked the cheap bedside clock. “Six hours. Car at five. Don’t stab the concierge.”

“He started it last time,” Rafe said.

“He asked if you needed help with your bags.”

“In a very suspicious tone.”

“Rafe.”

“Fine, fine,” he said, walking toward the bathroom. “No stabbing civilians. Tonight.”

The bathroom light flared on, a harsh rectangle under the door. Lena lay back on the pillow for a moment, staring at the ceiling, listening to the water run.

After a while, she reached over, flicked off the lamp on the nightstand, and let the room sink into near‑darkness, the city bleeding in around the edges of the curtains like a distant fire.

In the dark, her voice floated toward the bathroom door.

“For the record,” she said, “if you ever try that wire thing on me, I’m going to be very disappointed.”

His laughter, muffled by the running shower, came back through the door. “Please. If I ever try anything on you, it’ll be a long way away and you’ll never see it coming.”

“Good,” she said, closing her eyes. “I’d hate to have to argue about it.”

“I don’t like inefficiency,” she said.

“Explosions are inefficient,” he countered.

“Explosions are marketing,” she said. “Once in a while, people need to remember accidents can be very dramatic.”

“You like those?” she asked, surprised.

“Professionally,” he said. “The artistry. It’s like they never existed as a ‘thing that happened.’ Just data. Statistics.”

“That’s more my line,” Lena said. “Careful, you’re drifting.”

He smiled. “Maybe I’m mellowing out.”

“Maybe you’re getting lazy.”

“Maybe I’m getting smart.”

She closed the ammo box and pushed it aside. “I’ll believe that when you stop carrying that family heirloom around.”

He patted his pocket where the knife sat. “One day,” he said, “you’re going to be in trouble, and you’re going to be very happy I brought this instead of a spreadsheet.”

“If I’m in trouble,” she said, “it’s because you started a knife fight in a hallway with terrible lighting.”

He opened his mouth, considered, then shrugged. “Statistically possible.”

“Statistically guaranteed,” she corrected.

Outside, a siren wound up somewhere in the distance, then faded. Rafe got up, flicked the TV off with the remote, and the room fell into a gentler, more honest dimness.

“You ever think about what you’d do if the work dried up?” he asked, stretching his back until it popped.

“Learn to code,” she said instantly.

He snorted. “You’d last ten minutes in an office.”

“I lasted three weeks as a yoga instructor,” she reminded him. “I can fake whatever I need to.”

“That’s different. That had a conclusion.”

She slid her gun into the waiting foam of her case. “That’s the real reason I like this over all your wires and blades,” she said.

“What, the travel perks?”

“The finality,” she said. “There’s a moment where the job is just…done. No lingering. No wondering. Clean cut from one life to the next.”

Rafe leaned against the wall, folding his arms. “You like the full stop,” he said.

“Exactly.”

“And you think a bullet is a better full stop than a wire?”

“I think,” she said, closing the case with a precise snap, “that when it works, there’s nothing to argue about. No room for stories. Just cause and effect.”

He nodded slowly. “Me, I like the part right before that. The last sentence, not the period.”

“That,” she said, “is why you’re the one who gets recognized on the street sometimes and I don’t.”

He grinned. “You noticed that?”

“People remember drama,” she said. “They don’t remember…accounting.”

He chuckled, pushing off the wall. “You’re not accounting. You’re…infrastructure.”

“That’s worse,” she said, but she didn’t sound offended.

He picked up his knife, slid it into his pocket with a familiar, practiced motion. “So,” he said, “call time?”

She checked the cheap bedside clock. “Six hours. Car at five. Don’t stab the concierge.”

“He started it last time,” Rafe said.

“He asked if you needed help with your bags.”

“In a very suspicious tone.”

“Rafe.”

“Fine, fine,” he said, walking toward the bathroom. “No stabbing civilians. Tonight.”

After a while, she reached over, flicked off the lamp on the nightstand, and let the room sink into near‑darkness, the city bleeding in around the edges of the curtains like a distant fire.

In the dark, her voice floated toward the bathroom door.

“For the record,” she said, “if you ever try that wire thing on me, I’m going to be very disappointed.”

His laughter, muffled by the running shower, came back through the door. “Please. If I ever try anything on you, it’ll be a long way away and you’ll never see it coming.”

“Good,” she said, closing her eyes. “I’d hate to have to argue about it.”

Heat rolled off the pyre in waves that felt almost solid, pressing against faces even at the edges of the crowd. The air near the stake shimmered, the lines of the world warping as if the day itself were bending away from what was happening. Every breath tasted of dry wood and scorching resin, the kind of heat that licks at eyebrows, cracks lips, and turns the simple act of inhaling into an effort.

Smoke rose first in slow, gray coils, then in heavy, roiling sheets. It wrapped around the figure at the center, swallowing features, turning them into a shifting silhouette that lurched and strained against the ropes. The smell was thick and layered: pine and pitch, old straw, singed cloth, the acrid bite that made eyes water and throats close. It crawled along the ground and billowed upward at once, smearing the sky with a dirty, trembling veil.

Her screams cut through it all—raw, high, and ragged, more animal than human, tearing at the air. At first they were words, broken pleas and curses that tumbled over each other, but the fire stole syllables faster than she could form them. Soon there were only sounds: hoarse, cracking wails that hit a pitch no one wanted to recognize and no one could forget.

They rose and fell in frantic bursts, each one shorter than the last, each breath harder to drag out of smoke-scoured lungs. Then, abruptly, they faltered—one strangled cry, a gasping half-sound—before dwindling into a rough, scraping moan. The final noise was barely more than a breath, a thin, strained exhale swallowed by the roar of the flames and the restless murmur of the watching crowd. After that, there was only the crackle of burning wood and the low, relentless hiss of fire feeding on what remained.

results.model_response:
The moon was a thin, sickle-shaped wound in the sky, bleeding pale light over the broken plain.

They had buried the dead here in haste—mounds of upturned earth and splintered wagons half-submerged in the soil, rusted blades still clutched in skeletal fingers. The battle had ended weeks ago. The carrion birds had come and gone. What remained was a scabbed-over wasteland, crusted with old blood and tangled in dead banners that whispered as the wind worried at them.

The necromancer stood at the center of it all.

His robe—which might once have been black—was faded to a colorless, oily shade that seemed to drink in the light. Wide sleeves hung loose from his thin arms. A dozen talismans dangled from his throat: finger bones blackened with age, teeth drilled through and strung on gut-string, rust-scarred coins that had passed over dead men’s eyes. They knocked softly together with each small movement, a hollow, uneven rhythm like the rattle of dice in a coffin.

He raised his staff.

It was not carved wood, though it had the shape of a branch torn from a tree. It looked like something that had been grown rather than made, pale and ridged, a spiral of fused vertebrae capped with a glassy stone the color of congealed wine. Old runes had been carved along its length and then erased and carved again, so that nothing remained clear—only a jumbled, maddening pattern that refused to settle.

The air changed when he began to speak.

It went thin and sour all at once, as if the world had been holding its breath without knowing it and now suddenly realized it needed air. His voice was low, not loud enough to carry far, but the sound of it reached into the earth. Each word felt mispronounced, vowels bent in places they shouldn’t bend, consonants grinding together like broken teeth. The language was old, older than the kingdom whose dead lay beneath his boots. It had no place in the world of living things.

The wrongness of it scraped at the ears.

Shadows recoiled from the staff’s faint light. The wind faltered and then fled altogether, leaving the field unnaturally still. The cries of night creatures—the distant bark of foxes, the flap and croak of crows—thinned into silence, as if some larger predator had stepped into their midst and every instinct ordered them to hide.

The earth responded.

Not at first with drama or spectacle, but with a quiet shift, a subtle settling. The mounds of dirt rose a finger’s breadth as something beneath them pushed upward. Soil clotted and cracked. Roots that had grown down into the corpses tightened as if in protest, then tore free with small, snapping sounds.

The smell came next.

The battlefield had already stunk for weeks—old blood, turned soil, the ghost of smoke—but this was different. The magic teased the scent out of the ground, dragged it up, distilled it. Damp, cloying sweetness like fruit left too long in the sun. Sour flesh. The thick, chemical reek of decay pressed into the back of the throat. It was not the smell of something dying; it was the smell of something that *should have finished dying* and been allowed its quiet end.

The necromancer inhaled as if it were perfume.

He spread his fingers wide, palms facing the earth. As he chanted, a faint pallid glow seeped from his skin, draining the color from the air. It was not warm like fire’s light; it was dry and anemic, a light that revealed without offering comfort. Under its touch, the ground turned ashen. The grass, already yellowed, blackened and curled in on itself like paper in a too-hot flame.

The first hand clawed free.

It broke through the soil slowly, fingers splayed, nails split and fissured. Flesh sloughed loosely over the bones beneath, sagging in soft folds. Patches of skin had slipped away entirely, leaving gray-yellow muscle stretched like old cloth. The earth clung to it in wet clumps, mud filling the spaces where meat had rotted away. The fingers twitched once, convulsively, then stretched farther, as if reaching for a surface it did not remember but knew it wanted.

More followed.

Hands, arms, a skull pushing up like a pale, filthy stone, jaw yawning open. No breath came. No sound but the grinding of loose teeth and the wet, tearing hush of soil disturbed. Ribs surfaced in jagged rows, some still wrapped in ragged scraps of uniform, colors faded and crusted with old dirt. Cloth fused to skin in places, stitching decay into a single, disgusting whole.

As they emerged, the necromantic light slid over them, soaking into ruined flesh. It did not heal. It did not restore. Rather, it *asserted*. It clamped down, like a cold hand closing around a struggling throat. Tendons that had gone slack tightened again under its influence. Joints that should have frozen with rot flexed and grated into motion. Eye sockets, empty or filled with shrunken, milky orbs, turned toward the staff as if the dead could still sense its call.

And everywhere, beneath the movement, was the sense of something fundamentally misaligned.

It was not simply that the bodies moved when they should not. The magic scraped against the world itself, rubbing against its grain. The air felt strained, stretched thin over an idea it did not accept. Every step the dead took as they dragged themselves upward seemed half a step out of place, as if reality had to correct itself around their presence, shifting and shuddering with every unnatural twitch.

Shadows clung too tightly to them, or else not at all. A skull tilted just so would catch no shade where any living head would have been hooded in darkness. A ragged sleeve would trail a black stain on the ground where no object touched. The dead moved in studdering, uneven jerks, yet somehow each movement arrived a fraction of a heartbeat sooner than it should, as though time wasn’t quite flowing correctly around them.

The necromancer’s words grew faster, more insistent.

Lines of dark radiance crept out from the circle in which he stood, black veins spreading through the soil. Wherever they passed, the land withered further. Small stones cracked with a faint, brittle sound. Thin stems collapsed inward, turning to papery dust between one breath and the next. The lines pulsed with a heartbeat that was not his, something older and colder.

The corpses answered.

They did not cry out; they had no voice left. But they *aligned*. As one, heads turned toward the necromancer, eyes—or the absence of eyes—fixing on him with helpless, hollow focus. Some still wore helmets split nearly in half, rust glittering where metal had eaten through. Others had hair clinging in lank, discolored strands to half-bare skulls. Flies stirred weakly from their resting places, disturbed by new motion in old meat, then droned off uncertainly, unable to understand what had changed.

The bodies rose.

Some stood easily, half-shaped remnants of muscle still gripping bone. Others lurched clumsily, ribs protruding like the spars of broken ships. Knees buckled and then straightened, joints shuddering in their sockets. One corpse’s leg ended in tatters mid-calf; it hauled itself upright anyway, supported by unseen force, toes scraping, dangling uselessly above the ground. Another’s spine curved at an impossible angle, vertebrae slipped and misaligned, yet it walked as though its neck had never been broken, head lolling like a pendulum.

Still the necromantic power pushed on them, saturating each ruined form.

It was not life; it was its echo distorted in a cracked mirror. Where living flesh carried heat and subtle motion, this magic filled the dead with a chill density, the imitation of intention without the spark that gave it meaning. The bodies did not remember who they had been. There was no anguish in them, no recognition, no mercy. Only command.

Beneath their feet, the black veins of power dug deeper.

For a moment, something seemed to resist. A hush shivered through the field, as if the ground itself had clenched in refusal. The necromancer stiffened, teeth gritting, and drove his staff down hard. The bone shaft bit into the soil with a thud that felt more like a bruise than a sound. The crimson stone at its tip flared, and a wave of pressure rolled outward.

The resistance broke.

More mounds split open. More limbs pushed up, some so decomposed they were little more than stained bone with tattered, leathery strips of tissue clinging to them. The magic took them anyway, uncaring. A jaw with no tongue and only half its teeth clicked rhythmically as it rose, like a chattering puppet. Two empty sockets, packed with dirt and tiny roots, turned toward the necromancer with blind obedience.

They gathered around him.

Dozens at first, then scores. A ragged circle of upright corpses, swaying, adjusting, ordering themselves without thought. Flies buzzed in choked spirals, confused by creatures that smelled like food yet moved like predators. The stench became a living thing of its own, crawling across the skin, seeping into fabric, curdling in the lungs.

The necromancer fell silent.

The last echoes of his misbegotten words hung in the air a heartbeat too long, then snapped off, leaving a vacuum of stillness. Even the dead seemed to pause, bodies creaking faintly as they settled into expectant quiet. The world beyond the field held its distance, repulsed: no night breeze, no rustle of leaves, the stars above dimmed as if a haze had formed between them and this patch of earth.

He surveyed his work.

What stood before him were not soldiers. They were not men. They were *hollows*—emptied vessels jammed full of his will. The magic anchoring them was like icy wire wrapped through bone and tendon, wrenching them through the motions of a parody of life. The simple act of their existence pressed outward on the fabric of things, a constant, grinding dissonance humming just below hearing.

“March,” he whispered.

The word itself was harmless, a simple sound any farmer might say. But it fell into the pattern of his earlier speech like a stone into black water, and the necromancy seized it, twisted it, made it an edict.

The dead moved.

Feet that had forgotten the ground sought purchase. Bare soles and rotted boots met the earth with thuds and scrapes. Bones clicked in their sockets. Some walked cleanly, others dragged limbs behind them, but all obeyed. As they went, the world flinched—grass withered where they stepped, insects stilled in the soil, the night itself seemed to lean away.

Behind them, the battlefield lay more empty than before.

Not at peace; never that. The dead had not been given rest. They had been taken, wrenched from the slow, honest work of decay and thrust into a new shape. The wrongness of it hung over the plain like a taste on the air that would not wash out, like a note held too long in a song that had ended.

Under the wan, sickle moon, the army of the dead marched into the darkness, each step a quiet, unanswerable insult to the order of the world.

They met him under the freeway, where the concrete pillars turned the night into a kind of echoing tunnel. Headlights from a half-circle of parked cars threw long, warped shadows on the stained pavement. The air smelled of oil and old smoke.

Dre stood at the center of it all, the newest one, thin jacket zipped up to his throat though he was sweating through it. Around him, twenty men and boys formed a loose ring, hushed and attentive. They weren’t talking much—that had all been done earlier. This was the part where they watched.

On the hood of the middle car sat Rico, the one they all answered to. He didn’t raise his voice. He never had to.

“You say you’re family,” Rico said. “Family bleeds for each other. Family does what needs doing, no questions.”

His lieutenants flanked him like stone. Tone, with the spiderweb tattoo over one eye, clicked a lighter on and off, on and off, the tiny flame carving brief orange circles in the dark. Flex just stared at Dre, expression flat, arms folded over a sweatshirt that bore stains no one asked about.

Dre tried to keep his hands still at his sides. They trembled anyway.

“I said I’d ride,” he answered. His voice came out thin. “I meant it.”

Rico nodded slowly, as if that had settled something. “Then tonight you prove it.”

At his gesture, two of the older guys dragged someone from the backseat of a car. A man—late twenties maybe—hands tied behind his back, shirt ripped, knees scraping hard on the concrete as he was forced forward. A filthy rag was knotted around his mouth.

Dre’s eyes flicked to him, then away. He didn’t want to see the man’s face. He saw it anyway: blood at the lip, one eye swollen half shut, pupils wide with fear.

“He talked,” Rico said lazily. “Talked to cops, talked to other sets. Sold us out more than once. We got confirmation. He ain’t one of us anymore.”

Murmurs rippled through the circle, quiet but full of judgment, disgust. The group’s anger filled the space, directed at the kneeling man, but it washed over Dre like heat, pressing on the back of his neck.

“You want us?” Tone said, finally pocketing the lighter. “You gotta show we can trust you more than we ever trusted him.”

Flex stepped forward, something dark and heavy in his hand. He reached out, closing Dre’s fingers around the cold metal.

The weight of the gun made Dre’s arm sink a fraction. He stared at it, then at Rico, then at the man on his knees.

“Look at me,” Rico said.

Dre forced his gaze upward.

“You think this is about him?” Rico’s eyes were calm, unreadable. “This is about you. Cops come, they lean on you, your mom cries, your girl begs you to do the right thing—what do you do? You talk? Or you remember who put this in your hand, who put money in your pocket, who had your back out there?” He nodded around at the circle. “Us. Not them. Us.”

Dre swallowed. His mouth was dry, tongue thick like it didn’t fit.

“You walk away now,” Rico continued, “nobody’s gonna chase you. But every door in this neighborhood closes. You’re food. You’re a target. We see you on the street, we don’t know you. You bleed alone.”

The words didn’t come with shouting or threats. They were delivered like the weather report—just how it was.

From the ring, someone called out, “Make your choice, lil’ homie.”

Another voice: “Ain’t no halfway. You in or out.”

The kneeling man tried to say something through the gag, voice muffled, frantic. One of the lieutenants shoved him between the shoulder blades, forcing him to bend forward, exposed and helpless.

Dre’s heart slammed against his ribs. His vision tunneled; all he could see was the back of the man’s head, the chipped concrete, the gun in his own shaking hand.

Rico stepped off the hood, coming close enough that Dre could smell his cologne cutting through the car exhaust.

“We all did this,” Rico murmured, low enough only Dre could hear. “You think we were born hard? Nah. You become what you gotta be. We were scared same as you. Then we pulled the trigger. After that, nobody could ever say we weren’t down.”

He placed a hand on Dre’s shoulder, heavy, almost fatherly.

“You wanna be a ghost your whole life? Or you wanna be somebody?”

The circle tightened by inches, bodies edging closer. No one touched Dre, but he felt them anyway—their eyes, their hunger to see what he’d do. The peer pressure was a living thing, crawling over his skin, making his own will feel small and ridiculous.

If he refused, they’d watch him walk away. Maybe no one would follow. Maybe someone would. He imagined looking over his shoulder for the rest of his life, wondering which laughter on the block was about him.

“He’s already dead,” Tone said, motioning to the kneeling man. “He died when he snitched. All you’re doing is finishing the paperwork.”

Nervous laughter, dark and sharp.

Rico’s voice cut through again, steady. “Last chance. Walk, and you walk alone. Stay, and you prove you’re ours forever.”

The word “ours” clanged in Dre’s head. It sounded like belonging. It sounded like a sentence.

His arm felt separate from his body as he raised the gun. The man on the ground thrashed, tried to twist away, some desperate animal instinct, but the hands on his shoulders held him down.

“Look at him,” Flex ordered.

Dre didn’t want to, but he did. Their eyes met. For a second, the noise faded. It was just two people staring at each other, both of them scared, both of them knowing exactly what was about to happen.

That was the brutal part, more than anything else—the absolute certainty.

“Do it,” someone hissed behind Dre’s ear.

The command bounced around the underpass, picked up and repeated by the group, faster each time, a low chant building: “Do it. Do it. Do it.”

Rico didn’t chant. He just watched, silent, like a judge.

Dre’s finger tightened. He felt the resistance, the small mechanical protest before the break. The chanting blurred into a single, pounding note. He could have stopped. He didn’t.

The sound cracked the air, sharp and final. The kneeling man crumpled, the others letting him fall. For a half-second, there was nothing—no shouts, no movement—just ringing in Dre’s ears and a sick, hollow drop in his stomach.

Then the circle exploded in approval. Hands thudded against his back, fingers grabbed his shoulders, shaking him, turning him around. Voices crashed over him—“You did it!” “You in now!” “My boy!”—a tidal wave of praise and acceptance.

Rico moved through the crowd, parting it without effort, until he stood face to face with Dre again. He took the gun from Dre’s limp hand, wiped it casually with a cloth, then tucked it away.

He cupped Dre’s face briefly, forcing him to meet his eyes. There was a glint of satisfaction there, but no surprise. He’d known how this would end.

“Welcome to the family,” Rico said quietly. “Ain’t no going back now.”

The others roared at the word “family,” arms around Dre, drawing him into the center of their celebration. Behind them, on the cold concrete, the body lay still and unattended, already fading into the background.

In the middle of the noise, as someone draped an arm around his shoulders and pulled him close like a brother, Dre understood the real initiation: not the act itself, but the way they took his guilt and fear and wrapped it in belonging, so he’d never be able to separate one from the other again.

results.model_response:
He lifts the first forkful as if nothing in the world has changed.

It’s a small thing—slow roasted, lacquered in the sauce I stood over for an hour, stirring, tasting, adjusting. The dining room lights are low and flattering, catching on the rim of his wineglass, softening the edges of his face. He’s already had one glass. Half of the second waits, garnet-dark, patient.

“Smells incredible,” he says. “You’ve outdone yourself.”

“I keep telling you I’m getting better,” I say, and smile. It feels like lifting someone else’s mouth.

He takes the bite, chews. The sauce glistens on his lower lip before he licks it away, unaware of his own precision. Unaware of mine.

The first swallow is the important one. The rest is just time.

“How’s work?” I ask.

He rolls his eyes. “Don’t ask. New boss thinks ‘team building’ means three-hour meetings where we write our ‘hopes and dreams’ on sticky notes.” He lifts another forkful, larger this time. “This is really good, by the way. What did you put in this?”

“Trade secret,” I say.

The answer is technically honest.

The compound needs warmth and fat to open; it clings to the rich gloss on the meat, invisible, scentless. I watch it disappear into him, bite by bite, as if he’s eating threads only I can see.

He talks. I nod in the right places. The first effect is so subtle it could be anything: a blink that lingers half a second too long, a tiny furrow between his brows. The timeline runs behind my eyes like a second clock.

Five minutes: a faint tightening at the back of the throat, like swallowing dry air. He reaches for his water without breaking his sentence. He swallows, then swallows again.

“Ugh. Got something stuck,” he mutters, clearing his throat. “I don’t know how you eat so fast; I feel like I’m chewing for hours.”

“You do talk while you eat,” I say lightly. “Maybe focus on one or the other.”

He snorts, takes another sip of water, and returns to his plate. He eats a little more cautiously now, but habit is stronger than faint discomfort. Habit and trust.

Eight minutes: the first flush. It shows under his collar, at the base of his throat, spreading up. His skin takes on a damp sheen, as though the air has warmed only for him.

“Is it… hot in here?” he asks, frowning slightly. He tugs at his shirt collar with two fingers. A bead of sweat breaks at his temple and begins to slide down, catching the light as it goes.

“I can open a window,” I offer. “It might just be the oven. I had it on all afternoon.”

He gives a little laugh, half an exhale. “Nah, it’s fine. Just my metabolism finally waking up. About time.”

But his hand drifts to his chest as if something unfamiliar is moving there. He rolls his shoulders, then stops, as though some small invisible thread has pulled too tight.

“Anyway,” he says, forcing brightness back into his voice, “guess who finally got promoted?”

It’s an easy story to tell. I nod, ask, “Really?” at all the expected beats. The words pass around me like water around stone.

Twelve minutes: his breathing changes. Not enough that another guest would notice, but I know the measure of his breath the way a musician knows a familiar song. It’s just slightly off-tempo, a fraction shallower. He pauses mid-sentence to catch up to himself.

“You okay?” I ask.

He shifts in his chair. “Yeah. Just… weird day. I think I skipped lunch. Blood sugar’s probably all over the place.” He lifts his glass of wine. His hand is a touch unsteady, the rim ticking softly against his tooth when he takes a sip. A small, embarrassed flinch; he glances at me to see if I saw. I pretend I didn’t.

The flush has spread to his cheeks now, patchy and uneven. His pupils look a little wider than the low light requires. He blinks too slowly and then too fast, trying to find a rhythm that feels like normal.

“You’re pale,” I say. It’s almost true. The color sits on his skin in uneven splashes over a canvas that’s gone a shade too gray.

“Really?” He drags a hand over his face, then presses his fingertips into his eyes. “Huh. I feel… I don’t know. Off. Like I stood up too fast, except I’m sitting down.”

He laughs at himself, but the laugh frays at the edges. His hand remains at his temple a hair longer than it should.

“Maybe you’re getting sick,” I suggest. “There’s something going around.”

He shakes his head, then winces as if the motion scraped something along the inside of his skull. “No, I was fine all day. It just hit me now. Must be the week catching up with me.”

He reaches for his fork again. Reflex. He’s always finished his plate. It’s one of the things I used to like: that determined, thoughtless completion of whatever is in front of him.

Fifteen minutes: the first real misfire. The fork misses the edge of the plate and scrapes the table. It’s a fraction of an inch, nothing more, but his hand doesn’t correct in time. Silver-on-wood, a tiny metallic screech.

“Wow,” he says, chuckling weakly, “apparently I can’t even aim my fork now. Maybe it is the wine.”

He tries again, focusing, jaw tight with the simple effort of putting food on metal. He succeeds. I can see the pride flicker and sputter in his eyes at having mastered something a child does without thought.

“Eat,” I urge him, voice mild. “You’ll feel better if you get something in you.”

He nods. “You’re right. You’re always right about this stuff.”

He brings the fork to his mouth, but his lips don’t quite meet it correctly; a smear of sauce streaks the corner. He doesn’t wipe it away. His attention is turned inward now, testing the borders of his own body and finding them blurred.

Eighteen minutes: his sweat has a different shine, not just exertion but cold creeping through. A shiver crosses his shoulders as though a draft has passed, but none has. Gooseflesh rises along his forearms; I watch it roughen the skin.

“What’s wrong?” I ask. It isn’t concern, not exactly. It’s habit. Practice. The lines I’ve said a thousand times in a different world.

He hesitates, trying to pull together a feeling that keeps slipping away from words. “I don’t know. My hands are—”

He turns them palm-up, studying them. The fingers flex, then curl slowly into fists as if his joints have thickened. I notice the tremor: small, fast vibrations like the first ripple disturbing a still pond.

“Like when they fall asleep?” I prompt.

“No. I mean, sort of, but… not pins and needles. Just… wrong. Heavy.” He rubs thumb against forefinger as though he could rub the sensation back to normal. For a brief second, fear cracks through his practiced calm. It appears in his eyes, fast and bright, before he clamps down on it.

“Maybe lie down after dinner,” I suggest. “It’s probably nothing.”

He exhales. “Yeah. Yeah, probably nothing.”

Twenty minutes: the poison enters its confident phase. His heartbeat is visible now, fluttering at the hollow of his throat, too rapid, trying to compensate for something the rest of him hasn’t named yet. His words come slightly delayed, as though he’s hearing them from another room and repeating them.

He lifts the wineglass again. This time his hand betrays him more openly. The glass shudders, the trembling fine but constant. A dark arc of wine climbs the inside of the bowl.

To his credit, he notices. The fear returns, this time staying.

“Okay, that’s… that’s not normal,” he says, staring at his own fingers. “I’m really shaking. Look at that.”

I lean in. I let my brows pull together in a perfect, symmetrical frown. I touch the back of his hand. His skin is hot and damp, the tendons jumping under my fingers.

“Maybe you’re having a panic attack,” I say. “You’ve been stressed lately.”

“I don’t get panic attacks,” he snaps, too sharply. Then softer, “Sorry. Just… this is weird. My chest feels… tight. Not pain, just like it has to work harder.” He takes a deeper breath as if to prove that he can. It catches slightly on the way in. He notices. His eyes flick to mine.

“You’re okay,” I say. “Breathe in slowly. Like this.” I demonstrate, the old script. Inhale, exhale. Reassure, contain.

He tries to follow, but his chest can’t quite match the smoothness. His breaths come shallow, a little too quick, riding the edge of adequate.

Twenty-four minutes: coordination slips another notch. He tries to cut another piece of food—there’s barely anything left on the plate—but the knife tilts, skidding off the meat and clattering against the porcelain. The sound is louder than it should be in the warm, quiet room.

“Maybe stop eating,” I suggest gently. “If you’re not feeling well.”

He sets the utensils down, or tries to. The knife lands at an angle; the fork slips from between his fingers and hits the tablecloth. He stares at it, as though the sight doesn’t quite make sense.

“Hey,” he says. The word wavers, a touch slurred, as if his tongue has grown heavier. “This… seriously, this feels wrong. My arms are—”

He lifts one. It moves, but with effort, like something drawn up through deep water. Halfway up, his elbow wobbles and the limb drops back to the table, more from exhaustion than gravity.

“—weak,” he finishes, breathless from that simple motion. “This isn’t just being tired. Something’s… off. I think… maybe…”

The thought dissolves halfway through. He closes his eyes, trying to focus. Opening them again takes effort.

“Did you eat anything weird today?” I ask. “New restaurant? Old leftovers?”

He shakes his head. The motion is ragged. “Just the usual crap. Sandwich. Coffee. Donuts someone brought in. I don’t—” He breaks off, swallowing convulsively. His throat works hard around nothing. “Dry,” he mutters, reaching for his water.

His hand misses the glass entirely this time, knocking it over. Water cascades across the table, over his fingers, into his lap. He jerks in surprise, but the movement is slow, no real urgency in it, as though his body is receiving everything on a slight delay.

“Oh. Damn. I’m sorry,” he says, automatic. His tongue stumbles over the consonants.

“It’s just water,” I say. I rise, fetch a towel, blot the spreading pool, efficient and neat. His hand lies in it, unresisting, fingers barely curled. I lift his wrist to dab underneath. His skin slides strangely in my grasp: too loose over muscles that no longer answer.

He watches me, eyes widening a fraction as the implications assemble themselves.

“What’s happening to me?” he whispers.

Twenty-nine minutes: his breathing has gone from shallow to labored. Each inhale draws slightly more effort: nostrils flaring, ribs trying to expand against a weight that isn’t there. His mouth has fallen slightly open between words; his lips are losing color.

“Maybe you should go to the hospital,” I say.

The suggestion lands cruelly late, by design.

He seizes on it. “Yeah. Yeah, that’s… that’s a good idea.” He tries to push himself back from the table. His legs don’t quite cooperate; the chair tips a little, scraping the floor. For a moment, he freezes, as if simply sitting very still might reset whatever is wrong.

He tries again. His hands press on the arms of the chair. The muscles in his forearms bunch visibly, but the movement they produce is pitiful. His body lifts maybe an inch before sagging back, shoulders rounding, breath hitching with the effort.

“I can’t—” he says, and stops. The next word doesn’t come. His brows knit together, struggling with the idea that his own body can deny him something as simple as standing.

“Hold on,” I say. “Let me get my keys.” I don’t move.

Thirty-two minutes: the fine muscles in his face begin to lose their subtlety. His expression is stuck halfway between confusion and fear, each emotion dragging the slackening features in a different direction. A tremor works along his jaw. His lips move without sound for a moment, testing the reliability of speech.

“This…” He has to pause between syllables now to catch breath. “This doesn’t… feel like… panic. My chest—” He stops to inhale again, a shuddering, insufficient breath. “—can’t… can’t get… air.”

His hand goes to his throat, fingers splaying as if he could claw the problem away. His nails scrape weakly at his own skin, leaving fleeting red tracks that fade almost as soon as they appear.

Inside, the smooth, critical muscles are relaxing in the wrong order. The diaphragm is still fighting, but less efficiently. The intercostals are confused, some firing, some quiet. His body is trying to breathe through a mechanism that is coming apart screw by screw.

“Hey,” I say. My voice is very calm. “Look at me.”

He drags his gaze up to mine. It takes effort. His pupils are huge now, reflecting the room in tiny, fractured circles.

“You’re going to be okay,” I lie, the lie honed, perfect. “Just try to relax. If you fight it, it’s worse.”

He nods. The motion is barely perceptible. He tries to inhale calmly. The air rattles faintly at the top of his lungs and then stalls.

Thirty-seven minutes: his arms have gone heavy as sandbags, draped awkwardly on the table and in his lap. He tries to lift a hand. It twitches, then slumps. His fingers no longer grasp; they curl only because gravity encourages them to.

His words are fragments now, slipping out around the growing effort of breathing.

“Help,” he says. Or tries to. It comes out, “He…lp,” the second half more exhale than sound.

“I am helping,” I say. “I’m calling someone right now.”

My phone is in reach. The emergency number waits just three taps away. I could press them. I could.

I don’t.

His world is shrinking to the space between one breath and the next. Each inhale takes everything he has. The exhale trembles out of him in a frail rush. His shoulders jerk with the attempt to pull in more; the muscles along his neck stand out in strained relief.

The sky was the color of old bruises, heavy with a storm that refused to break. The *Maiden’s Woe* creaked and groaned as she rose and fell on the swell, lines humming in the wind like taut fiddle strings. Every man on deck had fallen silent.

“Bring him forward,” Captain Rourke said.

His voice was low, almost casual, but it carried from quarterdeck to bowsprit. Two sailors hauled the mutineer between them. Harlan’s wrists were bound in front of him with a length of tarred rope, but his legs dragged as if he’d forgotten how to walk.

They had stripped him to his shirt and trousers. The wind cut through the thin cloth, raising gooseflesh on his arms. Harlan’s eyes—usually narrowed and mocking—were wide now, darting from face to face, searching for someone to speak, to intervene, to do anything but stare.

No one spoke.

The plank had been drawn out from the port rail, a heavy oaken board stained dark from long use and sea-spray. It jutted over the water like a tongue from a rotten mouth. Below, the waves rolled and slapped the hull in lazy, hollow sounds.

And circling in the blue-green depths, fins stitched black crescents on the surface.

Rourke descended from the quarterdeck without hurry, boots ringing on each step. He stopped a few paces from Harlan, the wind flicking at his coat, his dark hair damp with salted spray.

“You broke faith,” the captain said. No anger, no shout, only the plain weight of fact. “You turned your hand against your own crew. Against me.”

Harlan swallowed hard. His throat clicked audibly.

“I—Captain, listen—Rourke—” His voice cracked around the name. “It was talk, that’s all. Just talk. We was drunk, all of us. Men gripe. You know that. I never laid a hand on you—”

Rourke’s eyes, cold and pale as winter glass, never flickered.

“You tried to win them to cut my throat in my sleep,” he said. “That’s more than talk.”

A murmur stirred among the crew—no outrage, no support, just the quiet rustling of men shifting weight, clearing throats, staring at the boards. None of them looked at Harlan for more than a heartbeat.

Harlan heard it anyway: their decision to live another day, on whatever terms Rourke gave them.

“You can’t,” Harlan whispered. Then louder, more desperate: “You *can’t*, Captain! We’ve sailed together six years. Remember Cartagena? Remember when I took that shot meant for—”

Rourke raised one hand. The memory was there, in the brief tension at the corner of his jaw, but it passed.

“Six years I fed you,” he said. “Six years I paid you your share. And in return I get a knife in the dark.” He nodded to the plank. “Walk.”

Harlan’s breath quickened to ragged gasps. He shook his head, rope scraping against his chafed wrists.

“Please,” he said. “Rourke, I beg you. Put a ball in my head. Tie me to the mast in the next gale. Anything but… not that. Not the sharks.”

Below, as if summoned by the word, a dorsal fin sliced a slow, lazy arc through the water. Another joined it, then another, gray shapes gliding just beneath the surface, drawn by the smell of men and ship and the promise they had learned long ago: where this hull drifted, meat sometimes fell.

Rourke’s mouth tightened. “You had no mercy in you when you whispered of cutting my crew in half to make them bend,” he said. “There will be none now. Walk, or I’ll have you dragged to the end and thrown.”

Two of the bigger sailors stepped forward, grim-faced. They took Harlan by the arms. He tried to pull back, boots sliding on the wet deck.

Harlan’s voice broke into a high, panicked babble. “Jeb, for the love of God, we drank together in Tortuga! Hargreaves, you owe me dice money—Hargreaves, you bastard, look at me! Benno—Benno, we’re kin—”

Benno, a hulking man with scarred knuckles, looked at him—just once—and then looked away.

They marched him to the base of the plank. Its wood was slick with salt, worn smooth by boots and water. Up close, Harlan could see scratches along its length—gouges from nails or rings dug in by men trying desperately to hold on.

Rourke stepped closer until they were almost nose to nose. The captain’s eyes were unreadable now.

“You’ll do it yourself,” Rourke said quietly. “On your own feet. That’s as much mercy as you get from me.”

He nodded to the sailors, and they let go.

For a heartbeat, Harlan simply stood—swaying, the sea and sky tilting around him. The rope bit his wrists; his fingers tingled, numb from the binding and cold. Sweat beaded at his temples, then ran into his eyes, stinging. He blinked hard.

The fins cut circles beneath the plank. One shark rolled just under the surface, pale belly flashing, rows of teeth a brief white blur before it slid deeper again.

Harlan’s gut turned to ice.

“I can’t,” he whispered.

“You can,” Rourke said. “And you will.”

Behind them: the creak of rigging, the soft slap of water against the hull, the low cough of a man clearing his throat. The crew watched him like men watching a noose being tightened.

Harlan set one barefoot step onto the plank.

The wood flexed slightly under his weight. Out here, beyond the rail, there was only wind and the long drop to the water. The void yawned under him, the sea suddenly vast and hungry.

Another step.

The world narrowed to the board beneath his feet and the ropes cutting his skin. He could hear his own breath, ragged and fast, and the harsh thump of his heart as if his ribs were a drum.

The sharks circled tighter. Their bodies cast shifting shadows that moved across the pale underside of the plank. One fin brushed the surface of the water with a soft hiss, then disappeared.

“Keep going,” came Rourke’s voice from behind. Distant, cold. “No stopping.”

Harlan shuffled forward, knees quivering so hard he could barely keep them straight. He stared at the far end of the plank, at the knife-scarred lip where so many boots had likely paused before his.

When the wind gusted, the board rocked, and he cried out, arms flying wide for balance—even bound, his body remembered how to try to live.

“Please,” he said, voice raw. “Please, Captain. I’ll swear an oath. I’ll—I'll take the lash, I’ll—”

The sea answered him with a hollow boom against the hull.

He reached the end.

The plank dipped perceptibly under his weight now. The sharks were a restless, swirling mass below, sleek backs sliding over one another, white-tipped tails flicking. Their movements were growing more agitated, anticipating the fall.

Harlan stared down. The water seemed impossibly far and yet horribly close, a shifting mirror that showed not his face but the grim, inhuman eyes and open mouths that waited.

His stomach lurched. His legs locked.

“I can’t,” he said again, hoarse, broken. “I can’t do it. I can’t.”

Behind him, boots strode on wood. Rourke’s hand fell on his shoulder—heavy, immovable. The captain leaned close, his words for Harlan alone.

“You already did it,” he said. “The moment you chose mutiny.”

And with that, he pushed.

The world dropped out from under Harlan. He fell with a tearing scream that seemed ripped from something deeper than his lungs. Wind smashed the sound out into the air; then the sea rose up and swallowed him whole in a great, frothing splash.

The crew crowded the rail.

For a heartbeat, there was only the spreading rings of the impact. Then the water erupted.

Dark shapes converged in a thrashing knot where Harlan had gone under. Foam boiled white, then stained dull and murky. The rolling bodies of the sharks crashed together, tails lashing, water churning as they fought and twisted in a frenzy.

A hand broke the surface—a flash of pale skin, fingers splayed, reaching blindly. A scream tore loose, thin and shrill and cut short as something yanked him down again. The hand vanished.

More splashing. More violent surges as the sharks collided and wheeled, each trying to seize its share. The water frothed and heaved, stained now with a spreading, cloudy red that the sea eagerly dispersed.

The crew watched in rigid silence as the commotion slowly subsided. The fins began to separate, sliding away, bellies distended, movements sated and sluggish. The red washed thin, broken apart by current and swell until it became just another streak of color on the vast, indifferent ocean.

Nothing of Harlan surfaced.

Rourke stepped back from the rail, his face as impassive as carved stone.

“Let this be the last time any man on my deck thinks of turning against me,” he said quietly. “Sharks are always hungry. I’m not lacking for ways to feed them.”

One by one, the sailors looked away from the sea and back to their work. The wind filled the sails with a heavy sigh, and the *Maiden’s Woe* turned her prow toward the horizon, leaving behind only the fading stain and a few circling fins that trailed after, patient as ever.

Harlan’s breath quickened to ragged gasps. He shook his head, rope scraping against his chafed wrists.

Two of the bigger sailors stepped forward, grim-faced. They took Harlan by the arms. He tried to pull back, boots sliding on the wet deck.

Benno, a hulking man with scarred knuckles, looked at him—just once—and then looked away.

They marched him to the base of the plank. Its wood was slick with salt, worn smooth by boots and water. Up close, Harlan could see scratches along its length—gouges from nails or rings dug in by men trying desperately to hold on.

Rourke stepped closer until they were almost nose to nose. The captain’s eyes were unreadable now.

“You’ll do it yourself,” Rourke said quietly. “On your own feet. That’s as much mercy as you get from me.”

He nodded to the sailors, and they let go.

For a heartbeat, Harlan simply stood—swaying, the sea and sky tilting around him. The rope bit his wrists; his fingers tingled, numb from the binding and cold. Sweat beaded at his temples, then ran into his eyes, stinging. He blinked hard.

The fins cut circles beneath the plank. One shark rolled just under the surface, pale belly flashing, rows of teeth a brief white blur before it slid deeper again.

Harlan’s gut turned to ice.

“I can’t,” he whispered.

“You can,” Rourke said. “And you will.”

Behind them: the creak of rigging, the soft slap of water against the hull, the low cough of a man clearing his throat. The crew watched him like men watching a noose being tightened.

Harlan set one barefoot step onto the plank.

The wood flexed slightly under his weight. Out here, beyond the rail, there was only wind and the long drop to the water. The void yawned under him, the sea suddenly vast and hungry.

Another step.

The world narrowed to the board beneath his feet and the ropes cutting his skin. He could hear his own breath, ragged and fast, and the harsh thump of his heart as if his ribs were a drum.

The sharks circled tighter. Their bodies cast shifting shadows that moved across the pale underside of the plank. One fin brushed the surface of the water with a soft hiss, then disappeared.

“Keep going,” came Rourke’s voice from behind. Distant, cold. “No stopping.”

Harlan shuffled forward, knees quivering so hard he could barely keep them straight. He stared at the far end of the plank, at the knife-scarred lip where so many boots had likely paused before his.

When the wind gusted, the board rocked, and he cried out, arms flying wide for balance—even bound, his body remembered how to try to live.

“Please,” he said, voice raw. “Please, Captain. I’ll swear an oath. I’ll—I'll take the lash, I’ll—”

The sea answered him with a hollow boom against the hull.

He reached the end.

The plank dipped perceptibly under his weight now. The sharks were a restless, swirling mass below, sleek backs sliding over one another, white-tipped tails flicking. Their movements were growing more agitated, anticipating the fall.

Harlan stared down. The water seemed impossibly far and yet horribly close, a shifting mirror that showed not his face but the grim, inhuman eyes and open mouths that waited.

His stomach lurched. His legs locked.

“I can’t,” he said again, hoarse, broken. “I can’t do it. I can’t.”

Behind him, boots strode on wood. Rourke’s hand fell on his shoulder—heavy, immovable. The captain leaned close, his words for Harlan alone.

“You already did it,” he said. “The moment you chose mutiny.”

And with that, he pushed.

The world dropped out from under Harlan. He fell with a tearing scream that seemed ripped from something deeper than his lungs. Wind smashed the sound out into the air; then the sea rose up and swallowed him whole in a great, frothing splash.

The crew crowded the rail.

For a heartbeat, there was only the spreading rings of the impact. Then the water erupted.

Dark shapes converged in a thrashing knot where Harlan had gone under. Foam boiled white, then stained dull and murky. The rolling bodies of the sharks crashed together, tails lashing, water churning as they fought and twisted in a frenzy.

A hand broke the surface—a flash of pale skin, fingers splayed, reaching blindly. A scream tore loose, thin and shrill and cut short as something yanked him down again. The hand vanished.

More splashing. More violent surges as the sharks collided and wheeled, each trying to seize its share. The water frothed and heaved, stained now with a spreading, cloudy red that the sea eagerly dispersed.

The crew watched in rigid silence as the commotion slowly subsided. The fins began to separate, sliding away, bellies distended, movements sated and sluggish. The red washed thin, broken apart by current and swell until it became just another streak of color on the vast, indifferent ocean.

Nothing of Harlan surfaced.

Rourke stepped back from the rail, his face as impassive as carved stone.

“Let this be the last time any man on my deck thinks of turning against me,” he said quietly. “Sharks are always hungry. I’m not lacking for ways to feed them.”

One by one, the sailors looked away from the sea and back to their work. The wind filled the sails with a heavy sigh, and the Maiden’s Woe turned her prow toward the horizon, leaving behind only the fading stain and a few circling fins that trailed after, patient as ever.
