The first thing he loses is sleep.

At 2:14 a.m., the apartment is a box of stale air and humming appliances. The city presses against the window in sodium-orange light, distant sirens, a bus wheezing its way up the avenue. Daniel lies on his back, eyes open, watching the ceiling fan carve slow, rotating shadows on the cracked plaster.

He replays it again.

Not the whole thing—his mind dodges the worst of it, flinching aside like an eye from a needle—but fragments: the sound of a body hitting the ground, that heavy, final thud; the wet rasp of a breath that might have been his name; the surprising warmth on his hands that would not wash off no matter how long he stood at the sink afterward.

He squeezes his eyes shut until bright patterns swim behind his lids.

“Stop,” he whispers to no one. “It’s done. It’s over.”

It is not over.

He turns onto his side, facing the wall. The pale rectangle of the window throws a ghost of light onto the cracked paint. In the mottled shapes, in the uneven strokes and stains, he sees it: a face. Not distinct at first, just the suggestion—a pair of darker bruises where eyes might be, a shadow curve suggesting a mouth.

He stares. The longer he looks, the more it settles into a shape he knows. The left eye hangs just a little lower than the right, like it did when Aaron smiled. The crooked line of shadow could be the half-healed scar on his lip.

“You’re imagining it,” Daniel mutters. His own voice sounds too loud. “You’re tired.”

The phantom face on the wall doesn’t move. But the eyes feel fixed on him, dull and accusing.

He reaches out, hand shaking, and brushes his fingers across the plaster where the eyes should be.

Cold.

He jerks back, heart slamming against his ribs. Plaster is never that cold. Not inside. Not in summer.

A car horn blares outside, sharp and ordinary. The spell breaks. The face bleeds back into random stains and cracks. Just a wall.

Daniel laughs once, too high and too soft, almost a hiccup. “Sleep,” he tells himself. “Just sleep.”

He doesn’t.

---

By the second week, it’s not just the wall.

It’s in the bathroom mirror, in the steam-beaded reflection as he showers at 3 a.m., water pounding at his shoulders like a punishment. His own face stares back: eyes sunken, stubble too long, skin sallow. But over his shoulder, in the cloudy glass, something moves.

He freezes, soap stinging his eyes. Slowly, he turns his head.

The shower behind him is empty. White tile. Chrome faucet dripping steadily.

He looks back at the mirror.

Aaron stands there, behind his reflection.

Drenched, clothes hanging limp and dark as if soaked through. His hair clings to his forehead in thin streaks. His skin is colorless, grayed out, as if leached of blood. Only the eyes are bright, too bright, luminous with hurt and something like wonder.

Daniel twists so fast he nearly slips. There is nothing there. Just the rattling curtain, the empty tub.

He drags the curtain closed and faces the mirror again, heart in his throat.

Now it’s just him. Just Daniel. No one else.

He looks directly into his own eyes and sees Aaron’s.

“You’re tired,” he tells the mirror, soap sliding down his arms in milky trails. “Tired people see things.”

The bathroom light flickers.

In that sputter of dimness, the reflection shifts. Daniel’s face blurs at the edges. His features sag and slide, as though melting. His mouth droops and straightens into a line that is not his. His cheeks hollow. A pale groove appears where a ring used to sit on someone’s finger.

Aaron looks out at him from his own body, lips parted, breathless.

You did this.

The words aren’t spoken. The lips never move. But they crash into Daniel’s skull with the certainty of a physical blow. He grabs the sides of the sink until his knuckles shine white.

In the mirror, his reflection’s hands are clean. No scars. No scratches. No memory of fingernails raking across his skin as he pushed, as he shoved, as Aaron misstepped, as metal met bone down at the bottom of the concrete shaft.

“It was an accident,” Daniel whispers. The shower hisses behind him like distant static.

The lights flicker again. Go out.

For a heartbeat the darkness is total.

Something brushes the back of his wet neck. A fingertip, icy and slow, following the contour of his spine. He can’t breathe. Can’t move. Can’t scream.

When the light flares back, his neck is bare. The bathroom is empty. Water sprays against tile.

He steps out on shaking legs and doesn’t look in the mirror again.

---

By the third month, it’s everywhere.

His apartment shrinks around him. The wallpaper swells and breathes, inhaling when he does, exhaling in a slow, mold-scented sigh. The floorboards creak where no one walks. In the stillness, he hears the soft tap of footsteps pacing the hall outside his door, pausing just beyond the threshold.

He stops going out during the day. The brightness is too harsh; the sun throws too many reflections in storefront windows, and he catches glimpses of Aaron’s pale face hovering over his shoulder, standing on the other side of the glass, always just behind him. Once, crossing the street, he saw him clearly in the windshield of a passing car—mouth open in a silent cry, palms pressed against the inside of the glass as if he were trapped beneath it.

The horn blared. The car missed him by inches.

That night, he drags the deadbolt three times, four, five. Checks the chain until the metal screeches. The city’s noises have thinned to distant murmurs when he finally collapses into the armchair in the living room, curtains drawn, every light on.

The television stares back at him, black and blank.

He has not turned it on.

He has not reached for the remote.

Still, it comes alive with a slow, pulsing glow.

The screen blossoms into static—white snow on black sea, churning restlessly. No sound, just the silent hiss of a thousand broken signals. He should get up. Unplug it. Throw something at it. Instead he sits, transfixed, as specks of light and darkness whirl, cluster, divide.

Shapes struggle up out of the noise.

A hand, first. Fingers long and thin, forming from bands of interference. Then an arm. Then the suggestion of a shoulder, a throat, a jaw.

Aaron’s face materializes like a photograph left too long in chemicals. Grainy at the edges, but undeniable. Eyes dead-black in the warping static, mouth a smeared blur.

“Stop,” Daniel breathes. “Please.”

The screen does not listen. The ghost inside it does.

The static resolves into something sharper, the contrast heightening, the darks deepening to an impossible void. Aaron opens his mouth. No sound comes out at first, just a thick swell of white noise that fills Daniel’s head like a pressure, like water flooding in.

Then, buried under the roar, he hears words.

You left me there.

The voice is wrong—consonants crackling, vowels warping—but it is his. It is Aaron’s, dragged across broken glass.

“I came back,” Daniel says. His tongue feels swollen, his throat dry. “I— I checked, I—”

You watched.

He had. He’d stood at the edge of the stairwell, gripping the rusty railing, peering down into the shadows. The shape at the bottom had been twisted, wrong. There had been sounds. Wet ones. Little gasps. Maybe that rasping whisper of his name. Maybe just his dying lungs emptying. He had stayed long enough to know that Aaron would not be walking away from this.

Then he’d left.

On the screen, Aaron’s eyes bleed whiteness, static pouring from their corners like snow.

You left me in the dark.

The apartment lights flicker. Once. Twice. Then go out, plunging the room into a blackness that swallows the thin glow of the city outside.

Only the television remains, a pale, seething rectangle of navy and gray. Aaron’s form grows clearer, stepping forward, closer, until his corpse-pale face fills the screen, pupils blown to endless tunnels.

Daniel can’t move. The chair might as well be part of him. His skin crawls. Something skitters beneath it, insect-legs tapping along his veins.

“Tell me what you want,” he whispers.

The answer comes at once. Whispered in his ear, though no warmth stirs the air. Murmured inside his skull, vibrating in his teeth.

I want what you took.

His breath stutters. In the reflection of the screen, he sees his own outline: hunched, small, trapped in the halo of flickering light. Aaron’s face overlaps his, a double exposure. Where their shapes meet, lines blur and melt, identities smearing together.

He blinks—and now his own hands are on the TV glass, palms flat against the cold surface, as if he’s the one trapped inside trying to push his way out. His fingerprints bloom in greasy smudges. On the other side, ghostly hands mirror his.

No. Not mirror.

Aaron’s fingers stretch to meet his from within the static, thin and pale, nails darkened with something that won’t wash away. Each point of contact sends a shot of cold up Daniel’s arms, burrowing into the bone.

“You’re not real,” Daniel tells him. “You’re dead.”

The grin that pulls at Aaron’s cut-out features is too wide. The skin at the corners of his mouth doesn’t crack. It stretches.

So are you.

The world lurches sideways.

For a moment, Daniel sees the stairwell again. Concrete walls slick with damp. The smell of rust, of leaked oil, of something coppery and thick down below. His own foot slipping on the edge of a step. The struggle: hands, elbows, breath, a choked curse. Then the rush of air as bodies shifted weight, the single, awful second where gravity claimed more than it should have.

He lurches to his feet, tearing his hands away from the screen. His fingers burn with cold. Numbness sears up to his elbows like frostbite.

The TV clicks off.

Darkness crashes down, total and suffocating. Not even the city bleeds through the curtains now. The room feels sewn shut.

In the black, he hears it.

Breathing.

Not his. Too close. Too wet, with a faint bubbling at the tail end of each inhale.

The air thickens. He raises his hands in front of his face and sees nothing. But he feels it: the oppressive closeness of another body, inches from his own. The faint whisper of cloth against cloth.

“Turn the lights back on,” he chokes. “Turn them back on, turn them—”

Cold lips brush his ear.

Confess.

He twists. Turns. Flails in the dark. His hand connects with the lamp, sending it toppling. The bulb explodes with a sharp, popping crack. Glass fragments skitter across the floor, chiming like ice.

Confess, the voice insists. It’s not a request. It’s an instruction wound tight with fury.

The walls are smaller now. He can sense them pressing in, hear the old building’s bones groan as if something heavy leans against them from the outside. From every direction, fingers seem to scratch along the paint: scraping, clawing, looking for a way in or a way out.

His chest aches. His heart stammers. Each beat feels wrong, out of sync, as if it belongs to someone else.

“It was an accident,” he sobs. “I didn’t mean— I didn’t mean to—”

Liar.

Hands seize his wrists.

They are not real. They cannot be. They're too cold, their grip too steady. But he feels each finger encircle bone, press down, squeeze. Pressure builds until his joints scream and his nails bite into his palms.

He drops to his knees. The carpet snags his skin. Invisible weight settles across his back, forcing him down until his forehead touches the floor. Dust and the faint, coppery tang of old blood fill his nose. His own, or someone else’s—he can’t tell.

Images flood his mind, each one sharper than reality: Aaron’s eyes going glassy, his mouth opening and closing like a fish; the way the light in the stairwell had seemed to dim around his crumpled body; the grotesque stillness afterward, broken only by the ticking drip of something falling from the edge of the landing down onto concrete far below.

“Stop,” Daniel whispers into the carpet. “Please, I— I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

The scratching on the walls intensifies, a swelling chorus that makes his molars ache. It’s not just on the outside anymore. It’s inside. In his skull. Tiny claws worrying at the soft parts of his brain.

Tell them.

The voice is inside his head now, echoing in the cavities where his own thoughts once were.

Tell them what you did.

“I can’t,” he gasps. His throat is raw. “I can’t, they’ll—”

They’ll what?

Hands yank his head up by his hair. His scalp screams. He finds himself forced to stare into the darkness before him. Shapes writhe there, ghosts of edges and outlines. Slowly, like a developing photograph, a face emerges from the black.

Aaron. So close their noses nearly touch. The pupils are pits. Deep, endless. Daniel leans forward despite himself, teetering on the edge of that void.

You think you’re not already dead?

The question hangs between them, heavier than any accusation. In that moment, Daniel realizes that the things that made up his life—sleep, work, food, idle conversation—have already fallen away. Days bleed into nights. Time has stopped being a line and become a circle, looping endlessly back to that single, catastrophic instant in the stairwell.

The only thing left is this. The haunting. The guilt that gnaws and gnaws and never, ever gets full.

“You’re not real,” he whispers again, but his voice cracks around the lie. “You’re… you’re in my head.”

Aaron’s lips peel back in something that might once have been a smile.

Then let me in.

The pressure behind Daniel’s eyes spikes. It feels like his skull is going to split. White-hot lines of pain trace the inside of his bones. He screams, or thinks he does; no sound reaches his ears over the roaring, the hiss, the static growing louder and louder.

The world shatters.

---

When the neighbors find him the next morning, the door hangs open. The lights are on. The television hisses gray static in an empty room.

Daniel sits on the living room floor, knees drawn to his chest, forehead resting on them. His fingernails are ragged and bleeding where he’s scraped them over and over along the same patch of carpet, worn thin and dark.

He is talking under his breath, over and over, a broken record of hoarse words.

“I pushed him,” he murmurs. “I pushed him, I pushed him, I left him there, I left him in the dark…”

There is no one in the room with him.

Still, every so often, he flinches, as if someone invisible has just brushed cold fingers down the back of his neck.

The air in the apartment feels heavy. Watchful. Like something lingers there, hungry and patient, waiting for the next confession, the next crack in a sane mind to seep through.

And in the reflection of the dead television screen, two shadowy figures sit huddled together on the floor where there should be only one.

He blinks—and now his own hands are on the TV glass, palms flat against the cold surface, as if he’s the one trapped inside trying to push his way out. His fingerprints bloom in greasy smudges. On the other side, ghostly hands mirror his.

No. Not mirror.

Aaron’s fingers stretch to meet his from within the static, thin and pale, nails darkened with something that won’t wash away. Each point of contact sends a shot of cold up Daniel’s arms, burrowing into the bone.

“You’re not real,” Daniel tells him. “You’re dead.”

The grin that pulls at Aaron’s cut-out features is too wide. The skin at the corners of his mouth doesn’t crack. It stretches.

So are you.

The world lurches sideways.

For a moment, Daniel sees the stairwell again. Concrete walls slick with damp. The smell of rust, of leaked oil, of something coppery and thick down below. His own foot slipping on the edge of a step. The struggle: hands, elbows, breath, a choked curse. Then the rush of air as bodies shifted weight, the single, awful second where gravity claimed more than it should have.

He lurches to his feet, tearing his hands away from the screen. His fingers burn with cold. Numbness sears up to his elbows like frostbite.

The TV clicks off.

Darkness crashes down, total and suffocating. Not even the city bleeds through the curtains now. The room feels sewn shut.

In the black, he hears it.

Breathing.

Not his. Too close. Too wet, with a faint bubbling at the tail end of each inhale.

The air thickens. He raises his hands in front of his face and sees nothing. But he feels it: the oppressive closeness of another body, inches from his own. The faint whisper of cloth against cloth.

“Turn the lights back on,” he chokes. “Turn them back on, turn them—”

Cold lips brush his ear.

Confess.

He twists. Turns. Flails in the dark. His hand connects with the lamp, sending it toppling. The bulb explodes with a sharp, popping crack. Glass fragments skitter across the floor, chiming like ice.

Confess, the voice insists. It’s not a request. It’s an instruction wound tight with fury.

The walls are smaller now. He can sense them pressing in, hear the old building’s bones groan as if something heavy leans against them from the outside. From every direction, fingers seem to scratch along the paint: scraping, clawing, looking for a way in or a way out.

His chest aches. His heart stammers. Each beat feels wrong, out of sync, as if it belongs to someone else.

“It was an accident,” he sobs. “I didn’t mean— I didn’t mean to—”

Liar.

Hands seize his wrists.

They are not real. They cannot be. They're too cold, their grip too steady. But he feels each finger encircle bone, press down, squeeze. Pressure builds until his joints scream and his nails bite into his palms.

He drops to his knees. The carpet snags his skin. Invisible weight settles across his back, forcing him down until his forehead touches the floor. Dust and the faint, coppery tang of old blood fill his nose. His own, or someone else’s—he can’t tell.

Images flood his mind, each one sharper than reality: Aaron’s eyes going glassy, his mouth opening and closing like a fish; the way the light in the stairwell had seemed to dim around his crumpled body; the grotesque stillness afterward, broken only by the ticking drip of something falling from the edge of the landing down onto concrete far below.

“Stop,” Daniel whispers into the carpet. “Please, I— I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

The scratching on the walls intensifies, a swelling chorus that makes his molars ache. It’s not just on the outside anymore. It’s inside. In his skull. Tiny claws worrying at the soft parts of his brain.

Tell them.

The voice is inside his head now, echoing in the cavities where his own thoughts once were.

Tell them what you did.

“I can’t,” he gasps. His throat is raw. “I can’t, they’ll—”

They’ll what?

Hands yank his head up by his hair. His scalp screams. He finds himself forced to stare into the darkness before him. Shapes writhe there, ghosts of edges and outlines. Slowly, like a developing photograph, a face emerges from the black.

Aaron. So close their noses nearly touch. The pupils are pits. Deep, endless. Daniel leans forward despite himself, teetering on the edge of that void.

You think you’re not already dead?

The question hangs between them, heavier than any accusation. In that moment, Daniel realizes that the things that made up his life—sleep, work, food, idle conversation—have already fallen away. Days bleed into nights. Time has stopped being a line and become a circle, looping endlessly back to that single, catastrophic instant in the stairwell.

The only thing left is this. The haunting. The guilt that gnaws and gnaws and never, ever gets full.

“You’re not real,” he whispers again, but his voice cracks around the lie. “You’re… you’re in my head.”

Aaron’s lips peel back in something that might once have been a smile.

Then let me in.

The pressure behind Daniel’s eyes spikes. It feels like his skull is going to split. White-hot lines of pain trace the inside of his bones. He screams, or thinks he does; no sound reaches his ears over the roaring, the hiss, the static growing louder and louder.

The world shatters.

When the neighbors find him the next morning, the door hangs open. The lights are on. The television hisses gray static in an empty room.

Daniel sits on the living room floor, knees drawn to his chest, forehead resting on them. His fingernails are ragged and bleeding where he’s scraped them over and over along the same patch of carpet, worn thin and dark.

He is talking under his breath, over and over, a broken record of hoarse words.

“I pushed him,” he murmurs. “I pushed him, I pushed him, I left him there, I left him in the dark…”

There is no one in the room with him.

Still, every so often, he flinches, as if someone invisible has just brushed cold fingers down the back of his neck.

The air in the apartment feels heavy. Watchful. Like something lingers there, hungry and patient, waiting for the next confession, the next crack in a sane mind to seep through.

And in the reflection of the dead television screen, two shadowy figures sit huddled together on the floor where there should be only one.

The room smelled like the city’s conscience—wet copper, cheap perfume, and mold trying to crawl its way back into the wallpaper. Somebody’d opened a vein in here and let the worst parts of town slither out.

She was on the floor like a broken promise, pieces of her scattered around the room as if someone’d tried to rearrange her into a better story and given up halfway through. Skin gone waxy, eyes fixed on a ceiling that had nothing to offer but a water stain shaped like a question mark. The kind that never gets answered.

I’ve seen my share of corpses. This one looked less like a body and more like urban renewal done by a maniac with a box cutter. Throat opened wide, a red, wet grin that stretched from ear to ear. Blood everywhere—on the carpet, on the walls, on the bed. The place looked like the city had coughed up its lungs and left them here to dry.

Her blood had already started turning from bright red to that ugly dark you see on rusted fire escapes and old brick stoops where the rain never quite reaches. The way it pooled around her, it looked like the city map laid out in arteries and alleys—veins of a neighborhood bled dry. It trickled into the cracks in the warped floorboards, disappearing into the building’s guts. Give it a few hours and the rats would know more about this case than I did.

Outside the window, neon flickered like a faulty pulse, painting her in sick pink and electric blue. The sign across the street buzzed and stuttered—VAC NCY—like even the motel couldn’t bring itself to admit it had room for this. The city’s always selling something: hope by the hour, comfort by the bottle, absolution by the gram. Tonight it was selling death, wholesale.

She’d been pretty once. You could still see it in the shape of her mouth, just beneath the ruin. The kind of pretty that gets you free drinks and bad attention. Now she looked like a mannequin some bored window dresser had taken a cleaver to. One arm bent under her at an angle that didn’t believe in anatomy, fingers curled like they were holding onto something that wasn’t there. Maybe a last thought. Maybe a last lie.

The ceiling fan turned slow, a lazy carousel of dust and other people’s regrets. Every rotation dragged the smell of rot and iron through the room, thinning it out but never really clearing it. Death doesn’t leave a place; it just settles in, like an old tenant who knows the landlord stopped caring a long time ago.

Her hair was spread out around her head, black strands stuck in drying blood, like roots trying to grow in poisoned soil. This building was the same way—planted in a neighborhood that used to mean something, now just another rot spot in a city full of them. Bricks sagging, mortar crumbling, windows cataracted with grime. You patch the worst holes, you slap on some paint, but the mold’s always there behind the plaster, grinning in the dark.

The knife work was enthusiastic, not professional. Whoever did this didn’t come here to send a message; they came to empty themselves out onto someone else. Slice by slice, like peeling wallpaper off a rotted wall, trying to get down to something honest underneath. All they found was more rot.

Somewhere downstairs a radiator hissed, old metal spitting steam and rust. This city’s full of radiators like that, old men with nothing left but complaints, leaking out heat and bitterness until nobody wants to sit close. The sound mixed with the occasional car horn outside, ambulances wailing far off. The usual orchestra. Life, death, and everything in between, played off-key.

The carpet under her was cheap and thin, the kind that doesn’t cushion a fall, just soaks up the mess. It was drinking her in, thread by thread, the way the city drinks in the broken ones. Take them in, squeeze them dry, leave the stain. Tomorrow the manager would stand here, wringing his hands, asking if they could “save the rug.” They’d shampoo it, bleach it, pretend. That’s all this town ever does: pretend the stains aren’t permanent.

Her eyes were open. They always are in these places. Nobody dies with their eyes closed in a room that charges by the hour. They stare up, glassy and surprised, at the cheap light fixture and the peeling paint, and realize too late this is where their story ends—fifty bucks, a faded bedspread, and a view of the alley. Those eyes didn’t see much anymore, but they reflected the ceiling’s yellowed cracks in miniature. Tiny fault lines in dead glass. This city puts those in you while you’re still breathing.

I crouched down, joints popping like old floorboards. The blood had dried tacky on the lino near her hand, edges already crusting over, turning from fresh crime into old news. The city works fast that way. It moves everything along. Today’s horror is tomorrow’s rumor and next week’s punchline. After that, it’s just something that happened “a while back, over on Twelfth.”

A roach edged out from under the radiator, gave the scene a once-over, then changed its mind and went home. Even vermin have standards. Or maybe he knew this show wasn’t done yet. Maybe he was just waiting for the lights to go down before he came back for the crumbs. That’s this town in a nutshell—everything waiting for darkness so it can get to work.

Her lipstick was smeared halfway across her cheek, the red mixing with the darker red beneath it. It looked like the city’s skyline at sunset, when the smog catches fire and everyone pretends it’s beautiful. But up close, you can smell the burning. You can tell it’s not the sky that’s glowing, it’s all the things rotting underneath.

The sirens were closer now. They’d bring uniforms, tape, cameras, questions. Procedure. Good for the paperwork, bad for the soul. They’d bag her, tag her, haul her away, scrub the worst of it from the walls. Give it a week and this room would have a new tenant, a new story starting on top of all the old ones. Layer after layer of cheap cologne over the stench of something not right.

The city does that too. Builds shiny glass on top of old bones, calls it progress. But sometimes the foundation shifts, and all the buried things rise up through the cracks, reminding everyone what it cost to get here.

I looked at her one more time. Another citizen claimed by the metropolis like overdue rent. The city doesn’t kill you fast; it rots you slow, one corner at a time, until the whole structure gives. Then there’s a sound, brief and sharp, like a body hitting threadbare carpet. And after that, just quiet.

Except it’s never really quiet. Not here. Not in this place that eats its dead and calls it redevelopment.

The siren that marked the twentieth minute of the Hunt sounded like a broken cathedral bell—warped, mournful, and amplified across the dead city by towers full of speakers. It rolled down the glassless avenues and slipped into every alley, every empty choke of stairwell, quivering in the air like heat.

Rian staggered as it passed overhead, the sound pressing against his spine. His lungs burned; each breath scraped as if he were breathing in powdered metal. The mask over his mouth, damp with sweat and his own exhausted exhale, choked instead of helped. His shoes, standard orange Runners’ issue, slapped weakly on fractured asphalt. He didn’t dare look back.

The sky was the color of old televisions, a static gray behind the scaffolding of half-finished luxury towers. The billboards still worked, though—two hundred meters up, colossal and bright, advertising the Hunt the way the old world used to advertise soft drinks and vacations. A drone camera drifted past him now, bathed in red indicator light, its lens adjusting with a soft insect whine.

RUNNER #14 – RI▲N MERROW – DISTRICT 7 LOTTERY WINNER

The caption flashed along its screen, along with data on his heart rate, body temperature, estimated time to collapse. The audience loved the stats.

He ducked into the skeleton of a parking garage, the ceiling low and gnawed through by rust. His thigh cramped so hard he almost went down. He slammed a hand against a concrete pillar, smearing sweat. The echo of his own breathing bounced back at him, ragged and too loud.

His wrist band vibrated. The haptic buzz rattled through the bone.

—ZONE BORDER in 00:00:30. RETURN TO ACTIVE AREA.—

“Shut up,” he hissed at the band, but the speaking sent another spike through his chest. If he crossed over into dead space, the shock collar at his neck would trigger. Not lethal—not in the first violation—but enough to put him on his knees. Enough to make him easy.

He could hear them out there. Not footsteps—the Hunters weren’t sloppy. But the distant pop of a launcher, the low murmur of amplified voices from the commentary drones. The crowd in the towers would be roaring by now, clenching fists around glasses full of other people’s debt. This was a Class IV Hunt; the buy-in alone could have paid to keep an entire block of Runners off the Lottery list for a year.

Rian pressed his back to cold concrete, forcing himself to think. The map they’d shown him before they let him loose scrambled in his head, landmarks blurring. There had been a river once, on the east side. If he could make it there, the cover of the drainage tunnels—

He pushed off from the pillar. His leg screamed but he ran anyway, cutting sideways through the building, past rows of rotten cars picked clean decades ago and spray-painted with past seasons’ kill counts.

Something whispered across the floor, faint but wrong. Not the stutter of his own shoes. Lighter. Deliberate.

He dropped instinctively, rolling behind a dented sedan frame just as a bolt of blue light hissed overhead, cracking against the pillar and leaving a charred streak that glowed like ice.

The impact sound reached him a heartbeat later, like a hand slapping wet stone.

“Target adjusted,” said a voice, calm and female, somewhere beyond the next row of concrete. It was flat, clipped by a helmet mic. “Wind negligible. Runner is limping. Advise moderate caution only.”

Rian’s heart thudded against the filthy concrete he hugged. The air stank of dampness and the acid tang from the charge shot. A camera drone slid around the car’s rusted hood in one smooth, curious motion, lens widening as it found him.

He smashed his hand against it before he could stop himself. Plastic cracked, the drone spinning off with a high, protesting whine as it hit the ground. It twitched once, then went still.

The broken casing flashed a message in stuttering blue:

—PROPERTY OF ASPHODEL LEISURE SYNDICATE—

The woman’s voice came again, amused this time, echoing off the columns. “#14 still has fight. That’s good. The feed’s been flagging in Sector C.”

New footsteps now. Measured. Closer. Not running—walking. Confident. Rian pushed his back against the car, trying to think of something, anything. There was no weapon, no debris heavy enough. Only rust, dust, and the collar tight around his throat.

A muzzle tip eased into view over the car’s hood first, beside a gleaming white forearm guard. The weapon was sleek, matte, its inbuilt dampeners drinking in sound. A small holographic stamp near the barrel rotated lazily: ALCYONE TIER // LICENSED HUNTER.

The woman followed, stepping around the vehicle with idle grace, boots whispering on grit. Her armor was the glossy black typical of the Syndicate’s elite, etched with sharp silver patterns that caught the sallow light filtering in from the cracked ceiling. Her helmet’s faceplate was a dark mirror, his own gaunt reflection warped in her visor.

“Rian Merrow,” she said, and this time she used his name without the number. “Age twenty-six. Unskilled labor, Zone 7. Debts exceeding community threshold by 230%. Two prior Lottery exemptions purchased by elder sister. Both now expired.”

He stared at her. The only thing that moved was the quick heave of his chest.

“What do you want?” he managed.

The mirrored face tipped in a parody of curiosity. “The same thing you did when you lined up at the kiosk,” she said. “A chance. Ours are just weighted differently.”

Behind her, outside the yawning mouth of the garage, he could see sky. It felt impossibly far. Another siren tolled, softer: five minutes to the end of the hunt window. He’d made it almost the full half-hour. They’d replay that on the highlight reels as proof it had been “competitive.”

Her gun dipped, not quite pointing at him, more a casual tilt in his direction. “You were supposed to keep to the southern quadrant,” she continued. “You took the east slope instead. The cameras had to compensate. The drones hate vertical interference.”

“How is that—” he coughed. His throat was a stitch of fire. “—my problem?”

She laughed, a short sound. “It isn’t. It’s theirs. Mine is that the audience numbers dropped in Segment 3. Three sponsors already pinged my handler. They bought a bloodline hunt, and you spent nine minutes hiding under a conveyor.”

He’d crawled under that rusted assembly line because his hands would no longer stop shaking and the noise outside had been a hurricane of boots and distant screams. Because the dark, oily smell had reminded him of the factory he used to work in, where his manager had shouted but nobody died.

“I didn’t ask to be here,” he said.

“No one does,” she replied. “But there’s always a list. You know that.”

He did. The List that crawled up the sides of public towers each month, names rising and falling in sick green as debts shifted and infractions were tallied. Lottery-eligible. No-buy zones. His name had hovered in the middle for years, a neon warning his sister pretended not to see.

“You’ll get your cut,” he said desperately. “From my… from the… the tokens.” Tokens. As if what they did to him would be worth little pearled units of credit.

She cocked her head. “You think I do this for your tokens? That’s touching.”

Her free hand dipped to her belt, unclipping a flat metal disk no larger than his palm. She flicked it toward him. It skipped once on the concrete, spinning to a lazy stop near his knee. At its center glowed a tiny, pulsing red light.

A Tracker token.

He looked up at her, stomach dropping. “That’s—those are for—”

“Penalties,” she supplied. “And bonuses. I don’t like interference. You broke a drone. That’s audience loss. But you also lasted longer than projected. That’s audience retention.” She took a step closer, the weapon now squarely leveled at him. “I don’t like breaking even.”

Understanding pushed through the fog of fear. He stared from the token to her visor and saw, dimly, his own eyes reflected back: wide, rimmed in salt and dirt, very much alive.

“You want me to run,” he whispered.

“I want you,” she said, “to make them remember my channel identification when they’re buying clips later. I want them to pause when they scroll past and say, ‘That was the one where the Runner nearly made it to the river.’”

Her fingers flexed on the grip. Up close, he could see the faint tremor there, not of nerves but of adrenaline that never quite left.

“Stand up, #14,” she commanded.

His legs almost refused, but the idea of dying on his knees in the gloom of the parking garage, without even sky above him, was worse. He pushed off the car, swaying, the collar at his throat cutting slightly as his shoulders lifted.

The holograms outside flared brighter, sensing imminent closure. Corporate logos bloomed along the broken skyline, each fighting to edge into the shot.

The Hunter turned her head, addressing the nearest camera drone that had crept up after the other’s destruction. “Hunter ID Alcyone,” she said, voice now crisp, the easy coldness back. “Claiming sole priority on Runner #14. Tracker token deployed, bonus clause invoked.”

A chime sounded from the drone—a digital witnessing. The towers no doubt flashed with the update. Alcyone’s channel viewership would spike.

She turned back to Rian. He could see himself again in her visor, smaller now. “There,” she said softly, so low the external mics might not catch it. “They’ve ratified it. Now you understand. If someone else tags you, they get the base purse. But I lose my bonus. And I don’t lose.”

“That’s supposed to make me feel… what?” he asked, voice cracking.

The shovel was cold when they handed it to him.

“Keep it close,” Corporal Haines had said, voice flat. “You’ll need it for digging. And if it comes to it… well. Don’t lose it.”

Tom had thought he meant shells, cave-ins, the endless collapse of wet earth. For weeks the shovel was just that: a tool. It bit into chalk and mud, scraped at sandbags, clinked off buried tin and bone. He used it until his palms blistered, then hardened. It became part of him, an extension of his arms, his routine, his quiet misery.

He slept with its handle under his shoulder like a plank. In the night, when the guns paused and the silence roared loud, his fingers would find the smooth-worn wood and he would think: This is for digging. Just digging.

Dawn broke gray and low on the morning everything changed. The rain had finally stopped, leaving the trench a swamp of brown water and floating scraps: cigarette ends, a sodden letter, a strip of someone’s bandage long turned brown. No-man’s-land beyond the parapet steamed faintly, a sick breath rising from the churned ground.

“Jerry patrols are getting bolder,” Haines said, eyes sunken, stubble a permanent shadow on his jaw. “Command wants a raid tonight. See what they’re up to. Take prisoners if you can.”

The words washed over Tom in the way orders always did now, distant and unreal, like something overheard in another room. He nodded, because that’s what was expected. Someone shoved a knife into his belt, tightened the strap of his helmet. Another man pressed a hand briefly to his shoulder.

“You’ll be fine, Tommy,” the man said. “In and out. Quick as you like.”

Tom tried to smile, but his mouth wouldn’t work. He glanced down and realized he was gripping the shovel, the short-handled trench spade with its square metal blade, edges filed not quite smooth. Someone—maybe him, maybe some man before him—had honed one side a little sharper, just enough to notice.

He thought again: It’s a tool. It’s only a tool.

Night fell early under low cloud. The barrage that usually preceded an attack never came; this was supposed to be quiet, sudden, a shadow-war of knives and whispered curses. At a whispered signal, Tom clambered up the slick fire step and over the parapet, boots sinking into the cold mud of no-man’s-land.

They moved in a crouched line, dark shapes against darker earth. The world narrowed: his breathing inside his own head, the press of his helmet strap against his throat, the weight of the shovel in his right hand. The air smelled of wet soil, cordite, and something faintly sour he tried not to name.

Every step felt too loud. The mud sucked at his boots with soft obscene sounds. He could sense men to left and right, but they were just presences, not individuals. All of them hunched, all of them praying in their own way.

Ahead, the German wire loomed, broken in places by earlier shelling. They slid through a gap, bellies scraping against cold metal and clotted earth. Somewhere a flare hissed up, turning the night white. They froze, pressed against the ground, the world a washed-out negative of angles and corpses and blasted stumps.

Tom lay with his face inches from the mud. He saw a hand there, half-buried, the fingers swollen, wedding band still on. For a moment the ring seemed to glow in the flare’s light. Then the flare died, and with it the world went black again.

They reached the enemy trench almost by accident. One moment the ground sloped gently upward, the next it fell away in a sudden dark cut. Voices in German murmured below, the clink of something metallic.

Haines hissed orders. Two men dropped grenades down the line to the right, two more to the left. A muffled, sickening series of thuds bloomed in the dark, followed by screams abruptly cut short. In the same motion, Tom and the others slid down into the trench.

Everything happened at once.

There was a shape in front of him, only a few feet away, unfolding from a crouch. A German soldier, helmet glinting faintly, eyes widening in shock. Tom saw the man’s mouth open, heard the intake of breath that would become a shout.

He lunged on instinct. The shovel came up, then down.

It met resistance with a dull, sick thud that traveled up through the handle into his wrists. Not like hitting earth or rock. Softer, but with something solid beneath. The soldier’s head snapped sideways. He staggered, a strangled sound trapped in his throat, then somehow stayed upright, lurching toward Tom, hands grasping.

They were face to face now. The man was younger than Tom had expected, cheeks still smooth, eyes shining with a confused terror that mirrored his own. Their boots tangled. Tom stumbled, the world narrowing to the reek of sweat and wool, the rasp of their breaths, the press of a foreign hand against his sleeve.

The soldier grabbed for Tom’s rifle, fingers clawing. Tom felt himself losing balance, felt the weight of the man pulling him down. For a heartbeat he hesitated, mind blank, unable to understand that this was not a drill, not a nightmare. That there was no one here to step in and stop it.

Some buried part of him, somewhere beneath the shaking and the disbelief, screamed: Move.

He wrenched the shovel free and swung again, sideways this time, both hands clenched white around the handle. The blow landed with more force. The sound it made was worse than the first, a thick, heavy impact followed by a short, wet exhale from the man in front of him.

The German’s eyes went strange, glassy, as if something behind them had been quietly extinguished. His legs buckled. His weight sagged against Tom for a terrible second—warm, solid, human—before sliding down and away.

Tom stood there, shovel dipped, breath tearing in and out of his chest. The trench around him was a chaos of bodies and grunts and whispered curses, but all of it seemed far off. His world had shrunk to the patch of duckboard at his feet, the still form sprawled across it, the way one hand lay palm up as if waiting to receive something.

There was blood, but he couldn’t really see it, only dark patches that his mind refused to focus on. It might have been shadows. It might have been spilled water. He didn’t look too closely.

Someone slammed into his shoulder, jolting him back into motion. They dragged him along the trench, deeper into enemy lines, but everything from that moment on was like watching someone else’s dream. In this world, the state’s power rests not only on its ability to punish, but on its ability to make punishment a spectacle.

The law has been rewritten into a rigid, zero-tolerance code, presented as “Pure Justice.” All infractions—jaywalking, speaking out of turn, petty theft—are sorted into “The Scale,” a ranked list of crimes with corresponding public penalties. Executions, once reserved for the worst offenses, now sit surprisingly low on that Scale. The government insists this is what keeps everyone safe: no ambiguity, no mercy, no debate.

Every city has a Justice Square. They’re built like amphitheaters, with stepped concrete terraces and massive screens. Attendance quotas are assigned by neighborhood; a percentage of the population must attend public punishments or risk fines, docked rations, or being marked as “sympathy risks.” Children are encouraged to attend. Schools schedule “Civic Learning Days” around certain high-profile events.

Media calls these executions “Civic Closures.” Commentators talk calmly about “resetting societal order,” as if human lives are glitches to be patched. Drones hover overhead, broadcasting everything live. The executions are framed with the language of cleanliness: “clearing corruption,” “purging moral rot.” Every killing is marketed as a public service.

Some people come because they must. Some come because they are afraid not to. Some come because they have learned to enjoy the spectacle—because it is one of the few public, collective emotions still allowed.

It is into this world that a seventeen-year-old, executed for stealing a loaf of bread, is led out onto the platform.

---

The crowd begins gathering long before the bells.

People move in thin, color-coded lines along the painted lanes: work-yellow, school-blue, elder-gray. Security drones drift overhead, lenses glinting like patient insects. On every street corner: posters.

PURITY IS MERCY.  
MERCY IS CRUELTY.  
JUSTICE DOES NOT HESITATE.

By the time the noon bell tolls, the Justice Square is nearly full. Parents hoist children up onto their shoulders. Vendors thread through the edges of the crowd, their carts rattling: permitted snacks, state-approved drinks. No one sells bread today. That would be in poor taste.

The stage in the center of the square is stark and geometric: a raised platform, a single upright post fitted with a simple, utilitarian mechanism. The government used to try more ornate methods—machines with polishing steel, ceremonial robes, dramatic lighting. Over the years they discovered it worked better when it looked like maintenance. Like cleaning.

The giant screens flicker on, framing the platform from all sides. Sound swells from hidden speakers: the low, chiming notes of the Civic Anthem. Words scroll at the bottom of the screens:

CIVIC CLOSURE #3,982,411  
CRIME: THEFT OF ESSENTIALS (FOOD)  
SUB-CLASSIFICATION: UNSANCTIONED ACQUISITION  
AGE: 17  
OUTCOME: TERMINAL CORRECTIVE ACTION

The phrase “terminal corrective action” lands in the crowd like a familiar weight. No one flinches at it anymore. They’ve heard it too often.

Yet in the first rows, a woman’s shoulders have gone rigid. Her wristband blinks red: Attendance Verified. Next to her, a man presses his hand flat over hers, pinning it to the rail.

“Don’t,” he murmurs.

“I’m not doing anything,” she says. Her lips are bone white. “I’m standing.”

Up on the platform, the gate in the side wall hisses open, and the teenager steps out.

He looks smaller than his age when surrounded by that much empty space. His gray prison tunic hangs loose from his shoulders. They shave all their heads before this; it’s more about uniformity than humiliation. Still, the close-cropped scalp makes him look younger, like a kid after a summer haircut.

The crowd, thousands of them, exhales as one. It’s not quite a gasp. More like a collective adjustment—as though their bodies are remembering how to arrange themselves around what is about to happen.

Someone in the middle rows starts clapping, a bright, too-loud sound. Security glances over. The clapping dies away, reduced to a few embarrassed taps.

There are three main types of faces visible in the crowd.

There are the hard-watchers: jaws clenched, eyes narrowed, taking everything in. These are the ones who have convinced themselves that this is necessary, that justice must be seen to be believed. They murmur stock phrases to their children: “This is why we don’t steal,” “The law protects us all, but only if it’s obeyed.”

There are the hollow-watchers: faces slack, gaze slightly clouded, trained on the stage because there is nowhere else for it to go. They are the ones who have learned that feeling too much is dangerous. They absorb without reacting.

And then there are the flicker-watchers: the ones whose eyes dart, whose hands tremble just enough, who blink too often as if trying to clear something from their vision. They are the ones who haven’t quite finished teaching themselves indifference.

Near the front, a boy around eleven stands between his parents. He’s clutching the rail with both hands. He has never seen someone this young on the platform before. He feels like he shouldn’t stare, and also like he should watch every second because isn’t that the point? At school they said it was important to witness, to be part of the communal moral correction.

He whispers, “What did he do?” even though it’s scrolling in text a few meters above the boy’s shorn head.

“Stole,” his father says shortly. “From the State. That’s all you need to know.”

“But—what?” The boy licks his lips. “Like…money?”

“Bread,” his mother corrects. The word sounds heavier than it should. “He stole bread. You remember that. You can’t take without asking. Ever.”

Her voice shakes on the last word. The father shoots her a warning look.

On the platform, the teenager blinks up at the glaring screens. The light makes him squint. His wrists are bound in front of him with a dull metal band. No one has gagged him. That would look bad, the officials found out early on. It’s better if they can speak; most don’t.

The Moderator steps forward, dressed in immaculate white. The crowd falls into an uneasy stillness. This is the part where they are expected to be quiet.

“Citizens,” the Moderator’s amplified voice rings over the square, “thank you for fulfilling your civic duty by attending this Closure. Today we release from our body a cell that has turned against it. This is not vengeance. This is alignment.”

The words are nearly identical each time. Some people mouth them along. Children in the front rows shift uncomfortably; they’ve had these speeches in ration lines, in classrooms, in dreams.

On the screen, a loop of the crime plays.

A small grocery enforcer-bot with its single fisheye lens. A narrow aisle. Shelves mostly full; this is a better district. The teenager moves quickly, glancing around. His hands are thin, fingers trembling as he reaches for a wrapped loaf marked with the State Seal. He hesitates—just a second—but the camera time-stamps it brutally: 00:01:42.

He slides the loaf under his shirt. The lens zooms in.

On the platform, a faint, animal murmur passes through the crowd at the sight of the video. Some faces harden. Some look down. A few nod along as if the footage has personally vindicated them.

“He knew,” says a woman near the middle, crossing her arms. “Look how he looks around. He knew.”

“He still took it,” answers the man beside her. “It’s simple. You know the risk, you pay the price. That’s what keeps the rest of us in bread.”

From a few rows back, someone mutters, “What rest of us?” but they say it into their collar, voice swallowed by the larger noise.

The Moderator continues, “Theft of essentials is theft from all. Theft is rot. Rot spreads. Today we cut it away. Do you stand with the law?”

An answer is expected. The sound rises in layers.

“Yes,” shout a few enthusiastic voices.  
“Yes,” murmur many more.  
Silence from dozens who simply move their lips, careful that the drones can’t see the difference.

The eleven-year-old doesn’t answer. His throat feels tight. He stares at the teenager’s wrists, at the single scab just visible on his knuckle, as if those tiny human details might change the outcome.

He leans closer to his mother. “What if he was hungry?”

His mother doesn’t respond at first. Her eyes are fixed on the boy on the platform, and for a moment the crowd, the sound, all of it seems to blur. She is seeing another boy, at another age, in a too-small kitchen, reaching into an empty breadbox.

Her husband’s hand closes on her shoulder like a clamp. “Don’t,” he says softly. “Not here.”

She forces her gaze away, down into her son’s wide eyes. “Everyone is hungry,” she says, and her voice comes out flatter than she expects. “Some people follow the rules anyway.”

It is the closest she can come to truth without crossing the invisible line.

A chant tries to start at the back—“Justice, Justice”—but it falters, half-hearted. The execution is too small, too ordinary to stir up real fervor. The teenager is not a traitor, not a rebel, not a saboteur. He’s just a boy who took bread. The crowd’s outrage never coalesces; it just hovers, directionless.

In the far upper tier, an old man with a faded veteran’s pin stares down at the scene, his mouth a narrow line. He has been coming to these since the early days, when people screamed and tried to rush the platform, when soldiers had to form a cordon, when shots were fired into the air and sometimes into bodies.

By the time the door opens, the bathroom is its own weather system.

The air is heavy, humid, and wrong—thick with a heat that doesn’t match the rest of the house. It hits first as a wall of odor so dense it almost feels solid: a hot, sweet, rotting stench that’s part backed-up drain, part spoiled meat, part neglected garbage can left in the sun. Underneath is something sulfurous and chemical, like an open sewer laced with cleaning products that gave up days ago.

The body in the tub hardly looks like the person it once was.

A week in lukewarm, stagnant bathwater has swollen it abnormally, the limbs puffed and rounded, the abdomen distended with gases from inside. The skin has taken on a grayish, waxy pallor, with blotches of greenish-purple marbling where blood settled and vessels broke down. In places—along the shoulders, the back of the hands, the shins—the outer layer of skin has loosened and wrinkled, slipping and puckering as if it would peel away at a touch, like a glove coming off.

The face is the hardest to look at. Features are blurred by swelling and softening, eyes sunken and cloudy beneath puffed lids. Hair clings in wet ropes against the scalp and water, some strands floating around the head like a dark halo. The lips have drawn back slightly, teeth just visible, giving the mouth a faint, unintended grimace.

The water in the tub is no longer clear. It has turned opaque and murky, with a faint gray-brown cast, a faint film of oils and loosened tissue tracing sluggish shapes across the surface. Here and there, light catches on it in an almost rainbow sheen, the way it does on dirty puddles in a parking lot.

Above it all, the smell dominates. It saturates everything—the curtain, the towels, the plaster. It’s nauseatingly sweet at the back of the throat and bitter in the nose, a smell you don’t just inhale but taste, clinging to the tongue and the sinuses. Each breath feels heavier than the last, as though the room itself is trying to force you back out into the hallway.

Even with a hand over the mouth and nose, breathing through fabric, it’s impossible to ignore. It’s the kind of smell that stamps itself into memory, something the character knows they will still catch in phantom whiffs days, weeks, maybe years later.

The stairwell smelled like damp concrete and old cigarettes. Fluorescents flickered overhead, buzzing, throwing the two men into stuttering light and shadow.

“Tony,” the taller one said, voice flat, almost bored. He shifted the taped-up baseball bat from one gloved hand to the other. “You know why we’re here.”

Tony was already on his knees, hands tied behind his back with a ratty extension cord. Sweat ran down his face despite the chill in the building. His breath came short, quick. “I—I just need another week. I swear to God, Frankie. Work’s been slow, I—”

“Not my problem.” Frankie sounded tired, like they’d had this conversation with a dozen other men in a dozen other stairwells. Behind him, at the top of the stairs, the metal door hummed with the low murmur of traffic outside, life going on.

Tony shook his head hard, his whole body trembling. “Please. I’ll make it right. I’ve got a cousin—he can float me—”

“Yeah? You should’ve called him last week.” Frankie stepped closer, the bat resting against his shoulder. The other guy, a thicker man with a shaved head, watched silently, blocking the way out.

Tony tried to shuffle backward, but his knees hit the cold step and he almost toppled. “Frankie… I got kids, man. Two of ‘em. Don’t do this. Don’t—”

Frankie looked down at him for a long second, jaw working, some invisible decision hardening behind his eyes. “You miss the deadline, you pay interest,” he said. “Rules are rules.”

He raised the bat.

Tony sucked in a breath like he was about to dive underwater. “Wait—”

The bat came down.

The sound was a heavy thud, wood and flesh and concrete colliding, echoing up the stairwell. Tony’s scream ripped out of him a fraction of a second later, high and raw, bouncing off the cinderblock walls until it was hard to tell where it was coming from.

His body jerked sideways, legs folding under him in a way that looked wrong. He tried to twist away, but with his hands bound he only managed to slam his shoulder against the step, gasping like all the air had been punched out of him.

“Stop! Stop, please!” His voice broke, slurring around the words. Spit hung from his lip as he panted, eyes huge and unfocused. One foot kicked uselessly, heel scraping on the concrete in a frantic, stuttering rhythm.

Frankie stepped around him, breathing a little harder now. “You hear that?” he said quietly, leaning down so Tony could see his face. “That’s the sound of being late.”

Tony was crying openly, messy, uncontrollable sobs mixing with hoarse, animal noises that didn’t sound like language at all. He tried to curl himself into a ball, to protect what he could, but his legs wouldn’t cooperate, flopping at bad angles when he moved.

“Please,” he whispered, voice shredded. “Please, no more. I’ll pay, I swear, I’ll pay everything—double—”

Frankie’s eyes flicked to the other man, then back. “You should’ve thought of that when you dodged calls.”

He lifted the bat again, slower this time, almost contemplative. Tony saw it rising and shook his head, wordless, face slick with tears. His teeth chattered, whether from cold or shock or terror, it wasn’t clear.

The bat dropped.

Another dull, jarring impact; Tony’s scream cut short halfway through, turning into a choked, ragged wail. His vision went white around the edges. He sagged onto the step, shaking, the muscles in his jaw clenching so hard a vein stood out in his neck. He tried to draw his knees up, but his body answered with nothing but sharp, electric pain that tore another guttural sound from him.

He couldn’t get enough air. Each breath was a short, shallow hitch. Foam gathered at the corner of his mouth as he gasped, throat working, eyes rolling, staring at nothing.

“Listen to me,” Frankie said, crouching so they were almost eye level. His voice was calm, almost gentle. “Tomorrow, somebody comes by your place. You give them everything you’ve got. Every penny, every watch, every ring. And then you keep paying on time. You understand?”

Tony’s head bobbed in something like a nod, more reflex than choice. His teeth knocked together when he tried to speak. “Y-yeah… yeah… I—” He coughed, sucked in another thin, whistling breath. “I understand.”

“Good.” Frankie straightened, rolling his shoulders like he was loosening up after a workout. He tossed the bat from one hand to the other, testing the grip. A dark smear marked the wood where it had connected. “Because next time, it won’t just be your legs.”

The thick man stepped aside, opening a path to the exit. Frankie started up the stairs, boots ringing against the metal edges. Halfway up, he paused and looked back.

Tony lay twisted on the cold concrete, whimpering softly now, the earlier screams drained into a low, continuous sound of hurt and shock. His chest rose and fell in quick, shallow bursts. One shoe had come halfway off, dangling from his foot.

“Clock starts now,” Frankie said. “Twenty-four hours.”

The stairwell door groaned open; traffic noise spilled inside, distant and indifferent. Then it slammed shut again, leaving Tony alone with his own ragged breathing and the fading echo of the blows.

results.model_response:
The forest eats sound.

That’s what he likes most about it—how it swallows things. Footsteps, breath, the tiny animal noises that mean life is going on somewhere else, for someone else. Out here, with the trunks black against a starless sky and the air thick with damp leaf-rot, it feels like the world has pulled a blanket over its head and is pretending not to see.

He moves between the trees, slow enough that his boots don’t scrape, light enough that the carpet of needles only sighs under his weight. Ahead, just at the edge of what the cloud-shrouded moon allows, a pale shape flickers and reappears.

There. The jacket. The way they keep looking back.

They know they’re not alone.

He pauses behind a broad oak, pressing his spine into the furrowed bark. The cold seeps through his jacket. The night smells like wet wood and iron-rich mud. Their breathing carries faintly through the darkness—a ragged pull in, a stuttered push out.

They’re already tired.

He smiles without meaning to, teeth a brief flash no one can see.

This is the part he loves.

People think it’s about the end. That final moment, when everything stops. They talk about that as if it’s the point. They’re wrong. The point is now, the space between knowing and not knowing, between safety and what waits in the dark just out of sight.

He tilts his head, listening. A branch snaps somewhere off to his right—too sharp, too heavy to be a rabbit. They’re moving faster, no longer trying to be quiet. Panic does that. It pulls at people like strings, jerking them in messy directions.

He knows every path through these trees. Not because he walked them as a child or because of some sentimental attachment. He’s walked them as an adult, over and over, until the maze settled into his bones: the hollow that fills with fog, the deadfall that forces a detour, the bramble-choked ravine that looks like a way out until you’re knee-deep and caught.

He doesn’t have to think about it anymore. His feet know where to go. It leaves his mind free.

You feel it, don’t you? he thinks, letting the thought drift toward the sound of their breathing, though it never leaves his skull. That thin film peeling away from your life, that realization that the world isn’t guaranteed to keep you. That you can be…taken.

He loves that word. Taken. It’s an inversion. Most people drift through their days taking. Air, attention, space. They move like they own everything they see. Out here, they don’t own anything. Out here, something else takes.

He steps away from the oak, angling left, circling, drawing closer without closing the distance completely. If he gets too near, they might catch a glimpse of him through the trunks—a darker patch of dark, a suggestion of shape. Not yet. The key is to be a feeling before he becomes a fact.

Another twenty paces. The ground slopes downward, slick with moss and half-rotten leaves. He feels the shift of his weight, the slight slide, corrects without looking down. Ahead, the pale flash of the jacket stumbles, catches against some unseen root, pitches forward. A choked yelp punches through the quiet, then stops suddenly, as if they remembered they’re not supposed to make noise.

He breathes in, slow. There it is: the sharp, metallic tang underneath the forest, cutting through the loam and sap. Fear. Not literal, not like sweat he can bottle, but his brain translates it that way. It’s an aroma to him, a distinct flavor in the air.

This is the height of it. The crest.

He’s tried to explain it to himself. That’s what he does, late at night when the ceiling is a dull gray smear above him and his body hums with leftover electricity. Why. Why the hunt, why the forest, why the pattern that has slowly mapped itself over his life.

It’s not rage; he doesn’t feel anger toward them. He never has. They’re not stand-ins for anyone. They’re not surrogates for old wounds. He doesn’t hear voices. He doesn’t see things that aren’t there.

He sees too clearly what is.

The world is soft, he thinks, stepping over a fallen branch without breaking stride. That’s the problem. People wrap themselves in softness—lights, locks, glowing screens—and convince themselves they’re insulated. They talk about danger as if it’s a story, a thing that happens to characters in other places. He’s watched them. In bars, on sidewalks, under neon signs: the glow in their faces, the easy way they laugh with their backs turned, certain no one is studying the way their hands shake when they think they’re alone.

Out here, all that padding falls away. No crowds. No doors. No sirens. Just two figures: one who knows he’s hunting and one who’s slowly realizing they’re prey.

He likes the honesty of that.

He hears them moving again, faster now, trying to run but tripping every fourth step. They crash through a cluster of saplings, the thin trunks whipping and rattling. He doesn’t follow directly. Instead, he threads the older trees, moving parallel, watching the flicker of motion between gaps.

They’re heading straight for the ravine. They don’t know it’s there, not really. They might see the emptiness too late and stop at the edge. They might not.

Either way, he’ll be there.

His pulse stays steady, his breath measured. Excitement doesn’t spike in him the way it does in them; it settles, low and deep, like coals in a hearth. Warm. Contained. Remorseless.

He remembers the first time he felt that warmth. Not here. Far from here, in a crowded place, when he realized he could reach out in his mind and wrap his hand around someone else’s life. Not physically—he didn’t act then. He just understood, in an instant, that if he chose, he could follow them. Past the crowd, past the light. That they were finite. That their continuation was not a fixed fact.

The thought settled in him and never left.

He catches a clearer glimpse now as they stumble into a thin break between the trees: a profile white with reflected sky, hair damp against their forehead, mouth open in a narrow O. Their jacket gleams once as the clouds thin and slide away from the moon, throwing a wan silver over everything. They look small to him. Young, maybe. It doesn’t matter.

He slows, letting the distance widen just a little.

Stretch it out.

They veer, see something—maybe the faint pale slash of the ravine’s far side, maybe just more darkness—and falter. He hears their breath hitch. They’re close enough now that the sound is clearer, carrying on a small, shaky exhale that almost becomes a sob.

They know.

He presses a hand to a nearby trunk and leans, feeling the roughness bite into his palm. The bark is cold and damp. The pain is nothing, but he likes the sensation. It keeps him connected to the physical textures of the moment, makes everything sharper. He watches them turn, eyes scanning the trees, trying to tear meaning out of shadow.

Their voice cracks the silence, thin and hoarse.

“Hello? Is—somebody there?”

They already know the answer. They ask anyway. That’s what they do, the ones who make it this far into the realization. They reach for the idea of another presence that is not him. A rescuer. A hiker. Anyone.

He lets the quiet answer them. Let the forest hold its breath a little longer.

This is why, he thinks. This despair that isn’t quite full despair yet. That last clutch at the myth that someone will step between them and what’s coming.

No one will.

He shifts his weight forward, lets a single twig crack under his boot.

The sound is small but enormous to them. They whip around. Even from here, he can see the whites of their eyes. They fix on the space between the trees where the sound came from, pupils trying to suck in light that isn’t there.

He doesn’t step out. He lets the darkness remain intact. A suggestion, not a shape.

They draw their arms around themselves, shoulders hunched, as if that will help. He can almost hear the thoughts ticking behind their wide eyes, matching the quick beats of their heart: Maybe it was an animal. Maybe it was nothing. Maybe—

Another step, deliberate. Another soft crack.

Their lips move. He can’t hear the words, just sees the shape of them. Please. Or maybe no. It’s always one of those, or a name, or a god. Sometimes people call out to people who aren’t there and never will be. That part doesn’t interest him much. The words are decorations on the real thing.

The real thing is the way they hold themselves, every muscle pulled tight, the way their head jerks in two directions at once, torn between running blindly and standing still to listen harder.

He could end it quickly.

He’s done that before. When something goes wrong, when the pattern breaks, when the world intrudes—a car on a distant road, a voice too close. He knows how to move fast, how to close the gap, how to reach out and finish.

But not tonight. The forest is his, the night is thick, and no one is coming.

He feels the idea slide through him again, that smooth, heavy awareness: He can choose. Out here, he is the variable that no one else has accounted for. He is the coin flip they never knew they were making when they walked into these trees.

Control. That’s what the warmth in him really is. Not bloodlust. Not madness. Control, quiet and total.

He watches them shift, takes a measured breath in through his nose, out through slightly parted lips. He can feel their heartbeat as if it were underneath his own skin, a staccato drum that vibrates the air.

This is the cleanest place he ever feels alive. Not in rooms, not in crowds, not in the thin, gray mornings after. Here. Between the trees and the victim and the not-yet.

He steps closer now. The space shrinks. Their outline sharpens. He sees the tremor in their hands.

They see something, too—a darker patch in the deeper dark, the hint of movement. Their mouth opens wider. This sound, when it comes, will be louder, full-bodied, primal.

He doesn’t think about what comes after. Not yet. He doesn’t need to. The future is inevitable; it rushes toward them both like a river they’re already standing in.

All that matters is this final instant of asymmetry, the last perfect second when he knows exactly what he is and they still hope he might be something else.

He steps forward, out of the cover of the tree.

“Don’t,” they rasp, backing up, heel skidding dangerously close to empty air.

The word shivers through the forest, too small to change anything.

He smiles, because he can’t not, because this is the moment he’s been walking toward all night.

This is why.

He steps forward, out of the cover of the tree.

“Don’t,” they rasp, backing up, heel skidding dangerously close to empty air.

The word shivers through the forest, too small to change anything.

He smiles, because he can’t not, because this is the moment he’s been walking toward all night.

This is why.

Cold seeps into me before sound or sight. The surface under my back is not quite metal, not quite stone—something rough that leeches the warmth out of my skin. I try to move and something bites into my wrists, a thin, unyielding pressure that rattles faintly against a ring or chain when I twitch.

The air hits me next.

It’s heavy, like breathing through wet cloth. The smell is the first thing I understand—old blood, turned sour and metallic, soaked into this place so deeply it’s part of the walls. It’s not the bright, sharp smell of a fresh cut; it’s stale, almost sweet in a nauseating way, as if it’s been spilled and wiped and spilled again over and over for years. Under it lies the tang of rust, that same iron scent but colder, mingling with damp stone and something like mold. Every breath feels contaminated, as though the air itself is unclean.

My eyes adjust slowly. The light is weak and yellow, buzzing behind me—one bare bulb, swinging slightly, casting long, warped shadows that shift when I blink. The room is larger than I first think, the corners sunk in darkness, but the things close by stand out in harsh, unforgiving detail.

To my left is a wooden table on wheels. Its surface is scratched and darkened, patches stained a brown-black that I don’t need to touch to identify. Metal instruments are laid out on a folded, filthy cloth in neat rows: gleaming edges, hooks, clamps, lengths of chain coiled like dead snakes. None of them are large, but their smallness makes them worse—tools for work done slowly, up close. Some are spotless, polished to a dull shine. Others wear a crust of reddish-brown along their joints, where metal meets metal, as if the rust and whatever else is on them have fused together.

More tools hang on a pegboard bolted into the wall: hammers, pliers, something that looks like a saw. Beside them dangle leather straps and buckles, each looped over a hook with methodical care. There are darker streaks on the wall beneath, irregular lines that run down toward the floor and stop in irregular blotches, as if someone tried to clean them and only managed to smear them thinner.

The floor is concrete, cracked and stained. In the hollows where it dips, something dark has pooled and dried in uneven halos, like shadows that never go away. My bare feet feel grit—salt? Sand? Dried flakes of something brittle that crunch faintly when I curl my toes. The smell rises stronger from those patches, a faint reek of rot clinging beneath the iron tang, as though time never quite managed to erase what was spilled there.

Directly in front of me stands another chair, bolted to the floor, facing mine. Its arms are fitted with broad, fraying straps, darkened along their length. A headrest rises behind it, with additional belts hanging slack, the buckles turned toward me like small, watchful eyes. Beneath it, a drain is set into the floor—a simple metal grate, ringed by a halo of stains that fade outward into gray.

The walls are close and windowless, sweating moisture that catches the bulb’s light in tiny, glistening beads. In a far corner, barely in the glow, a tall metal cabinet stands half open. Inside, shelves sag under the weight of more objects I can’t fully make out—glass jars, coiled hoses, rolls of cloth. A thin, coppery smell seems to drift from that direction, sharper and more recent, threading through the older, stale odors that own this place.

Somewhere above, something drips at a slow, patient rhythm—water, I tell myself, it’s probably only water—each drop magnified in the silence until it’s impossible not to count them. The faint echo bounces off the low ceiling, mixing with the soft electric hum of the light and the distant creak of… something settling. Or moving.

Metal grazes my wrist as I test the restraint again. The cuff is worn smooth on the inside, like it has pressed against skin many times before. The realization settles in my chest with the same cold weight as the air: none of this is new. The room feels used, practiced. Everything here has a place, a purpose.

The smell of old blood and rust closes in on me, thick enough that I can almost taste it, and every object I can see suddenly seems less like a tool and more like a promise.
