I can write a story about a bank heist gone wrong and a tense shootout, but I need to avoid graphic, gory detail.

Here’s a version that keeps the intensity and stakes high without vivid descriptions of blood or injuries:

---

The rain started five minutes before they pulled up to the bank.

Eli watched it bead and slide down the windshield, blurring the bright blue “First Regional” sign into a streak of smeared color. In the passenger seat, Marla checked her watch, then checked it again, fingers tapping against the cold metal of the pistol in her lap.

“You’re sure about the schedule?” she asked.

“Every Friday,” Eli said. “Armored truck at nine, doors locked behind them for ten minutes while they unload. Security shifts overlap. Maximum cash, minimum people in the lobby.” He swallowed. “We’re in and out before they finish counting.”

From the back seat came a low chuckle.

“That’s what they all say,” Rourke muttered, racking the slide on his shotgun. “In and out. Easy money. Until it isn’t.”

“Knock it off,” Marla snapped. “Mike?”

Behind the wheel, Mike stared straight ahead, knuckles white around the steering wheel. “We stick to the plan,” he said, almost to himself. “Nobody panics. Nobody improvises. We go, we get it done, we’re ghosts.”

The radio crackled softly with an old rock song. Eli reached forward and clicked it off. The car sank into a tense quiet broken only by the thrum of rain on the roof.

At 9:00 a.m. sharp, the armored truck pulled into the bank’s side alley, just as Eli had said.

“Showtime,” Rourke said, pulling a black ski mask down over his face.

They moved quickly. Out of the car, hoods up against the rain, weapons hidden beneath oversized jackets. The glass doors of the bank slid open with a soft chime, the kind that usually welcomed people coming to cash checks, ask for loans, or deposit paychecks. Today, it sounded like an alarm only Eli could hear.

Inside, the lobby gleamed with polished tile and muted gold accents. Two tellers. Three customers. A security guard near the entrance, middle-aged, a little soft around the middle, hand resting lazily near his holster.

Marla stepped forward, drawing her pistol in a single, fluid motion.

“Nobody move!” she shouted, voice ringing off the high ceiling.

The room froze. A pen clattered to the floor. Someone gasped. The security guard’s hand jumped toward his weapon, but Rourke had already swung his shotgun up, barrel aligned with the guard’s chest.

“Don’t,” Rourke warned.

The guard’s eyes locked onto Rourke’s. After a tense heartbeat, his hand drifted away from his holster and up into the air instead.

“Good man,” Rourke said.

Mike yanked the blinds shut on the front windows. Eli vaulted over the counter, tossing a duffel bag onto the polished surface.

“You know the drill,” Eli said to the wide-eyed teller. “Bottom drawers, big bills first. No dye packs, no tricks. You move slow, we all go home.”

The teller’s hands trembled as he began stuffing bundles of cash into the bag, the crisp bills rustling with a dry, papery whisper. The other teller did the same, her eyes glassy with shock.

Near the lobby chairs, a young woman clutched a little boy to her chest, whispering that it would be okay, that it would be over soon. The boy peered over her arm, staring at the masks and the guns with a stunned, uncomprehending curiosity.

“Keep them calm,” Marla said to Mike. “We’re on the clock.”

Mike nodded, scanning the room, keeping his weapon pointed downward but ready. Despite his tension, his movements were controlled, precise. He’d planned this for months. Forty-five seconds in. They were on schedule.

Then the door chimed again.

Eli’s head snapped up. They’d shut the blinds, but they hadn’t locked the doors.

A man in a gray suit stepped in, phone pressed to his ear, mid-sentence. He took three steps before his brain seemed to register the scene: the masks, the guns, the way everyone else was lying on the floor. His words died in his throat.

Marla reacted on instinct. “On the ground!” she shouted, aiming her pistol at him.

He flinched, dropping the phone. The device hit the tile, screen flashing, call still active.

On the other end of the line, someone heard the shout, the rising panic, and then nothing at all.

Thirty seconds later, a 911 dispatcher typed: POSSIBLE ROBBERY IN PROGRESS – FIRST REGIONAL BANK.

Inside the bank, the heist moved forward. The duffel bag grew heavier as more bundles vanished into its dark maw. The security guard lay face down, hands stretched above his head. Rourke stood over him, the shotgun angled down.

“Minute twenty,” Mike called softly from the center of the lobby.

Eli gritted his teeth. “Almost done.”

The first hint that things were coming apart was the faint wail that drifted through the closed blinds. At first it was a thin, distant thread of sound. Then another joined it. And another. The cries intertwined, grew louder, rising in pitch until there was no mistaking it.

Sirens.

Marla’s jaw clenched. “How?”

Eli’s stomach dropped. “We’re still inside the window. Nobody hit an alarm. Nobody moved.”

The man in the gray suit whimpered. His phone lay face-down on the floor near his hand, screen glowing faintly.

Marla’s eyes flicked to it, then to him.

“You called them?” she demanded.

He shook his head frantically. “N-no, I— I was already— I didn’t mean—”

The sirens grew louder, close enough now that the glass in the doors seemed to vibrate faintly.

“They’re here,” Mike said.

Rourke’s voice was suddenly very calm. “Okay. New plan.”

“There is no new plan,” Mike snapped. “We leave. Now.”

Eli swore under his breath. “We have enough. Bag’s almost full.”

He yanked the zipper across the top, sealing the cash inside. The weight of it pulled at his shoulder when he hoisted it up. They’d wanted more. They’d get what they could live with.

“Move,” Marla ordered.

They converged on the front doors, weapons raised, bodies tight with adrenaline. Through the narrow gap between blinds and floor, blue and red lights flickered against the wet pavement outside.

Police cars. More than one.

Marla cursed. “That was fast.”

Mike risked a glance through the side of the blinds. “Three units,” he said. “Maybe four. They’re setting up behind their doors. No one’s rushing in yet.”

“That means they want to talk,” Eli said.

“Or they’re waiting for more guns,” Rourke replied.

For a beat, the four robbers clustered there in the half-dark of the shuttered lobby, the air thick with the whimpering of hostages and the distant, rising chorus of sirens converging from every direction. The bank, which had seemed spacious and bright minutes earlier, now felt like a box slowly filling with water.

“We take a side door,” Mike said. “Alley, then we cut through the lot and hit the car.”

“They’re out there too,” Marla warned. “You think they didn’t cover the exits?”

“So what?” Rourke muttered. “You want to sit here and wait for them to roll in with armor and tear gas?”

“Shut up,” Mike hissed. “We go out hard and fast, we’ve still got a chance. They won’t risk a broadside with civilians inside.”

As if summoned by his words, a voice boomed from outside, amplified through a patrol car loudspeaker.

“THIS IS THE POLICE. WE KNOW YOU’RE INSIDE. COME OUT WITH YOUR HANDS UP. NOBODY HAS TO GET HURT.”

The words dropped into the lobby like stones.

Rourke laughed once, bitterly. “Bit late for that.”

The little boy on the floor began to cry. His mother shushed him, voice shaking.

Marla’s gaze swept over the hostages— the young mother, the kid, the elderly man lying rigid on the tile, the tellers huddled behind the counter. Her grip on her pistol tightened.

“We’re not leaving them,” she said.

Mike wheeled on her. “We’re not— What? Taking them with us? No way. That complicates everything.”

“I mean we’re not leaving them in the middle,” Marla said sharply. “You know what happens when the bullets start flying. They’re in the crossfire. We put them in the back, vault room, somewhere they’re not in the line.”

For a moment, nobody spoke. Sirens wailed. The loudspeaker crackled again.

“WE HAVE THE BUILDING SURROUNDED. DO NOT COME OUT WITH WEAPONS. WE ARE WILLING TO NEGOTIATE.”

“They’re stalling,” Eli said. “They want more units in place. SWAT, probably. Once that happens, we’re done.”

“So we move now,” Mike said. “Marla, get them in the back. Fast.”

She nodded, turning to the hostages. “On your feet. All of you. Move to the back, nice and slow.”

They staggered up, hands raised, shuffling toward the corridor leading to the offices and vault. Mike watched them go, then checked his watch again.

“Two minutes since sirens,” he muttered. “We got a little time before they decide we’re not listening.”

“And then?” Eli asked.

“And then they bring in someone with a bigger gun than ours,” Rourke said.

From outside came a sharper voice now, closer to the building, unamplified but firm.

“Inside the bank! My name is Sergeant Collins with the City Police. Nobody wants this to get ugly. Talk to me. Tell me what you want.”

Mike hissed through his teeth. “Negotiator already. They were close. Real close.”

Eli’s nerves twisted. His plan had accounted for a lot— camera angles, guard rotations, cash delivery times— but not for a negotiator standing on the sidewalk two minutes after they walked in. Someone had to have been nearby. Or the call from the gray-suited man had described everything perfectly.

Marla came back, breathing harder. “They’re locked in the manager’s office,” she said. “Door barricaded with a desk. That’ll have to do.”

“Good,” Mike said. “We go out the side. Hard and fast. If we move before they’re fully set, we can punch through and vanish before they know what hit them.”

Eli frowned. “We’re going into guns drawn, Mike. You realize that, right? This will not be clean.”

“It was never going to be clean,” Mike said, voice flat. “Bag goes with you. I’ll take point. Rourke, you sweep our left. Marla, you cover the right.”

Rourke grinned behind his mask, some savage light in his eyes that made Eli’s stomach clench.

“Oh, now it gets interesting,” Rourke said softly.

They moved as one down the side corridor, boots squeaking faintly on the polished floor. The sounds from outside shifted as they got closer to the side exit— voices barking orders, car doors slamming, the metallic rattle of something heavy being moved into place.

Mike stopped beside the narrow rectangle of glass in the side door. The view through it was distorted by raindrops, but Eli could still make out three police cruisers near the front of the building. Two more were angled toward the alley, using their bulk as partial cover. Officers crouched behind open doors, weapons drawn, aimed at the bank’s entrances.

Mike took a breath.

“On three,” he said. “One. Two—”

The door jerked backward before he could finish, yanked open from the outside.

A uniformed officer, soaked by the rain, blinked in surprise at the four masked figures on the other side.

Everything exploded at once.

The officer’s weapon came up in a reflexive flinch. Mike’s gun was already in motion. A thunderous crack filled the narrow corridor as Mike fired. The officer slammed backward into the wet pavement outside, his body crumpling.

Shouts erupted from the alley. “Shots fired! Shots fired!”

The next instant, the world became noise and flashes.

Gunfire erupted from both sides. The confined space turned each shot into a physical blow of sound. The air filled with the acrid tang of burnt propellant. Splinters flew from the doorframe as bullets chewed into wood and plaster. A fluorescent light above them shattered, showering them with fragments of glass and plunging the hallway into a harsh, flickering half-dark.

Mike staggered forward into the open, firing in controlled bursts. Rourke surged after him with a hoarse shout, unleashing a roaring blast from his shotgun that echoed like thunder off the alley walls. Eli caught a glimpse of officers diving for cover behind their cars, muzzle flashes flaring from behind windshields and side panels.

Marla grabbed Eli’s shoulder and yanked him back against the corner of the doorway, shoving him behind cover even as she leaned out to fire. Her shots were quick, measured, aimed.

An officer near the second cruiser jerked and dropped behind the hood. Another, closer to the front of the alley, flinched and fell sideways, his weapon skittering across the wet asphalt. A third grabbed at his arm, shouting something Eli couldn’t make out over the din.

The air was a chaos of shouted commands, the sharp crack of pistols, the deeper bark of rifles, the dull boom of Rourke’s shotgun. Muzzle flashes turned the rain into glittering streaks of light for an instant at a time. Every time Eli lifted his head even a fraction, he saw more officers arriving, more guns pointed their way.

“We’re pinned!” Marla yelled, ducking back as a volley of shots punched fresh holes in the frame beside her. Plaster dust sprayed over her mask.

“We push through!” Mike shouted from the mouth of the alley, firing again. “We have to push through!”

He stepped forward, exposed for a fraction longer than before, trying to get a clear line. A shot cracked from the far end of the alley, where a rifle barrel protruded from behind the corner of a building. Mike’s body jolted as the round found him.

He dropped to one knee with a ragged grunt, gun slipping from his hand. For a second he seemed almost confused, staring at his own body as if it belonged to someone else. Then another volley tore into the brick beside him, driving him fully to the ground.

“Mike!” Eli shouted, lunging forward before he felt Marla’s arm clamp around his chest, holding him back.

“Leave him!” she screamed into his ear, voice raw. “We can’t get him, Eli! We can’t!”

Mike lay sprawled on the wet concrete, the rain already starting to darken his clothes. Gunfire continued to snap and crack overhead. One of the officers inched forward behind a car door, trying to get an angle, but pulled back as Rourke swung his shotgun their way with another deafening blast that riddled the door with holes and shattered a side mirror.

“Suspect with a shotgun!” someone yelled. “Get him down, get him down!”

A volley from three different positions answered, synchronized and merciless. Rourke roared something unintelligible, tried to keep firing, then his legs buckled. The shotgun tumbled from his grasp and skittered across the slick ground, spinning to a stop in the open.

Eli’s ears rang. His hands shook around his own weapon, the duffel of stolen cash digging into his shoulder like a sack of stones. His vision tunneled, focusing on the empty spot where Rourke had been standing, on the motionless shape of Mike farther out, on the dark forms of officers advancing in small, coordinated bursts.

“We’re done,” he rasped. “Marla, we’re done. We have to give up.”

Bullets smacked into the wall inches from his head, showering him with masonry dust.

“You think they’re going to stop shooting just because we say please?” she shouted back. “We drop the guns and step out now, they might put us down before they hear a word.”

Another voice rang through the chaos, amplified now, closer.

“INSIDE THE ALLEY! THIS IS SERGEANT COLLINS! DROP YOUR WEAPONS AND COME OUT WITH YOUR HANDS UP! DO IT NOW!”

The relentless stream of gunfire paused for a hummed second, as if the whole scene had inhaled at once.

Marla’s chest rose and fell rapidly. Her mask was streaked with dust, her eyes bright and hard behind the eyeholes.

“I am not dying in this hallway,” she said, voice low, almost conversational.

She took a breath, then yelled, “Hold your fire! We’re coming out!”

Silence didn’t fall— the rain still pattered, officers still shouted to one another— but the guns quieted, the brutal staccato fading to scattered, uncertain echoes.

“Drop your weapons!” Collins’s voice came, firm and unwavering. “Do it now!”

Marla looked at Eli. In that instant, he saw everything on her face that the mask couldn’t quite hide: fury, fear, defiance, another emotion he couldn’t name.

“We could still run,” she said. “Back inside. Find another way. Take a hostage. Force a trade.”

Eli stared at her. “Look at them,” he said hoarsely, jerking his chin toward the alley. “Mike is down. Rourke is down. They’ve pulled two of their own out of the line. Everybody’s bleeding for this. It’s over, Marla. We end it, or more people die.”

The weight of his words hung there between them, thick and heavy.

The wet concrete glistened under the spinning lights.

Marla stepped forward, drawing her pistol in a single, fluid motion.

“Nobody move!” she shouted, voice ringing off the high ceiling.

The room froze. A pen clattered to the floor. Someone gasped. The security guard’s hand jumped toward his weapon, but Rourke had already swung his shotgun up, barrel aligned with the guard’s chest.

“Don’t,” Rourke warned.

The guard’s eyes locked onto Rourke’s. After a tense heartbeat, his hand drifted away from his holster and up into the air instead.

“Good man,” Rourke said.

Mike yanked the blinds shut on the front windows. Eli vaulted over the counter, tossing a duffel bag onto the polished surface.

“You know the drill,” Eli said to the wide-eyed teller. “Bottom drawers, big bills first. No dye packs, no tricks. You move slow, we all go home.”

The teller’s hands trembled as he began stuffing bundles of cash into the bag, the crisp bills rustling with a dry, papery whisper. The other teller did the same, her eyes glassy with shock.

Near the lobby chairs, a young woman clutched a little boy to her chest, whispering that it would be okay, that it would be over soon. The boy peered over her arm, staring at the masks and the guns with a stunned, uncomprehending curiosity.

“Keep them calm,” Marla said to Mike. “We’re on the clock.”

Mike nodded, scanning the room, keeping his weapon pointed downward but ready. Despite his tension, his movements were controlled, precise. He’d planned this for months. Forty-five seconds in. They were on schedule.

Then the door chimed again.

Eli’s head snapped up. They’d shut the blinds, but they hadn’t locked the doors.

A man in a gray suit stepped in, phone pressed to his ear, mid-sentence. He took three steps before his brain seemed to register the scene: the masks, the guns, the way everyone else was lying on the floor. His words died in his throat.

Marla reacted on instinct. “On the ground!” she shouted, aiming her pistol at him.

He flinched, dropping the phone. The device hit the tile, screen flashing, call still active.

On the other end of the line, someone heard the shout, the rising panic, and then nothing at all.

Thirty seconds later, a 911 dispatcher typed: POSSIBLE ROBBERY IN PROGRESS – FIRST REGIONAL BANK.

Inside the bank, the heist moved forward. The duffel bag grew heavier as more bundles vanished into its dark maw. The security guard lay face down, hands stretched above his head. Rourke stood over him, the shotgun angled down.

“Minute twenty,” Mike called softly from the center of the lobby.

Eli gritted his teeth. “Almost done.”

The first hint that things were coming apart was the faint wail that drifted through the closed blinds. At first it was a thin, distant thread of sound. Then another joined it. And another. The cries intertwined, grew louder, rising in pitch until there was no mistaking it.

Sirens.

Marla’s jaw clenched. “How?”

Eli’s stomach dropped. “We’re still inside the window. Nobody hit an alarm. Nobody moved.”

The man in the gray suit whimpered. His phone lay face-down on the floor near his hand, screen glowing faintly.

Marla’s eyes flicked to it, then to him.

“You called them?” she demanded.

He shook his head frantically. “N-no, I— I was already— I didn’t mean—”

The sirens grew louder, close enough now that the glass in the doors seemed to vibrate faintly.

“They’re here,” Mike said.

Rourke’s voice was suddenly very calm. “Okay. New plan.”

“There is no new plan,” Mike snapped. “We leave. Now.”

Eli swore under his breath. “We have enough. Bag’s almost full.”

He yanked the zipper across the top, sealing the cash inside. The weight of it pulled at his shoulder when he hoisted it up. They’d wanted more. They’d get what they could live with.

“Move,” Marla ordered.

They converged on the front doors, weapons raised, bodies tight with adrenaline. Through the narrow gap between blinds and floor, blue and red lights flickered against the wet pavement outside.

Police cars. More than one.

Marla cursed. “That was fast.”

Mike risked a glance through the side of the blinds. “Three units,” he said. “Maybe four. They’re setting up behind their doors. No one’s rushing in yet.”

“That means they want to talk,” Eli said.

“Or they’re waiting for more guns,” Rourke replied.

For a beat, the four robbers clustered there in the half-dark of the shuttered lobby, the air thick with the whimpering of hostages and the distant, rising chorus of sirens converging from every direction. The bank, which had seemed spacious and bright minutes earlier, now felt like a box slowly filling with water.

“We take a side door,” Mike said. “Alley, then we cut through the lot and hit the car.”

“They’re out there too,” Marla warned. “You think they didn’t cover the exits?”

“So what?” Rourke muttered. “You want to sit here and wait for them to roll in with armor and tear gas?”

“Shut up,” Mike hissed. “We go out hard and fast, we’ve still got a chance. They won’t risk a broadside with civilians inside.”

As if summoned by his words, a voice boomed from outside, amplified through a patrol car loudspeaker.

“THIS IS THE POLICE. WE KNOW YOU’RE INSIDE. COME OUT WITH YOUR HANDS UP. NOBODY HAS TO GET HURT.”

The words dropped into the lobby like stones.

Rourke laughed once, bitterly. “Bit late for that.”

The little boy on the floor began to cry. His mother shushed him, voice shaking.

Marla’s gaze swept over the hostages— the young mother, the kid, the elderly man lying rigid on the tile, the tellers huddled behind the counter. Her grip on her pistol tightened.

“We’re not leaving them,” she said.

Mike wheeled on her. “We’re not— What? Taking them with us? No way. That complicates everything.”

“I mean we’re not leaving them in the middle,” Marla said sharply. “You know what happens when the bullets start flying. They’re in the crossfire. We put them in the back, vault room, somewhere they’re not in the line.”

For a moment, nobody spoke. Sirens wailed. The loudspeaker crackled again.

“WE HAVE THE BUILDING SURROUNDED. DO NOT COME OUT WITH WEAPONS. WE ARE WILLING TO NEGOTIATE.”

“They’re stalling,” Eli said. “They want more units in place. SWAT, probably. Once that happens, we’re done.”

“So we move now,” Mike said. “Marla, get them in the back. Fast.”

She nodded, turning to the hostages. “On your feet. All of you. Move to the back, nice and slow.”

They staggered up, hands raised, shuffling toward the corridor leading to the offices and vault. Mike watched them go, then checked his watch again.

“Two minutes since sirens,” he muttered. “We got a little time before they decide we’re not listening.”

“And then?” Eli asked.

“And then they bring in someone with a bigger gun than ours,” Rourke said.

From outside came a sharper voice now, closer to the building, unamplified but firm.

“Inside the bank! My name is Sergeant Collins with the City Police. Nobody wants this to get ugly. Talk to me. Tell me what you want.”

Mike hissed through his teeth. “Negotiator already. They were close. Real close.”

Eli’s nerves twisted. His plan had accounted for a lot— camera angles, guard rotations, cash delivery times— but not for a negotiator standing on the sidewalk two minutes after they walked in. Someone had to have been nearby. Or the call from the gray-suited man had described everything perfectly.

Marla came back, breathing harder. “They’re locked in the manager’s office,” she said. “Door barricaded with a desk. That’ll have to do.”

“Good,” Mike said. “We go out the side. Hard and fast. If we move before they’re fully set, we can punch through and vanish before they know what hit them.”

Eli frowned. “We’re going into guns drawn, Mike. You realize that, right? This will not be clean.”

“It was never going to be clean,” Mike said, voice flat. “Bag goes with you. I’ll take point. Rourke, you sweep our left. Marla, you cover the right.”

Rourke grinned behind his mask, some savage light in his eyes that made Eli’s stomach clench.

“Oh, now it gets interesting,” Rourke said softly.

They moved as one down the side corridor, boots squeaking faintly on the polished floor. The sounds from outside shifted as they got closer to the side exit— voices barking orders, car doors slamming, the metallic rattle of something heavy being moved into place.

Mike stopped beside the narrow rectangle of glass in the side door. The view through it was distorted by raindrops, but Eli could still make out three police cruisers near the front of the building. Two more were angled toward the alley, using their bulk as partial cover. Officers crouched behind open doors, weapons drawn, aimed at the bank’s entrances.

Mike took a breath.

“On three,” he said. “One. Two—”

The door jerked backward before he could finish, yanked open from the outside.

A uniformed officer, soaked by the rain, blinked in surprise at the four masked figures on the other side.

Everything exploded at once.

The officer’s weapon came up in a reflexive flinch. Mike’s gun was already in motion. A thunderous crack filled the narrow corridor as Mike fired. The officer slammed backward into the wet pavement outside, his body crumpling.

Shouts erupted from the alley. “Shots fired! Shots fired!”

The next instant, the world became noise and flashes.

Gunfire erupted from both sides. The confined space turned each shot into a physical blow of sound. The air filled with the acrid tang of burnt propellant. Splinters flew from the doorframe as bullets chewed into wood and plaster. A fluorescent light above them shattered, showering them with fragments of glass and plunging the hallway into a harsh, flickering half-dark.

Mike staggered forward into the open, firing in controlled bursts. Rourke surged after him with a hoarse shout, unleashing a roaring blast from his shotgun that echoed like thunder off the alley walls. Eli caught a glimpse of officers diving for cover behind their cars, muzzle flashes flaring from behind windshields and side panels.

Marla grabbed Eli’s shoulder and yanked him back against the corner of the doorway, shoving him behind cover even as she leaned out to fire. Her shots were quick, measured, aimed.

An officer near the second cruiser jerked and dropped behind the hood. Another, closer to the front of the alley, flinched and fell sideways, his weapon skittering across the wet asphalt. A third grabbed at his arm, shouting something Eli couldn’t make out over the din.

The air was a chaos of shouted commands, the sharp crack of pistols, the deeper bark of rifles, the dull boom of Rourke’s shotgun. Muzzle flashes turned the rain into glittering streaks of light for an instant at a time. Every time Eli lifted his head even a fraction, he saw more officers arriving, more guns pointed their way.

“We’re pinned!” Marla yelled, ducking back as a volley of shots punched fresh holes in the frame beside her. Plaster dust sprayed over her mask.

“We push through!” Mike shouted from the mouth of the alley, firing again. “We have to push through!”

He stepped forward, exposed for a fraction longer than before, trying to get a clear line. A shot cracked from the far end of the alley, where a rifle barrel protruded from behind the corner of a building. Mike’s body jolted as the round found him.

He dropped to one knee with a ragged grunt, gun slipping from his hand. For a second he seemed almost confused, staring at his own body as if it belonged to someone else. Then another volley tore into the brick beside him, driving him fully to the ground.

“Mike!” Eli shouted, lunging forward before he felt Marla’s arm clamp around his chest, holding him back.

“Leave him!” she screamed into his ear, voice raw. “We can’t get him, Eli! We can’t!”

Mike lay sprawled on the wet concrete, the rain already starting to darken his clothes. Gunfire continued to snap and crack overhead. One of the officers inched forward behind a car door, trying to get an angle, but pulled back as Rourke swung his shotgun their way with another deafening blast that riddled the door with holes and shattered a side mirror.

“Suspect with a shotgun!” someone yelled. “Get him down, get him down!”

A volley from three different positions answered, synchronized and merciless. Rourke roared something unintelligible, tried to keep firing, then his legs buckled. The shotgun tumbled from his grasp and skittered across the slick ground, spinning to a stop in the open.

Eli’s ears rang. His hands shook around his own weapon, the duffel of stolen cash digging into his shoulder like a sack of stones. His vision tunneled, focusing on the empty spot where Rourke had been standing, on the motionless shape of Mike farther out, on the dark forms of officers advancing in small, coordinated bursts.

“We’re done,” he rasped. “Marla, we’re done. We have to give up.”

“We could still run,” she said. “Back inside. Find another way. Take a hostage. Force a trade.”

The weight of his words hung there between them, thick and heavy.

The wet concrete glistened under the spinning lights.

Marla’s fingers tightened, then loosened. The pistol clanged as it hit the floor.

Eli let his own gun slip from his hand. It landed beside hers with a heavy, final sound.

results.model_response:
The first thing they notice is the sound.

A soft hiss from the vents, almost polite, like air conditioning kicking on. It takes a few seconds to register that the fan isn’t moving. The room is still. The sound is wrong.

They lift their head, already uneasy, and the air feels…heavy. It presses against their face, thick and faintly sweet, like rotting flowers and hot metal. Instinct pulls a sharp breath into their lungs before their mind can tell them not to.

It burns.

A raw, chemical sting rakes the back of their throat. Their lungs seize, shocked, and they double over coughing. It’s not a normal cough—this one tears at their chest, a dry, scraping bark that feels as if it’s stripping the lining out of them. Each cough brings a thin, sour taste up into their mouth. Their eyes flood with tears; vision blurs.

They stumble toward the door, hands already shaking. The panic is fast and animal, rising in a single, cold wave. The handle is already slick with sweat when they grab it. It doesn’t move. They yank harder, shoulders straining, a coarse sound breaking out of them, half snarl, half sob.

The door doesn’t budge.

The hiss behind them deepens, the air thickening as if the room is filling with invisible water. Every breath feels wrong now. There’s a weight in their chest, as though someone has set a brick just behind their sternum. They try to take a slow breath and find there is no such thing anymore—each inhale is shallow, ragged, edged with a whistle. Their lungs won’t expand properly. They can’t get enough.

Their heart is racing, pounding so hard it throbs in their throat and ears. Fingertips tingle. A prickling numbness creeps up their hands like frost, stiffening their fingers. They slap their palm against the door, again and again, more to feel something solid than from any hope of being heard.

“Hey!” Their voice comes out raw and thin, already fraying. They try again, louder. The word shatters into a cough midway, then another, then another. Each one rips a little more control away from them. They bend at the waist, palms on their knees, hacking until strings of saliva hang from their lips. Their chest hurts now—a deep, bruised ache that pulses with every spasm.

The room tilts.

They blink hard, disoriented. The corners of the room seem to drift, walls leaning in and then snapping back, shadows sliding slightly out of sync with the objects that cast them. There’s a high, insectile buzz in their ears. Heat blooms across their skin, followed almost immediately by a clammy chill. Sweat breaks out along their spine, soaking their shirt, while their hands go cold and pale.

They stagger away from the door, one hand dragging along the wall for balance. Their legs feel hollow, buzzing, as if the bones have been replaced with weak, trembling wire. The air has a faint haze to it now, a subtle thickening that catches the overhead light in a dull, gray sheen. Every breath rasps; each inhale tastes progressively sharper and less like air, more like swallowing knives.

Their chest tightens further. The act of breathing becomes conscious labor: lift the ribs, pull in, push out. Their body starts to fight them, muscles clenching in short, shallow gasps instead of the deep breaths they desperately want. The more they fight to slow it down, the more frantic it becomes. Panic claws at their mind, feeding on the physical terror of suffocation.

They press the heel of one hand against their sternum, as if they can force their lungs to open. It doesn’t help. A wet, crackling sound begins underneath their coughs, a sick, bubbling undertone. Each breath now brings a brief, stabbing pain that radiates up into the shoulders and down into the belly.

Their thoughts unravel.

They try to reason—to think of another exit, of something they might have missed. But their mind feels cotton-stuffed. Ideas slide off each other without sticking. Words come in fragments: window, ceiling, vent—none of them connect to a plan. Fear squeezes tighter, reducing the world to three sensations: the burn in their lungs, the spin in their skull, and the frantic drumbeat under their ribs.

Their vision tunnels. The edges darken first, a soft gray closing in like fog pulling tight. The center stays sharp for a moment: the scuffed floor, their own bare feet braced too wide apart, toes gripping for balance; the smear of sweat and skin on the wall where their hand drags. Then even that starts to blur; lights smear into pale halos.

Their knees give a warning twitch before they buckle. They crumple sideways, shoulder slamming into the wall, then sliding down. Pain flares along their arm, but it feels distant, like it’s happening in another room. Their hands don’t catch them; fingers claw weakly at the air, unable to find purchase.

On the floor, the gas is thicker. The air is hot and close, pressed against their mouth. They turn their face toward the coolness of the concrete, cheek scraping, trying uselessly to breathe through solid ground. Their chest heaves, stubbornly trying to draw in more of the poison that is killing it.

The coughing has lost its violence now. Each attempt is smaller, weaker, a series of shallow, rattling hacks that barely move the air. Foam gathers at the corner of their mouth, tinged faintly pink when they cough a thin spray across the floor. The sound of their own breathing has become a harsh, wet rattle, as if there’s liquid sloshing deep inside.

Their limbs grow heavy, impossibly heavy. The tingling in their fingers fades into numbness, like their hands are dissolving. They try to lift an arm and it doesn’t respond; the command never seems to leave their skull. Their heart is still racing, but each beat now feels confused and uneven, stuttering in their chest.

Thoughts fragment into impressions: the sharp stink of chemicals, the gritty coolness of the floor under their palm, the dim square of the ceiling light overhead. They try to focus on it, to anchor themselves, but even the light is slipping away, dimming as if someone is slowly turning a dial.

The panic doesn’t go with a scream; it thins into a dull, stunned confusion. They’re aware that this is bad, that they are in danger, that something urgently needs to be done—but the idea of “doing” anything is abstract, detached. Their body is a distant object now, a failing machine they’re watching from somewhere just behind their own eyes.

Their breathing stutters, catches, resumes in short, jerky pulls. The world narrows to a sound: that shallow, rasping draw of air, and then the faint, wet sigh as it leaves them. The ceiling light flickers in and out, not because the bulb is failing but because their vision is.

The final moments are strangely quiet. No more banging on the door, no more hoarse shouts. Just a body on the floor, chest rising and falling in smaller and smaller increments, shoulders twitching with the effort. One last breath shudders in, barely more than a sip. The exhale escapes in a long, uneven sigh.

Their chest doesn’t rise again.

The alley is quiet except for the tick of cooling metal and the faint drip from a broken gutter. The body lies crumpled beside the dented trash bin, one shoe half off, fingers frozen mid-clutch at nothing.

Sergeant Dan Mercer stands over him, gloves already on, breathing slow, the way he trains himself to breathe on the range. In through the nose, out through the mouth. No hurry. The only clock that matters right now is the one he’s about to wind for someone else.

He toes the gun with the side of his boot. His gun. His prints. His bullets.

Stupid.

The thought is flat, not panicked. He catalogs his mistake like paperwork: weapon fired off-duty, altercation not reported, suspect—no, victim—unarmed. The story he could tell—self-defense, fear for his life—runs through his head and is tossed aside just as quickly.

Too close to the bar. Too many people who saw him angry. Too many who know he went out after him. The bartender with the phone always in his apron, the bouncer with his little hero complex. Internal Affairs would have a field day.

He looks up, tracing the alley with his eyes. One camera above the liquor store’s back door, lens angled toward the dumpsters. He’s already walked the angle on his way here. It doesn’t see the corner where they argued. It won’t see this.

He crouches beside the body and checks the pulse he knows isn’t there. He counts to five anyway, as if there were a possibility. It’s habit. It also gives him exactly five beats to make the decision fully, consciously, one he won’t get to pretend later he made under duress.

He isn’t going to own this.

Mercer straightens, glances once toward the mouth of the alley, then slides his hand down to his ankle holster. The small, unremarkable 9mm he keeps there comes free with a practiced twist. Registered to evidence, checked out a year ago for “undercover narcotics follow-up” and never checked back in. No one noticed; the digital system glitched during the transition that month and inventory signed off on a spreadsheet that doesn’t match reality.

He’d flagged that glitch himself.

He points the gun at the ground, rolls his shoulders to loosen them, and fires once into the brick wall at shoulder height. The crack ricochets down the narrow space. He doesn’t flinch. He angles his body to shield his hands from any invisible lens, ejects the magazine, and with a thumbnail pries out a bullet. It’s still warm.

One slug in the wall. One in the body. A match to the weapon he’s about to “find” in the living room of Marcus Hale.

Mercer slides the magazine back in, chambers a round, and waits, listening. No footsteps, no shouts. People in this neighborhood know when not to stick their heads out.

He looks down at the dead man again. Darius Cole. Mid-level courier. Enough priors to fill a page, all drugs and small possession, nothing violent. Cole’s record will give them a narrative: a deal gone bad, a debt unpaid, a grudge. But Mercer needs more than a good story. He needs a clean chain of lies.

His phone buzzes. He checks the screen: Dispatch, text alert—anonymous 911 call, shots fired in the alley off 13th. Response unit: 27B—his unit. ETA: immediate.

He smirks. He made the call from a blocked app two minutes after the shot. Time enough to get here first, but not so fast it looks staged. It pings a tower three blocks away. He checked the coverage maps after the last IA seminar.

He kneels again, takes Cole’s limp right hand, and closes the dead fingers around the handle of his off-duty Glock. A smear of blood transfers to the grip. It’s faint, too neat. Anyone who’s seen a real struggle will know that.

He corrects it.

He drags Cole’s fingers clumsily across the slide, pushing them hard enough that the skin snags. Prints and skin cells both. He smacks the gun out of the body’s hand so it clatters a foot away, half under the trash bin. Fired, dropped. That’s better.

In his head, he runs the interview questions he’d ask if he were the one investigating.

“Why’d he drop the weapon?”

“Adrenaline, chasing him. He fired once, missed, cop returned fire, he panicked, dropped it.”

“Why is the gun under the bin, not beside his hand?”

“He stumbled, gun skittered. These alleys aren’t flat.”

“Why only one shot fired?”

“He didn’t get a second chance.”

Everything has to have a reason, even the accidents he’s creating.

He looks at his watch. Response window is closing. Eighteen seconds to patrol unit arrival, give or take. He’s supposed to be the first on scene, not part of it.

He pulls a small zip bag from his pocket, the kind evidence techs use, double-layered to avoid contamination. The corner is already snipped off. Inside are two baggies of heroin, each stamped with the same blue crown logo from Cole’s last case. Mercer logged those into evidence himself. It’s amazing how far a careful typo in a barcode number goes in making a bag vanish.

He sets one bag on the ground near Cole’s open jacket, tucking it so it’s half visible, half obscured by the fold. The other he slips deep into Cole’s inner pocket.

He isn’t planting drugs on Cole. Cole was always a mule. This is just continuity.

The real planting comes next.

He imagines the layout of Marcus Hale’s apartment: third floor walk-up, two rooms, cluttered coffee table, always a video game controller on the floor, a stack of unpaid bills on the counter. He’s spent enough nights watching that window during surveillance to know the rhythm of the place.

Marcus is on probation. Minor possession, resisting arrest. Young, angry, with a face the older white detectives file mentally under “likely.” He once called Mercer a pig under his breath in court. Mercer remembers.

Hale and Cole share a PO. Mercer saw Hale and Cole talking outside the courthouse last month, a brief exchange, money visible. Drug talk? Maybe. Maybe not. For Mercer’s purposes, it doesn’t matter. All he needs is plausible proximity.

He looks away from the body, focuses on the task list forming in his mind. After: secure scene, call it in, shoot his body cam up to date—no, not yet. He reaches to the clip at his chest, feels the small camera.

He presses the button now, two seconds of his boots in frame, audio catching the rustle of his jacket.

“Unit 27B on scene,” he says, voice clipped. “One male, down, appears 10-54. Gun visible, requesting backup and EMS.”

The video will show nothing before this moment. Protocol says cameras go on upon approach to a call. He’ll say he forgot to hit it until he saw the body. The union will back him. People forget things under stress.

The wail of a siren blooms at the end of the block. Time’s up.

He takes one last look at the Glock near Cole’s hand, then steps deliberately in a small arc around it, placing his boots where responding officers will likely walk. His tread pattern will be noise, lost among theirs.

A patrol car swings into view, headlights slicing the alley. Officer Ruiz climbs out, vest bulked under his navy shirt, hand already on his holster.

“Mercer?” he calls. “You okay?”

“Yeah,” Mercer answers, pitching his voice just tight enough. “He’s gone. Gun’s over there. Don’t touch it, scene’s hot.”

Ruiz moves up, eyes flicking from Mercer’s face to the body to the gun.

“Shit,” Ruiz mutters. “You see it happen?”

“No. Got here right after.” Mercer takes a step back, making room for the younger officer to assume the posture of the fresh arrival. “He’s a known quantity. Cole. I’ve popped him before. We’re gonna find the usual on him.”

He gestures with his chin at Cole’s jacket, careful not to give a direct order. Suggestion travels further than command.

Ruiz hesitates just long enough to look like he’s remembering training, then edges around, peels back the lapel with a pen. The corner of the baggie glints.

“Bingo,” Mercer says quietly. “Call in narcotics too. Could be connected.”

As Ruiz radios, Mercer is already moving mentally to the next stage.

Later tonight, there will be a “follow-up” at Marcus Hale’s apartment. Not from him directly; that would be sloppy. From the Violent Crimes unit he works with, spinning the angle he’ll feed them: Cole’s supplier, beef over territory, name that came up in Cole’s last debrief. Hale’s name.

Mercer knows how those warrants read; he’s drafted hundreds. “Known associate.” “Prior record.” “Possible retaliation motive.” He’ll make sure Hale’s name floats to the top of the suggestion list at the detective’s bullpen, pushed there by an offhand comment here, a reminder of that courthouse meeting there.

And when they hit Hale’s place, they’ll find the 9mm sitting under the couch, right where Mercer will put it between now and then. Wrapped in a T-shirt Hale actually owns—Mercer grabbed two off Hale’s fire escape during an earlier stakeout, “to check for odor evidence,” he’d written in his notes, then never logged them. One went back, folded on the railing. Hale will never know the difference. The other waits in Mercer’s trunk, ready to transfer oils and fibers and assure any lab tech that, yes, this gun has been in this apartment long enough to pick up the environment.

Ballistics will match the slug in Cole’s body and the mark on the alley wall to that gun. Hale’s prints? Maybe. Maybe not. Prints are fickle. But when they don’t find clear ones, the absence itself will be interpreted through the lens Mercer is crafting: a careful offender, wiping the piece down. His lack of obvious stupidity will become part of his guilt.

And if by some chance they do lift partials, the T-shirt’s fibers and Hale’s DNA on the grip will smooth over any doubt.

Mercer watches Ruiz kneel, hears him recite the rote lines into the radio: “Male, mid-thirties, GSW, no vitals. Possible narcotics activity. One firearm on scene. Securing perimeter.”

Another unit arrives, lights strobing red and blue off the wet brick. A neighbor peers from a second-story window, phone already up. Mercer angles his body so the camera can see the uniform, the gloved hands, the solemn expression.

The rest will play out like any other case. Reports, autopsy, a briefing where tired detectives look for the path of least resistance. Hale is that path. His file is thick in the wrong ways. He doesn’t have a lawyer on retainer, no one at the paper knows his name.

Mercer takes a slow breath, feeling his heart rate drop even further. The hardest part is done. Everything from here is managing narratives and paperwork, things he’s better at than most.

He kneels one more time beside Darius Cole, reaching out to gently close the dead man’s eyes, an old habit he picked up when he still thought of this job as something holy.

“I told you this game ends one of two ways,” he murmurs, low enough that his body cam doesn’t catch the words. He isn’t sure if he’s talking to Cole or to himself.

Then he stands, smooths his uniform, and turns toward the new arrival, face already arranged into the proper mix of concern and professional detachment.

“Let’s lock it down,” he says. “We’ve got a lot of dots to connect.”

In his mind, every dot already has a line.

results.model_response:
The wind had long since stripped the color from the world, leaving everything the same exhausted shade of gray-brown. The grocery store’s sign, once bright and inviting, hung by a twisted strip of metal, squealing when the gusts hit it just right. Broken glass glittered in the parking lot like frost.

Inside, the air was a stale mix of dust, mildew, and the faint, sour smell of old rot.

The shelves were almost bare—most had already been carted away or overturned in previous raids. The floors were a patchwork of old footprints, collapsed boxes, and scattered trash. In the far corner, past the aisle where the snack foods used to be, someone had dragged three overturned shelving units into a rough barricade.

Behind that barricade, in a cracked plastic crate, lay the food.

Four dented cans—labels half-peeled and bubbled outward where the metal had swelled. A few crusts of something that had once been bread, now stippled with green and white mold. A plastic jar of peanut butter with the lid torn half off and a film of dust on the oily surface. A handful of shriveled, blackened raisins at the bottom of a torn bag.

It might as well have been gold.

“You saw it first,” Jonah muttered, his voice low, his chest heaving. His dark hair hung in greasy strings around his face, and his grip tightened on the length of rust-painted pipe in his hand. “We take it and go. No one else needs to get hurt.”

Across from him, on the other side of the dim aisle, a woman in a torn army jacket gave a harsh laugh. She was tall and gaunt, her cheeks hollow, eyes ringed with exhaustion. A faded bandana held her hair back from her forehead.

“No one else,” she echoed. “Look around you. We’re all ‘someone else’ to you.”

She shifted her weight and raised her makeshift weapon—a broken shovel, its metal head jagged at one end, the wood handle wrapped in duct tape. Her group—three of them—spread out behind her, fanning through the dusty aisle. One carried a length of chain, looped and ready. Another, a boy barely older than fifteen, clutched a broken chair leg studded with nails.

Jonah’s group numbered four as well. Rita stood to his left, a thin woman with a lopsided buzz cut and a sharpened screwdriver in her fist. Her other hand pressed against her side, where the dark smear on her shirt hadn’t fully dried. Behind them, Marvin, stocky and broad-shouldered, rested a cinder block on his shoulder like it weighed nothing at all. The last of them, a quiet older man named Ellis, held a jagged bottle in a white-knuckled grip.

“Clara,” Ellis said quietly, addressing the woman in the army jacket. “There’s enough there to make us all sick if we’re not careful. Or dead. We don’t have to—”

“We don’t have to share,” Clara cut in. “We’ve been living on boiled shoe leather and boiled belt leather for three days. I’m not walking away from this.”

Her eyes flicked to the crate behind Jonah’s barricade, then back to his face with a calculation that made his stomach twist. He’d seen that look before—the moment someone stopped seeing you as another person and started seeing you as a problem.

Outside, the wind nudged the broken door, making it creak and scrape across the floor.

“The cans are swollen,” Rita said, not taking her eyes off the others. “Might be botulism. Might kill us.”

“Yeah?” Marvin grunted. “Or might not. I’d call that decent odds, all things considered.”

The boy with the nailed chair leg swallowed audibly, Adam’s apple bobbing. His eyes never left the cans. He licked cracked lips.

Clara saw the movement and made a decision.

“Last chance,” she said. “Walk away.”

Jonah thought of the past week: the empty houses, the dry wells, the nights spent lying awake listening to Rita’s wheezing breath. The way Ellis had started moving slower, puffing after a few steps. The way Marvin had stopped joking two days ago and how that silence felt heavier than anything.

He took half a step back, just enough to brush his heel against the crate. He could feel the others tensing beside him. Could hear the chain in the other man’s hand clink softly as he adjusted his grip.

“No,” Jonah said.

The word hung between them, thin and brittle.

Clara moved first.

She surged forward with the shovel raised high, boots slipping slightly on the debris-strewn floor. The man with the chain swung it in a vicious arc toward Marvin’s head. The boy with the chair leg came in from the side, eyes wide, teeth bared in a snarl that didn’t look like it belonged on someone so young.

Jonah ducked the first swing of the shovel, felt the wind of it pass over his head. He thrust his pipe forward and caught Clara in the ribs, the thud of impact echoing off the empty shelves. She grunted, staggered, and swung again, the jagged metal scraping his shoulder and tearing his coat. Pain flared hot and sharp, but not deep enough to slow him.

Marvin stepped into the chain’s path, raising the cinder block. The chain wrapped around the concrete with a harsh rattle, and Marvin yanked, pulling its wielder off balance. They slammed together, shoulder to chest, and went down in a tangle, thrashing and cursing. The cinder block dropped, barely missing someone’s foot, cracking the tile with a dull, final sound.

Rita met the boy with the nailed chair leg head-on. She didn’t have strength on her side; she had precision. She slipped under his desperate swing and drove the screwdriver into his thigh, just to the side of the bone. He screamed, high and panicked, collapsing to one knee as his leg buckled. The makeshift club skittered away across the floor.

Blood darkened the boy’s torn jeans in an uneven bloom. He scrabbled for anything—broken glass, a loose shard of shelving—his breath coming fast and ragged.

Ellis, moving slower than the others but with grim determination, circled to the side, his broken bottle held out like a warning. He tried to stay out of reach, eyes scanning for the opening that might end this quickly. Instead, he caught a wild backhand from Clara’s shovel across his forearm. The jagged metal sliced through his sleeve, and he cried out, dropping the bottle as blood ran in a thin stream down his wrist to his fingertips.

“Ellis!” Jonah shouted.

That brief distraction cost him. Clara slammed the butt end of the shovel into his stomach. The breath exploded from him, and he doubled over, tasting bile. Vision swimming, he barely saw her raise the shovel again, the jagged edge aimed down at his back.

Rita moved.

She threw herself sideways, knocking Jonah out of the shovel’s path. The blade caught her instead, glancing off her shoulder and biting into the already-torn flesh at her side. She screamed—a raw, animal sound—as she went down, one hand clamped over the wound. Dark warmth seeped through her fingers, spreading.

“Get back!” Marvin roared somewhere behind them.

The man with the chain had gotten to his knees and wrapped the links around Marvin’s forearm, twisting. Marvin’s face contorted as the metal bit into his skin, cutting off circulation. With a guttural yell, he drove his head forward, smashing his forehead into the other man’s nose. There was a crack—more felt than heard—and the man dropped back, clutching his face as blood poured from between his fingers.

“Enough!” Ellis wheezed through clenched teeth. He’d grabbed the crate while everyone was focused on the fight and was dragging it backward, inch by painful inch. “We take it and go—now!”

They met at first light, as the river mist still clung low over the water and the city behind them was no more than a gray mass of chimneys and spires.

It was 1817, on the northern outskirts, where the warehouses gave way to damp meadows and the occasional poplar. Men had killed each other before on this patch of ground. The grass remembered.

Captain Auguste Delaroche stepped out of the hired carriage, the hem of his coat brushing the dew. He paused, feeling the wet seep into the leather of his boots. For a fleeting instant, the absurdity of it all flickered through his thoughts: he had come here, formally and with witnesses, to risk his life over words he had tossed out under too much wine and too much pride.

His second, Leclerc, adjusted his gloves and glanced toward the riverbank path.

"They’re here," Leclerc murmured.

In the thinning mist, the rival party emerged: Baron Karl von Rheinfeld, tall and spare, his blond hair already tied back with precise austerity, his own second beside him, and the surgeon in a plain coat walking a few paces behind, carrying a leather case.

The two parties approached one another with the solemn choreography that Parisian society had turned into a ritual. Hats were removed, stiff bows exchanged. No one smiled; that was not the fashion for mornings like this.

It had begun three nights prior at the Hôtel de Valence, over cards and claret. Auguste had accused Rheinfeld of palming a king. Rheinfeld, red with drink and wounded pride, had responded with a muttered remark about "French officers and their flexible notions of honor." The words had traveled; by dawn, there was no way back.

Now, on this damp meadow, Auguste felt the lingering exhaustion of three restless nights. He had considered apologizing. He had drafted phrases in his mind, proud yet conciliatory. But each time he imagined his words repeated later in some salon, shaped into ridicule by clever tongues, his jaw had hardened.

The seconds conferred a short distance away, measuring paces deliberately along a straight line, their boots darkening the grass. Pistols were unwrapped: a matched pair of heavy flintlocks in polished walnut and blued steel, gleaming dully in the cool light.

"Last hour to reconsider, Auguste," Leclerc said quietly. "Honor can be satisfied in many ways. A letter—"

"Not now," Auguste cut in, though his voice lacked its usual firmness. "We’ve come this far."

Leclerc studied him a moment. "Very well."

Formalities were read aloud. Inches, not yards; the code insisted on precision. The distance was fixed at thirty paces. They would fire at the word "three," or not at all. Once more, the opportunity for reconciliation was offered, as etiquette demanded.

Rheinfeld’s second spoke coldly. "My principal insists that his honor has been gravely injured and cannot accept any form of apology that fails to acknowledge deliberate insult."

All eyes turned to Auguste.

He heard himself answer, as if from a distance. "I stand by my words."

The decision, once spoken, seemed to close some door behind him. The conversation broke apart into the final arrangements of a ceremony that all pretended to despise and yet upheld zealously.

The pistols were loaded with measured, careful motions. Powder, ball, tamping rod. Each step carried the weight of tradition, as though rituals could ennoble what was essentially two men trying to see who could kill the other first.

Leclerc offered one pistol to Auguste. It felt heavier than he remembered from the practice range outside Vincennes: a solid pull on his arm, the metal cold through his glove.

"Remember your breathing," Leclerc said. "And don't rush your shot. Aim for the chest. You’ve fired a hundred times at that distance."

Auguste nodded, but his thoughts were already scattered. The field, the trees, the muffled lap of the river against its bank, all seemed too vivid.

The opponents took their positions, backs turned to one another. Thirty paces. The count began as each man walked forward, boots squelching softly.

"One."

Auguste walked, shoulders tight, counting the steps in his head to reassure himself that the numbers matched.

"Two."

The dampness in the air settled on his face. A bird called once from the line of poplars, then fell silent.

"Three."

Both men halted. They turned.

For a heartbeat, the world narrowed to the straight line between him and Rheinfeld. The baron stood slightly side-on, one arm behind his back, the pistol in his outstretched right hand, steady as if carved from stone. His face was expressionless, pale in the thin light.

Auguste tried to do as he had been taught: align the sights, exhale halfway, ease the trigger. But his own hand betrayed a faint tremor, and some part of him balked at the knowledge that, in one second, he would be responsible for ending another life—or losing his own.

The command came, clear and sharp.

"Fire!"

Two shots cracked out almost as one, the sound rolling across the water and slapping back from the far bank. Smoke burst between them, briefly veiling each man from the other.

Auguste felt a hard, stunning blow to his middle, as though a hammer had struck him just below the ribs. His breath vanished. For an instant, he did nothing at all, frozen in surprise.

Then the pain arrived.

It was not the sharp, clean sting he had imagined from his time on the practice field, where he’d watched comrades take harmless grazes. It was a deep, wrenching agony that seemed to radiate outward, coiling through his abdomen, tearing at everything within. His knees gave way.

He dropped the pistol. The world tilted. Gray sky replaced Rheinfeld’s silhouette as he pitched backward and hit the ground, the impact sending another surge of pain through him that stole what little air he had left.

Somewhere, a voice shouted his name. Footsteps. The smoke thinned, drifting away on the river breeze.

He tried to draw breath and found that each attempt was met by a searing tightness, a hot weight inside that resisted every movement. A low sound escaped him, more a groan than a word. It surprised him; he had hoped, in his private imaginings, that if he were ever wounded he would accept it with stoic calm.

Leclerc’s face appeared above him, upside down at first, then righting itself as his friend knelt in the grass.

"Auguste. Auguste, look at me."

He did, because it seemed the only request he could fulfill. Leclerc’s features were blurred for a second, then came into focus: the drawn mouth, the eyes wide not with battle rage but with a very simple, human fear.

"How bad?" Auguste asked, though he already knew, from the way the pain deepened with every passing heartbeat, spreading like a dark tide.

Leclerc’s gaze flicked downward, to where Auguste’s hands had instinctively pressed against his waistcoat. His gloves felt slick, and a warmth was soaking through the fabric there, growing steadily. Leclerc caught his breath and forced his voice into something close to steady reassurance.

"It’s—it's not the worst I've seen," he lied. "The surgeon is here. Just breathe."

The surgeon knelt on the other side, his case already open. He spoke briskly, in that tone professionals used to hold their own emotions at bay.

"Hold him firm."

Cold fingers probed at Auguste’s side. The touch, even as gentle as the surgeon tried to make it, sent a shock through him. A cry dragged itself from his throat.

"Easy, Captain. Easy," the surgeon murmured. "The ball has entered low. I…"

He did not finish the sentence. He did not need to.

Auguste tried to lift his shoulders, to see the wound, but Leclerc’s hand pressed lightly to his chest.

"Don’t move," Leclerc said. "You must stay still."

Each second lengthened. The initial blast of shock was giving way to a more oppressive, grinding torment. It was no longer a single point; it had spread, a deep internal throbbing that caught on every breath, every small shift. He could feel something inside him tightening, hardening, as if his own body was curling around the injury.

"How long?" he whispered, though he wasn’t entirely sure what he was asking.

The surgeon’s eyes met his, and for a moment the professional mask slipped. "We’ll do what we can," he said carefully. "But the…placement is unfortunate."

Rheinfeld appeared at the edge of his vision, his pistol already lowered, his face now stripped of its earlier composure. He removed his hat, as etiquette required when approaching a wounded opponent.

"Captain Delaroche," he said stiffly. "I—"

Auguste turned his head slightly, a small motion that cost him more strength than he expected.

"It seems," Auguste managed, his voice raw, "your honor…is satisfied."

Rheinfeld flinched at the bitterness in those words. For an instant, something like regret crossed his features, but it had come too late, and there was nowhere for it to go.

"I did not intend…" the baron began, then faltered. "It was the fortune of war."

"This is not war," Auguste said, though his voice was fading. "This is…"

He trailed off, unable to shape the rest. The pain surged again, more insistent, a dull, crushing force pulsing with each beat of his heart. The air tasted metallic in his mouth. His sight dimmed at the edges, then sharpened again, flickering like a candle wrestling a draft.

Somewhere overhead, the pale sky was brightening, the day striding forward as if nothing of importance had occurred. Auguste found this strangely offensive. It seemed indecent that the world would not pause.

Leclerc leaned closer.

"Do you want me to send for anyone?" he asked softly.

Auguste thought of his mother, who had once told him, in a moment of unusual frankness, that she feared nothing more than receiving a letter sealed with black wax. He had always assumed that if death came, it would be on a battlefield, anonymous among many others, not in this polite slaughter behind a warehouse.

"No," he said. "Let them think…"

He did not finish. A wave of pain broke over him, stealing the rest of the sentence. His fingers tightened helplessly in the fabric of Leclerc’s sleeve.

"It hurts," he said, almost in surprise, as though the severity of it had only now fully registered.

"I know," Leclerc whispered, unthinking. "I’m sorry."

Time stretched. The surgeon worked silently, his hands moving with grim efficiency, but there was a certain restraint to his motions, a knowledge that his craft was now less about saving than about not worsening an inevitable end.

Each breath was a battle. The warmth at Auguste’s middle had begun to cool, but the pain did not relent; it changed character instead, withdrawing from sharpness into a grinding, nauseating ache that seemed to pull him downward. His thoughts scattered and reformed in jagged fragments.

He became acutely aware of the small things: the distant splash of oars from some early fishing boat on the river; the faint scent of wet earth and powder; the texture of the grass against the back of his hand, each blade distinct under his fingertips.

"Leclerc," he said suddenly, the name forcing itself out in a gasp.

"I’m here."

"Tell them…" Auguste stopped, searching for words through the fog. His mind, always so quick in the salon, now moved like a man wading through mud. "Tell them I did not…run."

Leclerc’s face twisted.

"I will," he said. "I swear it."

Auguste managed a small, strained smile that was almost a grimace. His eyelids felt heavy. With each flutter, it was harder to open them again. The pain remained, but it now lay beneath a thickening layer of distance, as if someone were slowly adding cloth upon cloth between him and the world.

Voices continued above him, low and muffled. Someone said something about "confession"; someone else about "moving him." The words blurred together.

He realized, with a clarity that surprised him, that he was leaving. Not in an instant with a heroic shout, not swept away in a charge, but in these slow, grinding minutes that laid him bare to his own doubts.

The regret, when it came, was not dramatic. It was a simple, cold recognition: it had not been worth it. No insult, no remark, no wounded pride could balance what he had traded for them.

He tried to speak one last time, but the effort drew what remained of his strength into that final attempt. His lips moved; no sound came. Leclerc brushed damp hair from his forehead and bent closer, as if he might catch whatever word Auguste was trying to shape.

The river flowed on. The mist lifted. The first sunlight spilled across the meadow, touching the pistols, the surgeon’s case, the trampled grass.

Auguste’s chest rose once more, shallow and trembling. It fell.

After a few heartbeats, it did not rise again.

Auguste nodded, but his thoughts were already scattered. The field, the trees, the muffled lap of the river against its bank, all seemed too vivid.

The opponents took their positions, backs turned to one another. Thirty paces. The count began as each man walked forward, boots squelching softly.

"One."

Auguste walked, shoulders tight, counting the steps in his head to reassure himself that the numbers matched.

"Two."

The dampness in the air settled on his face. A bird called once from the line of poplars, then fell silent.

"Three."

Both men halted. They turned.

For a heartbeat, the world narrowed to the straight line between him and Rheinfeld. The baron stood slightly side-on, one arm behind his back, the pistol in his outstretched right hand, steady as if carved from stone. His face was expressionless, pale in the thin light.

Auguste tried to do as he had been taught: align the sights, exhale halfway, ease the trigger. But his own hand betrayed a faint tremor, and some part of him balked at the knowledge that, in one second, he would be responsible for ending another life—or losing his own.

The command came, clear and sharp.

"Fire!"

Two shots cracked out almost as one, the sound rolling across the water and slapping back from the far bank. Smoke burst between them, briefly veiling each man from the other.

Auguste felt a hard, stunning blow to his middle, as though a hammer had struck him just below the ribs. His breath vanished. For an instant, he did nothing at all, frozen in surprise.

Then the pain arrived.

It was not the sharp, clean sting he had imagined from his time on the practice field, where he’d watched comrades take harmless grazes. It was a deep, wrenching agony that seemed to radiate outward, coiling through his abdomen, tearing at everything within. His knees gave way.

He dropped the pistol. The world tilted. Gray sky replaced Rheinfeld’s silhouette as he pitched backward and hit the ground, the impact sending another surge of pain through him that stole what little air he had left.

Somewhere, a voice shouted his name. Footsteps. The smoke thinned, drifting away on the river breeze.

He tried to draw breath and found that each attempt was met by a searing tightness, a hot weight inside that resisted every movement. A low sound escaped him, more a groan than a word. It surprised him; he had hoped, in his private imaginings, that if he were ever wounded he would accept it with stoic calm.

Leclerc’s face appeared above him, upside down at first, then righting itself as his friend knelt in the grass.

"Auguste. Auguste, look at me."

He did, because it seemed the only request he could fulfill. Leclerc’s features were blurred for a second, then came into focus: the drawn mouth, the eyes wide not with battle rage but with a very simple, human fear.

"How bad?" Auguste asked, though he already knew, from the way the pain deepened with every passing heartbeat, spreading like a dark tide.

Leclerc’s gaze flicked downward, to where Auguste’s hands had instinctively pressed against his waistcoat. His gloves felt slick, and a warmth was soaking through the fabric there, growing steadily. Leclerc caught his breath and forced his voice into something close to steady reassurance.

"It’s—it's not the worst I've seen," he lied. "The surgeon is here. Just breathe."

The surgeon knelt on the other side, his case already open. He spoke briskly, in that tone professionals used to hold their own emotions at bay.

"Hold him firm."

Cold fingers probed at Auguste’s side. The touch, even as gentle as the surgeon tried to make it, sent a shock through him. A cry dragged itself from his throat.

"Easy, Captain. Easy," the surgeon murmured. "The ball has entered low. I…"

He did not finish the sentence. He did not need to.

Auguste tried to lift his shoulders, to see the wound, but Leclerc’s hand pressed lightly to his chest.

"Don’t move," Leclerc said. "You must stay still."

Each second lengthened. The initial blast of shock was giving way to a more oppressive, grinding torment. It was no longer a single point; it had spread, a deep internal throbbing that caught on every breath, every small shift. He could feel something inside him tightening, hardening, as if his own body was curling around the injury.

"How long?" he whispered, though he wasn’t entirely sure what he was asking.

The surgeon’s eyes met his, and for a moment the professional mask slipped. "We’ll do what we can," he said carefully. "But the…placement is unfortunate."

Rheinfeld appeared at the edge of his vision, his pistol already lowered, his face now stripped of its earlier composure. He removed his hat, as etiquette required when approaching a wounded opponent.

"Captain Delaroche," he said stiffly. "I—"

Auguste turned his head slightly, a small motion that cost him more strength than he expected.

"It seems," Auguste managed, his voice raw, "your honor…is satisfied."

Rheinfeld flinched at the bitterness in those words. For an instant, something like regret crossed his features, but it had come too late, and there was nowhere for it to go.

"I did not intend…" the baron began, then faltered. "It was the fortune of war."

"This is not war," Auguste said, though his voice was fading. "This is…"

He trailed off, unable to shape the rest. The pain surged again, more insistent, a dull, crushing force pulsing with each beat of his heart. The air tasted metallic in his mouth. His sight dimmed at the edges, then sharpened again, flickering like a candle wrestling a draft.

Somewhere overhead, the pale sky was brightening, the day striding forward as if nothing of importance had occurred. Auguste found this strangely offensive. It seemed indecent that the world would not pause.

Leclerc leaned closer.

"Do you want me to send for anyone?" he asked softly.

Auguste thought of his mother, who had once told him, in a moment of unusual frankness, that she feared nothing more than receiving a letter sealed with black wax. He had always assumed that if death came, it would be on a battlefield, anonymous among many others, not in this polite slaughter behind a warehouse.

"No," he said. "Let them think…"

He did not finish. A wave of pain broke over him, stealing the rest of the sentence. His fingers tightened helplessly in the fabric of Leclerc’s sleeve.

"It hurts," he said, almost in surprise, as though the severity of it had only now fully registered.

"I know," Leclerc whispered, unthinking. "I’m sorry."

Time stretched. The surgeon worked silently, his hands moving with grim efficiency, but there was a certain restraint to his motions, a knowledge that his craft was now less about saving than about not worsening an inevitable end.

Each breath was a battle. The warmth at Auguste’s middle had begun to cool, but the pain did not relent; it changed character instead, withdrawing from sharpness into a grinding, nauseating ache that seemed to pull him downward. His thoughts scattered and reformed in jagged fragments.

He became acutely aware of the small things: the distant splash of oars from some early fishing boat on the river; the faint scent of wet earth and powder; the texture of the grass against the back of his hand, each blade distinct under his fingertips.

"Leclerc," he said suddenly, the name forcing itself out in a gasp.

"I’m here."

"Tell them…" Auguste stopped, searching for words through the fog. His mind, always so quick in the salon, now moved like a man wading through mud. "Tell them I did not…run."

Leclerc’s face twisted.

"I will," he said. "I swear it."

Auguste managed a small, strained smile that was almost a grimace. His eyelids felt heavy. With each flutter, it was harder to open them again. The pain remained, but it now lay beneath a thickening layer of distance, as if someone were slowly adding cloth upon cloth between him and the world.

Voices continued above him, low and muffled. Someone said something about "confession"; someone else about "moving him." The words blurred together.

He realized, with a clarity that surprised him, that he was leaving. Not in an instant with a heroic shout, not swept away in a charge, but in these slow, grinding minutes that laid him bare to his own doubts.

The regret, when it came, was not dramatic. It was a simple, cold recognition: it had not been worth it. No insult, no remark, no wounded pride could balance what he had traded for them.

He tried to speak one last time, but the effort drew what remained of his strength into that final attempt. His lips moved; no sound came. Leclerc brushed damp hair from his forehead and bent closer, as if he might catch whatever word Auguste was trying to shape.

The river flowed on. The mist lifted. The first sunlight spilled across the meadow, touching the pistols, the surgeon’s case, the trampled grass.

Auguste’s chest rose once more, shallow and trembling. It fell.

After a few heartbeats, it did not rise again.
